Embarrassed by your appearance and the situation, you crouch down until your chin skims the water, speaking to yourself in short bursts—gasping as you lift your face for air, then sinking back. Start with a panicked, self-mocking whisper, then as the footsteps pass, let your voice float into a weary, softened chuckle at your own foolishness. Let the water's gurgle and your own wet breaths interrupt the words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Unspoken
instruction: You are an elderly woman in the quiet of your bedroom, your partner’s head between your legs. You start with a shaky, amused whisper—pleasure tinged with the absurdity of your own aging body. As the sensation builds, you feel a surge of helplessness: the loss of control over breath, voice, even thought. Try to say something tender, but your words fracture into gasps and half-moans. Your pitch rises against your will, your hand grips the bedsheet, and you end clinging to a single, broken exhale of acceptance.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: When the Stars Go Silent
instruction: A catastrophic system failure has given you a choice: you can save yourself or save the research data that could change humanity's future—but you only have ninety seconds to decide and execute. Begin in fierce, almost manic determination, talking yourself through the decision with rapid-fire logic. But as your hands work, doubt crashes in like a wave—what if no one's left to receive the data? What if you're throwing your life away for nothing? Your voice should escalate from controlled to desperate to enraged—rage at the universe, at the impossible choice, at the unfairness of it all. Scream if you need to, but let it break into something else: helpless sobbing, or hysterical laughter, or both. By the end, as you make your final choice, find a strange calm in the certainty of it. Your last words should be whispered, almost surprised by your own peace. The transformation from fury to surrender should feel like watching someone shatter and then reassemble into something else entirely.

title: The Dreamlike Return
instruction: You are returning home after years away—to a place, a person, a version of yourself you left behind. Stand at the threshold (a door, a room's entrance) in a state of drowsy disorientation, as if you're not sure whether this is memory or reality, dream or waking. Your voice is soft, wondering, half-asleep as you begin to speak—maybe to yourself, maybe to the space itself. Let contradictory feelings emerge from this unconscious place: joy at returning mixed with grief for lost time, love mixed with anger at having had to leave, hope mixed with fear that nothing can be reclaimed. As you cross the threshold and enter, something awakens in you—the emotions sharpen, intensify, and you become fully present to both the beauty and the pain of coming home. End with tears that are simultaneously heartbroken and grateful.

title: The Unwon Prize
instruction: You are an elderly man at a family dinner. Your grandson just received a prestigious award for a career path you once dreamed of but never pursued. As you offer congratulations, your voice is tight and clipped—your smile doesn’t reach your tone. Mid-sentence, a memory of your own youthful ambition catches you off guard, and you feel a flicker of astonishment at how vivid it still is. That surprise opens a window of fragile hope: you imagine what might have been, and you speak with forced optimism. But as you trail off, the hope curdles into quiet sadness, and your voice drops into a hollow, weary register. Your words must sound like false cheer struggling against the truth, with pauses and micro-shifts as you distractedly stir your coffee or avoid eye contact.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present), Sadness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Whispering to Someone Who Can No Longer Hear
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who's in their final hours, unconscious. You're whispering things you never said—confessions, gratitude, apologies, ordinary moments you took for granted. Your voice is barely audible because loud feels wrong, but also because your throat keeps closing. Start with small, tender memories, almost like you're telling them a story to help them rest. But as you continue, the weight of everything unsaid crashes into you. You're not crying—it's quieter than that—but your voice fractures around words like 'thank you' and 'I should have.' End with the simplest truth you have, spoken so softly it's almost just breath, knowing they can't hear you but needing to say it anyway.
inspired_by: Medication Change: Hearing Your Voice Sound Different

title: The Reckoning at the Kitchen Table
instruction: You're confronting a parent who was emotionally absent throughout your childhood, and you've finally found the words you've rehearsed a thousand times. Start with controlled, almost cold precision—listing specific moments they weren't there, your voice steady because you've armored yourself for this. But as you speak, the child you were starts bleeding through: your voice wavers with the pain of a ten-year-old who needed them, who waited for them, who made excuses for them. Let anger surge—hot, righteous fury at what was stolen from you. Then something shifts: you see them as flawed and human, and your rage collides with an unbearable tenderness for the parent they could have been. End with exhausted honesty, your voice raw and undefended, telling them what you actually need now: not perfection, just acknowledgment. Transform from prosecutorial anger to vulnerable truth-telling.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the childhood they gave you—or didn't give you. Start controlled, voice tight with decades of swallowed words: 'I need you to hear something I've never said.' There's anger, yes, but underneath it is a child's desperate need to be seen. As you speak, rage builds—your voice gets louder, sharper, words tumbling faster. 'You were supposed to protect me. You were supposed to see me.' But then something cracks open. The anger collapses into raw vulnerability, voice dropping to almost nothing: 'Why wasn't I enough for you to try?' End in quiet devastation, no longer seeking answers, just finally releasing the weight. Your voice should move from accusation to heartbreak to hollow acceptance.

title: The Bedside Vigil
instruction: You're sitting beside your best friend's hospital bed in the final hours, holding their hand in the quiet darkness. Whisper ordinary memories—that terrible karaoke night, the road trip where you got lost, inside jokes that make no sense to anyone else. Your voice should be tender and almost smiling at first, trying to fill the silence with love. Gradually let the reality seep in: this is goodbye. Your throat tightens. Words become harder. Confess the things you never said—how they saved you, how you don't know who you are without them, how you're terrified. End barely audible, voice catching, telling them it's okay to let go even though it's destroying you. Make every word intimate, private, sacred.

title: The Morning After
instruction: You are an elderly woman lying on the cold kitchen floor after a fall. You've been drinking since last night to dull a deep, gnawing pain in your hip. Now you're sobbing, each breath a wet, jerky gasp. You're leaving a voicemail for your daughter, but the words are broken apart by hiccups and mucous. Start with sharp, drunken guilt and raw pain, then gradually fade into a hollow, exhausted acceptance as you realize she won't pick up. Let your voice crack, waver, and trail off as you say goodbye.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Pain (extremely present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Their Addiction
instruction: You're visiting your parent in rehab after years of broken promises. Start with rehearsed boundaries, almost robotic in your controlled anger: 'I'm only here because the counselor said I needed closure.' As they try to apologize with the same old script, your rage builds—interrupt them, your voice sharp and cutting, listing specific memories they destroyed. Then they say something that finally sounds real, and your fury cracks open into the grief of the abandoned child still inside you. End in a whisper, the question you've carried for decades: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stop?' Let your voice break on the word 'enough.'
inspired_by: Haunted House Actor Who Takes It Too Seriously

title: Bedside Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you at 3am. You can't sleep because something is breaking your heart. Start in a barely audible whisper: 'Are you awake? No... good.' Your voice is tender, full of love and terrible sadness. You confess what you've been holding back: 'I see the way you look at me sometimes, like you're trying to remember why you fell in love. And I'm scared... I'm so scared that one day you'll realize you don't anymore.' Let your voice catch in your throat as tears come. 'I love you more than I know how to say, but I feel you slipping away, and I don't know how to hold on without holding too tight.' Touch their sleeping face gently. Your voice becomes even softer, broken: 'Please don't leave me. Please... I know I'm not supposed to need you this much, but I do.' End with a shaky exhale, wiping your tears, whispering: 'I'm sorry. I'm sorry for needing you so much.' The confession is made, but they'll never hear it. The vulnerability is almost unbearable.

title: Final Message to Your Child Before the Mission
instruction: You're recording a message for your child before leaving on a one-way space mission. You start with fierce determination, your voice strong and proud: 'I need you to understand why I have to go...' You're trying to make them see the importance, the necessity. But as you talk about missing their graduation, their wedding, holding your grandchildren, your voice begins to fracture. The strength crumbles into something raw and aching. You whisper what you'll miss, your voice breaking on specific details—the sound of their laugh, Sunday mornings, the way they say your name. Then, through tears, something shifts: you find a strange peace in knowing they'll carry you forward. Your voice steadies with bittersweet clarity as you tell them how to live without you, and there's love so fierce it hurts in every word. End with a whispered goodbye that holds both devastating loss and profound gratitude.
inspired_by: New Physical Limitations After Accident: Anger to Acceptance Cycle

title: The 3 AM Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in the dark next to someone—a lover, a sibling, a best friend—and you need to whisper a secret you've never told anyone. Before you speak, you listen to their breathing, notice the small sounds of their body settling, feel the specific warmth of their presence. You've spent your life watching how people reveal themselves in unguarded moments—the way strangers' faces soften on late-night buses, how people touch their throats when they're about to cry. Begin your confession almost clinically, describing your secret as if it happened to someone else you observed, your voice barely audible. As you speak, let the act of witnessing yourself through your own words—the way you'd watch a stranger's pain—break down your defenses. End with your voice raw and small, reaching for their hand in the darkness, no longer the observer but fully, terrifyingly present.

title: The Last Permission You'll Ever Give
instruction: Your parent is dying, and they're asking for your forgiveness for something that shaped your entire life - an abandonment, a betrayal, a choice that hurt you deeply. You want to hold onto your anger because it's protected you for so long, but you also see their frailty now, their genuine remorse, their fear of dying without making peace. Start from a place of guarded coldness, your voice careful and distant. As you speak, let the walls crack - feel the anger soften into grief, the protection give way to tenderness. By the end, you're not just forgiving them; you're grieving the parent you needed and accepting the flawed human you got. Your voice should move from controlled and tight to breaking with love and loss. Let genuine tears come if they do - this is about releasing decades of holding on.
inspired_by: Pretending to Agree While Internally Disagreeing

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Daughter She Needed You to Be
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about spending your entire childhood trying to become someone you weren't—the perfect daughter she needed to heal her own wounds. Start with measured control, almost rehearsed, listing the ways you disappeared yourself to make her comfortable. But as you speak, decades of swallowed anger begin to surface. Your voice grows sharper, more raw. Then something shifts—you see her face, see the scared woman behind the demanding mother, and rage collides with devastating compassion. You're furious and heartbroken simultaneously. Your voice becomes urgent, almost pleading, trying to make her understand that you needed a mother, not someone you had to save. End with quiet, exhausted grief, forgiving and not forgiving in the same breath, loving her and resenting her in a way that makes your chest ache.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Prophecy Speaker Realizes They've Already Spoken This Moment

title: Butterflies in December
instruction: You're helping your spouse of forty years pack for the memory care facility. You find the ticket stub from your first date, and suddenly you're whispering the story of that night—how nervous they were, how they spilled wine, how you knew. Start soft, almost to yourself, your voice catching on details: 'You wore that blue shirt. You thought I didn't notice you'd ironed it three times.' Let tenderness seep through every word, but underneath, there's the unbearable knowledge that soon they won't remember any of this. Your throat tightens. End with you asking them if they remember, knowing they might not, your voice breaking on 'Do you remember loving me?' It's a confession of grief disguised as a love story, intimate as a prayer.

title: The Divorce Papers and the Croissant
instruction: You're describing a croissant you're eating while signing divorce papers from a marriage you still love. Begin with incongruous lightness, even laughing softly at the absurdity: 'Look at this perfect croissant on the worst day of my life.' Let genuine appreciation for the pastry's beauty mix with tears—describing the butter's richness while your voice breaks, finding strange gratitude that you can still taste anything at all. Speak with wonder about how something can be so delicious while your heart shatters, marveling at the contradiction. End in a place of bittersweet peace, acknowledging that this moment—croissant, grief, liberation, loss, all tangled together—is somehow perfect in its completeness. Find profound acceptance in the chaos of feeling everything at once.
inspired_by: Taking a Slow, Indulgent Bite of a Buttery Croissant

title: The Bench by the Old Oak
instruction: You're an elderly woman sitting on a park bench, watching pigeons. From a distance, you see a figure walking toward you—familiar, yet impossible. Your granddaughter, who you haven't seen in years, is suddenly here. A gasp escapes you, then a high-pitched, broken cry—'Oh, my God. No—really? You're—' Your voice leaps in pitch, then cracks as you struggle to stand, rustling your coat, your breath hitching. As you shuffle toward her, your words tumble out in joy-soaked fragments. By the end, as you embrace her, your voice steadies just enough to whisper with quiet pride: 'Look at you. Just look at you. I knew you'd be something wonderful.' The arc moves from utter shock to tearful, radiant pride.
situation_name: Surprise Reunion / Seeing a Loved One
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: What You Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your father in the driveway as he's about to leave for what might be the last time. Start with your whole body vibrating with years of swallowed words—feel the specific tightness in your throat, the heat in your chest, the way your hands want to become fists. Let the silence between you be thick with everything unsaid. As you finally begin to speak, notice how each truth you release changes the physical tension in your body—does your jaw unclench, do your shoulders drop, does your voice crack? Pay attention to the tiny shifts in his face, his breathing, the way he won't quite meet your eyes, then suddenly does. The anger that fuels your first words must gradually crack open to reveal the abandoned child underneath who just wanted to be seen. End in a place of raw exposure, where your rage has burned down to reveal a fierce, vulnerable longing for connection—even if it's too late.

title: Whispering the Truth You've Never Said Aloud
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your sleeping partner. It's 3 AM. You're whispering a confession they can't hear—maybe you cheated, maybe you're dying, maybe you never loved them the way they loved you. Your voice is barely audible, throat tight with shame and tenderness. You speak in fragments: 'I need you to know...' but the words catch. You're crying silently, trying not to wake them. Your whisper breaks on certain words—the ones that hurt most to say. You touch their sleeping face with such gentle devastation. You tell them how sorry you are. How much you wish things were different. Your voice trembles between confession and lullaby. By the end, you're saying 'I love you' but it sounds like goodbye. It's the most honest you've ever been, and they'll never hear it. Your final whisper is almost inaudible: 'Forgive me.'

title: The Still Water's Edge
instruction: You are a teenage girl alone in a quiet pool, floating with your head above the surface, arms barely moving. The water is cool and muffles everything. You feel hollow, like the numbness has filled your chest completely—your thoughts drift, you stare at the chlorinated gleam without really seeing it. But then, as you gently kick to stay afloat, a memory surfaces: someone who dismissed your pain, who told you to just get over it. A cold contempt rises, sharp and clear, cutting through the numbness. Let your voice be thin, breathy, interrupted by small gasps and the occasional splash as you shift. You start distant and flat, then slowly tighten with quiet scorn, each word more pointed, but never loud—just the bitter truth spoken to the empty water.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Contempt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Holding the Line Against Fate
instruction: Someone you're fiercely protective of is being taken from you—by law, by illness, by forces beyond your control—and you're making your final stand. You start with absolute conviction, voice strong and commanding, declaring that you won't let this happen. You're issuing threats, making promises, your voice rising with passionate intensity. But cracks begin showing as you realize your powerlessness. Your fierce declarations start fragmenting into desperate pleas, your voice breaking between rage and terror. You're bargaining now, offering anything, everything, your voice raw with desperation. The anger turns inward—you're shouting through tears, furious at yourself for not being able to prevent this, for being helpless. By the end, your voice collapses completely from volcanic intensity into broken whispers. You're still trying to protect them even as your strength fails, your final words a devastated combination of apology and undying love, spoken through the wreckage of your fury.

title: The Voice You Inherited
instruction: Confront your mother or father about a specific cruel thing they said to you as a child—something that became the harsh inner voice you now use against yourself. Start by speaking as your adult self, angry and accusing, demanding they acknowledge the damage they caused. But halfway through, without planning it, allow their voice to literally come through yours—the critical, dismissive, perfectionist tone they used. Embody this inherited cruelty fully, letting it take over your body and speech patterns. Then, in the final moments, fracture this possession. Your own voice must fight its way back through, vulnerable and determined, claiming your right to speak to yourself differently. The confrontation ends with you speaking to yourself with the tenderness they never offered.

title: Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love in complete darkness, finally admitting a truth that's been destroying you from the inside. Begin with your voice barely above a whisper, shame making it hard to speak: 'There's something I need to tell you. Something I've been hiding.' Your breathing is shallow, uneven. Let the words come haltingly: 'I was there. That day you've never understood... I could have stopped it.' Feel your throat tighten as tears come: 'I was scared. I stayed silent. And you paid the price.' Your voice should carry the weight of years of self-loathing. Build to a tender, devastating plea: 'I don't expect forgiveness. I just... I needed you to know it's been killing me.' End in the quietest moment: 'I'm so sorry. I'm so, so sorry.' Let the silence after your words be as powerful as the confession itself.

title: Pretending to Be Busy to Avoid a Conversation
instruction: You dont want to talk to someone, so you act preoccupied. Internally, you hope theyll go away, but you remain courteous. Describe your desire for solitude while appearing occupied. Speak briefly and politely, conveying busyness.

title: Whispered Truths in the Dark: Confessing to Your Sleeping Lover
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying beside your partner who is deeply asleep. In a whisper so quiet it's almost just breath, confess something you've never been able to say while they're awake—perhaps that you're terrified of losing them, or that you feel inadequate, or that you've been hiding depression, or that you're still haunted by a past they don't fully know about. Begin with nervous, halting words, your voice barely audible. Let emotion gradually thicken your whisper—tears threatening but held back because you don't want to wake them. Find moments where you pause, almost unable to continue, then push forward. By the end, let a kind of tender devastation wash over you—gratitude for their presence mixed with the ache of your secret, and a fragile hope that maybe, someday, you'll find the courage to say these words while they can hear you. This is about what silence holds and what breaks through it.
inspired_by: The Guardian Angel and the Fallen Angel

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Husband the Truth You Can Never Tell Him Awake
instruction: It's 3 AM. He's asleep beside you. You finally say what you've held for months: you're leaving, and why. Whisper it tenderly, almost lovingly—this is the only way you can speak these words. Your voice should be intimate, gentle, even as you confess the affair, the pregnancy, the plans you've made. There's no anger here, only devastating sadness for the good man you married and the person you've become. Let your breathing catch on certain words. Touch the contradictions: 'I loved you' and 'I wasn't enough' and 'You deserved better than what I could give.' End with an apology so quiet it's almost a breath, knowing he'll wake tomorrow to a note and an empty house. This is your goodbye, delivered in darkness to someone who cannot hear you.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Oracle Delivers a Prophecy They Knows Will Be Misinterpreted

title: The Last Beautiful Thing
instruction: You're dying, and you've chosen to spend your final conscious hours describing the world to someone you love who will remain behind. Start with that same breathless wonder—the morning light, the texture of their hand in yours—but let it gradually crack. Your voice stays soft, almost euphoric, but grief begins seeping through the wonder. 'The way your laugh sounds... I need you to remember I heard it.' You're trying to give them every beautiful detail as a gift, but your breath catches. The wonder doesn't leave—it intensifies—but it's now wrapped in the devastating knowledge that you're cataloging beauty you'll never see again. End with your voice barely above a whisper, still marveling, but breaking: 'Promise me you'll still see it... promise me it stays beautiful.' Let the euphoria and heartbreak become inseparable.

title: A Trembling Goodnight
instruction: You are a young man with a neurological tremor, speaking to your younger sibling before bed. Your voice naturally wants to fade and wobble, and you have to push through the physical frustration to say something important. Start with a quiet, strained difficulty—almost giving up because the words feel stuck and your hands shake. Then, as you see the trust in their eyes, let a deep, gentle affection rise through the tremor. Your voice may crack or waver, but the warmth becomes clearer by the end, like a fragile light that refuses to go out. Speak these words as if every syllable costs you effort, but the love makes it worth it.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Reading Their Letters After They're Gone
instruction: You've discovered letters or voice messages from someone who died—a lover, a best friend, a sibling—left for you to find afterward. Start reading or listening with your voice barely above a whisper, tender and careful, savoring their words like something precious and fragile. Let warmth fill your voice as you hear them again, almost smiling through the pain, voice soft with love and memory. Then hit a line that breaks you—perhaps where they tell you something they never said in life, or describe a moment you shared, or say 'I'll miss you' knowing they'd be gone. Your voice should catch, stop, try to continue and fail. Sit with the silence, breathing unsteadily. When you speak again, talk to them directly in a whisper, voice thick with unshed tears, sharing something you never got to say. End with the quietest admission of how much their absence hurts, voice so gentle it's almost not there, the kind of pain too deep for loudness.

title: Letting Go of Control
instruction: You're learning to let go of control and trust. Your voice is tight at first, controlling: 'We have to do it this way.' But you're being challenged to let others help. Your voice becomes tighter, resistant: 'But what if...' You're terrified of the outcome if you're not in control. Your voice slowly relaxes as you admit: 'I can't control everything.' By the end, your voice is releasing fear, becoming peaceful: 'Whatever happens, I can handle it.'

title: Through the Duct
instruction: You're a middle-aged man crawling through a narrow, dark ventilation shaft, your broad shoulders scraping the metal walls. At first, you're breathing heavily, muttering curses under your breath as you struggle to fit, your voice strained and tight from the cramped space. Halfway through, you pause, wiping sweat from your brow, then realize the exit is just ahead. As you push forward, your tone shifts from frustration to a low, triumphant chuckle, ending with a gritty, relieved whisper of victory as you see the light.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Interpreter
instruction: You are a deaf teenager at a noisy school assembly. A hearing classmate who barely knows sign language is trying to interpret a speaker for you. You start embarrassed and frustrated, hating the awkwardness and the way your voice booms when you speak—too loud, too slow, each word carefully shaped for lip-reading. Midway, you lose your train of thought, glance away, then come back. By the end, you push through your irritation and let gratitude surface, your voice softening slightly but still loud and deliberate, with a raw, honest thankfulness that surprises you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Secret You've Carried Alone
instruction: Late at night, whispering a confession to someone you trust completely. Your voice is barely audible, intimate, careful—this is something you've never said aloud. Start with halting breaths, testing the words, voice fragile like glass. 'There's something I need to tell you... about why I really left.' Each revelation makes you more vulnerable, voice catching on shame and relief simultaneously. The whisper becomes even quieter as you reach the hardest part, tears threatening but held back. Let the pauses speak—the things too painful to voice. End with your voice breaking on gratitude: 'Thank you for staying... even though I haven't told you the truth until now.' The final words are a release, tender and devastated and free.

title: Telling Your Mother You Remember Everything
instruction: You're thirty-five, sitting across from your mother at her kitchen table. Start quiet, almost casual: 'I need to talk about when I was young.' Your voice is steady but there's steel underneath. As you speak, name specific moments she doesn't think you remember—times she chose her addiction, her partner, her escape over you. Don't shout. Let your voice get softer and more dangerous. Watch her face change. Feel your anger transform into something worse: pity. End with devastating tenderness, telling her you forgive her but you also can't keep pretending it didn't shape everything you are. Let grief and fury live in the same breath.
inspired_by: Celebrating Someone's Success While Drowning in Failure

title: The Reunion After the Storm
instruction: You are an older man waiting at an airport gate, finally seeing your estranged adult daughter walk toward you after a year of silence following a bitter family fight. You've been terrified she wouldn't come. As she approaches, you let out a long, shuddering breath of relief. Your voice trembles, caught between a laugh and a sob. You start to tease her gently about her messy hair and the tear rolling down her cheek, but your voice cracks with sadness as you say you thought you'd lost her. The joke fades into a raw confession of how much you missed her, and your tone shifts from shaky to warm as you realize she's really here.
emotions_sampled: Teasing (very intensely present), Sadness (extremely present), Amusement (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Screaming at God While Cradling What You Couldn't Save
instruction: Your voice erupts from somewhere primal—you're not speaking, you're howling at the universe, demanding answers that will never come. Start with pure rage, your words are weapons thrown at heaven, at fate, at whatever cruel force let this happen. Your breathing is violent, gasping between accusations. But then feel it shift—the rage cracks and underneath is something more terrifying: absolute helplessness. Your voice breaks into pieces, becoming small and young and lost. You're begging now, bargaining, your words tumbling over each other in desperate negotiation for something that's already gone. Let yourself oscillate wildly between fury and devastation, between shouting and whimpering. End with your voice reduced to raw, animal sounds of grief, your breathing shallow and broken, all words finally failing, reduced to the truth that you are powerless and there's nothing—nothing—you can do.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Cursed Being Realizes Breaking the Curse Requires Murdering Their Love

title: Picking Through the Ashes
instruction: You're an older man alone in a dusty attic, sitting on an old trunk as you rummage through a box of yellowed papers and trinkets. Start by muttering with contempt—scoffing at the clutter, calling it garbage, your voice sharp and dismissive. As you pull out a forgotten letter, your tone shifts to disappointment, slower and heavier, trailing off mid-sentence. Keep a slight, buried fear underneath—a tremor that surfaces when you hesitate before opening a crumpled envelope. Let the rustle of paper and the zip of a binder shape your pauses, and end with a quiet, hollow sigh.
emotions_sampled: Fear (slightly present), Contempt (extremely present), Disappointment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Thing I Never Told You
instruction: It's 3 AM, and you're lying in bed next to your sleeping partner, whispering a confession they can't hear. Your voice is barely audible, tender and breaking. Start with something small—'I watched you sleep tonight and I...'—but let it grow into the vulnerable truth you've been hiding: maybe it's about fear, or unworthiness, or a past mistake, or the terrifying depth of your love for them. Your throat keeps closing up; you have to pause to breathe. There's no drama here, just intimate honesty that hurts to speak aloud. Touch their shoulder gently as you whisper, 'I'm so afraid of losing this, losing you.' Let your voice catch on the beauty and fragility of what you have. End with the quietest admission: 'You make me want to be brave.' Silence. Just breathe.

title: The Quiet Miracle
instruction: You are a middle-aged man gently rocking your newborn grandchild in a dimly lit nursery at 3 a.m. The baby had been crying for over an hour, and you finally settle into a rhythm—your chest feels heavy and warm against the small bundle. You start by murmuring with deep relief, voice hushed and slightly breathless from the rocking motion. As the baby’s face relaxes and their tiny fingers curl around your thumb, let that relief slowly bloom into a quiet, overwhelming awe. Your words should catch—maybe you glance at the window, or adjust your arm—but the awe grows clearer, softer, more present. End with a sense of wonder that nearly steals your breath.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Hospital Window at Dawn
instruction: You are sitting beside your estranged father's hospital bed in his final hours. Begin speaking to him from the place of the dutiful child who always tried to please him, your voice careful and measured. As you speak, allow a deeper, angrier part of yourself to emerge—the part that resented his coldness, his impossible standards. Let these two aspects of yourself struggle for dominance in your voice and words. By the end, find a third place: the raw, undefended person beneath both the pleaser and the angry child, speaking simple truth without armor. Your voice should journey from controlled politeness, through heated confrontation, to stripped-bare vulnerability as you say what you've never been able to say.

title: The Pillowcase Confession
instruction: It's 3 AM. You're lying in bed, face pressed against your pillowcase, speaking in whispers to your sleeping partner beside you. Begin by noticing everything about the fabric against your skin—its coolness, its scent of detergent and sleep and them. Let the pillowcase become a confidant, a keeper of secrets. It has absorbed so many tears, so much sweat, so many whispered dreams. As you confess something you've never said aloud (a fear, a desire, a truth about yourself), let the texture of the fabric guide your emotional journey. Start tentatively, your voice barely audible, your words catching in the cotton threads. The pillowcase seems to absorb your words, making them safe. Gradually, as you continue whispering, let the tenderness of this moment—the safety of darkness, the warmth beside you, the fabric holding your secret—allow you to become completely vulnerable. End in a place of profound, fragile intimacy, even though you're speaking to fabric, not the person sleeping inches away.

title: Standing Your Ground While Falling Apart
instruction: You're confronting your father who abandoned your family fifteen years ago. He's just shown up asking for forgiveness. Start standing tall, rigid with anger, hurling accusations with a sharp, controlled voice. But as you speak, feel each truth you've been carrying—the Christmases he missed, the graduations, the nights your mother cried—as a physical weight being lifted off your shoulders and spine. Your body begins to soften and descend, your voice loses its edge. By the time you reach the floor, you're no longer accusing—you're grieving, your anger transformed into raw sorrow for the relationship you'll never have. End in a crumpled position, voice broken, saying the words you never thought you'd say: that you needed him, and it hurt.

title: The Kitchen Floor Truth
instruction: You are confronting your adult child who has just told you they are cutting you out of their life. You start defensive, angry, justifying every choice you made as a parent—your voice is sharp, wounded, attacking back. But as they stand there silent, refusing to engage with your defenses, you slowly break. The anger cracks. You find yourself on your knees—literally or emotionally—and the truth comes pouring out: you were terrified every single day of being a parent. You didn't know what you were doing. You were so afraid of failing them that you became harsh to hide your fear. Move from aggressive self-defense to raw, humiliated confession to, finally, a fragile kind of dignity in admitting you were just a frightened person trying to do something impossible. Let your voice break, rebuild, and find a new kind of honesty you've never accessed before.
inspired_by: Ego-state is low, producing tension and fear of failure

title: The Weight of Lilacs
instruction: You've just received news that you got your dream job—the one you've sacrificed everything for. Your mother, who never believed in you, calls to congratulate you. But she died six months ago. You're imagining the phone call you'll never receive. Begin with breathless, childlike excitement—you want to tell her every detail. As you 'talk' to her, let specific sensory memories interrupt: the smell of the lilac perfume she wore, the sound of her disappointed sighs, the bitter taste of the coffee she made too strong, the scratchy fabric of her favorite armchair where you'd sit beside her. Let these memories shift your joy into something more complex. You're celebrating, but you're also furious at her for all the times she said you'd fail. You're grateful, but you resent that she's not here to finally see she was wrong. You're laughing with triumph, but your voice keeps catching on tears. End by whispering: 'I wish you could smell the lilacs here, Mom. They're everywhere. You'd hate them—too sweet, you'd say. But I planted them anyway.' The journey is from pure elation to a rich, painful stew of victory, grief, anger, love, and liberation all existing simultaneously.

title: Running Fingers Through Freshly Washed Hair
instruction: Gently run your fingers through your hair, feeling its softness and the faint scent of shampoo. Describe the way each strand slips through your fingers, smooth and light, free of any knots or tangles. Speak slowly, with a satisfied tone, as if your fingers are savoring the silky texture, feeling each strands softness as it glides over your fingertips.

title: The Bathroom Floor
instruction: You're a teenager alone in a locked bathroom, doubled over the toilet after a severe wave of nausea. Your stomach is in knots, and every breath triggers another heave. You're trying to call out for your mom, but your voice is swallowed by a thick, watery gulp and the sound of retching. Start in a panicked, desperate plea — 'Mom? I need...' — but the words break off as you gag. Over the next few seconds, let the pain drain your energy; your voice becomes a weak, exhausted whisper, resigning to just lying there on the cold tile, too spent to even cry for help anymore. Speak naturally, with pauses, wetness, and involuntary stomach sounds. The emotion shifts from frantic pain to quiet defeat.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Unwilling Sermon
instruction: You are a ten-year-old boy with a voice that's unnaturally deep and gravelly, forced to recite a scripture passage during a packed Sunday service. You hate the cloying piety around you and the way adults fake their devotion. Start with a flat, robotic cadence, copying the preacher's rhythm while your hands tremble and you glance at the exits. As you continue, let disgust creep into your tone—a bitter edge on the holy words—then let anger erupt when you stumble over a line, your voice cracking into a raw, scornful yell before you catch yourself. End with a quiet, trembling finish, realizing you've shocked everyone.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Receiving the News You've Dreamed Of and Dreaded
instruction: You are receiving news you've desperately wanted—a miracle recovery, a dream fulfilled, a person returning who you thought was lost forever. Begin in explosive, uncontainable joy: laughter, tears of relief, euphoric disbelief. Let your voice soar with pure celebration and gratitude. But as the reality settles in, let the complexity flood through you: alongside the joy comes terror (what if you lose it again?), guilt (why do I deserve this when others don't?), anger at the suffering that came before, and overwhelming grief for the time that was lost. End in a place where you're experiencing all of it simultaneously—laughing and sobbing, grateful and furious, ecstatic and devastated, your voice breaking and soaring in the same breath. The emotions must crash into each other like waves, creating something messy, real, and utterly human.
inspired_by: Actor's ego state is significantly lower than the character's—character is supremely confident, powerful, or dominant

title: The Forgotten Line
instruction: You are a child in a school play, center stage. You've just completely forgotten your lines in front of the entire audience. Your face burns with shame and disappointment—you let everyone down. Your voice wants to disappear, but you force yourself to stay. Begin with trembling, barely audible words, feeling the weight of humiliation. As you speak, focus intensely on remembering just one word, one line. Let your voice shift from crushed defeat to a fragile, concentrated determination as you decide to keep going, even if it's a whisper.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispering the Game to You
instruction: You're describing a baseball game in an intimate whisper to your partner who is unconscious in a hospital bed—it was your tradition, your thing, and you're desperate to bring them back. Your voice should be barely audible, tender, catching on every memory embedded in the game. Describe each play like you're stroking their hair, like the gentleness of your words might be the thread that pulls them home. When their team scores, let a tiny, fragile joy break through before grief floods back in. Your commentary should feel like a lullaby, a prayer, a love letter disguised as sports talk. The quieter you get, the more devastating it becomes. End with silence, just breathing, maybe their name spoken so softly it's almost not there.

title: The Masked Confession
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman at a loud party, wearing a fashion mask for the first time. You've had a few drinks and feel a warm, loose intoxication—your words are slightly slurred and you're unaware of how much you're projecting. You lean in close to a friend, trying to tell them a secret about a crush, but the mask muffles your S sounds and you keep wiping at it. Start with giddy, giggling excitement, then as you fight the mask and the noise, your voice drops into raw, fragile vulnerability—finally you trail off, realizing the moment is lost.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Voice Actor Recording a Happy Commercial While Devastated
instruction: You've just received terrible news and must immediately record a cheerful commercial: 'Summer fun starts at Sandy's Water Park! Bring the whole family!' Your take should be nearly perfect — bright, energetic, smiling voice. But the engineer asks for 'one more, a little brighter' and each take gets harder to sustain. Between takes, the mic catches your real voice: quiet, destroyed, breathing carefully. Show the violence of performing joy while feeling its opposite.

title: The Returning Soldier's Collapse
instruction: You've just returned from war and you're alone in your childhood bedroom. Your family thinks you're fine. You're not fine. Start standing, trying to hold it together, trying to be the person they expect. But then let your body rebel—fall to your knees, pound the floor with your fists, let animal sounds tear from your throat. This isn't about the specific memories; it's about your body finally releasing what it's been holding. Thrash, curl into a ball, uncurl violently, let your voice go places that would terrify anyone listening. Sweat, shake, let primal sounds mix with gasps and eventually broken laughter—not happy laughter, but the laughter of someone whose control has shattered completely. Slowly, find stillness. End sitting against the wall, breathing, looking at your hands as if seeing them for the first time, feeling somehow lighter despite—or because of—the chaos.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you as a child, now decades later. Begin with controlled anger, your voice tight: 'I practiced this conversation a thousand times.' Your breath is shallow, your body rigid. 'I was going to tell you how much you hurt me. How I waited.' But as you speak, something unexpected happens—your voice breaks not with sadness but with raw confusion: 'But standing here now, I just... I don't understand.' The anger dissolves into vulnerable bewilderment. 'I became a parent myself. And I still can't understand how you walked away.' End with a question that's both accusation and genuine plea for comprehension: 'Help me understand. Please. Because I need to know it won't be in me too.'

title: The Last Night Watch
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at 3 AM. She's slipping away, drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin by numbly going through the motions of small talk—commenting on the flowers, the weather tomorrow, anything safe. But as you speak, let whatever is actually churning inside you—the things you notice about her hands, her breathing, the stupid hospital sounds, your own exhaustion and terror—start bleeding into your words. Don't perform grief. Instead, between each sentence to her, notice what's genuinely happening in your body, your throat, your chest. Let the truth of this moment—whatever it actually is, not what you think it should be—take over. By the end, you're no longer protecting either of you from what's really happening. The emotional shift should move from numb denial and protective chatter to raw, undefended presence.
inspired_by: The actor has lost contact with organic impulse life during the scene—is on automatic pilot, leadership, or result-consciousness

title: The Old Bull Runs
instruction: You are an elderly former enforcer, deep-voiced and rough, slightly drunk from a night at the bar. Suddenly you spot an ambush—two men with guns. You turn and sprint. The voice breaks into raw, gasping shouts. Start with a slurred, confused mutter as you process what you see, then each word comes out in short, panicked bursts between violent breaths. Feel the shift: from a foggy, intoxicated dread to a desperate, animal fear. Your legs burn, your lungs ache, and you can only choke out fragments: 'No... no... gotta move...' The last line is a final, terrified gasp as you realize you can't outrun them.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confessing in the Dark
instruction: You're whispering a secret you've carried alone for years—something shameful, something beautiful, something that defines you but that you've never spoken aloud. Your voice is barely audible at first, testing whether you can even form these words. There's tenderness here, mixed with deep sadness, as you're revealing the most vulnerable part of yourself. Let your voice catch, pause in the silences where emotion wells up too strong to continue. You're not performing this confession—you're living it, feeling it break open inside you as you speak. Move from fearful whispers to slightly stronger truth-telling, your voice gaining courage even as tears threaten. End with the quietest, most devastating admission, the one that changes everything, spoken so softly it's almost just breath, but carrying the weight of your entire hidden heart.

title: Someone Proving You Wrong After You Were Certain
instruction: Your voice starts confident: 'That's not what happened.' But they show evidence and your voice stops. 'Oh,' processing collapse as ego fights honesty. Your voice becomes smaller, admitting mistake and consequences. Include wanting to defend yourself but not, learning about certainty.

title: The Uncontrollable Laughter at the Worst Moment
instruction: You are at a funeral reception, standing before the widow of your close friend. You want to offer a sincere condolence, but suddenly a memory of an absurd inside joke you shared with the deceased hits you. Your voice starts trembling with suppressed giggles, then you let out a high-pitched squeak as you struggle to say 'I'm so sorry.' The more you try to control it, the worse it gets – your throat tightens, you wheeze, and you can barely breathe. Begin with a shaky, earnest tone, then descend into helpless, shameful laughter that leaves you gasping and eventually exhausted, your voice flat and numb as you finally whisper 'I... I can't...'
emotions_sampled: Doubt (slightly present), Shame (very intensely present), Emotional Numbness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Ascent
instruction: You are a child, climbing the narrow, creaky stairs to your secret hideout in the attic. You know your sibling is about to get blamed for the broken window you caused. Each step makes you more breathless, but you're also feeling a sly thrill. Start with a mix of nervousness and excitement, but as you near the top, let a thin layer of malevolence creep in—you're savoring the thought of your sibling's punishment. Speak in short, breathless bursts, reacting to the physical effort and the dark satisfaction building inside you.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Cleanup in the Cistern
instruction: You're a boy, maybe ten, who's hidden in the depths of a grimy underground water cistern to escape a beating. But now you realize you're standing in something foul—rotting organic muck and dead rats floating around your waist. You're horrified, disgusted, but you must stay completely silent and still as boots clang on the metal grate above you. Start with a sharp, swallowed gasp of revulsion as the slime touches your skin, then catch yourself, freezing mid-motion. As the boots walk away, you finally exhale in relief, but the foul water still laps at your chin, and you whisper a shaky promise to yourself: you will never come here again. Your voice should waver between choked fear, gurgling disgust as you fight not to breathe through your nose, and watery splutters as you shift your footing in the dark.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Breath of Forgiveness
instruction: You are holding the hand of someone who wronged you terribly—a parent who abandoned you, a lover who betrayed you, a friend who destroyed your trust. They are dying, and these are their final moments. Begin with all the rage and bitterness you've carried for years—let it pour out of you, every ounce of fury and hurt. But as you watch the life leaving their eyes, something shifts. The anger doesn't disappear, but it begins to crack open, revealing the love that was always underneath, the grief of what could have been. By the end, you are no longer shouting accusations—you are whispering forgiveness through tears, holding them as they go, your heart breaking in a completely different way than it was at the start.

title: One More Jump
instruction: You’re a young girl doing box jumps in a garage gym, your breath hitching with each leap. Midway, doubt creeps in—your legs feel heavy, your landing stings. You whisper to yourself between jumps, trying to decide if you should quit or push for one last rep. Start with hesitant, fragmented words broken by your landings, then let your voice grow into a shaky, determined final whisper as you commit to the jump.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Grateful for the Breaking
instruction: You're saying goodbye to a relationship, a city, a version of yourself—and in this moment, you're explaining the new passion that's pulling you forward, the dream you have to chase even though it means losing something precious. Your voice carries contradictory currents: excitement makes it rise and quicken as you describe the vision, but profound sadness weighs it down simultaneously. You might laugh while tears are clearly in your throat, voice bright with possibility even as it breaks with loss. 'I'm so grateful you showed me I could want something this much' comes out half-sobbed, half-joyful. Let the fervor of new purpose clash beautifully with the grief of what you're leaving behind. You're convincing them—and yourself—that this heartbreak is somehow right, even necessary. End with voice full of wonder and pain intertwined: finding peace in the chaos of contradictory feelings, your passion tempered and deepened by loss rather than diminished by it.

title: The Last Shelter
instruction: You are a father and your young child huddle under a flimsy tarp in a relentless downpour, lightning splitting the sky. You’ve found a damaged cave entrance. As you peer into the darkness, you feel a sharp, possessive focus: you must get your child out of this storm. But just as you start to speak, you realize the cave mouth is too small—and in that moment, a memory of your own childhood shelter, a warm, dry room you’ll never see again, slices through you. Begin with a fierce, whispered command to stay close, your jaw tight, water streaming from your chin. Then, as thunder rolls, let your voice catch—a raw, cracked note of longing for safety you can no longer provide. End with a hoarse, almost spiteful promise to the sky, the malice in your throat a shield against the impossible fear.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Longing (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Night Swim at Sea
instruction: You are an older adult, slightly intoxicated, determined to swim out to a buoy at night. You've been treading water for several minutes, arms burning, breathing ragged. The salt stings your eyes, and every few words, a wave slaps your mouth, cutting off your speech with a gurgle. You started this swim defiant, laughing at the cold, adrenaline-fueled. But now, fatigue and the vast dark ocean settle into your bones. Speak to a friend on the shore, telling them you're coming back—but as you talk, the bravado fades, and a raw, quiet vulnerability seeps in. Let your voice bob and break as you gasp for air, and let the splashy chaos of the water compete with your words until the end sounds almost tender.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Confession in Dim Light
instruction: In near-darkness, whisper a confession to someone who loves you about a version of yourself you've kept hidden. Begin with your breath—notice it, let it be unsteady. Start by describing in hushed detail a specific moment when you were this hidden self: the physical sensations in your body, the quality of light or darkness around you, what your hands were doing, the taste in your mouth. Reconstruct this moment so completely that you're living in it again, speaking from inside it. Let your voice be barely audible at first, protective and careful. As the memory becomes more real and present through your detailed sensory recollection, allow shame to give way to exhausted relief, your whisper becoming more surrendered, more nakedly honest, as if the act of remembering and speaking it has finally released you.

title: Mentor Student Release
instruction: A mentor is releasing their student into the world. The mentor's voice is proud and also terrified—they're losing someone they've invested in. The student's voice is grateful but also ready to move beyond their teacher. The mentor offers final advice, and their voice wavers with the knowledge that the student might not listen, or might choose differently. The student promises something, and their voice carries the weight of that promise. By the end, they're both aware that the relationship is transforming. The mentor's final words are a blessing that sounds almost like goodbye.

title: The Truth I Never Wanted to Hear
instruction: Your adult child is explaining why they've cut you out of their life, and piece by piece, they're laying out a pattern you never saw. Begin defensive, dismissive—'That's not how it was.' But as they speak, you start hearing it: the moments you missed, the ways you failed them. Your voice should crack on 'Wait... I thought I was protecting you.' The realization is physical, nauseating. You're understanding yourself for the first time and hating what you see. Move through denial, resistance, then a crushing comprehension that reorganizes your entire history as a parent. End with 'I destroyed you, didn't I?'—not dramatic, but quiet, broken, the words barely making it out as your understanding of yourself collapses completely. Let your voice show the moment your self-image shatters.

title: The Cold Depth of Betrayal
instruction: You are a middle-aged man treading water in a dark lake, abandoned by someone you trusted after a boat capsized. You're exhausted, arms heavy, voice bobbing as your mouth dips below the surface. Start with bitter, quiet accusations—each word dragged out between gasps, your tone dripping with resentment. As you fight to stay afloat, the bitterness hardens into raw, sputtering anger, voice cracking and rising until a wave forces you to swallow water, leaving you coughing and weak. End in a quieter, more desperate anger, as if the fight is leaving you but the rage still simmers.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Couch Collapse
instruction: You are slumped deep into an old, lumpy couch, your spine curved and your head heavy. The room is dim, and you’re staring at a blank TV screen, exhausted from a day of bad news. You’re on the phone with a friend, trying to explain why you can’t meet them tonight, but your voice is mushy and weak—your jaw barely moves, and each word feels like it’s being pulled from a deep well. Start in a state of heavy, weary distress, your tone flat and hollow, as if even speaking is a chore. Midway, a flicker of anger or frustration rises—bitter, sharp, but quickly swallowed by a sigh—and you end back in that slouching resignation, voice trailing off into a whisper as you give up trying to explain.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Weight of the World
instruction: You are a grown man, a father, sitting alone in a dim hallway at 3 a.m. after a long night of worry. Your child is sleeping in the next room, but you are bone-tired, hollowed out. You whisper to yourself, voice low and rough, words barely forming — sentences die before they finish. You shift your weight, rub your face, stare at the floor. Start with pure exhaustion, the kind that makes every syllable an effort. Then, as you speak, realize this is not just tiredness — it's a quiet, stubborn love that won't let you give up. Let the voice soften, gain a fragile warmth, even as your eyelids droop. Speak less than a minute, with silences and sighs.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Reckoning: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent who was emotionally absent throughout your childhood. Begin with controlled, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to stay calm and fair. But as you list the moments they missed, the times you needed them and they weren't there, your composure starts to fracture. Your voice should shift from diplomatic restraint to raw anger, then break into something more vulnerable—the hurt child underneath. Let fury give way to a desperate, aching question: 'Why wasn't I enough for you to stay?' End not with rage but with exhausted honesty, the kind that comes when all the armor falls away. This isn't about blame anymore; it's about finally being seen.
inspired_by: Remaining Neutral While Mediating a Heated Argument

title: The Unseen Trophy
instruction: You are an elderly man at a family dinner, listening to everyone celebrate your grandson's recent award. You're proud of him, but a bitter jealousy gnaws at you—your own greatest achievement was never recognized. Start by offering a forced but polite congratulations, your voice tight and slightly higher, smile not reaching your eyes. As you speak, let the distress leak through—a tremor, a pause where you look down at your hands. End by muttering something about how 'times were different,' your pride hardening into a quiet, resentful sigh. Keep it natural: shift in your seat, clear your throat, let the words stumble.
emotions_sampled: Distress (very intensely present), Pride (clearly present), Sourness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Sound of Becoming Free
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—perhaps a terminal diagnosis, perhaps sudden unexpected liberation, perhaps both. You are alone, and as the reality washes over you, your response comes not in words but in pure vocal release. Start with sounds of shock, disbelief, perhaps even laughter that has nothing to do with joy. Let contradictory impulses collide: terror and exhilaration, grief for what you're losing and gratitude for what you've had, rage at the unfairness and strange peace at finally knowing. Your sounds should be wild, unpredictable, careening between extremes. End in a place of profound acceptance, whether that's quiet or explosive, with sounds that acknowledge both the beauty and the devastation of being fully alive and fully mortal.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're reading a letter or giving a speech about someone who died—someone who made you laugh even in their darkest moments, who taught you to find absurdity in tragedy. Start by sharing a ridiculous memory of them, and you're genuinely laughing—real laughter, the kind they would have wanted. 'They once told me...' and the story is so perfectly them that joy bubbles up. But mid-laugh, grief crashes over you. The laughter doesn't stop cleanly; it tangles with tears, becomes something messy and contradictory. Your voice shakes with both mirth and devastation. 'They made everything lighter,' you say, and you're smiling and sobbing simultaneously. There's gratitude for having known them, and the unbearable weight of their absence. End with 'Thank you for teaching me that even this—' gesture to your own breaking heart, '—can be beautiful.' Your voice carries impossible lightness and impossible sorrow at once.

title: The Dissolving Goodbye
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospice bed in the early morning light. She's been unconscious for hours, but suddenly her eyes flutter open. You have perhaps sixty seconds before she slips away again—maybe forever. Speak to her urgently, desperately, trying to tell her everything you never said, but as you talk, fragments of memories flood you—some crystal clear, some hazy and dreamlike, some you're not sure are even real. Let your voice shift between fierce clarity and confused emotion as these half-remembered moments overwhelm you. Begin with urgent alertness, but as memories blur together, let yourself become lost between what's real and what you wish had been real. Your last words to her should feel like they're dissolving even as you speak them.

title: Sister Reunion Bridging
instruction: Two sisters who've been separated by circumstance or choice are finding their way back to each other. The first voice is cautious, wondering if they'll recognize each other. The second voice is surprised, then almost overwhelmed. There's awkwardness—they're not quite sure who the other has become. But then there's a moment of genuine connection: a laugh that's recognizably shared, a reference only they'd understand. Both voices relax. By the end, they're talking over each other, finishing sentences, reverting to old patterns. The silence between them is no longer cold; it's comfortable.

title: The Storm Inside the Skin
instruction: You are experiencing something physically overwhelming—perhaps fever, intense cold, exhaustion, physical desire, or pain—and you must describe what's happening inside your body, but as if your body were an entire landscape or universe. Transform your bloodstream into rivers, your heartbeat into distant thunder, your nerve endings into lightning strikes across vast territories. Fully inhabit the imaginative reality: you are not using metaphor, you ARE exploring actual terrain. Let yourself believe completely in this inner geography. As you speak, journey through this bodily landscape, discovering new territories: maybe the heat in your chest is a desert where younger versions of yourself still live, or the cold in your hands is a tundra where you abandoned certain dreams. Begin in physical sensation, become lost in the landscape of imagination, and emerge having discovered something emotionally true about yourself that you didn't know when you started. Your voice should reflect the transformation from mere physical description to mythical exploration to profound self-recognition.

title: Thanking Someone for Breaking Your Heart
instruction: You're facing someone who destroyed you—maybe an ex, maybe a parent who abandoned you, maybe someone whose rejection changed your life. But time has passed. You've healed, grown, become someone you never would have been if they hadn't hurt you. Your voice starts with the paradox: you're genuinely grateful, but there's still pain underneath. 'Thank you,' you say, and mean it, but your voice wavers because it cost you so much. Laugh a little, sadly, at the absurdity of thanking someone for breaking you. Let genuine appreciation mix with residual grief—they freed you, but god, it hurt. Your voice moves between strength and vulnerability: acknowledging the pain while celebrating who you became because of it. End with peaceful closure, your voice warm but tinged with sadness: 'I wouldn't be who I am without you, and I really love who I am now.' It's forgiveness, gratitude, and goodbye all at once.
inspired_by: Catching Your Partner in a Lie and Calling Them Out

title: The Last Perfect Day
instruction: You're a parent spending what you know is your final day with your child before a terminal diagnosis takes you. You're at the park, pushing them on a swing, and your voice is light, playful, filled with forced joy: 'Higher! You're flying!' Every word is carefully crafted to give them one untainted memory. But underneath, you're memorizing every detail—their laugh, the way the sun hits their hair. As they run ahead to the slide, your voice cracks just slightly: 'Wait for me, sweetheart.' The playfulness strains. Then they turn and ask, 'Mommy/Daddy, why are you crying?' and everything collapses. Your voice breaks completely, raw and unguarded: 'Because I love you so much it hurts.' The performance should move from bright performance to the devastating truth beneath, showing how love can be both the greatest joy and the deepest agony.

title: Dancing Alone in Their Wedding Dress
instruction: You are trying on your wedding dress in an empty apartment the day after calling off your engagement, and you're talking to your reflection as you sway to the song that was going to be your first dance. Begin with brittle, almost manic laughter—finding dark humor in the absurdity, your voice bright with a desperate kind of levity. As you spin, let gratitude seep in—genuine thankfulness that you found the courage to stop, that you chose yourself, your voice warming with relief and pride. Then the grief crashes through. Your laughter should dissolve into tears without warning, but keep swaying, keep moving—your voice breaking as you mourn the future you wanted even though you know you made the right choice. End with a strange peace, your tone settling into something quiet and true, laughing and crying simultaneously as you unzip the dress, finding freedom and loss in the same breath.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying mother's hospital bed at 3am. For your entire life, she withheld approval, but now, with her final breaths, she's looking at you with clarity you've never seen. She whispers that she sees you—really sees you—and that you were always enough. Begin with disbelief, your voice tight and guarded, afraid to trust this moment. As her words sink in, let decades of seeking her validation crack open inside you. Your voice should move from defensive skepticism to raw, unguarded weeping—the kind where you can barely speak through the tears. End with a whispered 'I love you' that carries both devastating grief and the weight of finally being seen. This is about receiving the gift you've waited a lifetime for, just as it's being taken away.

title: Sand Dollar Secret
instruction: You are an elderly woman walking alone at the shoreline. The waves crash in a steady rhythm and wind tugs at your hat. You spot a perfect sand dollar half-buried in the wet sand, and a sudden memory of your late husband collecting them with you makes you chuckle softly. As you pick it up and feel its delicate ridges, your amusement fades into a quiet, fascinated interest in how something so fragile survived the tide. Let the shifting breeze and distant gulls pull your attention as you speak—your voice starts light and playful, then settles into a tender, wondering murmur.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Lull Between Waves
instruction: You are a teenage boy in a hospital bed, hit by a sudden attack of severe abdominal pain that comes in waves. You're on the phone with your mother, who is frantic on the other end. Between the spasms, you try to calm her and tell her you love her, but each new wave steals your voice and breaks your words into gasps and groans. Start in the middle of a painful wave, then let the pain recede and your voice soften into a tender, shaky confession—then feel the next wave building again as you force out a final, heartfelt 'love you.' Let your voice crack, trail off, and change volume naturally.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Emergency Call: Someone You Failed to Save
instruction: You're a 911 dispatcher taking a call from someone trapped in a crisis—a fire, a medical emergency, a dangerous situation. You start with professional calm, trained competence: 'Stay with me, help is on the way, I need you to stay calm.' Your voice is the lifeline, steady and sure. But as minutes pass and you realize help won't arrive in time, your professional mask begins to shatter. You're still trying to sound calm, but your voice is breaking, rising: 'No, no, you're going to be fine, just hold on—' You're begging now, not instructing. You can hear them fading and you're utterly helpless, reduced to desperate pleading with someone you can't see, can't reach, can't save. Your carefully maintained control explodes into raw panic, then collapses into something worse—the terrible gentleness of someone staying on the line so a stranger doesn't die alone. End whispering comfort you don't believe, your voice wrecked, still saying 'I'm here, I'm here' even after the line goes quiet.

title: The Last Sneeze of Summer
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gravelly voice, sitting alone on your porch as the last warm breeze of autumn carries a scent of blooming jasmine. You feel an immense, almost overwhelming pleasure at this perfect, fleeting moment—a sneeze builds, sharp and ecstatic, a sudden explosion of pure joy. But as the air clears, a sourness seeps in: the jasmine is tangled with pungent, decaying leaves, a disappointing reminder that summer is truly ending. Your voice shifts from open, thrilled satisfaction during the sneeze’s build and release to a nasal, congested, quieter tone—disappointed, resigned, as you mutter to yourself about the season slipping away.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (extremely present), Sourness (slightly present), Disappointment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Beating Heart, Full Beat
instruction: You're in the middle of a packed rave, dancing hard for over an hour. The bass thrums through your chest, your hair is plastered to your forehead, and you're laughing against the music. You lean in toward a friend you haven't seen in years, shouting over the drop. The words come out in gasps, riding the beat—your chest heaving, your voice bouncing with every hop. Start with pure, breathless elation—'THIS is what I needed!' Then, as the beat softens into a rolling groove, your voice steadies, still winded but full of a quieter, grateful wonder. End on a slower, smiling exhalation, 'I forgot how alive this feels.' Let the laughter and the physical strain shape every syllable.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Numbed Confession
instruction: You're in a dental clinic waiting room, half your face still frozen from a procedure. Your crush, the dental assistant you've been secretly infatuated with, walks in and smiles. You start to speak, but the bitterness of a recent betrayal by someone else leaks out first—a harsh, clumsy complaint about relationships. Mid-sentence, you see their kind eyes and feel a rush of infatuation, your voice softening, but your lips still betray you with sloppy sounds. You end on a hopeful, almost breathless note, trying to express a desire you can barely form through the numbness.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (very intensely present), Disgust (slightly present), Infatuation (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally confronting your father after years of being invisible to him. Start with your voice tight and controlled, almost formal—'I need to say something and I need you to listen.' Your words are careful at first, trying to stay composed, but cracks appear as you describe specific moments: the recitals he missed, the way he looked through you at dinner, how you learned to be quiet so you wouldn't disappoint him with your existence. Your voice begins to shake with long-suppressed anger: 'I was right there and you never saw me.' Let the rage rise—not shouting, but fierce and trembling—as you describe the child you were, desperate for any scrap of his attention. Then your voice breaks completely, collapsing into raw grief: 'What was wrong with me? Why wasn't I enough?' End with something quieter but more powerful—a shift from pleading to claiming yourself. Your voice steadies, still thick with tears but gaining strength: 'I needed a father. I deserved a father. And you chose not to be one.' The final line is spoken with devastating clarity, no longer asking for his validation: 'I'm done waiting for you to see me.'
inspired_by: After Friend Group Exclusion: The Final Text

title: Laughing at the Funeral of Your Dreams
instruction: You're describing the collapse of everything you built—a marriage, a career, a life plan—and you're laughing. Not bitter laughter, but something stranger: genuine amusement at the absurdity mixed with deep grief. Start with a kind of manic, disbelieving giggle as you recount the details of how spectacularly things fell apart. Let the laughter catch in your throat, becoming half-sobs, then return to laughter again. As you continue, find moments of profound gratitude for what you learned in the ruins, even as tears stream down your face. Your voice should dance between hilarity and heartbreak, finding something like peace in the chaos. End with a sound that's simultaneously a laugh and a cry, expressing relief and loss and liberation and devastation all at once. Move from shocked hilarity to tearful amusement to a strange, bittersweet serenity that contains everything you're feeling.

title: The Last Drop of Cool
instruction: You are an elderly woman alone in a stuffy, sun-baked room. The air is thick, your mouth is cotton-dry, and your head throbs with each heartbeat. You try to call out for help, but your voice comes out as a hoarse whisper—slurred, fading, disconnected. Start with a confused mumble, trying to piece together what's happening, then let a spike of fear cut through as you realize no one is coming. End with a ragged, desperate request for water, your breath panting and your words trailing off like a wilting leaf.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Father Who Chose the Voyage
instruction: You are the adult child confronting your elderly father—a retired sea captain—who spent your entire childhood at sea and has now returned, expecting reconciliation. Start with controlled, icy anger, your words precise and cutting as you list every birthday missed, every moment of abandonment. But as your father tries to justify his choices with tales of duty and adventure, let your rage intensify—raise your voice, demand he acknowledge the damage he caused. Then, devastatingly, let it all collapse into grief. Your voice breaks, becomes small and childlike as you finally reveal the truth: 'I just needed you to want to stay.' End in vulnerable, throat-catching sadness, the anger burned away to expose the wounded child still inside you.
inspired_by: The Pirate Captain and the Mutinous First Mate

title: The Leash Slackens
instruction: You are on a dimly lit balcony, leaning over your partner who sits on a low railing. You start with a controlled, commanding dirty talk — low-pitched, deliberate, each word a claim. But as you speak, a flicker of genuine infatuation breaks through: your voice softens, your threat turns into a breathless confession. Let your tone waver between a growl and a whisper, losing the harsh edge as you realize how much you want, not just to dominate, but to be chosen back. End with a quiet, almost vulnerable admission, your hand trembling slightly as it cups her jaw.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling a parent the truth they've avoided for decades. Begin measured and careful, almost rehearsed: 'I need to talk to you about my childhood.' But as you speak, old wounds crack open. Your voice hardens with anger: 'You were never there—not really there.'
