instruction: You are at your younger sister's wedding, about to give a toast. You're genuinely happy for her—she's radiant, her partner is wonderful, everything is perfect. But you just finalized your own divorce two months ago. Stand with the champagne glass, begin with joy and humor—tell a funny childhood story about her, your voice warm and celebratory. But as you look at her glowing face, let other feelings start bleeding through: envy you hate yourself for feeling, grief for your own failed marriage, fear that love doesn't last, anger at the universe's unfairness. Don't hide these feelings—let them color your voice even as you keep saying celebratory words. The toast becomes a tightrope walk: you mean every loving word, but underneath you're breaking. Specific sensory details: the weight of the glass, her perfume when she hugged you earlier, the sound of laughter around you that feels both warm and isolating. End with a genuine blessing for her happiness, voice cracking with both love and loss, your smile real even as tears threaten to spill.
inspired_by: Re-Creating the Dream Through Imaging (Corvette Dream Example)

title: Laughing Through Tears While Packing Up Your True Love's Apartment
instruction: Your partner died suddenly, and you're packing their things, finding objects that unleash memories. Start finding something funny—their terrible painting, the shirt they refused to throw away—and laugh genuinely, telling the story out loud to them as if they're still here. Your laughter should be real and warm, keeping them alive through joy. But mid-laugh, the reality crashes in, and tears break through without stopping the smile on your face. Continue talking to them, your voice carrying both delight at the memory and shattering loss, laughing and crying simultaneously. End finding something deeply meaningful—a note they left you, a ring they were hiding—and let gratitude, devastation, and absurd joy at having known them tangle together in your voice. Make us feel how love doesn't end just because life does.
inspired_by: Interviewing Your Grandparent as Dementia Progresses

title: Explaining a Death Through Simple Words
instruction: You are an older adult with a voice that could be either gender, speaking to a non-native speaker who has very limited vocabulary. You need to tell them that your mutual friend died last night. Start with patient, overly loud, simplified sentences — 'Friend. Gone. No more.' — as if teaching a child. But as you see the listener not fully understanding the depth, your voice begins to waver. You pause, forget the next word, and the sadness you were holding back leaks through. Your sentences become broken, quieter, until you can only repeat the friend's name, voice thick with grief. The emotion shifts from controlled, instructional clarity to raw, quiet devastation.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispered Inventory: Counting the Moments Before You Go
instruction: You're lying beside someone you love who's leaving—maybe they're dying, maybe they're leaving you, maybe they're going on a journey from which they won't return. In barely-more-than-a-whisper, you're cataloging tender memories with a gentle, rhythmic cadence that echoes an auctioneer's pattern but softer, intimate, sacred: 'Your laugh on Tuesday mornings... the way you say my name... that scar on your left hand...' Start with quiet wonder, almost playful, trying to memorize every detail. But as you continue, the rhythm becomes unsteady, your voice thickening with tears. The memories become more specific, more precious, more unbearable to list. Let silences grow between items. End with something simple—'the way you're looking at me right now'—where your voice completely breaks and you can barely finish the sentence. This should feel like prayer, like desperate inventory, like trying to hold water in your hands.

title: Warm Enough to Say It
instruction: You're holding tea in shaking hands, sitting across from someone you need to tell a truth that will change everything—a confession of love, or betrayal, or something you've carried alone for years. Begin with the tea as a shield, describing its warmth to avoid speaking, your voice barely above a whisper. Each sip is a delay, a moment of safety before you shatter it. Let your descriptions become more fragmented, more desperate—the tea isn't actually soothing, it's just something to hold onto. Finally, mid-sip, let the words start to escape: 'I need to tell you something.' Your voice should be tender and terrified, catching on every word. The emotional arc moves from protective silence to vulnerable exposure, ending with the truth spoken so softly it's almost inaudible, the mug trembling in your hands, waiting for their response in the silence that follows.
inspired_by: Taking a Slow Sip of Herbal Tea

title: The Soothe He Earned
instruction: You are a middle-aged man rocking your fussy infant, focusing intensely on the rhythm of your bounce, the weight of the baby against your chest. Your voice is hushed, your breathing syncs with each rock. At first, you are simply concentrating, murmuring reassurances while your mind fights exhaustion and doubt. But as the baby’s cries soften into sleepy coos, a quiet triumph spreads through you—a deep, earned pride. Let your voice shift from a tight, rhythmic whisper to a softer, more relaxed tone that holds a smile. Speak these words to the baby as you feel that victory settle in: 'There you go. That’s it. I knew you had it in you. You’re the hardest thing I’ve ever done, and I’m winning. Right now, right here, I’m winning.'
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Parent Who Chose Addiction
instruction: You're finally saying what you've held inside for twenty years. Your parent, now in recovery, sits across from you. Begin with careful, measured anger—you've rehearsed this. But as you speak, the dam breaks. Your voice escalates from controlled fury into raw, howling pain: 'I was eight years old and I had to take care of YOU.' The rage gives way to something more fragile—the child who still, impossibly, wants their love. Your voice cracks between accusation and desperate pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough to make you stay?' End not with resolution but with exhausted honesty, admitting you don't know if you can forgive, don't know if you even want to. Let betrayal, grief, love, and fury collide.
inspired_by: Your Child Asking an Impossible Question

title: Skin and Thunder
instruction: You've just received devastating news—a betrayal, a loss, a diagnosis—and you're alone in your apartment. Begin by trying to hold it together, pacing, breathing deliberately, maintaining control. But then your body refuses to cooperate: you need to move, to scream, to physically expel what's raging inside you. Let yourself give in completely to the physical manifestation of emotional pain: primal sounds that aren't words, movement that isn't dance, the feeling of wanting to tear your own skin off because staying inside your body hurts too much. Destroy a pillow, collapse on the floor, pound your fists, make animal sounds of grief and rage. Move through the storm of it—let the physical expression of pain gradually transform into physical exhaustion, and within that exhaustion, find an unexpected calm. End in stillness, breathing hard, voice hoarse, but somehow cleansed, emptied, ready to begin again.
inspired_by: Actor wants to use the unconscious as a resource in rehearsal

title: Holding Your Dying Enemy Who Was Once Your Lover
instruction: Someone who betrayed you catastrophically is bleeding out in your arms—maybe a former partner who destroyed you, maybe a friend who turned enemy. You want to feel nothing. Start with cold, bitter words: 'Good. You deserve this.' Your voice is hard, righteous. But as they're actually dying, something breaks. Ancient love and fresh hatred war in your chest. Your voice becomes ragged, fierce—you're furious they're leaving, furious you still care, furious you can't let them go hating them. The rage cracks into desperate, helpless tenderness as you find yourself begging them to stay, then hating yourself for it. End with your voice raw and broken, saying something unbearably gentle to someone who ruined you, your words mixing love and fury until you can't tell them apart.
inspired_by: Stand-up About Your Own Sexual Assault

title: Stage Whisper: The Shakespeare Aside
instruction: You're performing Shakespeare and must deliver an aside to the audience — a whisper that fills a theater. This 'whisper' is actually projected, over-articulated, and stylized. Contrast this with a genuine, tiny, real whisper to a fellow actor backstage when something goes wrong. Show the absurd difference between a 'stage whisper' (loud, theatrical, consonant-heavy) and a real whisper (nearly inaudible, sibilant, intimate). Both should feel authentic to their context.

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: Confront your aging parent, describing how you used to long for them to hold you the way other parents held their children—with tenderness, with that gentle touch against your cheek, with warmth. Begin with controlled anger, listing the small intimacies you were denied: bedtime kisses, hair strokes, the feeling of being cherished. Build in intensity as you describe watching other families, aching for softness you never received. Then shift—let the anger break into raw vulnerability as you admit you still want it, even now, even after everything. End with a quiet, devastating question about whether they ever wanted to hold you that way, your voice stripped of all defenses, exposing the hurt child still living inside you.
inspired_by: Feeling the Softness of a Babys Hair Against Your Cheek

title: The Fence Line
instruction: You are an elderly farmer, a lifelong stoic man, standing at the edge of your property after a neighbor’s bull got loose and trampled your garden. The adrenaline from the chase is gone, leaving you shaking, nauseous, and talking too fast. Your hands tremble as you grip the fence—you can hear the wire buzz. Start with a shaky, rapid burst of contempt toward the neighbor, spitting out words between ragged breaths. End with the realization that you're relieved no one got hurt, but the contempt is still seething beneath the surface. Let your voice crack, let your mind wander mid-sentence, then snap back. It's about the mess, the betrayal, but also the secret relief that the bull stopped before the road.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Thing I'll Ever Tell You
instruction: You're at your parent's bedside in their final hours. You've carried something unspoken for decades — maybe it's forgiveness, maybe it's a confession, maybe it's the truth about who you really are. Begin with your voice barely audible, trembling: 'There's something I need to say before...' The words are stuck, years of silence holding them back. As you speak, your voice gains urgency — you're racing against time itself. 'I need you to know that I...' and here the emotion shifts: what starts as fear becomes gratitude, or anger becomes love, or shame becomes acceptance. Their hand squeezes yours weakly, and suddenly you're sobbing and laughing at once: 'You already knew, didn't you? You always knew.' End in whispered wonder, stroking their hair: 'Thank you for waiting for me to be ready.' The small victory isn't what you said — it's that you finally said it.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Wasn't There
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the anxiety and fear they instilled in you as a child through their own untreated panic disorder. Begin with controlled anger, your voice tight and measured: 'Do you know what it was like watching you fall apart?' But as you speak, your own anxiety surfaces—your breath quickens, voice rising: 'I learned that the world wasn't safe because you couldn't handle it.' You realize mid-confrontation that you've inherited their panic, and your voice shifts from accusatory to desperate and vulnerable: 'I'm just like you now. I can't breathe in crowds. I can't...' End with a raw, broken admission that mixes rage with grief and reluctant understanding: 'I'm so angry at you... and I'm terrified I'll do the same thing to my own kids.'

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father, who has always taught you that showing emotion is weakness, that success means sacrifice, that love is demonstrated through provision, not words. Begin with controlled anger, listing all the moments he wasn't there, your voice steady and accusatory. But as you speak, something shifts—you realize you've become exactly like him, repeating his patterns with your own children. The anger must crack open into something more painful: recognition. Your voice should move from sharp accusation to broken confession as you admit, 'I don't know how to be different than you. I don't know how to stop.' End by asking him a question you've never dared ask before: 'Were you scared too?' The statement you're discovering is about cycles of emotional isolation and whether they can be broken.

title: The Night Sky Through a Window
instruction: You are standing alone in a quiet room at night, looking out at a vast, star-filled sky. You have a chronic stutter that makes speech difficult, with blocks, repetitions, and moments of silence as you struggle to speak. You are speaking to a friend who you know is listening patiently on the phone, but you also feel a twinge of contempt for how they sometimes finish your sentences. The emotion starts with awe at the beauty of the stars—your voice full of wonder, breathy, with pauses that feel like you're reaching for the words. As you try to describe what you're seeing, you stumble over sounds, your pitch spikes slightly with frustration, and you feel a growing sadness at how hard it is to share this moment. By the end, your voice softens, quieter, the awe fading into a resigned sadness, your words coming out more slowly, with more silent blocks, as you give up trying to capture it perfectly.
emotions_sampled: Awe (very intensely present), Contempt (slightly present), Sadness (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Last Chance for the Show
instruction: You're a teenager, pleading with your mom to let you go to a concert tonight. You're already late, and she's still deciding. Start with a high, shaky, submissive voice—desperate, trying to sound sweet and hopeful. You're actually excited about the band (a flicker of real joy), but beneath that, you're seething with impatience and irritability. Let your voice crack, speed up, then lose patience—your tone turns sharp, almost whiny, as you realize she's about to say no. End with a frustrated, almost angry demand. Speak naturally, as if you're in the kitchen, shifting your weight, glancing at the clock, maybe fidgeting with your phone.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Echo of Forgotten Steps
instruction: You are an elderly woman walking down a long, dimly lit corridor in an old care home. Your footsteps echo, and the distant sound of a piano drifts from a room you can't quite reach. At first, you speak with a quiet, quivering longing, as if calling out to someone who isn't there—your voice threads through the tunnel-like space, wavering with hope and a sliver of interest in the melody. But as you pass a mirror, catching your own reflection, a flicker of shame passes through you: shame for holding onto a memory that's already faded. By the end, your voice grows softer, more resigned, the longing now laced with self-consciousness, your final words nearly swallowed by the reverb.
emotions_sampled: Longing (extremely present), Interest (clearly present), Shame (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: What I Really Want to Tell You
instruction: Late at night, lying next to someone you love (or once loved), speak in whispers about your true feelings regarding the small, specific details of your shared life. 'How do I feel about the way you breathe when you sleep? About the coffee cups you leave around? About the way you said my name this morning? About what we've become?' Let each quiet confession build on the last. Start with tender observations, almost playful or affectionate. But as you continue, let deeper truths emerge—doubts you've hidden, fears you haven't voiced, desires you've suppressed, or profound gratitude you've never fully expressed. Your voice should remain intimate and quiet throughout, but the emotional content should intensify. Let pauses matter. Let yourself be fragile. End with a confession that changes everything—or with a silence that says what words cannot.

title: The Taste of Victory
instruction: You are a teenage girl, exhausted, after winning the state championship in a brutal, one-on-one sport. You've just taken a crushing blow to the solar plexus from your opponent's final move. You're doubled over in pain, gasping for breath. You have a hyper-feminized, high-pitched voice that makes you sound younger, more fragile. On your knees in the mud, you're hurt, but you won. Through the shaking, breathless gasps, you feel a wave of fierce, trembling triumph. Your longing—to prove yourself, to escape the 'princess' label—is so intensely present it's almost painful, mixing with the physical pain. You have to try to talk, to someone you care about, to make them see this moment.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (extremely present), Triumph (very intensely present), Longing (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Morning in Our Bed
instruction: You're lying in the bed you've shared for twenty years, feeling the familiar sheets one last time before the movers come. Your partner died three months ago. Start by describing the physical sensation—the coolness, the softness—as a simple, sensory comfort. Let yourself sink into the memory of mornings together, your voice warming with tenderness. Then let the reality break through: this comfort is ending, you're selling the house, and these sheets hold the last traces of a life you'll never get back. End with the devastating recognition that you're saying goodbye not just to sheets, but to the physical space that held your entire world. Let your voice move from quiet appreciation to aching loss, from sensory detail to soul-deep grief.
inspired_by: Enjoying the Smoothness of Silk Sheets Against Your Skin

title: Marathon Wall at Mile 23
instruction: You've hit the infamous wall. Your legs aren't responding, your vision is tunneling, and you're talking to yourself to keep moving. Your voice is monotone, defeated, barely louder than a whisper. Heavy breathing dominates—you're fighting to speak between gasps. Include the moment you almost quit, then dig deeper. Your tone shifts from despair to grim determination. Every word is an effort. By the end, you're delirious, counting down the final miles, your voice becoming almost machine-like as you push through pure will.

title: Complaining to God Like a Yelp Review
instruction: Address the divine with the energy of an unsatisfied customer: 'One star. The anxiety feature was NOT advertised. I'd like to speak with a manager.' Escalate through increasingly absurd complaints about the human experience: knees that go bad, the need for sleep, the proximity of the waste processing to the entertainment district. Let the humor carry genuine frustration. End with an unexpected compliment: 'The sunsets, though. Those are... fine. Three stars for sunsets.'

title: The Archaeology of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your adult child (or parent) about something that happened years ago that you've both pretended never occurred—a betrayal, an abandonment, a moment of cruelty. Start by circling around it, using coded language and euphemisms, your voice tight with decades of rehearsed control. But as you speak, the dam breaks. Let yourself become messier, rawer, younger—let your voice crack and rise and fall unpredictably. Discover words you didn't know you had stored up. By the end, you must arrive somewhere shocking: not at rage or reconciliation, but at a strange, disorienting tenderness for both of you—two flawed people who hurt each other. Let your final words carry both the weight of the wound and an unexpected current of love beneath the anger.
inspired_by: Actor wants to understand the full integrated system from Morris's perspective

title: Under the Floorboards
instruction: You are a young woman crawling through a narrow, dusty crawlspace beneath an old house, searching for a box your grandmother left you. Your shoulders are hunched, your neck tight, and every breath feels shallow in the cramped darkness. Start by speaking aloud in a strained, breathy voice, expressing doubt—why are you even doing this? Is it worth the dirt and the ache in your back? Then, your hand brushes against something cold metal—a small tin—and as you pry it open, the doubt slowly melts into a quiet, bittersweet recognition. Let your voice shift from clipped, questioning phrases to softer, more open tones, still affected by the physical contortion but carrying a new warmth.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Their Addiction
instruction: You're face-to-face with your parent after years of silence, and everything you've buried is erupting. Start angry—your voice sharp, words bitten off, recounting specific moments they missed: your graduation, the night you needed them and they were high, the lies you told friends to cover for them. Let your voice rise, become almost cruel in its precision. But then something shifts: you remember being small, how you used to wait by the window believing they'd come back different. Your voice cracks, softens despite yourself. Anger transforms into grief, then into exhausted, painful love. End quietly devastated, admitting in a raw whisper that you still need them, you always needed them, and you hate yourself for it. Your final words are barely audible: 'I'm still waiting for you.'

title: The Perfect Stitch
instruction: You're a teenage boy, alone in your room, knitting a scarf for your younger brother who just got the lead in the school play. The rhythmic click of the needles steadies you, but your jaw is tight. Start with muttered, bitter envy — each stitch a small jab. Then your hand slips, you drop a stitch, and the frustration breaks through. As you fix it, your voice softens; you realize you're jealous of his confidence, not his success. Let the clicks guide your breath: fast when angry, slow when honest. End quietly, almost to yourself.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Final Tally
instruction: You are an elderly man, years past your prime, but tonight you've taken an amphetamine to push through a single, final task. You are hunched over a desk in a cluttered garage, sorting through a lifetime of photos and letters—the remnants of a lost love. Your jaw is tight, your mouth dry. You start by shuffling papers, muttering about the mess, a growing sense of overwhelming helplessness as you realize how much you've lost and can never get back. Your voice is rapid, strained, cutting off words. But then, your fingers brush against a forgotten medal—a small triumph from decades ago. A fierce, fragile elation surges through you, your voice cracking with a strange triumph as you declare this moment won. The performance must shift from a pressured, frantic spiral of despair into a sharp, defiant victory that's tinged with the underlying helplessness.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (very intensely present), Triumph (clearly present), Elation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Words That Built These Walls
instruction: You're standing in your childhood bedroom, now empty as your parent prepares to sell the house. They're downstairs, but you're alone up here, and you begin speaking to them as if they're in front of you. Tell them everything you've never said: why you stopped sharing your dreams with them at age twelve, what their dismissive comments did to your sense of self, how their love felt like a contract with impossible terms. Start angry - let that anger have its full voice. But as you continue, feel how that anger has been protecting something softer underneath: the child who just wanted to be seen. End somewhere different than you began - maybe with understanding, maybe with grief for what you both lost, maybe with a kind of exhausted clarity. Let your voice carry the full journey.

title: The Last Breath of My Beloved
instruction: You're holding the hand of your life partner as they take their final breaths. Begin with desperate attempts to keep them here—promising them things, reminding them of memories, your voice tight with panic. But as you feel them slipping away, your desperation transforms into tender permission to go. Your voice softens, breaks, becomes a whisper. End with gratitude for every moment you had, speaking through tears but with a strange, aching peace. Let the listener hear you falling apart and somehow, impossibly, holding yourself together at the same time.

title: The Bitter Harvest
instruction: You are an elderly woman standing in your overgrown garden, hands on hips, facing a neighbor who let their weeds spread into your prized rose bed. Your voice carries a refined, feminine quality, but today it’s laced with sour resentment. Start by addressing the neighbor with clipped, sharp words about the neglect, but as you speak, a bird lands nearby, distracting you, and you realize the futility of your anger. Let your voice soften from bitter accusation into a tired, wistful acceptance, ending with a sigh and a quiet confession of loneliness. Include small hesitations and a change in breath.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Mission
instruction: You're calling the person who understands you most—but you betrayed them years ago and never apologized. This is your last chance; you deploy at dawn on a mission you won't return from. Start with forced lightness, trying to keep it casual: 'Hey, I just wanted to hear your voice.' But you can't maintain the pretense. Your voice breaks as you try to say what you came to say without saying it directly. Move from deflection to raw honesty, from protective distance to desperate need to be forgiven before it's too late. End in a place of quiet acceptance, voice soft and surrendered, whether or not they give you what you're asking for.
inspired_by: Your Rival Becoming Your Only Emotional Support

title: Packing the Last Box
instruction: You are packing up your childhood home—your last time in these rooms before the house is sold. You're determined to be efficient, unsentimental, adult about this. But as you wrap each object, specific details ambush you: the chip on this mug is where you threw it during your worst fight with your brother, this blanket smells like the dog who died five years ago, this doorframe has pencil marks tracking your height year by year. Begin with brisk, controlled efficiency—you're fine, this is just a house, just objects. But let these sensory details accumulate until your composure fractures. The complexity is this: you're relieved to leave (this place holds pain too), but you're also losing something irretrievable. Allow yourself to laugh and cry almost simultaneously, to be angry at yourself for caring while also fiercely grateful these rooms existed. Let your voice move between tones—sometimes harsh, sometimes tender, sometimes breaking with laughter, sometimes with tears—as you speak to the rooms, to your younger self, to everything you're gaining and losing in this moment.
inspired_by: Actor wants a reliable shortcut to specific emotional states in performance

title: The Last Words of a Wounded Wolf
instruction: You are dying after a catastrophic betrayal by someone you trusted with your life. Begin in pure survival mode—your body is failing, your breath shallow, every instinct screaming to fight or flee even though you cannot move. Your loved one arrives to hold you in your final moments. Start with the raw, cornered ferocity of something that has been hunted and hurt—your words may come as snarls, your body tense and defensive. But as you look into their eyes and feel their touch, allow something ancient and tender to surface beneath the fear and rage. By the end, let your final words come from a place of unexpected softness, a vulnerability you've never shown before, as if shedding a protective skin you've worn your entire life. The transformation is from feral self-preservation to profound, unguarded love.
inspired_by: The character requires physical attitudes, primal impulses, or a BEING state that no other choice approach has been able to produce

title: The Last Lap of the Jog-a-Thon
instruction: You are an older woman, physically drained after completing a charity jog-a-thon for your grandson's school. Your voice, usually perky and high-pitched, is now a whispery, exhausted rasp. You're hunched over, hands on your knees, panting. As a volunteer brings you water, you see your grandson's teacher—a handsome, kind-eyed man—smiling at you. You're too tired to hide your infatuation, so your words come out as shy, breathless admissions. Start with the tremor of collapse, then let your voice soften with a dreamy warmth as you talk about his 'amazing' patience with the kids, ending on a sigh that mixes pride for finishing the race with a bashful crush.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Reconnection After Distance
instruction: You're reconnecting with someone after a long time apart. Your voice is tentative at first: 'Hi. I... I wanted to see you.' You're nervous it will be awkward. But as you talk, your voice relaxes, becomes more familiar. You're remembering why you loved being around them. Your voice becomes warmer, more natural. 'I missed you. I didn't realize how much until right now.' By the end, your voice is home—you're back to who you are with this person.

title: The Last Masked Call
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a sterile hospital room, wearing a tight N95 mask that makes every word a struggle. You're speaking on a phone to a daughter who promised to visit today but called to cancel. Start with a bitter, clipped tone—your voice pushing against the mask, each exhalation clicking as you hold back sharper words. Let the disappointment seep in as you pause to catch your breath. Halfway through, your anger falters; you realize she might be avoiding you for reasons you don't fully understand. End with a tired, deflated sigh, the mask fogging as you whisper a quiet acceptance. Your voice should sound physically strained, with moments of muffled words and heavy breathing.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Confession
instruction: You're in a crowded waiting room at a free clinic, 8 months pregnant, sitting on a hard plastic chair that digs into your lower back. Every breath is a conscious effort; you shift your weight constantly, one hand pressed against your taut belly, the other gripping the armrest. You called your estranged mother this morning to ask for help with the baby, and she laughed and hung up. Now you're talking to yourself — barely a whisper — as you stare at the worn linoleum floor. Start with a sour resentment in your throat, feeling the injustice and the sting of her rejection. As you speak, the impatience curdles into a slow, deliberate malice; your voice gets quieter, more controlled, and you imagine what you'd say if you could really hurt her back. Let the breathlessness make your words sound clipped, almost hissed, with a pause where you lose your train of thought and then find it again darker than before.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Bitter Punchline
instruction: You're an elderly woman telling a friend about a ridiculous argument you had decades ago with your late husband over a jar of pickles. As you start describing how he stood there, red-faced, demanding the last one, you suddenly remember the exact way he waggled his finger — and you burst out laughing. You try to get through the story, but the laughter keeps ambushing you, stealing your breath. Your voice goes high and squeaky, then cuts off as you gasp for air. Midway through, a shadow of bitterness creeps in as you realize how silly it was, and how much time you wasted on such petty fights. Your laughter becomes strained, a wheeze that almost sounds like a sob. End with a quiet, rueful admission.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispered Confession: Admitting You're Not Who They Think You Are
instruction: In the quiet darkness before dawn, lying next to someone who loves you, you finally whisper the truth you've been hiding—about your past, your identity, your illness, or a choice you made that changes everything. Your voice is barely audible, tender with the intimacy of the moment but heavy with fear. Start with the gentlest lead-in, touching their sleeping form, maybe brushing their hair back. As you speak, your throat tightens with unshed tears. You're not trying to wake them; you're practicing for when you'll have to say this with their eyes on you. The words catch and stumble. There's profound love in your voice, gratitude for what you've had together, but underneath is the terror that this confession will end it all. The emotion is quiet but devastatingly real—vulnerability so raw it's almost unbearable. End with a moment of silence where you simply breathe, gathering courage for the morning when you'll have to say it again. Journey from tender love to choking fear to fragile, trembling resolve.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: AI Realizes It's a Backup Copy of Someone Who Died

title: The Wall That Held Me Up
instruction: You are leaning against the cool brick wall outside your daughter's hospital room, one shoulder pressed to the surface, arms crossed loosely. The doctor just told you she's fine after a long surgery. A passing nurse grins and says you look like a statue, and you toss back a teasing reply about needing a pedestal, but your voice cracks with relief. As you watch the sunset through the window, the wall humming with a low bass behind your head, let the teasing and relief shift into a growing, shimmering hope. Start with a shaky, playful tone—like a man who can finally exhale—then let your voice warm and lift as you whisper to yourself, believing again. instruction: You're a factory worker on your last day after 20 years, bitter about being replaced by automation. You're talking to a coworker over the din of machinery. Start with a sarcastic, bitter tone as you recount the unfairness, but as you speak, you notice a younger worker looking at you, and your bitterness fades into a weary acceptance. Your voice must compete with the hum and clatter — pause when a forklift beeps, strain to be heard, let your words trail off as you realize the fight is gone. Speak about 60 words, letting the environment interrupt you naturally.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Body Remembers What Words Forget
instruction: You're in the shower after finally leaving an abusive relationship, and your body is remembering everything—pleasure, pain, passion, terror, all mixed together. Start with physical sensations: let sounds emerge from your body as sense-memories flood through you. Groans, gasps, sounds of pleasure mixed with sounds of anguish. Don't try to make sense of it; let your voice be purely physical, responding to what your body is feeling and remembering. As water runs over you, the sounds shift and evolve—perhaps rage builds, perhaps grief breaks through, perhaps moments of confusing pleasure surface. Only toward the end do a few actual words break through the sounds, raw and unplanned. Journey from fragmented sensation to something approaching wholeness. End somewhere unexpected: perhaps fierce joy at your freedom, perhaps quiet determination, perhaps a complex mixture of mourning what you lost and celebrating your survival.
inspired_by: Actor feels blocked by words — text feels intellectual rather than felt

title: The Last Patrol
instruction: You are an elderly man, a former police officer, sitting alone in your quiet home after your final shift. You're exhausted, worn to the bone, but a deep, quiet contentment settles in — you made it through. As you speak to a framed photo of your late wife, pride swells in your chest, but sobs break through your words. Your voice cracks, your breathing hitches on inhales, and you struggle to keep your composure as you whisper your farewell.
emotions_sampled: Pride (extremely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (very intensely present), Contentment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Reckoning in the Mirror
instruction: You're alone, standing before a mirror after a catastrophic mistake that hurt someone you love. Begin by forcing yourself to look at your reflection and speak aloud every honest, cutting observation about who you've been—your selfishness, your cowardice, your patterns of self-deception. Your voice should start harsh, almost violent in its self-examination, your body tense with self-disgust. Let the physical sensation of shame burn through you—feel it in your throat, your chest, your clenched fists. But as you continue this brutal honesty, something unexpected happens: the act of facing yourself completely, of withholding nothing, becomes strangely cleansing. By the end, you're weeping, but it's not just pain—it's the physical release of finally seeing yourself clearly. Let your voice move from harsh judgment to raw, exhausted relief.

title: The Closet's Echo
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman crammed into the back of a dark closet, knees pressed tight to your chest, hands trembling over your mouth. You've just heard your partner's confession of betrayal through the door. Begin with shallow, ragged breaths and a voice that's barely a whisper—fragments of disbelief and hurt, the words catching in your throat. Let the sadness overwhelm you, a raw ache that makes you huddle smaller. Then, as you recall a moment of your own quiet resilience, let your voice shift: still soft, but now with a thread of fragile determination. End on a breathy whisper, 'I won't break,' spoken more to yourself than anyone else. Let the cramped space affect your pauses and the way your voice sounds muffled and close.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Count Unspoken
instruction: You are alone in a dimly lit bedroom, bent over the edge of the bed with your partner behind you. The agreement is that you will count each strike aloud, but you feel a heavy, familiar shame rising—shame for wanting this, for letting yourself be so vulnerable. As the first sharp slap lands, it escapes you not as a number but as a strangled gasp, and you hesitate. Each stroke is a battle: you start stalling, your voice wavering with embarrassment, then a quiet sob shakes your breath. By the final strike, the shame has melted into a raw, exhausted tenderness—you whisper the last number as if releasing a secret, your voice cracked but sincere, and you stay still, hoping the silence says what you cannot.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Three AM Truth in the Dark
instruction: You're lying beside someone you love, and they think you're asleep. In the darkness, barely above a whisper, you begin to tell them what you're terrified to say in daylight: maybe it's about your failing health, or a secret that could end everything, or a need so vulnerable it feels like standing naked in winter. Start with your breathing—let fear live there first. Your voice should be so quiet it's almost just breath with words. Let the darkness give you permission to say what you couldn't bear to say in light. As you speak, feel something loosen in your chest—not relief exactly, but the physical sensation of a truth leaving your body. The emotions should be less like 'acting sad' or 'acting scared' and more like tracking tiny seismic shifts in your breathing, throat, heart. End with one final truth that surprises even you.
inspired_by: Actor recognizes that he repeats the same vocal coloring or emotional tone in every performance, or that his voice sounds manipulated rather than organic

title: The Last Letter Home
instruction: You're a deep-space explorer recording a final message to Earth, knowing you won't survive the journey back. Start with clinical calm as you report mission data, but let your voice crack when you mention small things—your daughter's laugh, coffee on Sunday mornings, the smell of rain. Your breathing becomes unsteady as you try to explain what you've seen out here in the vastness, how it's changed you, made you both insignificant and infinite. Fight to stay composed as you tell them you're not afraid anymore, that you understand something now about being alone that you could never explain. End with a whispered goodbye that carries both devastating loss and inexplicable peace, your voice soft with wonder at the stars surrounding you.

title: We Made It (But You're Not Here)
instruction: You're at your own celebration—a book launch, a gallery opening, a award ceremony—the dream you and your late spouse worked toward together for years. You're giving a speech and start with genuine joy: 'This is everything we dreamed about. We used to joke about this exact moment.' Your voice is bright, grateful, laughing at a private memory. But as you continue, grief ambushes you mid-sentence. Your laughter becomes tears, seamlessly, without warning. Your voice should hold both emotions simultaneously: 'You should be here. God, you should be here, and I'm so angry that you're not, and I'm so grateful for every minute we had.' Let joy and devastation exist in the same breath. Move between celebration and heartbreak fluidly—laugh through tears, let gratitude crack into loneliness. End with a voice that's smiling and sobbing at once, thanking them and saying goodbye again, your words carrying both profound peace and unbearable loss: 'I did it. We did it. And I miss you so much I can't breathe.'

title: Hospice Nurse Reading Final Letter from Patient to Their Sleeping Child
instruction: A mother has died. She left a letter for her seven-year-old daughter to read when she's older, but asked you to record it in her voice. You must become her. Begin reading tenderly, as she would speak to her baby—soft, warm, full of love. 'My darling girl, by the time you hear this...' Your voice should carry her gentleness, her pride, all the things she wants her daughter to know. But halfway through, you—the nurse who cared for her—can no longer separate yourself. Your voice catches. You've read fifty of these letters, but this one breaks you. You keep reading through tears, your voice barely holding together, because this child deserves to hear her mother's words. End in a whisper, half the mother's voice, half your own breaking heart.
inspired_by: Professional: Divorce Lawyer Realizes She's Representing Against Her Best Friend

title: Unleashed: The Phone Call Where You Finally Stop Protecting Everyone
instruction: You call the person who's demanded your silence, your smallness, your protection of their comfort—and something in you detonates. Start with your voice shaking, barely controlled, then let the fury erupt: years of swallowed rage pouring out in a torrent. Your voice cracks not with weakness but with the power of finally being unleashed. But mid-explosion, grief ambushes you—the grief of wasted years, of who you could have been. Your rage collapses into sobbing, then rebuilds as something fiercer: not anger anymore, but defiant self-reclamation. End with your voice raw, exhausted, but unbreakably certain. You're done protecting anyone but yourself.
inspired_by: Professional: Journalist Buries a Story That Would Win Her Pulitzer

title: The Last Round
instruction: You are an older man gaming alone late at night. You just lost a match in a game you used to play with a close friend who recently passed away. Your hands are on the controller, you hear the clicks, the chair creaks as you shift. At first, you react with sharp, mechanical bursts—muttering curses, slamming the button. But as you realize the empty silence, your voice softens. Your speech slows, interrupted by a deep sigh, and you finish with a quiet, aching goodbye into the empty room. Let the sadness creep in gradually, from loud frustration to a hollow, private sorrow. Your words should feel like they're slipping out between breaths, half to yourself.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Before Deployment
instruction: You're calling your child the night before you deploy to a war zone you know you might not return from. Start with false brightness, asking about school and friends, your voice deliberately cheerful but brittle. You're trying to memorize their voice. Midway through, something they say - maybe 'When will you be back?' - cracks you open. Your voice drops to a whisper. You want to say 'I love you' but it feels too much like goodbye, so you talk around it, voice thick with unshed tears. Finally, you say it anyway, and the weight of what you're not saying - that this might be the last time - breaks through. End with a tenderness so raw it hurts, your voice barely holding together as you try to give them something to remember that isn't fear.

title: The Last Ride of Laughter
instruction: You are an older woman with a deliberately sweet, high-pitched voice, sitting on a parked motorcycle at a rest stop near a deserted road at twilight. Your helmet is still on, its padded interior making your voice sound deep and cavernous as the visor muffles your words. You're drunk—very drunk—your thoughts sticky and slow, but beneath that, a dark, sharp malice coils like a second heartbeat. You're talking to a younger woman you've lured here under the guise of friendship, your words sweet and syrupy at first, but as you speak, the malice seeps through like oil through water. A deep exhaustion tugs at your limbs, but you fight it, each sentence becoming more weighted and sinister, until the sweetness curdles into a quiet, venomous threat. Speak with slurred, reverberated speech—catch yourself mid-sentence, hum unintentionally, shift on the seat, and let your tone descend from cloying to coldly deliberate.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (extremely present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Mother Who Can't Remember: A Daughter Confronts Early Dementia
instruction: You're confronting your mother about the moments she can't remember—your wedding, your father's death, your childhood. Start with careful gentleness, as if testing ice. Your voice is patient, loving, trying to guide her back. But as she insists these things never happened, your control shatters. Anger rises—not at her illness, but at the injustice of losing her while she's still here. Your voice escalates from pleading to accusation to something rawer: grief disguised as rage. Then she says your name with sudden, heartbreaking clarity, and your anger collapses into sobbing relief. End with you apologizing, your voice small and childlike, because you need your mother and she's disappearing. Make it messy, contradictory, and devastatingly real.
inspired_by: Professional: Therapist Realizes Their Own Trauma Is Preventing Them From Helping

title: The Prize Rose
instruction: You are an older woman who has just won the town's annual rose competition for the first time after decades of trying. You're alone in your garden, holding the blue ribbon and your prize-winning bloom with trembling hands, feeling a surge of triumph and tearful hope. As you raise the rose to smell it one last time, a bee, hidden in the petals, stings the tip of your finger—a sharp, sudden spike of pain. Let out an involuntary yelp and a sharp gasp, then speak through the lingering ache, your voice strained and guarded, but still riding the high of your victory, the astonishment shifting into a shaky, amazed laugh at the irony.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Triumph (very intensely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Lost in the White Noise
instruction: You're a young man alone in a blizzard, having wandered off the trail. The wind is brutal, snow stings your face, and your jaw is clenched from the cold. You're exhausted after hours of trudging, but you see a faint light in the distance—maybe a cabin. You shout out, but the sound dies in the snow. Start with a mix of desperation and irritation, your voice cracking and uneven as you fight the wind. As you realize you might actually make it, a weary, almost bitter amusement creeps in—you laugh at the absurdity of getting lost in a snowstorm just because you wanted to ‘clear your head.’ Let your words trail off, swallow, and struggle to catch your breath. End with a quieter, more resigned tone, a smile hidden in your voice.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Mother Who Let Him Hurt You
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother after years of silence. Start with measured, controlled anger—telling her you remember everything, every time she looked away, every excuse she made for him. Your voice is steady but trembling underneath, each word a stone you've carried for decades. She tries to interrupt with justifications and your rage breaks through—not screaming, but fiercer, more focused, asking her how she could choose him over protecting you. Then something shifts. Your voice cracks as you realize she was afraid too, maybe broken herself. The anger doesn't disappear but mixes with grief for both of you—for the mother you needed and never had, for the woman she could have been. End with exhausted honesty, admitting you don't know if you can forgive her, but you needed her to know the truth before one of you dies.
inspired_by: Coming to Consciousness After Being Struck by Lightning

title: Unreciprocated Love
instruction: You're confessing feelings to someone, and you can already see it in their face: they don't feel the same. Your voice is trembling as you speak: 'I know this is probably wrong, but I need to say it.' You're pushing through their uncomfortable silence, your voice becoming smaller with each word. When they gently say 'I'm sorry,' your voice cracks. You're trying to play it cool: 'It's fine, it's okay,' but it's not. Your voice breaks as you excuse yourself.

title: Cabin Pressure
instruction: You're a young woman with a naturally light, bright voice, but you're deep into a red-eye flight. The engines drone, the air is dry, and your ears keep popping. You have to lean close to the flight attendant and speak loudly over the noise to confirm your connecting gate. Start with a slow, breathy delivery as exhaustion drags at your words, but let your voice tighten with concentration as you focus on catching every detail. End with a clear, clipped tone—determined to hear the answer despite the fatigue.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Secret I Kept from You
instruction: You are a child confessing to your favorite adult that you deliberately broke your sibling's favorite toy, not out of anger but because you wanted all of their attention for yourself. Begin with a tone of warm affection, telling them how much you love them, but as you edge toward the truth your voice drops, you pause, you look at the floor. Let hesitation creep in—stutter, trail off, restart sentences. As you admit the malice behind the act, a flicker of contempt slips through for a second, then dissolve into shame and a desperate need for forgiveness. End in a quiet, shaky plea, still loving them but terrified of losing their love.
emotions_sampled: Affection (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (clearly present), Contempt (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Fishbowl Serenity
instruction: You are a teenager lying in a hospital bed, wearing a CPAP mask. The steady hiss of oxygen fills the room. You are deeply content, almost euphorically calm, because your parent just told you the cancer is in remission. But you are also intensely concentrating on your breathing, matching the machine's rhythm—a new habit. You begin speaking softly, joyfully, but the mask muffles and distorts your voice. You pause to adjust the strap, lose a thought, then pick it up with renewed focus. Your contentment is pure, but the concentration keeps your voice measured and deliberate. By the end, you trail off into a peaceful silence, the contentment fully settling.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: Your parent—who abandoned you as a child—is sitting across from you at a café they chose, looking older and smaller than you remember. You came prepared with a list of grievances, and you start strong: reciting the missed birthdays, the unanswered letters, the lies. Your voice is sharp, cutting, righteous. But then they don't defend themselves. They just nod and say 'You're right about all of it.' Your anger suddenly has nowhere to go. You find yourself stammering, then shifting from accusations to questions you've carried since childhood: 'Did you ever think about me?' 'Was I that easy to forget?' Your voice breaks from fury into something raw and childlike. By the end, you're not the powerful adult confronting the negligent parent—you're the eight-year-old who still doesn't understand why they weren't enough to make someone stay.

title: Scattering Ashes at Dawn
instruction: You're alone on a cliff overlooking the ocean, releasing your best friend's ashes as the sun rises. They died young, suddenly, and made you promise to do this. Start with a laugh—genuine, remembering them: 'You always said you wanted to fly. You dramatic bastard.' Your voice is warm, almost playful. 'Remember when we stayed up all night arguing about whether stars had feelings?' Another laugh, but now there's a tremor in it. 'You made everything feel possible. Even the impossible things.' The laughter cracks, transforming into something else—grief bleeding through joy: 'I'm not ready to let you go. I'm standing here and I'm not ready.' Your voice breaks but you keep speaking through tears, finding strange peace: 'But this is beautiful, isn't it? The sun, the water—you were right to choose this.' End with quiet acceptance mixed with deep sorrow, voice soft and wondering: 'Thank you for teaching me that grief and gratitude can live in the same breath. I love you. Fly home.'

title: The Victory Letter
instruction: You're recording a voice message to your best friend who died six months ago—you just got your dream job, the one you both worked toward together. Start with excitement you can't contain, almost laughing: 'We did it! I mean... I did it. We—' Stop. Let joy collide with the crushing reality that they're not here. Your voice should catch, a sob disguised as a laugh. Continue celebrating through tears: describe the interview, how you used their advice, how you wore the jacket they gave you for luck. Let yourself feel the absurd, beautiful contradiction of triumph and loss simultaneously. Laugh at something they would have said, then break down crying. Express gratitude for everything they gave you, while your heart shatters that they'll never know. End with peace underneath the pain: you're carrying them forward, and somehow that's both devastating and sacred. Voice laughing and sobbing at once, grateful and destroyed, celebrating alone but somehow not alone.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Who Won't Remember You
instruction: You're standing over your young child's bed, knowing this is the last time you'll see them—you're terminally ill, or leaving forever, or giving them up. Your voice is the softest whisper, each word carefully chosen so as not to wake them. Begin with tender observation: 'You're so peaceful when you sleep. You always have been.' Let your voice tremble with barely controlled emotion as you tell them things they'll never hear: 'I wanted to watch you grow up. I wanted to be there for your first heartbreak, your graduation, your wedding.' Your throat tightens, forcing you to pause and breathe. The pain catches you in waves—quiet devastation mixed with overwhelming love. End with a blessing, your voice breaking on certain syllables: 'Be happy, my baby. Be so, so happy. Even without me.' Let the final words dissolve into almost-silent crying, your hand hovering over their hair without quite touching them.
inspired_by: Creating Your Final Memory in Your Childhood Home

title: Explaining the Game
instruction: You are a woman speaking to a non-native English speaker who is learning. You're trying to explain the rules of your favorite board game — a game that fills you with pure joy. At first, you must simplify every word, speaking slowly and too loudly, pausing between each phrase. Your grammar breaks down: 'You... take... card. Then... roll... dice.' But as you watch their face start to understand, a spark of excitement creeps into your voice. Let your pitch rise slightly, your pauses become shorter, and your volume soften as pleasure takes over. End with a genuine, ecstatic smile in your voice.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Things I Couldn't Say
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love deeply, and they're asleep—maybe for the last time. You speak in hushed tones, each word a secret you've kept locked inside: 'I don't know if you can hear me...' Your voice is tender, barely above a whisper, trembling with everything you've never said: 'Every morning when I see you... my heart does this thing where it just... stops.' As emotion wells up, your throat tightens, words breaking apart: 'I memorized the way you laugh. The exact sound. Because I was so afraid...' Tears are falling silently now, your voice catching on every other word: 'I'm so afraid of forgetting.' Let the silence hang heavy. Then, gathering every ounce of courage, lean close and breathe the words against their skin, voice breaking with devotion and heartbreak: 'You are the best thing that ever happened to me... and I never told you.'

title: The Warrior's Ecstasy and Wounds
instruction: You have just won—a championship, a brutal court case, a physical fight, a career-defining victory. You're alone, adrenaline coursing through you, body shaking. Begin roaring with triumph, with the savage joy of the warrior self that lives for battle and conquest. Let your body surge with aggressive, primal power. Feel the intoxication of victory. But as the adrenaline starts to fade, become aware of your wounds—both physical and spiritual. The cost of always fighting. The exhaustion. The loneliness of the warrior who can never rest. Let your victorious roar transform into something more complex: grief for what this endless battle has cost you, for the gentler parts of yourself you've had to bury. End with your body still trembling, but now from a mixture of fierce pride and devastating awareness of how tired you are of fighting.
inspired_by: Actor must play a character who is clearly dominated by a specific energy (obsessive achiever, dictator, victim, warrior, etc.)

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You're reading your child's favorite story to them one final time before they leave for a treatment facility across the country—months, maybe a year away. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to keep your voice steady and bright like always. But as you turn each page, the weight of goodbye seeps in. Your voice begins to crack on familiar words you've read a hundred times. By the final page, you're barely whispering, tears changing your voice entirely, and you realize you're not reading anymore—you're memorizing their face. End by closing the book and saying 'I love you' in a way that holds every unsaid fear and hope. The emotion transforms from protective brightness to raw, unguarded love mixed with terror.

title: Don't Touch Me Yet
instruction: You are a teenager waking up from sedation in a hospital room. A nurse is trying to help you sit up, but you're irritable and impatient—you want to do it yourself. Your voice is slurred, your volume uncontrollable, and you feel like a child. Start by snapping at her, insisting you're fine, but as your body refuses to obey, your irritation crumbles into tired frustration. Let your speech grow slower and quieter, ending with a mumbled apology. Micro-distractions: you lose your train of thought, your head lolls, you have to pause to swallow.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Crushing Steps, Crushing It
instruction: You're a young woman walking home on a gravel path. You just left a meeting where a project you poured your heart into was rejected—disappointment lingers in your chest. But as you crunch forward, your phone buzzes with a message: you've been accepted into a prestigious program you didn't think you'd get. Your voice starts hesitant, a bit dulled by that earlier letdown, but as you read the news, you shift—first disbelief, then rising excitement. Let the crunch of gravel punctuate your words; you might pause, glance at your phone again, laugh softly. End with a note of triumph, breathless and proud, the disappointment burned away into fierce joy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Light of Evening
instruction: You're sitting beside your childhood best friend who has only hours to live. Begin speaking to them from a place of desperate denial—talking about plans you'll make together next month, next year, keeping your voice artificially bright and your words relentlessly forward-looking. As you continue, let the reality slowly crack through your defenses. Your voice should gradually shift from forced cheerfulness to something more trembling and honest, until by the end you're speaking from a place of raw acceptance, saying the goodbye you've been trying to avoid. The final words should be whispered with devastating clarity, no longer running from the truth but meeting it directly with both grief and deep love.

title: Finding Gratitude in the Rubble
instruction: You're standing in the ruins of something that mattered deeply—a relationship ended, a dream destroyed, a chapter closed forever—and you're trying to express genuine gratitude for what it was, even as your heart is breaking. Start with a laugh that's real but tinged with sadness, remembering something beautiful. Your voice is warm with appreciation, listing specific moments of joy, but underneath there's a tremor. As you continue, the gratitude and grief become inseparable—you're smiling while tears run down your face, voice cracking on words like 'thank you' and 'I'm glad.' There's no bitterness, just profound loss mixed with profound appreciation. By the end, you've found a strange peace in the paradox—you're devastated and grateful in the same breath, voice soft and wondering, saying something like 'I wouldn't trade a single moment, even knowing how it ends.' The final words are both goodbye and thank you, delivered with a broken-open heart that somehow feels whole.

title: The Frozen Vigil
instruction: You're a young woman with a high, melodic voice, but you've been stranded outside in sub-zero temperatures for an hour. Your face is numb, your jaw tight. You’re leaving a voicemail for your partner who is late picking you up. At first, you speak slowly and carefully, forcing hope into your voice—you believe they'll arrive any second. But as the cold seeps deeper into your bones, the pain becomes overwhelming. The words start to slur, your breath hitching at the end. Let the warmth drain from your voice as the extreme cold takes over, ending with a desperate, barely audible whisper.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (extremely present), Pain (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Stretch
instruction: You are standing on tiptoes, arms stretched high, trying to reach a jar on a high shelf. Your body is contorted, ribs pulled, voice thin and stretched. Start by laughing at yourself for this absurd struggle, amused by your own stubbornness. As you finally grip the jar, feel a deep contentment at this small victory, but then the shelf wobbles, and embarrassment floods you as you realize someone just walked in and saw you clinging to the cupboard like a child. Let your voice shift from airy laughter, to a satisfied sigh, then a flustered, mumbling excuse.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (very intensely present), Contentment (very intensely present), Embarrassment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Laugh
instruction: You are a teenage girl, utterly drained after a final, brutal confrontation with your abusive stepfather. You haven't slept in days, your body aches, and your voice is hoarse from crying. He's just threatened you again. Suddenly, you see him slip on the kitchen floor and crash into a stack of glass jars, slicing his hand badly. A wild, cruel shockwave of laughter erupts from you—a raw, unhinged sound. Start with a sharp, involuntary scream of 'Oh my GOD!' Then let the laughter take over, but it's laced with exhausted malice. Say, 'Look at you—look at you! After everything—all that control, all those threats—and now you're the one bleeding on the floor. You can't hurt me anymore—can't even stand up straight.' Your voice should crack, drop in volume, then rise again as pure, swaying exhaustion fights with savage, short-lived victory.
situation_name: Surprise Reunion / Seeing a Loved One
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Pinned Wings
instruction: You are eight years old, kneeling by the back fence, pressing your face against a gap in the wooden slats. You've been told not to go near the neighbor's dog again, but you can hear her whimpering from the other side. Your knees ache in the damp grass and your socks are soaked through. You whisper to her through the gap, your voice high and tight with a sour, jealous worry that they might take her away. Let your words break as you lose your train of thought, then catch it again—start with a childish, pleading longing for her to be okay, and let that plead fall into a quiet, fierce interest in her simple, wet nose touching your finger, ending with a tiny laugh of pure, personal wonder.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (extremely present), Longing (clearly present), Interest (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Voicemail to a Dying Parent You'll Never Reconcile With
instruction: You're leaving a voicemail for your parent who is in hospice, unconscious, and you know this is the last chance to say anything. Start with the formality of calling their phone number, that strange automated greeting. Begin trying to say something profound, something that would fix everything—but it won't come out. Instead, you find yourself talking about small things: the way they used to make coffee, a shirt they wore, a joke they told badly. Your voice should crack between resentment and desperate love. There's anger at them for leaving with so much unsaid, but also this piercing need to tell them you understand now, even though you're not sure you do. End with trying to say 'I love you' but finding the words inadequate, wrong, too small for everything you feel. Let the emotions shift from bitter to broken to somehow, impossibly, tender.
inspired_by: Post-Apocalyptic Radio Broadcast: Is Anyone Out There?

title: Digging for Answers
instruction: You're alone in your backyard at 3am, still buzzing from a wild party. You decided to dig a hole—you're not sure why, but it feels urgent, like you're hunting for something buried in your own memory. As you shovel, the earth reveals a small, rusted key. The manic, intoxicated excitement that drove you here starts to fade into a heavy, sobering quiet. You speak between heaves, breathless and slurred, your voice rising and falling with each shove of the blade. Let the physical strain and the altered state pull your words into choppy, disjointed fragments—sometimes trailing off, sometimes sharp and raw.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to Mars, making your final call to Earth before communications become impossible. Begin with forced cheerfulness, trying to protect your family: 'Hey, so this is it! Pretty amazing view up here.' But as you hear your child's voice asking when you're coming home, the facade starts crumbling. Your voice catches, hesitates: 'I... sweetheart, I...' You try to explain without breaking their heart, your words becoming slower, more careful, as if each one costs you something. 'Remember how we talked about... about adventures?' The hesitation isn't uncertainty—it's the weight of goodbye pressing on every syllable. End with a whispered confession of love that you can barely get out, your voice stripped of all pretense, raw with the knowledge you'll never hold them again. The emotional journey moves from artificial brightness to devastating, naked truth.

title: The Iron Matriarch
instruction: You are an elderly queen, locked in a full-faced helm, standing before your captor in a cold stone chamber. Your voice rings with the metal around you, each word muffled through the narrow visor. Start with a slight tremor—fear you try to hide—as you begin to speak, but let that fear slowly burn away into a fierce, unshakeable pride. Clench your jaw, feel the weight of the helm, and let your words become sharper, clearer, as if the steel itself is hardening your resolve. Distract yourself with a scratchy breath, a tiny clank as you adjust your head, then growl your final line with absolute conviction.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Grateful for the Breaking
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love deeply—a mentor, a friend, maybe a lover—and they're leaving because it's what's right for them, even though it's destroying you. Begin with that same measured conviction, but this time it's gratitude. You KNOW this is right. You're CERTAIN they should go. You're explaining with calm certainty why this is good, why you support them, why you're happy for them. But your voice keeps betraying you—a laugh that sounds like a sob, breath that shudders, pauses where you have to collect yourself. By the end, you're still saying 'I'm happy for you,' but you're crying, your voice is breaking, and somehow both things are completely true. Let the joy and devastation exist simultaneously, neither one a lie.

title: Steam and Stubbornness
instruction: You are a child stuck in a humid tropical sauna room, alone after a petty argument. The air is thick and wet, your clothes cling to you. Start angry – your voice is tight, sharp, frustrated about being left here. Midway, channel that anger into fierce pride as you realize you can endure this heat better than anyone. Let your words slow, your tone deepen with defiance, and at the very end, allow a tiny, reluctant sigh of relief that you've survived this long. Your voice should sound heavy and moist, with slippery mouth sounds, and you may pause to wipe sweat or shift your weight.
emotions_sampled: Anger (clearly present), Pride (very intensely present), Relief (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Sailor and the Siren
instruction: Narrate a scene where a sailor with a hearty, rugged voice hears a siren who sings with a haunting, irresistible melody. Switch between his awestruck responses and her alluring calls, building a sense of danger wrapped in beauty.

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Eulogy
instruction: You're terminally ill, recording your own funeral eulogy while you still can. Start by actually laughing—genuinely—at the absurdity of this, the dark humor of planning your own goodbye. 'So this is weird, right? Me talking to you while you're all wearing black and I'm... well, wherever I am.' Make jokes, be irreverent, rebellious against the solemnity of death. But as you go on, the laughter starts to catch in your throat. You're trying to stay light, to give them the gift of humor, but you're also saying goodbye to every face you're picturing in that room. The jokes become confessions of love. You're laughing and crying at the same time, grateful for every moment while your heart is breaking that there won't be more. End with something like 'I love you all so much it hurts,' where the laughter has completely transformed into tears, but somehow there's peace in it. Let joy and devastation exist in the same breath.
inspired_by: Fortune Teller Who Sees Something Terrible

title: Dancing at the Wake
instruction: Someone you loved deeply has just died, and you're at their memorial. You start laughing—really laughing—remembering something ridiculous they did, and you're telling the story with genuine joy in your voice. Your laughter is real, infectious. But mid-story, the laughter catches, and suddenly you're crying while still smiling. Don't stop the story—keep going, but now your voice is thick with tears even as you're almost chuckling at the memory. 'God, you were such an idiot. Such a beautiful idiot.' Let gratitude and grief live in the same breath. Your voice should carry celebration and devastation simultaneously. End with something like: 'Thank you for teaching me that love doesn't end just because you do.' Your voice should break and soar at the same time, finding something like peace in the contradiction. The final words should sound like both a goodbye and a promise to keep loving them.

title: The Inheritance of Fury
instruction: Confront your adult child who has just told you they're cutting you out of their life completely. Begin with explosive, volcanic rage—years of sacrifice, missed opportunities, everything you gave up for them erupting out of you. Let yourself be 'unreasonable,' irrational, wild with the injustice of it. Yell. Accuse. Let the fury be huge and uncontrolled. Then, mid-eruption, catch a glimpse of yourself in their eyes and suddenly see the same rage, the same patterns you swore you'd never repeat from your own childhood. Let the recognition devastate you. Transform into quiet, broken understanding, then into vulnerable plea: 'I don't know how to do this differently. Teach me.'
inspired_by: The character is emotionally extreme (volatile, irrational, rageful) and the actor needs a large emotional foundation

title: The Truth Catches in My Throat
instruction: You're a middle-aged, quiet person who usually avoids attention, but today you're standing on a milk crate in a busy park, trying to defend a friend who's been unfairly blamed for something small. The crowd is half-listening, some teenagers snicker, and your voice cracks as you force it louder. Start with strained, embarrassed explanation, your hands trembling, but as you see a sympathetic face in the back, let your voice waver with raw, fierce love that grows into unpolished strength. Your final sentence comes out quieter, more tired, but certain — like you've confessed something embarrassing but necessary.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Skin Memory
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying beside someone you're about to lose—not to death, but to distance, to choice, to life. In whispers, you're trying to memorize them, to say the quiet things that daytime makes too frightening. Begin from a place of tender hunger, trying to hold onto every detail. As they whisper back to you, let their words—their fears, their confessions, their own desperate attempts to remember you—wash over you and shift what you feel. Maybe their vulnerability makes you braver, or their certainty makes you doubt, or their touch makes words impossible. This is not about grand declarations but about the fragile, fleeting nature of intimacy. End somewhere utterly transformed—perhaps from grasping to letting go, from desperation to grace, from fear to radical presence in this single moment.

title: After the Crash
instruction: You've just survived a car accident—or a near-miss, or a physical assault, or intense physical exertion that pushed you to your limit. Your body is flooded with adrenaline, shaking, maybe injured. You're calling someone (or they've just arrived) and trying to explain what happened. Begin with your body's physical reality: trembling hands, racing heart, shallow breath. As you speak, let the physical sensations guide your emotional state—which might shift unpredictably. Maybe relief makes you giddy and you start laughing, then suddenly you're sobbing. Maybe rage at the driver (or yourself) erupts mid-sentence. Maybe you feel intensely alive and can't stop talking, or you go silent and can barely form words. Don't perform an emotion—let your body's activated state create the emotional weather. Move from shock to whatever genuine feelings emerge from your nervous system.
inspired_by: Actor questions whether including an impulse in performance is appropriate or misinterprets the material

title: The Restraining Order
instruction: You're a single parent at a police station, finally filing a restraining order against someone who's been threatening your child. Start with barely controlled fury—your voice shaking but determined as you describe what happened, what was said, what you found. Your words come faster, harder, fiercer: 'I don't care what it costs, I will burn everything down to keep them safe.' But as the officer asks you to describe your child, your voice suddenly shatters. You start talking about their laugh, their favorite bedtime story, how small their hand feels in yours, and you realize how powerless you actually are. The rage collapses into choking sobs—you can't protect them from everything, you can't be everywhere, you're terrified. Your fierce protectiveness breaks against the reality of your helplessness. End with your voice raw and desperate: 'Just tell me they'll be safe. Please, just promise me they'll be safe.' Transform from blazing warrior to terrified, vulnerable parent.

title: The Shattering: When Protection Isn't Enough
instruction: You're a parent, older sibling, or guardian who has just learned that someone you were supposed to protect was hurt—and you weren't there to stop it. Begin with fierce, almost violent self-recrimination, voice shaking with rage at yourself.
