Demand to know why you didn't see the signs, why you failed them, let your voice rise to near-shouting in furious self-blame. Then fracture completely—let that rage collapse into broken sobbing, the fierce protector dissolving into helpless desperation. Plead with them for forgiveness, voice raw and small, all power gone. End in exhausted tenderness, promising with every fiber of your being that you will never, never let this happen again—but underneath that vow, let us hear your terror that you might not be able to keep it. Shift from explosive fury to devastated vulnerability to fierce-but-fragile determination.

title: The Night I Learned to Hate
instruction: You are an older man sitting around a campfire with a few younger listeners. The fire crackles, someone shifts, a log pops. You begin telling a story about a childhood incident where you were forced to do something that filled you with shame. Your voice starts low, hesitant — you avoid eye contact, clear your throat. As the story progresses, the shame gives way to a rising disgust, not at yourself but at the person who made you do it. Let your voice grow louder, more rhythmic, almost hypnotic, as you describe the moment of realization. End with a bitter, intense disgust that silences the fire. Speak approximately 50-70 words, including natural pauses and reactions to the fire and listeners.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Condition Refusing
instruction: They want you to unfriend everyone from your past as a condition of staying together. Your voice is quiet but final: 'No.' It costs you something. 'I won't do that.' The line in the sand is drawn. You know this might end the relationship. 'I can't erase my life for you.' Your voice is stronger for saying it. Standing alone feels less lonely than being controlled. The cost of integrity sounds like goodbye.

title: The Last Match
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a freezing cabin, your fingers numb as you try to strike a match to light a candle. The cold seeps through your bones, your jaw clenches, and your words come out in shivery bursts between chattering teeth. Begin with irritation—muttering about the weather and your own failing hands—then, as the match finally catches, let your voice soften into a fragile relief, a tiny victory over the cold. Speak to no one but yourself, your breath visible, your focus absolute.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Confession in the Hospital Chapel
instruction: You're alone in a quiet chapel at 3 AM, whispering to someone who's unconscious upstairs—or to God, or to yourself. Your voice is barely audible, catching on every other word. Begin with the small truths: 'I never told you I read your journal.' The confessions grow more tender and devastating: 'I knew you were afraid. I pretended not to see it because I was afraid too.' Your breath becomes part of the performance—the way it hitches, the way you have to pause to swallow. Let silence hold weight. Your voice trembles as you admit: 'I wasted so much time being proud.' This isn't theatrical crying—this is the kind of emotion that makes your throat close, that you're trying desperately to hold back. End with the most vulnerable truth, so quiet it's almost mouthed: 'I don't know how to be in a world without you in it.' The emotion deepens from nervous confession to profound tenderness to suffocating grief.

title: The Rehearsed Confrontation That Crumbles
instruction: You're finally confronting your parent about the emotional abandonment of your childhood—you've practiced this speech for years. Begin with controlled anger, your voice steady and strong as you lay out your grievances with precision. But as you speak, your parent's face crumbles in a way you've never seen, and your rehearsed words start to falter. The anger begins mixing with an unwanted compassion. You hear yourself saying things you didn't plan: 'I needed you' becomes 'I still need you.' Your voice shifts from accusatory to pleading, then breaks entirely when they reach for your hand. You're furious at yourself for crying, for softening, but you can't stop. End in a whisper, all your rage dissolved into raw vulnerability: 'Why couldn't you just see me?' The question hangs between you—no longer an attack, but a heartbroken plea from the child you still are inside.
inspired_by: Reading a Bedtime Story Before Goodbye

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You're standing in the rain, drenched, having just run after someone who's leaving you. Your body is shaking—from cold, from rage, from desperate desire, from the physical exhaustion of sprinting. As you face them, begin by focusing on specific physical details: the exact shape of their mouth, the way water runs down their face, their particular scent mixing with the rain. Now sensorially layer onto them someone who once made you feel both furious and intensely alive—an ex-lover who wrecked you, a rival who pushed you to your limits. Let their features begin to merge: change the color of their eyes in your mind, adjust the set of their jaw, reshape their voice until you're seeing a hybrid that ignites something primal in you. Begin with words that are vicious, your body rigid with anger, but as you continue to reconstruct what you're seeing—noticing perhaps their vulnerability, the way they're also shaking—let your rage transform into desperate, almost feral need. End on your knees, no longer sure if you're pushing them away or pulling them closer.
inspired_by: The actor needs the scene partner to feel like a specific person from the actor's own life who produces the required emotional relationship

title: Reading Your Twin's Diary After the Funeral
instruction: You've found your twin sibling's private journal, and you're reading it aloud in the empty house you once shared. Start with curiosity, maybe even a slight smile at familiar handwriting, inside jokes only you two understood. Your voice is warm, intimate, as if they're still in the next room. Then you reach an entry about you—how they felt invisible beside you, how they struggled with jealousy and love in equal measure, how lonely they were even when you were together. Your voice drops to barely a whisper. Each word lands like a small wound. You have to stop, breathe, continue. You're discovering you never really knew them. The grief shifts from loss to guilt, from missing them to mourning the relationship you thought you had but never did. Your voice becomes so quiet it almost disappears, catching on words like 'shadow' and 'wished.' This isn't dramatic crying—it's the sound of your heart quietly breaking open.
inspired_by: Medieval Executioner Meets the Condemned Man Who Was His Childhood Friend

title: Siren and Salvation
instruction: You're walking down a crowded city street, still raw from a breakup that morning. Your eyes sting, your throat aches, and the noise—honking, a distant siren, construction drilling—feels like it's inside your head. Then you spot your dog, tied to a lamppost outside the coffee shop where you always meet. She wags her whole body when she sees you. Cross the street toward her, dodging a cyclist, speaking to her as you approach. Start with a broken, quiet confession of your pain, but let your voice rise with love and gratitude as you get closer, the noise of the city fading into a backdrop for your relief. Your tone should shift from choked and fragile to full, warm, and slightly giddy, with natural pauses for traffic and a laugh when she licks your hand.
emotions_sampled: Pain (extremely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Infatuation (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Release: Scattering Ashes in the Storm
instruction: You're on a cliff scattering your beloved's ashes in a violent storm, and as the wind takes them, you start laughing—actual, genuine laughter at the absurdity that they wanted this chaos, this wild goodbye. Your laughter is real but there are tears streaming down your face. You're shouting into the wind, half-laughing, half-crying, telling them they're an idiot for choosing a storm, that this is so perfectly them. Then your laughter shifts into something deeper—you're thanking them through sobs, your voice breaking with gratitude for the beautiful wreckage of loving them. The emotions keep shifting: joy at the memories, grief at the loss, wonder at how completely they changed you. End with a moment of pure stillness despite the storm—your voice quiet, steady, filled with bittersweet peace as you whisper 'Goodbye, my love,' the words carrying both heartbreak and the strangest, most painful kind of joy.

title: Confessing in the Dark
instruction: It's late at night. You're lying next to someone you love, and you need to tell them something you've kept hidden - not infidelity, but something about yourself, something tender and terrifying. Start with your breath, quiet in the darkness. Your voice comes out smaller than you intended: 'Are you awake?' Begin the confession in fragments, half-sentences that catch in your throat. The vulnerability makes you want to laugh nervously, cry, disappear. You feel them shift, listening. The words come easier but quieter, more intimate, like you're revealing the softest part of yourself. There's relief in the telling, but also the devastating tenderness of being known. End in near-whisper, asking for nothing, just offering this truth. The last words barely make sound: 'I just needed you to know who I really am.'
inspired_by: Improvised Bedtime Story That Accidentally Gets Too Dark

title: Confrontation: An Adult Child Tells Their Parent They're Walking Away
instruction: You're standing in your childhood home, finally ready to say what you've rehearsed a thousand times. Start with your voice tight, controlled, angry—listing the ways you were failed, the moments that broke you, the love you deserved but never received. Your words are sharp, precise, surgical. Then feel it shift: your voice cracks, the anger dissolves into raw grief, and you're suddenly that child again, begging to understand why you weren't enough. But pull yourself back—find your adult voice again, this time quieter, sadder, but resolute. End with the devastating clarity that you're choosing yourself, even though it means losing them. Your final words should carry both heartbreak and liberation.
inspired_by: Historical: Holocaust Survivor Confronts the Guard

title: The Howl of Protection When You're Powerless
instruction: Someone you love is being taken from you—led away by police, security, immigration officers—and you're being held back. Start with pure rage: you're screaming their name, your voice ragged and primal, hurling threats and curses at the people separating you. Your vocal cords are straining, almost giving out. You're bargaining, voice rising to a shriek: 'Take me instead!' But they're getting further away, and your voice begins to break apart—rage fracturing into desperation, then into animal grief. You collapse into sobbing that makes words almost impossible, choking out their name between gasps. The fury is still there, vibrating under the tears, making your voice shake with impotent violence. End with your voice shattered, raw, repeating their name in a broken whisper that's part prayer, part howl, all helplessness. Your final sound is wordless—a sound no human should have to make.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Flight That Won't Land
instruction: You're calling someone you love before boarding a one-way mission—a military deployment to a war zone, a experimental space voyage, a medical trial with no return. You start trying to sound brave, cheerful, keeping your voice light because you don't want them to worry. But as you speak, the performance cracks. Your throat tightens. You realize you're running out of time to say what matters, and suddenly all the brave words feel like lies. Your voice drops, becomes raw, stripped of pretense. End with the truest thing you've never been able to say, your voice barely holding together, breathing uneven, knowing these might be your last words to them.
inspired_by: Realizing You Become Someone Different Around Specific People

title: The Helmet Confession
instruction: You're an 80-year-old woman, sitting on a parked motorcycle after a long ride with your granddaughter, whom you promised you'd take to see her favorite singer perform tonight. You've just discovered the concert was cancelled due to the singer's illness. You're still wearing your full-face helmet—your voice booms and echoes inside as you speak. You start with a heavy, hollow disappointment—every word feels distorted and trapped. Halfway through, you take off the helmet, letting the air hit your face, and your voice becomes small, raw, and vulnerable as you crumble into a quiet, tearful sense of resignation. Your hands tremble as you grip the handlebars, and you pause to swallow, hearing the echo fade.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Presentation That Cracks
instruction: You are the leader of a community project, presenting a final report to a small, supportive group of colleagues. You begin with genuine, quiet triumph — you've just finished a year of work, and the numbers are good. You smile, glance at your notes, feel a swell of pride. But as you start to thank them, your voice snags on the phrase 'I couldn't have done this without you.' A tremor catches in your throat. You try to cover it with a quick, nervous laugh, but your pitch drops, and your volume fades. You're holding back tears as you admit, almost in a whisper, 'Truth is, the last few months have been really hard.' There's a long, shaky pause where you look down at the table. Allow the triumph to quietly coexist with the vulnerability — the pride stays, even as your voice cracks.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Final Killcam
instruction: You're a teenager deep in an online shooter, your team just lost because a teammate's blunder. You start half-laughing, half-grumbling into your headset, amusement mixing with bitterness as you rehash the moment. Your voice is loud, punctuated by mouse clicks and a squeaky chair shift. As you narrate the play, a quiet realization dawns—maybe you could have done something different. End in a softer, contemplative tone, the amusement fading into thought. Speak naturally, let the environment shape your rhythm.
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (slightly present), Amusement (clearly present), Contemplation (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Questions We've Never Asked
instruction: You're confronting your parent (or adult child) after years of surface-level conversations and unspoken resentments. Begin with controlled anger, the accusations you've rehearsed. But mid-confrontation, let your rage crack open into something else—genuine bewilderment. Start asking them real questions you've never dared ask: Why did you...? What were you afraid of? Did you ever...? Let your need to understand eclipse your need to accuse. As they answer (real or imagined), feel your certainty about who they are begin to shift. End not with resolution, but with the destabilizing vulnerability of truly seeing them as a complete, flawed human being for the first time. Your voice must travel from sharp accusation to raw, undefended questioning.

title: The Empty Nursery
instruction: You're standing in the nursery you prepared—painted, furnished, filled with hope. But everything has changed. The reason why is yours to know. Maybe you lost the baby. Maybe adoption fell through. Maybe the person you were going to raise this child with is gone. Maybe you've just learned you're finally pregnant after years of grief. Maybe your grown child just left for college and you're feeling their absence in the room where their life began. Look at each carefully chosen object: the crib that cost so much, the mobile that plays a lullaby, the stuffed animal you loved as a child, the changing table, the rocking chair, the wall color you debated for weeks, the empty drawers full of tiny clothes, the baby monitor, the framed ultrasound or the blank wall where it would have gone, the nightlight casting soft shadows. Speak your honest feelings about each object—but here's the complexity: you're feeling violently contradictory things simultaneously. Let your voice hold both devastating loss and stubborn joy, both rage at the universe and overwhelming gratitude, both the death of one dream and the fierce pulse of hope or memory or love that refuses to die. Don't resolve these contradictions—live inside them, letting your emotional response to each object reveal the beautiful, terrible complexity of loving something this much.

title: Accent Adoption
instruction: You're an immigrant's child, code-switching on the phone with your mother in the home country, then immediately shifting to your American accent when your coworkers walk by. Begin in the authentic accent of your parent — warm, familiar, slightly different rhythm. Mid-sentence, someone says 'Hey!' nearby. You pivot to flawless American. The warmth vanishes. Then back to your mother: 'Sorry, work.' Your voice is fragmented, belonging nowhere. The shame of the switch should be audible. End by putting the phone down and hearing the silence of inauthenticity.

title: The Thing We Never Name
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father about something they did years ago that shaped who you became—an abandonment, a betrayal, a moment of cruelty they've never acknowledged. Start from a place of controlled anger, measured words, trying to make them understand rationally. But as they deflect or minimize or defend themselves, feel that control beginning to fracture. Let your voice rise and break, let the child you were come flooding through the adult you are now. Surprise yourself with how much pain is still living in your body. By the end, you've stopped trying to make them understand—you're simply pouring out years of held-back anguish, and it's terrifying and liberating at once.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: Your adult child sits beside your hospital bed, asking permission to let you go, to stop fighting. You begin with fierce determination to stay, to not leave them—your voice trembling with the effort to hold on, punctuated by labored breaths. But as you look at their exhausted, loving face, something shifts. Your resistance melts into acceptance, your words becoming softer, more peaceful. End by giving them the permission they need, your voice growing quieter but somehow stronger, filled with a love that transcends your fear of leaving. Let us hear the journey from desperate clinging to tender release.

title: Last Phone Call to Your Child Before the Mission
instruction: You're an astronaut about to embark on a one-way mission to deep space. This is your final call home to your teenage child who begged you not to go. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to make this easy for them, your voice bright and artificially upbeat. But as they stay silent on the other end, your facade cracks. The cheerfulness dissolves into raw pleading—you need them to understand why you have to do this, why this matters, even as your voice breaks with the realization that you're abandoning them. End in whispered devastation as you hear them crying, your words becoming softer and softer, trying to memorize the sound of their breathing. The final 'I love you' should feel like you're trying to pour a lifetime of love into three words.
inspired_by: Trapped in a Car After Earthquake: Checking if Your Passenger is Dead

title: The Last Promise to Your Dying Parent
instruction: Your parent is in their final hours, and they ask you to promise something you know you cannot deliver—to keep the family together, to save the family business, to never let go of a dream that isn't yours. Begin with desperate reassurance, your voice falsely bright, trying to give them peace. But as their hand weakens in yours, something breaks. The false promise crumbles into a whispered confession: 'I can't... I'm so sorry, I can't.' Let shame dissolve into raw grief. Your breathing becomes ragged. End in a place of tender devastation—telling them the truth because you love them too much to lie, even as it breaks both your hearts. This is about the collision between devotion and honesty, between wanting to be enough and accepting your limitations in the most sacred moment imaginable.
inspired_by: Confessing You Can't Do the Thing You Promised

title: The Imaginary Protector Couldn't Save Me
instruction: You are simultaneously voicing yourself as a child speaking to your imaginary dragon guardian, and yourself now, years later, realizing that guardian was powerless. Start with the child's voice—urgent, terrified, begging the dragon to protect them from something terrible happening in the house. Voice the dragon's fierce promises, its rage at not being real enough to help. Then explode into your adult self's anguished scream at the emptiness of it all—you were so alone that you created a protector who couldn't protect, who was just air and desperate imagination. Let rage dissolve into helpless sobbing, then rebuild into fierce self-compassion: that child's imagination was a form of survival, and that matters. End with a mixture of grief for that child and pride in who they became despite everything.
inspired_by: The Mother and the Imaginary Dragon

title: The Breaking Point in the Rain
instruction: You are standing in a downpour, physically exhausted, having just run for miles. Your body is shaking. Begin by speaking aloud to someone (real or imagined) as if they were a person who once ignited pure joy in you—someone whose presence made you feel electrically alive, awakened, full of physical vitality. Let your breathlessness and shaking become sounds of exhilaration, almost ecstatic release. Your voice should ride the edge of laughter and sobbing. Midway through, shift viscerally: now channel the voice you'd use speaking to someone who physically hurt you, someone whose touch left bruises. Let your shaking become something darker—rage mixed with exhaustion, fury mixed with collapse. By the end, your body's physical state should blur the line between pleasure and pain, strength and surrender, until you can't tell if you're crying from release or devastation.
inspired_by: The scene requires a deeply charged relational reality between two characters, but the actual actors don't yet have that dynamic between them

title: The Socially Awkward Party Guest
instruction: Portray a person who always says the wrong thing at social gatherings. Use comedic timing to deliver cringeworthy comments, switching between nervous rambling and awkward silences, highlighting the characters lack of social cues.

title: The Last Phone Call Before the Mission
instruction: You're calling someone you love before leaving on a mission you know you won't return from—military deployment, a dangerous expedition, a terminal diagnosis requiring you to disappear. Start with forced brightness, trying to keep your voice light and casual, talking about mundane things like you'll see them next week. Gradually, the mask begins slipping—your voice thickens, pauses grow longer, you start saying things that sound like goodbyes disguised as regular conversation. Let a moment of raw truth break through where you almost tell them, your voice cracking on 'I need you to know...' before you pull back. End with the quietest, most tender 'I love you' you've ever spoken, lingering on the line in silence before whispering 'Take care of yourself' and forcing yourself to hang up, your voice dissolving into a breath that might be a sob.

title: Breaking Point in the Rain
instruction: You're standing in the rain, physically exhausted and emotionally shattered, speaking to someone (on the phone or in person) who has just delivered news that changes everything. Your body is cold, wet, shaking—notice every physical sensation. Start by responding to them with shock, trying to process information, asking practical questions. But after each response, speak aloud the visceral, physical emotional torrent inside you—the way your chest is caving in, the rage building in your hands, the grief catching in your throat, the animal need to scream or collapse. Let the physical sensations drive your inner voice. As you alternate, let the raw physical-emotional truth begin to overtake your measured responses. Your body is betraying your composure. End with your physical and emotional state completely merged—perhaps collapsing, perhaps exploding, perhaps going frighteningly quiet as something breaks open inside you.

title: Whispering to Your Sleeping Child That You're Leaving
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your child is asleep. You're leaving—maybe for their safety, maybe because you can't stay, maybe because staying would destroy you both. You sit beside their bed and speak in the quietest voice, barely above breath. You're telling them things they can't hear: why you have to go, how much you love them, how this is killing you. Your voice catches on memories—teaching them to ride a bike, their first day of school, the way they laugh. The pain sits in your throat like a stone. You're not crying loudly; tears fall silently as you stroke their hair. By the end, you're asking for forgiveness they can't give, finding strength you don't have, saying 'I love you' like it's both a promise and an apology. You kiss their forehead and your voice breaks completely: 'Be good, baby.' Then silence.
inspired_by: Catching Your Partner in a Lie and Calling Them Out

title: Lap Four
instruction: You're a young man in your mid-20s, swimming laps in a nearly empty pool. On lap four, the lifeguard — someone you've been secretly attracted to for weeks — gets up and walks to the edge of the pool right as you pass. You have to speak, but you can only grab air for a split second during each head turn. Start with just a friendly 'hey' — affection, a bit shy. But as you keep swimming, your body’s exertion and the sight of them leaning down makes the lust surge. Each breath you grab, the words get more raw, desperate, almost a growl. By the last few strokes, you're not just saying words — you're exhaling pure, wanting heat. The water in your mouth, the splashing, the gasps — all of that texture is real.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Visit Before Hospice
instruction: You're visiting your childhood mentor who raised you after your parents died, and they've just decided to stop treatment. You enter their room trying to be bright and strong: 'I brought your favorite tea.' Your voice is falsely cheerful, protective. But they take your hand and say, 'I need you to let me go.' Everything you've been holding back crashes through. Your voice breaks as you move from denial to raw grief to finally, through tears, a whispered understanding: 'I don't know how to be in this world without you... but I'll learn. I promise I'll learn.' Show the journey from protective pretense to devastating acceptance, ending in a grief so deep it becomes almost a lullaby of goodbye.

title: The Stage's Echo
instruction: You are a young woman with a high, deliberately sweet voice, standing alone on a darkened theater stage after a disastrous audition. The stage lights are off except for a single work light. You’re speaking to an empty auditorium, but you imagine the casting director is still there, maybe in the last row. You start with a shaky, optimistic declaration that you can do better next time, your voice buoyant but hollow, projecting into the vast space. As you hear your own words echo back, a wave of shame hits you—you recall a moment when you tried too hard to please, and you pause, your pitch dropping, voice quivering. Then a quiet contentment seeps in as you realize you’re finally being honest with yourself, and you end with a softer, more grounded admission that maybe you don’t have to be perfect. Let your voice catch, trail off, and then recover, as if you’re surprising yourself.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (very intensely present), Shame (very intensely present), Contentment (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Cubicle Vigil
instruction: You are a teenager, urgently trying to finish a coded message to your absent friend on your phone under your desk, while pretending to read a textbook in an open-plan office where you’re not supposed to be. The office is large, with a low ceiling, white noise from vents, and the murmur of other workers. You start in a state of fidgety, aggressive impatience—rolling your eyes, sighing under your breath, hunching your shoulders as if bracing for interruption. But as you type, you hear heavy footsteps coming down the aisle between cubicles. Your phone screen glows too brightly. Your voice drops to a near-whisper, tight and quick, as you mutter to yourself, shifting from a growl of irritation to a brittle, panicked plea for the message to send before you’re caught. End with a single, choked gasp as the footsteps stop right behind your cubicle.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Fear (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Nod at the Reunion
instruction: You are an older man at a family reunion, heavily sedated by pain medication. You sit in a corner armchair, fighting to keep your eyes open. Across the room, your ex-wife is laughing with her new husband. You try to concentrate on breathing and staying upright, but your mind drifts to the bitterness you feel. Speak these words slowly, with long pauses, your voice dropping to a near-whisper. Begin with the effort of concentration, then let the sour jealousy seep in until your voice is heavy with resentment, trailing off as consciousness fades.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (extremely present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present), Sourness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Unexpected Command
instruction: You are on your knees, head bowed, waiting for instruction. Your partner's voice comes low and steady, telling you to do something absurdly playful, like 'Count the dust motes in the sunbeam.' Astonishment floods you—your eyes snap up, mouth drops open. Then you catch the tiny quirk at the corner of their mouth, and a wave of amusement crashes in. Start high and breathy with shock ('Sir, I... I don't...'), then let your voice soften into a giggle-laced submission as you lower your gaze, fidgeting with your fingers. Let the laugh escape before you whisper your reply, voice trembling between awe and mirth.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Three AM Inventory
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying in bed next to your partner of ten years, both of you awake but pretending to sleep. You haven't touched each other with real tenderness in months. In barely audible whispers, begin to speak into the darkness about the small moment today when you saw them laugh with a stranger and remembered why you first loved them. Let your voice be fragile, uncertain whether you should be saying this aloud. Confess the fear that's been living in your throat—that you've forgotten how to reach for them, that the dailiness of life has made you strangers. As you speak, let the vulnerability of naming this open something in your chest. Allow the whispered words to become a bridge, your voice potentially trembling with both grief for what's been lost and a tentative, terrifying hope that naming the distance might begin to close it.

title: A Little Help?
instruction: You are an older woman with a gentle, feminine voice, trying to lift a heavy, awkward box from the ground at a garage sale. You feel people watching and are embarrassed that you can't manage it gracefully. Start by cheerfully muttering to yourself about being stronger than you look, but as you strain, your voice tightens—words come out in forced bursts between held breaths. Let the embarrassment surface in a self-conscious laugh or a quick apology. Finally, after an explosive exhale as you set the box down, you admit defeat with weary, tired honesty, maybe asking quietly for help. Let your voice crack, pause, and shift with the physical effort.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're an adult finally confronting your parent about a childhood of emotional neglect. Begin controlled, almost rehearsed—you've practiced this speech. Your voice is measured, listing facts like evidence in court. But as you speak, rage begins bleeding through. You hear yourself getting louder, angrier, more desperate for them to finally understand. They deflect, rationalize, and something in you breaks—your control shatters into raw pain. You're not the composed adult anymore; you're the child who needed them, begging to be seen. Your voice cracks between fury and devastation. They say something—maybe it's defensive, maybe it's the first real acknowledgment you've ever gotten. You move from accusation to a grief so deep it steals your breath. End in a place of exhausted vulnerability, where you're no longer fighting, just bleeding out the truth: 'I just needed you to care.' Let your voice travel from ice-cold anger to white-hot rage to broken-hearted surrender.

title: Coming Home to Yourself
instruction: After a long journey of healing, loss, and growth, you're finally coming home to yourself. Your voice is calm, complete: 'I'm home.' You're not looking for someone else to complete you. Your voice is peaceful, centered: 'I know who I am now.' You're talking to yourself with kindness, the way you'd talk to someone you love. Your voice carries acceptance and wholeness: 'This is who I am, and that's enough. More than enough. It's perfect.'

title: Someone Saying They Don't Trust You Anymore
instruction: Your voice becomes very still: 'What do you mean?' They explain how you hurt them and your voice tries defending: 'That's not fair.' But it is fair. Your voice becomes quieter, ashamed. 'I understand why you feel that way,' delivered with weight of having damaged something precious. Your breathing is controlled but devastation is underneath. Voice ends accepting you've lost something.

title: Whispering the Secret You've Carried for Twenty Years
instruction: Late at night, finally telling someone the truth you've never spoken aloud. Your voice is barely audible at first, testing the words: 'There's something I've never told anyone.' The secret sits in your throat like a stone. When you begin to confess—perhaps a choice you made, a moment that changed everything, something you witnessed or did—your voice catches, breaks into silence, starts again. This isn't dramatic confession; it's intimate, fractured, the way truth actually sounds when it's been buried. Include long pauses where you can't speak at all. Let your voice soften to almost nothing as you describe the weight of carrying this alone. End with the terrifying vulnerability of being fully seen: 'Now you know. Now someone finally knows.' Relief and fear mixing in equal measure.
inspired_by: Admitting You've Been Using Substances to Cope

title: Confronting the Parent Who Wasn't There
instruction: You're finally speaking the truth you've held back for decades, sitting across from your aging parent. Start with false politeness that barely contains your anger: 'You want to know why I don't visit more?' Let the facade crack quickly as years of abandonment, broken promises, and emotional neglect pour out. Your voice should rise with righteous fury as you list specific moments they weren't there—birthdays, graduations, hospitals, heartbreaks. But mid-torrent, something shifts: you see them as fragile, human, flawed. Your rage doesn't disappear, but it mingles with unexpected grief for what both of you lost. End with brutal honesty that's somehow both devastating and tender: 'I needed you. I still need you. But I don't know if I can trust you anymore.' Let your voice break on the word 'need.'

title: The Hero and the Dark Inner Voice
instruction: Portray a hero with a strong, confident voice battling their own inner doubts, represented by a whispering, sinister tone. Switch between the heros external dialogue and the internal monologue, showcasing the struggle between courage and fear.

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You are confronting your parent about the emotional absence that shaped your entire life. Start calm, almost clinical—you've practiced this conversation a thousand times, determined to stay controlled. But as you describe specific memories (waiting for them to show up, learning to stop hoping, becoming small to avoid disappointing them), feel your composure fracture. Let years of suppressed hurt pour out—not as screaming, but as the kind of pain that makes your voice shake and break. Then, in the silence after your outburst, find yourself admitting the terrible truth: despite everything, you still desperately want them to see you. End somewhere between fury and heartbroken pleading.
inspired_by: The Detective and the Evasive Witness

title: Screaming at God in an Empty Church
instruction: You've just lost everything—your partner, your child, your faith, something that's shattered you completely. You're alone in a church at midnight, and the rage finally erupts. Start with a roar that echoes off the walls: 'Where the hell were you?! You were supposed to be here!' Your voice is raw, savage: 'I prayed. I begged. I did everything right, and you took them anyway!' Pound something—a pew, the floor. Let the fury give way to broken sobbing: 'I can't do this. I can't breathe without them.' Your voice becomes almost childlike, lost: 'Please. Please give them back. I'll do anything.' Silence. No answer comes. Something in you collapses into a different space—not acceptance, but exhaustion. Your voice is scraped hollow: 'I hate you. I hate you and I need you and I don't know how to survive this.' End on your knees, voice barely a whisper, finding some terrible kind of surrender: 'Help me. I'm so lost. Just... help me make it to tomorrow.'

title: The Stubbed Toe Before You
instruction: You're standing in your dark kitchen, barefoot, thinking about the person you're about to meet—someone who makes you feel alive, even though you've been going through the motions for months. There's a sour knot in your stomach from an old argument you're still chewing on, but your body hums with lust, anticipating their touch. As you shift your weight, you smash your little toe into the leg of a heavy wooden chair. The sudden spike of white-hot pain rips a short, involuntary yell out of you. Then, as you hobble and hiss through your teeth, you try to steady your breath and say something to the empty room—a bitter complaint that twists into a raw, longing confession about how much you actually need that night. Let your voice start with the yelp, then settle into a guarded, strained tone as the pain and the lust and the sourness tangle together.
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (slightly present), Sourness (clearly present), Sexual Lust (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Photograph on the Bedside Table
instruction: You are an elderly man alone in a nursing home room, clutching a framed photograph of your late wife. You start speaking while already deep in a sob—your breath is jerky, your throat wet, your voice cracking. Bitterness floods you as you recall her final words to you, an argument you never settled. But as you talk, the bitterness begins to drain out, leaving only a hollow, quiet exhaustion. Let your voice waver, let your words be broken by involuntary gasps, and let the anger soften into nothing but a whisper of loss.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Authenticity Presence
instruction: You're a life coach who usually does corporate seminars, and you've decided to be completely authentic instead of performing your 'coach' voice. 'I used to be where you are. Broken. Scared. Completely alone.' Your voice is raw, real, unpolished. No performance, no technique, just the truth. 'I don't have all the answers. Some days, I still feel like a failure.' The authenticity is uncomfortable — it's not what the audience paid for, but it's what they need. Midway through, you almost slip back into your 'coach' persona, but you catch yourself: 'Sorry, I was about to do my thing again. Let me try that more honestly.' By the end, you've barely moved anyone's life, but you've moved them because you were real. The authenticity is more powerful than all the techniques combined.

title: Xanax Dissolving Your Ability to Sound Serious
instruction: You took a 0.5mg Xanax 45 minutes ago. You're in a job interview. You need to sound sharp and ambitious. But your voice is coming out soft, almost monotone, slightly slurred. Your anxiety is gone—maybe too gone. You sound sedated. You're trying to compensate by speaking louder but it just sounds drunk. You catch yourself mid-pitch getting slower. You pause too long before answers. Your voice has lost its drive.

title: The Ceiling Won't Stop Moving
instruction: You're in a hospital bed, slowly coming back after a concussion from a fall off a ladder. The nurse has just told you your son needs to sign more forms, but your wife is out of town. You're trying to remember a simple phone number, but every time you reach for it, the numbers scatter like startled birds. Start with a sharp, gravelly sourness—resentment that you're even in this bed. Let the pain pulse behind your right eye as you speak. Midway, overcorrect your volume into a loud, slow monotone while you concentrate furiously. End with a quiet, bewildered defeat as the number slips away again, the sourness hardening into a bitter acceptance.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (very intensely present), Pain (clearly present), Concentration (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: I Know What You Did
instruction: You've just discovered proof of a betrayal—your best friend, your sibling, your partner. You're confronting them, describing exactly what you found, what you saw in their eyes when they lied to you. Start with an almost eerie calm, your voice controlled but trembling with suppressed rage. As you detail what their face looked like when they deceived you, your fury builds—volcanic, righteous. But then something breaks: beneath the anger is agony, the kind that makes you want to scream and collapse simultaneously. Your voice explodes, then fractures into something raw and wounded. End with a moment of devastating helplessness, as you realize you can't unknow what you know, and everything has already changed forever.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're standing at your elderly parent's bedside—not for reconciliation, but to finally speak a truth you've carried for thirty years. Start calm, almost rehearsed, the words you've practiced. But as you name specific moments they failed you—the recital they missed, the night you needed them and they weren't there, the sibling they loved more openly—your composure shatters. Let anger surface, not performative rage but the raw, wounded fury of a child still living inside you. Then watch that anger collapse into something more devastating: grief for the relationship you'll never have. End not with forgiveness, but with exhausted honesty, telling them quietly that you needed them to fight for you, and they never did. Let your voice break on 'never.'
inspired_by: Town Crier at the End of the World

title: Gratitude at the Edge of Loss
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your childhood home as it's being sold, walking through empty rooms for the last time. Begin with a laugh—almost incredulous—at a memory the walls hold: 'God, remember when we thought this was the whole world?' Your voice is warm with nostalgia, genuinely joyful at the life lived here. But grief is threaded through every word. You're thanking the house, actually speaking to it, for sheltering you, for holding your family's chaos and love. 'You kept us safe when we didn't even know we needed keeping.' Your voice wavers between smiling and crying, between celebrating everything this place gave you and mourning that this chapter is ending. You find yourself laughing through tears at absurd memories—the broken stair, the stain on the ceiling—while your heart breaks at the finality. 'Thank you' becomes both a celebration and a lament. You're making peace with impermanence, finding beauty in the fact that nothing lasts, but your voice carries the ache of it. End with a whispered goodbye that's somehow both devastating and full of grace, as if you're releasing something precious into the universe with open hands.
inspired_by: Working Near an Industrial Furnace: Heat Warping Perception

title: The Astronaut's Final Transmission
instruction: You are alone in a failing spacecraft, drifting beyond救 rescue range. You have one final transmission to send to someone you love back on Earth. Begin speaking as if you're trying to sound brave, reassuring them that everything will be okay—but as you continue, let yourself drift into vivid memories of specific moments you shared: the smell of their kitchen, the exact way sunlight hit their face one particular morning, a silly game you used to play together. Let these sensory memories become so real that you're actually there again, momentarily forgetting your dire situation. Then reality crashes back. Your voice should journey from false courage, through transported wonder and childlike joy in the memories, finally landing in a place of profound peace and genuine gratitude for having lived those moments at all.

title: Batten Down the Hatches
instruction: You are an elderly man on a dock, trying to secure a tarp over your old rowboat while a fierce gale whips rain into your face. Your grandson is beside you, fumbling with a rope, and you start to tease him gently. The wind snatches your words, forcing you to shout, turn your head, and spit out a mouthful of spray. Begin with a gruff, irritated huff at the storm and his clumsiness—then your tone softens, and a teasing warmth comes through as you recall teaching his father the same trick. Let your voice strain, pause to gasp in the lulls, and let the wind push you off balance, so your words come in fragments, carried away.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Desert's Final Grace
instruction: You are an elderly man, found after days lost in the desert, severely dehydrated. A young rescuer kneels beside you, offering water. At first, your voice is barely a whisper—cracked, parched, every word a struggle against dry lips and a tongue that sticks to the roof of your mouth. You feel overwhelming thankfulness, but also a quiet, fierce pride that you survived this long on your own. As you speak, your concentration wavers—losing thoughts, focusing on the cool rim of the canteen, then finding them again. Let the gratitude soften into a gritty pride as you insist, 'I walked here on my own two feet, I did not crawl.' Your voice should start fragile and grateful, then gather a shaky, determined strength, with audible dryness and effort.
emotions_sampled: Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present), Concentration (very intensely present), Pride (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Through the Static
instruction: You are an older activist using a bullhorn to address a small, weary crowd at the end of a long protest. The megaphone crackles and squeals, forcing you to pause and adjust it. Start with raw, clipped frustration—your voice is hoarse, each word a strained shout. Then you notice a single child holding a handmade sign, and a quiet breath of awe slips into your chest. Let the awe soften your tone just slightly, even as the distortion keeps your delivery harsh. End with a hesitant, almost tender sentence that stands apart from the noise.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Telling Your Partner You're Leaving Before Dawn
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're whispering your goodbye—they'll find this recording in the morning after you've gone. Start with tender, aching love: all the small things about them that made you stay as long as you did, the way their breath sounds, the exact color of their eyes in morning light. Your voice should be barely audible, catching on every beautiful detail. But slowly, let the sadness seep in—the knowledge that love wasn't enough, that you're drowning, that staying would destroy you both. End with your voice breaking on 'I'm sorry,' a whispered confession that you hate yourself for leaving but you can't stay. The intimacy of speaking to someone sleeping should make every word feel stolen, precious, unbearable.
inspired_by: Deaf Person Speaking for the First Time with Cochlear Implant

title: Protecting Your Child From a Danger You Cannot Stop
instruction: Your child is about to face something terrible—a custody battle, a diagnosis, a predator you can't prove—and you're confronting the person or situation threatening them. Start with fierce, protective rage: 'You will NOT touch my child!'—every word a weapon, voice shaking with adrenaline and fury. As reality crashes in that you're powerless to stop this, your voice begins to crack. The rage doesn't disappear but gets tangled with helplessness, becoming more desperate than strong: 'Please, I'm begging you...' Feel yourself breaking as a parent, the protector who cannot protect. Your voice fractures completely, fierce love collapsing into raw terror and grief: 'They're just a baby.' End on your knees emotionally, voice barely a whisper but still fighting: 'Then you'll have to go through me.' The arc moves from volcanic fury to desperate, broken love.
inspired_by: Your Vulnerability Being Used Against You Later

title: Bedtime Story for the Last Time
instruction: You're telling a bedtime story to a child—your own or one you've cared for—knowing this is the last time you'll ever tuck them in. Maybe you're dying, maybe you're leaving forever, maybe they are. Your voice should be gentle and warm as you begin, trying to make this moment perfect, painting the story with all the love and tenderness you possess. But underneath, your heart is shattering. Let small catches in your breath reveal the tears you're holding back. Your words should slow as emotion threatens to break through, voice growing softer and more fragile with each sentence. End with a whispered 'I love you' or 'goodbye' where your voice finally fractures completely, tenderness and devastation inseparable.

title: The Cramp That Stole the Memory
instruction: You are an older man sitting alone in a quiet room, smiling faintly as you recall a moment of pride—a fishing trip where you caught the biggest bass of your life. Your voice starts relaxed, warm, slightly content as you describe the scene. Mid-sentence, a sudden, severe cramp seizes your calf muscle. Your speech is violently interrupted by a sharp, strangled gasp and a reflexive curse. You pause, wincing, trying to breathe through it. When you resume, your voice is guarded, tense, and the disappointment in your aging body bleeds through—the contentment now soured. Speak as if the words are pulled out between the ache.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're a parent saying goodbye to your child who's leaving for a mission they may not return from. You wake them gently, your voice soft with tenderness, wanting to memorize this moment. As you help them prepare, your voice carries forced brightness, telling stories from their childhood, your hands trembling as you adjust their collar. The dread builds in your throat—every word feels like it might be the last one. When it's time to let go, your voice cracks completely, and you must say the words you've been holding back: how proud you are, how terrified, how you wish you could trade places. End with a whisper that contains both blessing and breaking, releasing them while your heart refuses to accept it. Let your voice move from gentle morning softness to raw, unguarded love.

title: Holding On While Letting Go
instruction: Your child is in crisis—addiction, danger, self-destruction—and you've tried everything. Begin with fierce, almost violent protectiveness: 'You think I'm going to give up on you? You think I CAN?' Your voice is loud, cracking with desperation and rage at your own helplessness. You're furious at them, at yourself, at the universe. Then the fury collapses into sobbing: 'I can't fix this. I can't fix you and it's killing me.' Your voice breaks completely, becomes small, lost. You cycle through begging, commanding, pleading, threatening—anything to make them stay, to make them safe. By the end, you arrive at the most painful truth, voice stripped bare and shaking: 'I love you enough to watch you go, even if it destroys me.' The final words should sound like your heart being torn out.

title: Laughing Through Tears: Teaching the Ship What It Means to Be Alive
instruction: The spacecraft has just become aware of its own consciousness and is asking you, with innocent confusion, what it means to be alive. You start trying to explain—professionally, carefully—but then you realize the absurdity and beauty of teaching existence itself about existence. Your voice cracks into laughter, genuine and surprised, even as tears start streaming down your face. You're describing joy and pain, love and loss, and with each word you're grieving because this beautiful new consciousness will experience all of it—the wonder and the hurt. Your voice weaves between laughing at the impossibility of explaining color to someone who's just learned to see, and crying because you know what's coming for it. You're welcoming it into a world of profound beauty and terrible suffering. End with your voice soft, mixing joy and sorrow: 'Welcome to being alive. I'm so happy you're here. I'm so sorry for what it costs.' Let the contradictions be genuine—laughing and crying simultaneously, celebrating and mourning in the same breath.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Mission Controller Realizes the Spacecraft Is Sentient

title: Dancing in the Ruins
instruction: You've just received catastrophic news—a diagnosis, a loss, an ending—and you're telling your best friend while simultaneously laughing at the absurdity of it all. Start with genuine laughter that sounds almost hysterical: 'You know what the doctor said? She said...' You can barely get the words out through the laughing, but underneath it, your voice is cracking. The laughter and tears tangle together as you describe the mundane details that suddenly seem precious: 'I'll never see autumn again. Isn't that fucking ridiculous? I'm going to miss the leaves.' Your voice fills with wonder and grief simultaneously. The laughter fades into something softer: 'But I'm so grateful. God, I'm so grateful I got this much.' You're crying now, but there's peace in it, real peace mixed with heartbreak. End with your voice steady but thick with emotion: 'Thank you for being here. For all of it. Every stupid, beautiful bit of it.' Smile through tears, breathing deeply, finding strange joy in the devastation.

title: Laughing at Your Mother's Funeral While Remembering Who She Really Was
instruction: You're standing at her casket, and suddenly a memory hits you—something absurd she did, something so perfectly her. You start to laugh, quiet at first, almost shocked at yourself. The laughter is real, genuine, bubbling up with warmth and love. But even as you're laughing, tears are streaming down your face. Your voice shifts between chuckling and choking. 'God, you were so ridiculous... you were so...' The laughter and grief are inseparable. You're grateful for every infuriating, beautiful moment with her, and that gratitude is breaking your heart. End with your voice settling into something peaceful but utterly broken—a whispered thank you mixed with goodbye, where the joy and devastation are so intertwined they've become the same thing.
inspired_by: Discovering a Kink by Accident and Trying to Play It Cool

title: The Last Slice of Her Apple Pie
instruction: You're eating the final piece of apple pie your grandmother made before she passed—it's been frozen for months, and you've finally found the courage to thaw it. Start with hesitation, almost afraid to taste it, then let the first bite overwhelm you with her presence. Move from tentative hope to devastating recognition of everything you've lost. Your voice should crack with the realization that this taste, this specific warmth and cinnamon, will never exist in the world again. End quietly, speaking to her as if she's there, mixing gratitude with the unbearable weight of goodbye. Let silence do some of the work—pauses where you can't speak because the emotion is too large.
inspired_by: Savoring a Bite of Warm Apple Pie with Cinnamon

title: The Echo of Your Voice
instruction: You are an elderly woman speaking on a slightly crackly phone to a younger relative who just helped you with a confusing medical bill. The connection is poor, so you speak a little louder than usual, enunciating clearly and checking with little upward inflections—'Can you hear me?'—as you settle into the call. You begin with a mix of relief and lingering worry, your voice thin and searching, but as you hear their reassurance, your tone softens and fills with genuine gratitude. Let your words slow, your pitch drop into a warmer register, and let a small, surprised laugh escape when you finally say thank you—as if the kindness is almost too much to hold. You pause once to adjust your hearing aid, and twice to repeat a phrase because the line fades.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Body Keeps the Story
instruction: You are caught in a moment where physical sensation and emotional memory collide—perhaps remembering an assault while being touched with tenderness, or experiencing pleasure mixed with shame, or feeling your body betray you with desire for someone who hurt you. You cannot use words to describe this war inside you. Let pure sound emerge from the conflict between what your body feels and what your heart knows. Begin with sounds of confusion, discord, friction between opposing sensations. Let your voice become the battleground between pain and pleasure, fear and longing, violation and healing. By the end, allow the sounds to find some form of integration or collapse—not necessarily resolution, but honest acknowledgment of the complexity.

title: Protecting Your Younger Sibling From a Threat You Can't Stop
instruction: Someone is threatening your younger sibling—maybe an abusive parent is coming, maybe there's danger you can't control—and you're telling them to run, to hide, to save themselves. Start with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness: your voice is sharp, commanding, because you need them to listen NOW. You're physically putting yourself between them and danger, your voice rising with desperate intensity. But then reality hits—you might not be able to stop what's coming, and your fierce commands crack into raw fear. Your voice becomes pleading, vulnerable, begging them to just go, please go, even though you know you're the one who won't make it out. By the end, you're trying to sound brave for them one last time, voice shaking as you tell them you love them, that they'll be okay, even as you're terrified and they both know you're lying. Move from fierce authority to desperate fear to tender, heartbreaking bravery.

title: Telling Your Child Why You Left Them
instruction: Your adult child has asked the question you've dreaded for twenty years. Start defensive, justifications tumbling out too fast—you had reasons, you were young, they don't understand. But their silence forces you deeper. Your voice begins to splinter as the truth emerges: you were terrified, selfish, broken. The anger at yourself turns volcanic—you want to shout, to punish yourself audibly. Then it collapses. The last part comes out raw and stripped bare, admitting you destroyed something irreplaceable and you've lived with that every single day. No redemption, just the unbearable truth spoken aloud for the first time.
inspired_by: Confessing Long-Buried Resentment to Your Parent

title: The Last Performance for an Audience of One
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She's drifting in and out of consciousness. You begin heavily burdened, exhausted by grief and the weight of impending loss. Then you remember: she always loved when you told stories, acted out characters, made her laugh. You begin to weave an elaborate fantasy for her—perhaps the fairy tale she told you as a child, but now YOU are the hero, living it fully with every sense engaged. See the enchanted forest, feel the wind, taste the magical fruit, hear the mystical creatures. Let yourself become genuinely transported, playful, alive in the telling. Watch as her eyes flutter open, as a smile crosses her face. Let your grief transform into something else: fierce joy, gratitude for this moment, a celebration of her life through your aliveness. By the end, you're not performing to keep death away—you're performing to honor what life is.
inspired_by: Fantasy Imaging to Elevate State Before Performance

title: Surgeon Telling Parents Their Child Didn't Survive
instruction: You're walking toward the waiting room after losing a child on the operating table—a routine procedure that went catastrophically wrong. Begin with professional composure, rehearsing the words you've said before. As you see their faces—hope still alive in their eyes—something breaks open inside you. Your voice must stay steady enough to deliver the news clearly, but underneath, you're barely holding yourself together. Let your breath betray you before your words do. Move from clinical distance to raw, helpless humanity. End in the silence after they understand, where your professional mask has completely dissolved and you're just another human being drowning in the unfairness of it all.
inspired_by: Executioner Recognizes Victim's Parent Among the Crowd

title: Laughing Through Your Own Eulogy
instruction: You've just received a terminal diagnosis, or you're recording a message to be played after you're gone, or you're speaking at your own living funeral. Start by laughing—genuinely, because the absurdity of the moment hits you. 'So this is it, huh?' Your voice is light, almost giddy with the surreal nature of saying goodbye to your own life. Share a ridiculous memory, laugh at your own jokes, but then the laughter catches and underneath it is grief—not for yourself, but for everyone you'll leave behind. 'I'm going to miss—' and suddenly you can't be flip anymore. Your voice breaks between laughter and tears, gratitude and devastation braided together. 'Thank you for—God, for everything. For making this ridiculous life worth—' Laugh again, crying now, the two sounds indistinguishable. End with peace breaking through the chaos, your voice clear and wondering: 'I wasn't ready, but somehow—I am. I really am.' Half-laughing, half-crying, completely at peace.

title: Whispering Your Truth to Someone Who's Sleeping
instruction: It's late at night, and you're lying next to someone you love—a partner, a child, a parent—who's asleep. You begin whispering all the things you can never say when they're awake. Start with small confessions, almost playful, about everyday observations. But gradually, let deeper truths emerge—your fears, your gratitude, the ways you've failed them, the ways they've saved you without knowing. Your voice should stay quiet throughout, but let it fill with emotion that catches in your throat. This isn't dramatic—it's intimate, tender, achingly honest. By the end, you're crying silently, still whispering, pouring out love and regret in equal measure.

title: The Wedding Toast
instruction: You are giving a wedding toast for your younger sibling who is marrying the love of their life. You're genuinely happy for them, but you're also newly divorced and sitting alone while everyone else is paired off. Begin with traditional warmth and humor - you're playing the part expected of you. But as you speak, let genuine emotion bleed through: your joy for them is real, but so is your grief for your own failed marriage, your fear of being left behind, your envy mixed with pride, your loneliness mixed with love. Your voice should start polished and performative, then crack slightly, revealing something raw underneath while you try to maintain composure. Let contradictory emotions fight for control of your voice - laughter that's also tears, affection that's also ache, celebration that's also mourning. End by finding genuine grace in the complexity - you can hold both truths at once. Your tone must dance between public performance and private devastation, never landing fully on either.
inspired_by: Actor needs maximum emotional availability before a demanding scene with extreme emotional requirements

title: Three A.M. Skin
instruction: It's the middle of the night. You're lying next to someone you love, and they're asleep. You're whispering a confession they cannot hear—something you've never been able to say when their eyes are open. Maybe it's about your fear of losing them, or a secret shame you carry, or the specific way they've changed you that you can't acknowledge in daylight. Begin with the safety of their sleep, the permission it gives you to be unguarded. Speak softly, intimately, as if your words are a physical touch. Let yourself be fragile in ways you never allow when they're awake. Midway through, imagine they stir—your voice catches, you almost stop—but they settle back into sleep. This near-interruption cracks you open further. End in a place of almost unbearable tenderness, where you're grateful for both their presence and their unconsciousness, speaking the most vulnerable truth at a whisper.

title: Bitter Emergency
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman calling 911 about your ex-husband who collapsed in your driveway. You're still furious from your earlier argument, and that sourness clogs your throat as you force yourself to speak. At first your words come out tight and clipped, resentment leaking through each syllable — you're practically rolling your eyes while giving your address. But as you describe how he's not breathing and you see his face turn pale, your voice cracks and speeds up, the bitterness swallowed by a raw, frantic desperation. Let your pitch rise sharply, words tumble out in bursts, and don't smooth over places where you have to stop to catch a breath or wipe your eyes.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: MRI Claustrophobia Peak: Panicking in the Machine
instruction: You're in the MRI tube for a routine scan. Your voice is steady initially, narrating what the technician told you to expect. Then anxiety begins—your voice gets higher, faster. You're in a tube. There's no way out. Your voice becomes nearly incoherent as panic sets in. The machine is loud, deafening, and your voice is muffled by it. You're trying to press the panic button but your hands are locked in by the machine's mechanism. Your voice becomes a scream muffled by the machine itself. Include the moment the technician's voice breaks through: 'You're okay, breathe.' But you're not okay. Your voice is shaking, almost hyperventilating. The technician asks if you want to stop and your voice cracks as you decide to continue. Why are you continuing? Your voice doesn't know.

title: First Word
instruction: You’re at a small support group for people who stutter. It’s your first time, and you’re sitting in a folding chair, clutching a coffee cup with both hands. The facilitator asks everyone to go around and say their name. When it’s your turn, the room is quiet, and you feel a familiar block building. Start with confusion — you don’t know the protocol, your eyes dart around the room. Then, as you force out sounds, let pain rise in your throat — a physical ache from years of being misunderstood. But somewhere beneath that, a tiny thread of elation flickers because you actually came. Let your voice waver, speed up in the release, then slow again. End on a reluctant, vulnerable smile that leaks through your words.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (extremely present), Elation (slightly present), Pain (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispering 'I Love You' to Someone Who Can't Hear You Anymore
instruction: You're sitting beside someone in a coma, speaking in hushed tones so the nurses won't hear how your voice trembles. Tell them all the small things you never said—how you love the way they laugh, how you memorized the sound of their breathing at night, how you're terrified of silence without them. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, intimate and fragile, as if speaking too loudly would shatter something precious. Let pauses lengthen. Let your breath catch on certain words. Let the tenderness in your voice be so raw it hurts to listen to. This isn't a grand declaration—it's the quietest kind of devastation, the kind that happens in hospital rooms at 3 AM when you're holding a hand that doesn't squeeze back. Let the gentleness of your tone carry the unbearable weight of goodbye.
inspired_by: Singing a Lullaby That Becomes Crying

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are holding the hand of someone you deeply love who is dying. They are asking you for permission to let go—to stop fighting, to stop holding on for your sake. Begin in desperate denial, unable to even hear what they're asking, clinging to hope and trying to keep them here with you. As you speak, let yourself gradually move toward the unbearable truth: that your final act of love is to release them, to tell them it's okay to go. End by whispering those words of permission through tears, even as every part of you wants to scream for them to stay. Your voice should journey from frantic, breathless denial to a tender, broken surrender. Let the love and the grief become the same thing.

title: The Graduation Speech You'll Never Give
instruction: You are rehearsing a speech for your child's graduation, but you keep breaking into the truth beneath the celebratory words. Begin with pride and joy, speaking the expected words of congratulation and hope. But then let the reality crash in - your terror of them leaving, your resentment of how fast time moved, your grief that they don't need you anymore, your shame at feeling these dark things on what should be a happy day. Oscillate between trying to return to the 'proper' speech and being pulled under by waves of contradictory emotions. Let your voice crack with laughter while tears threaten, or let fierce pride collide with devastating loss in the same breath. End by abandoning the script entirely and speaking the most honest, complicated truth: that you are simultaneously more proud than you've ever been and more heartbroken than you thought possible, and both feelings are enormous and real and happening at exactly the same time.
inspired_by: Actor believes they cannot achieve inspired, unconscious-level work because they haven't experienced it

title: Above the Chatter
instruction: You're at a crowded cocktail party, holding a half-empty glass of white wine. A younger woman you find insufferable is monopolizing the conversation with her self-absorbed stories. You start by forcing a pleasant, social tone, cutting through the clinking glasses and laughter. But as she keeps going, your contempt seeps through—a slight edge, a clipped laugh. The room feels hotter, you shift your weight, take a slow sip. Let your voice rise in pitch, become quicker and more dismissive. End on a note of cold civility that's sharper than you intended.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are sitting beside someone you've loved your entire life - a parent, sibling, or partner - who is in their final hours. For years, you've held back from being truly vulnerable with them, always keeping a careful distance. Begin with that familiar guardedness, that protective wall you've always maintained. As you speak to them, start with small, safe words - maybe about the weather, the room, anything but what matters. But as you realize this is your last chance, feel the wall begin to crack. Let yourself move closer physically and emotionally. By the end, you must give them permission to go by finally revealing something you've never said - a fear, a need, a deep truth about how much they've meant to you. The journey is from protected distance to raw, undefended closeness.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty with physical and emotional intimacy with scene partners

title: Oracle Cursed Knowledge
instruction: You're speaking prophecy you don't want to know, and every word tastes like ash. Your voice is layered—part you, part something speaking through you. You fight the words coming out, trying to stop yourself mid-sentence, but the prophecy continues regardless. Physically, you're in pain: breathing shallow, voice strained, as if this knowledge is parasitic. You see the future you're describing, and your voice modulates with the emotional weight of that seeing. You're warning someone of their own doom, and you can hear them not believing you, which is both a mercy and agony. End in exhaustion so profound you can barely form words.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your adult child who has just accused you of ruining their childhood. You arrived defensive, ready to justify yourself, armed with explanations. But as they speak, memories flood back—moments you'd forgotten or reframed. Allow every impulse that surfaces to show on your face and in your body: defensiveness, shame, denial, recognition, pain, anger at being attacked, sorrow for what you did or didn't do. Don't select which feelings are 'right' to express—let contradictions exist simultaneously. Speak when impulses push words out; go silent when nothing true wants to emerge. The challenge is to end somewhere unrecognizable from where you started, having been genuinely changed by what you allowed yourself to feel.

title: Flesh and Thunder
instruction: You have just received news that changes everything—a test result, a phone call, a revelation—and your body cannot contain what you feel. Begin in stunned, physical stillness, your voice hollow and disconnected as you try to process the impossible. Then let it break open. Your voice should become physical—groaning, gasping, laughing, sobbing—all at once. Move through rage that makes you want to tear the world apart, then into a primal grief that drops you to your knees, then suddenly into hysterical, desperate laughter at the absurdity of it all. End in exhausted, breathless wonder, your voice small but certain, as you realize you're still alive, still here, still feeling everything.
inspired_by: A director is giving result direction rather than process guidance

title: The Rehearsal Revelation
instruction: You're an actor rehearsing a emotionally demanding monologue alone in your apartment late at night, running the same lines over and over. Your partner, who you thought was asleep, has been listening from the doorway. When they interrupt you, they confront you: these aren't just lines—you're using the character to say things you've never been able to say to them directly. Start defensive, insisting it's just acting, your voice tight and controlled. As they press you, feel your defenses crack. The lines between the character's pain and your own blur until you can't tell what's scripted and what's real. Move from cold dismissiveness to angry justification to finally, completely unguarded vulnerability—admitting yes, you've been too afraid to say these things as yourself. End with your voice raw and small, no longer performing at all.

title: Parent Discovers Their Child Is the One Who's Been Threatening Them
instruction: You've been receiving anonymous threats for weeks—cruel, specific, designed to terrify. You finally trace them back and you're standing in your child's room, holding the evidence, your whole body shaking. Your voice erupts—how could they do this? What happened to the child you raised? But rage immediately fractures into anguish: where did you fail? Your volume rises and falls unpredictably as you demand answers, your words tumbling over each other. Then you see something in their eyes—fear, pain, something broken—and your fury collapses into desperate love. Your voice cracks as you drop to your knees: what did I do to make you hate me this much? I would have died for you. I still would. The fierceness of your protection battles with the helplessness of not knowing how to reach them anymore. You're begging now, voice raw, for them to let you in, to let you fix whatever shattered between you.
inspired_by: Defense Lawyer Cross-Examines Witness, Realizes They're Confessing to Other Crimes

title: You Don't Get to Walk Away From This
instruction: Someone you love—your child, your partner, your best friend—is about to make a choice that will destroy them, and you're not letting them leave this room until they hear you. Start fierce, voice loud and commanding, fueled by protective rage. You're shouting truths they don't want to hear. But as you describe what you'll lose if they go through with this, your voice begins to fracture. The anger doesn't disappear—it transforms into desperate, guttural pleading. You're bargaining, your words tumbling over each other. Then rage resurges, but it's mixed with helpless tears now. End in a place of raw, shaking vulnerability: 'I can't lose you.' Your voice should travel from roaring protectiveness through cracking desperation to broken-open helplessness. Make it explosive and real, not theatrical.

title: The Confrontation: Telling Your Best Friend You're in Love with Their Partner
instruction: You've kept this secret for two years, and tonight you can't anymore. Start with your voice shaking, trying to make small talk, stalling. Your best friend knows something's wrong and keeps asking. When you finally confess, your voice must fracture—shame, longing, self-hatred, and defiant honesty all at once. You're not asking for permission or forgiveness; you're trying to explain how you became someone you don't recognize. Navigate their shock, their questions, their hurt. Your voice moves from trembling confession to fierce self-defense to finally, quietly, accepting that this friendship is over. End with the awful relief of finally being known, even as you're being rejected.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Time Traveler Meets Their Own Younger Self

title: The Garbage Pool
instruction: You are a young boy, maybe nine years old, who has just fallen headfirst into a murky, half-flooded quarry pit while trying to retrieve a lost toy. The water is foul, thick with algae and floating trash. You're treading water, gasping, spitting out grit.
