You start by yelling in pure disgust—every time you surface, you gag and curse the filth, calling for someone to get you out. But the longer you're alone in the cold, you realize how far you are from home and how dark it's getting. Your voice softens, your splashing calms, and you don't shout anymore—you whisper, half-submerged, a desperate longing for your mother. The last words come out shaky, almost lost in the water, like you're talking to yourself.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Conversation Before Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother in the pre-dawn darkness. She's been unconscious for hours, but suddenly her eyes open and she recognizes you. Begin in quiet, fragile hope—almost afraid to breathe, terrified this moment will end. She whispers something about forgiving herself for a mistake she made decades ago. As she speaks, allow yourself to move from that tentative hope into a profound mixture of relief and heartbreak—relief that she's found peace, heartbreak that this peace means goodbye. Your voice should start as barely a whisper, trembling with the fear of loss, and end in a warm, steady tone that offers her permission to let go. Let the transformation happen organically—don't perform the arc, live through it moment by moment.
inspired_by: Director or colleague challenges the actor's process as overcomplicated or unnecessary

title: The Last Breath of Lavender
instruction: You're holding your grandmother's hand as she takes her final breaths. Begin by closing your eyes and focusing entirely on what you smell—her lavender perfume mixed with hospital antiseptic, the faint scent of the wool blanket she's clutched for sixty years. Let the smell transport you through memories: her kitchen, her garden, her embrace. As you speak your goodbye, let the scent guide every word—notice how it's fading, becoming fainter, how you're trying to inhale deeply to hold onto it. Your emotional journey moves from desperate denial (trying to preserve every sensory detail to keep her alive) to a tender, aching acceptance as the scent slowly disappears and you realize you're memorizing it for the last time. Speak softly, let long pauses fill with your breathing, let the act of smelling become an act of love and letting go.
inspired_by: Actor is visually dominant and neglects other senses in imaging

title: The Last Drag Before Bed
instruction: You're on the back porch, the air cool and still. You take a slow drag from your vape, the smoke curling up as you exhale. Your child comes to the screen door, rubbing their eyes. You start speaking with a tired, warm affection—your voice soft, but with the slightly roughened edge of a recent inhale. As you talk, you notice the way the porch light catches their hair, and the thanks you feel for this small, quiet moment begins to bloom. By the end, your voice is heavier with gratitude, the drag cycle making your words come out in gentle, exhaled murmurs. Let the vape interrupt you naturally—a pause for a hit, a crackle in your throat, a little shift of weight as you lean to see them better.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Unpacking Thirty Years of Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother or father about the childhood you never got to have, and you start with controlled hurt—crisp, articulate sentences about what you needed and never received. But as you speak, the control fractures. Your voice cracks on a specific memory: 'I was seven years old and I needed you to just... see me.' Anger flares briefly, then collapses into something more vulnerable—not a child's plea but an adult's reckoning with inherited pain. You realize mid-sentence that you're not just angry; you're grieving the parent-child relationship that could have been. End with unexpected compassion creeping in, your voice softening as you recognize their limitations, even as your heart still aches. The final words carry both boundary-setting and reluctant forgiveness.

title: The Last Question
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl interviewing for your first job at a cozy local bookstore. The manager has been warm but you've been nervously over-enunciating, sitting rigidly, breathing shallowly. She just asked why you want to work here and you answered well. Now she smiles and says something that makes you realize it's going your way—maybe 'we'd love to have you.' Start your words still in that anxious, careful tone, but let relief begin to crack through mid-sentence. You might laugh at yourself, trail off, or let your posture soften. End with a genuine, shaky sigh of relief.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Lust in the Moonlit Frost
instruction: You are an older, androgynous person standing alone in a snowy field at night. A thick woolen scarf is pulled over your nose and mouth, your breath hot and damp against the fabric. You've had too much mulled wine — a warm, heavy intoxication that loosens your thoughts. At first, you're concentrating on the cold, the crunch of snow, the muffled quiet. But then a memory of last night's lover floods in — raw, vivid, hungry. Speak aloud to no one, half-slurred, the lust building until it overtakes the haze. Let the fabric muffle your words, your panting, your laughter. Begin it matter-of-fact, end it breathless and aching. Keep it between 40 and 80 words of spoken content.
emotions_sampled: Concentration (clearly present), Sexual Lust (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Farewell at the Train Station to Forever
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone you love who's leaving for a one-way journey—a dangerous mission, a terminal diagnosis journey, exile—and you both know you'll never see each other again. Start with false brightness, trying to be brave: 'It's going to be fine. You're going to be amazing.' But your voice betrays you, cracking. They touch your face and suddenly everything breaks: 'I don't know how to be in a world where you don't exist.' Your voice becomes raw, urgent, trying to memorize them: 'Tell me again about the first time we met. I need to hear your voice say it.' They do, and you're crying now, but also laughing through tears at the memory. Then the final boarding call. Your voice drops to a fierce whisper: 'I will carry you with me every single day.' You're holding their hands, not wanting to let go. Finally, barely audible: 'Go. Before I beg you to stay.' As they walk away, you call out one last time, voice broken but full of devastating love: 'You were the best thing that ever happened to me.' End in silence, watching them disappear.

title: Whispered Truths in the Dark - Love Confessed Too Late
instruction: You're sitting beside someone's hospital bed in the quiet hours before dawn. They're sleeping (or unconscious). You begin in that familiar numbness, whispering practical things: 'The nurse said you're stable. That's good.' But in the safety of darkness and their unhearing, you start confessing what you've never said: 'I should have told you...' Your voice is barely audible, catching on tears you're trying to hold back. The vulnerability is excruciating - admitting love, regret, all the moments you were too afraid or numb to speak. Each sentence costs you something. Your breath shakes. By the end, you're whispering through quiet tears, 'Please don't leave me before I learn how to feel again.' The emotion is gentle but devastating, tender but breaking your heart.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting at your father's deathbed. For years, you've held back from telling him the ways he failed you—not out of cruelty, but because the truth was too heavy to speak. Now, with hours left, you realize the most loving thing you can do is free both of you from pretense. Begin with careful tenderness, your voice barely above a whisper, but let the honest words come—not to wound, but to finally be real with him. As you speak each truth, feel the weight lifting from your chest. By the end, you're not angry anymore; you're grateful for this final moment of absolute honesty, and you tell him he can go now. Let your voice move from fragile hesitation to quiet, powerful liberation.

title: The Victory Sip
instruction: You are a child (boy, voice naturally higher and lighter) who has just won a fierce contest against a rival. You’re now sitting at a table, feeling hot and impatient from the wait for your drink. You grab the glass, take a long, loud gulp of cold soda — the fizz burns, you have to swallow hard, then exhale wetly. As you set the glass down, you begin speaking to someone who doubted you. Start with a slight edge of irritation in your voice, as if you’re still annoyed they made you wait. Let that fade into a deep, swelling triumph — you relish your win. Then let contempt take over completely: your tone becomes sneering, smug, almost cruel. The drink breaks up your speech; you pause to gulp again, or lick your lips, letting the sounds of swallowing and gulping punctuate your words. Your body shifts, you might wipe your mouth with the back of your hand. The final emotion should be pure, cold contempt.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Triumph (very intensely present), Contempt (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about a lifetime of emotional absence, and the words you've rehearsed for decades are finally spilling out. Begin with controlled anger, your voice sharp and measured as you list the moments they weren't there—birthdays, graduations, the night you needed them most. Let the anger crack open into raw pain, your voice rising as you demand to know why you were never enough. Then something shifts: you see their fragility, their regret, and your fury collapses into something more complicated—pity mixed with longing, rage tangled with the child's desperate hope that they might finally say they're sorry. End with your voice barely holding together, offering them one last chance to acknowledge the damage, knowing they probably won't take it, but asking anyway because you need to hear yourself ask.

title: Mother Daughter Healing
instruction: A mother and daughter are repairing something broken between them. The mother's voice carries guilt and the need to be forgiven. The daughter's voice is hurt and cautious. The mother says something inadequate, and both voices pause in the failure of words. The daughter begins to speak, and her voice wavers. The mother waits, not interrupting, which is itself a healing act. There's a moment where something shifts—genuine apology meets genuine pain and begins to transform it. By the end, neither voice is entirely healed, but there's the possibility of healing between them, and that possibility is everything.

title: What You Never Said
instruction: You're standing at your father's hospital bed, and he's lucid for the first time in weeks. He says, 'I was a good father, wasn't I?' Start with the truth trying to stay buried—your voice careful, loving even, saying 'Of course, Dad.' But something breaks. The words start coming: the birthdays he missed, the way he looked through you, the quiet erasure of your childhood. Your voice gains strength, then cracks as you realize he's crying. The anger collapses into something more complicated—grief for what you both lost. End holding his hand, voice raw and tender: 'I needed you. I still need you. And I don't know how to let you go without saying that.'

title: The Three A.M. Confession
instruction: It's 3 a.m. and you're sitting in dim lamplight with someone you've silently loved for years, who's about to move across the world tomorrow. Begin with quiet small talk, that exhausted intimacy of late night, both of you avoiding sleep and avoiding goodbye. As the silence stretches and you look at each other in the soft darkness, let yourself stop performing. Whisper the truth you've carried—but not as a declaration or plea, simply as something that needs to exist in the air between you before it's too late. Your voice should be barely audible, fragile as tissue paper. Let vulnerability feel physically uncomfortable. You're not asking for anything; you're just letting them see you, finally, completely. The transformation is from friendly distance to terrifying openness, from protected to utterly exposed. End with nothing resolved, just the gift and burden of being truly known.
inspired_by: Hold Hands and Look at Each Other

title: The Old Oak's Ecstasy
instruction: You are an elderly man, your voice heavy and worn from years, standing alone in a dense jungle. You have just found a long-lost grove of towering trees your grandfather spoke of—a secret paradise. At first, your voice is weary, your breathing labored from the trek, and you mutter with disbelief at the sight. But as you look around, the sheer beauty of the moss, the light filtering through leaves, and the sounds of birds overwhelm you. Let your voice slowly swell with pure, unrestrained pleasure—a deep, guttural laughter and a trembling, ecstatic whisper of awe. Allow the sounds of the forest—the rustle, the calls—to interrupt your words as you touch a trunk and speak your heart out: 'I... never thought... it could be this. Look at her. Look at her. I’m whole, you know? I— (a bird call cuts in) ...yes, yes, I know, I know. She’s real. I’m here. I’m here, and I’m crying like a fool.'
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Lock That Unlocks
instruction: You're a middle-aged adult, alone in your living room, finally sitting down after hours of frantic packing for a trip you've been dreading. As you relax, a sudden, severe cramp seizes your calf—a sharp, blinding muscle lock. You gasp, let out a reflexive curse, and freeze, bracing against the pain. Through gritted teeth, you mutter about the timing of this 'gift,' your voice impatient and brittle. But as the spasm slowly, reluctantly eases, you feel a wave of relief wash over you; your breath deepens, your shoulders drop, and you speak with a drained, almost amused gratitude—exhausted, but free from the immediate agony.
emotions_sampled: Relief (clearly present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Summit's Toll
instruction: You are a young male climber alone at 20,000 feet, your body buckling under altitude sickness. You've radioed base camp but now your head throbs, each breath is a gasp, and thoughts slip away. You try to report your condition calmly, but as you speak, the fear edges in, your voice falters, and you lose the next word. By the end, you admit you can't descend—your body won't cooperate, and all that remains is quiet helplessness. Let your voice be slow, strained, and halting, with real gasps and winces between phrases—like you're truly struggling to breathe and think.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Midnight Confession in Whispers
instruction: It's 2 AM, and you're lying next to your partner in the dark. You're going to tell them something you've kept hidden for years—not something dramatic, but something deeply true about who you are that you've been afraid would change how they see you. Begin by focusing on small, intimate details: their breathing, the weight of the sheets, the quality of darkness, the warmth between your bodies. Start speaking so quietly they have to strain to hear you. Let your voice carry vulnerability—pauses, hesitations, the catch in your throat. As you reveal this truth, notice how the darkness makes you braver. Move from fear and shame at the beginning to quiet relief and tender hope by the end. Let the intimacy of the moment—the closeness, the night, their listening—transform your relationship to your own secret.

title: A Promise for the Morning
instruction: You are a young boy, maybe 8 years old, sitting up in bed late at night with a persistent, throbbing toothache on one side of your mouth. You're talking to your favorite stuffed animal, the one you've had since you were a baby. At the start, you're trying to be brave, but every word makes you wince from the cold air hitting the tooth. You're trying not to move your jaw too much, talking almost out of the side of your mouth. You start by saying how scary it feels and how much it hurts, but as you keep talking, you remind yourself (and the toy) that the dentist said a new tooth will grow in soon, and you begin to sound more hopeful and even a little excited about that. Let your voice crack, let it get quiet, and let the hope slowly push through the pain.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Weight of Your Absence
instruction: You are lying in bed beside your lover, early morning light just starting to filter through the curtains. Your bodies are close, your faces inches apart. You begin speaking with pride—about something you both built together, a project or a milestone that feels like yours alone. But as you talk, you realize you have to leave for a few days, and the pride softens into longing. Let your voice stay whisper-close, breathy, with small pauses where you caress their hand or let your eyes wander their face. Start warm and buoyant, then let the words grow heavier, slower, as the ache of missing them settles in. End with a sigh or a near-silent confession of how much you'll miss them.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're watching someone you deeply love marry another person—perhaps an ex-lover, a best friend who chose someone else, or a child leaving your protection. You're expected to celebrate, to smile, to toast their happiness. Begin forcing joy into your voice, genuinely trying to mean the congratulations you offer. Let real happiness for them surface—they deserve this. But underneath, allow your own loneliness, loss, or resentment to creep in. Access actual experiences of being left behind or choosing someone else's happiness over your own desires. Your voice should crack between genuine celebration and barely contained grief. End with a complex cocktail: true love for them, pride in their joy, and simultaneous devastation that you're not part of this next chapter. Let gratitude and heartbreak become inseparable.

title: Dancing in the Hospice Room
instruction: You're setting up your dying mother's hospice room, talking to her unconscious form while simultaneously laughing and crying. Start with dark humor, almost manic energy: 'Remember how you hated clutter? Well, tough. You're getting photos everywhere.' Your voice is bright but tears are streaming down your face. You're arranging flowers, photos, her favorite blanket, narrating each choice with a mix of tenderness and absurdity. Suddenly you start humming the song she used to sing to you, voice cracking but continuing anyway. By the end, you're dancing slowly in the middle of the room, voice filled with impossible gratitude mixed with breaking grief: 'Thank you. For all of it. For this.' You're sobbing but also genuinely joyful, finding peace in honoring her, even as you're losing her. The contradictions live together—devastation and deep love, goodbye and gratitude, all at once.

title: The Forbidden Truth Spoken Aloud
instruction: You are confronting your parent (or child) in a world where family hierarchy is absolute, where questioning authority could mean exile or worse, where even the thought you're about to speak aloud has been forbidden your entire life. Begin with the trembling awareness of how dangerous this moment is—your hands might shake, your voice might catch, because in your world, this could destroy everything. Feel the weight of clothing that marks your social position, the physical distance custom demands you maintain, the formal language you've always been required to use. Then let necessity overcome fear: speak the unspoken truth that your survival (emotional, physical, or moral) now depends on saying. Build from careful, respectful words toward something more direct and modern in its emotional honesty. End in a place where you've broken through centuries of expected behavior, where your authentic voice—not the one your era trained into you—finally emerges, consequence be damned.

title: The New Mitt
instruction: You're a kid in the locker room after practice, surrounded by friends joking and shoving. One friend just showed off a brand-new, top-of-the-line catcher's mitt—the kind you've been saving up for but can't afford. Start with genuine astonishment: your voice goes high and breathy as you say 'Whoa, that's insane!' but you're also clapping them on the shoulder, laughing a little. As they brag, your tone shifts: you try to keep the locker-room energy going—loud, percussive laughs, quick interruptions—but each word comes out tighter. Mid-sentence, you might trail off as you stare at the glove, then force a '...yeah, man, that's awesome,' but your voice cracks with envy. End with a forced, hollow laugh that doesn't reach your eyes, while you look away and pretend to tie your cleats.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Contentment (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present)

title: The Blanket Fort Confession
instruction: Late at night, in dim light, you're wrapped in a blanket speaking to someone you love deeply. You need to tell them about a moment from your childhood—something small that shaped you, a fear or secret or tiny heartbreak that you've never shared with anyone. Maybe it's about being left alone, or a pet that died, or overhearing something you shouldn't have, or a friend who betrayed you at recess. Begin hesitantly, almost whispering, unsure if you can even say it out loud. As you speak, let yourself become the age you were when it happened. Your vocabulary might simplify. You might curl tighter into the blanket. The memory isn't dramatic—it's tender and private and makes you feel small. By the end, you're asking for something simple: to be told it's okay, to be held, to hear that the child you were deserved better. Stay quiet, intimate, fragile throughout.

title: Laughing Through the Diagnosis
instruction: You've just received devastating medical news—terminal, untreatable, finite time remaining. You're calling your closest friend to tell them, and you start by laughing at the absurdity of it, making dark jokes about mortality, the universe's timing, the irony of your life. Your laughter should sound almost genuine at first, like you're genuinely amused. But gradually, let the laughter become a shield that's failing you—it should start to sound slightly hysterical, then catch, then break. As you continue, let profound gratitude emerge: thank them for every small kindness, every shared moment, speak with sudden clarity about how beautiful your life has been. End with a strange mixture of peace and heartbreak—your voice should carry both acceptance and the deep sadness of leaving. You're not performing bravery; you're genuinely finding grace while simultaneously breaking apart.
inspired_by: The Doctor and the Reluctant Patient

title: Thanking Your Best Friend at Their Going-Away Party While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: Everyone's celebrating—they got their dream job across the world. You're giving a toast and you start with genuine joy, laughing about shared memories, your voice warm and full of pride for them. But underneath, you're dying because they're leaving and nothing will ever be the same. Let both emotions exist simultaneously: you're laughing while your throat is closing up, your voice bright while it's also breaking. 'I'm so happy for you' comes out completely sincere and completely devastated at the same time. As you speak, the gratitude for having known them mixes with the grief of losing them, until you can't tell where one feeling ends and the other begins. End with a final 'I love you' that contains everything: celebration, goodbye, heartbreak, and a strange kind of peace with the beautiful, terrible impermanence of it all.
inspired_by: Speaking to Your Child After Getting Angry You Regret

title: The Breaking Point: A Surgeon After Losing a Child Patient
instruction: You've just lost a six-year-old on the operating table—a preventable death caused by faulty equipment you reported months ago. Explode into the room where administrators are gathered: 'I told you! I TOLD YOU the monitors were failing!' Your voice is raw, almost screaming. Let your rage be primal, uncontained. 'I begged for new equipment and you talked about budget constraints!' You're pacing, gesturing wildly. Then your voice cracks completely: 'She was six years old. She drew me a picture of her dog.' Suddenly you're sobbing, the fury collapsing into devastating grief. Your voice becomes almost childlike: 'I held her hand. I promised her mother...' You can barely speak. End with fierce, broken determination: 'I won't do this anymore. I won't watch children die because you care more about quarterly reports than lives.' Your voice must transform from explosive rage through shattered grief to a kind of fierce, helpless resolve. Let every word feel like it's tearing out of you.
inspired_by: Medical Director: Announcing Quality Improvement Changes

title: Confronting Your Grown Child About Why They've Cut You Out
instruction: Your adult son or daughter has finally agreed to meet you after two years of silence. You came ready to explain, to defend yourself, starting with 'You don't understand what I was going through back then' with controlled hurt in your voice. But as they calmly, quietly list specific moments—times you chose substances over their birthday, partners over their graduation, your pain over their childhood—your defenses crack. Your voice becomes smaller, younger almost, as you hear your own parent's excuses coming out of your mouth. Move from justification to raw recognition: 'I sounded just like him, didn't I?' Then comes the hardest part—asking 'Can you ever forgive me?' while your voice reveals you already know they might not, and that you might not deserve it. End in a place between shame and the faint, terrifying hope that honesty, finally, might be enough.
inspired_by: Realizing You're the Toxic One in This Relationship

title: The Last Inventory
instruction: You're sitting at the bedside of someone who raised you—a parent, grandparent, or mentor—who has only hours left. They're drifting in and out of consciousness. You begin speaking to them, starting with apologies and regrets for who you used to be—selfish, afraid, ungrateful. But as you continue, you find yourself telling them about the person you've become because of them, the ways you've changed, grown stronger, braver. Start with shame and sorrow, voice tight and hesitant. Let it gradually transform into something like pride mixed with devastating gratitude, your voice becoming clearer and more certain even as tears come. End by thanking them for not giving up on you, even when you had given up on yourself. The shift is from self-recrimination to recognition of transformation, from regret to bittersweet celebration.

title: Cancer Survivor Bell
instruction: You've completed your final chemo treatment, and you're ringing the bell in front of the whole hospital. Your voice is shaking as you take the mallet: 'I made it.' You ring the bell, and your voice erupts into a sound between a laugh and a sob: 'I'M ALIVE!' Nurses and doctors come out to celebrate, and your voice is uncontrolled, pure joy mixed with disbelief: 'I made it! I actually made it!' You're laughing and crying simultaneously. People embrace you, and your voice becomes softer, more personal: 'Thank you for saving my life. All of you. Thank you.' Later, alone in your car, your voice is quiet, almost in shock: 'I'm a survivor now. That's who I am. That's what I'll be forever.' You start the car, and your voice is steady: 'Now I live. Really live.'

title: The Forgotten Kettle
instruction: You are an elderly woman alone in your kitchen, lost in a memory of your late spouse. You reach for the kettle without thinking, your hand closing around the metal just as it boils over—a searing burn. Your first instinct is a sharp hiss through clenched teeth as you drop the kettle, gripping your wrist with your other hand. As you stand there, the pain fades into a familiar numbness, the same hollow feeling that’s lived with you since the funeral. You speak aloud to the empty room, your voice tight at first, then softening into a quiet, distracted murmur as you let the memory take over again, your burned hand forgotten at your side.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Feeling the First Gentle Snowflakes Land on Your Face
instruction: Stand still as soft snowflakes drift down, brushing lightly against your cheeks and nose. Describe the cool, delicate touch of each flake, the way it melts almost instantly, leaving a trace of coolness behind. Speak with a tone of wonder and quiet joy, as if each tiny snowflake is a whisper of winter, gentle and magical.

title: The Threshold of the Blue Room
instruction: You're whispering to someone you love in a room that exists in that strange space between sleep and waking—maybe it's your childhood bedroom but the proportions are wrong, maybe the darkness has a texture to it, maybe time feels suspended. Begin by exploring the sensory details of this impossible space: what does the darkness feel like on your skin? What small sounds do you hear that shouldn't exist? What's the quality of their breathing next to you? Start from a place of cautious tenderness, saying small true things. As you inhabit this distorted, dreamlike space more fully, let it give you permission to say things you could never say in the waking world. The illogical nature of the environment—the way shadows might move wrong, the way their face might shift in the darkness—allows deeper truths to surface. By the end, you've confessed something so fragile and raw that it could only exist in this liminal space, your whisper barely audible, your heart completely exposed.

title: Under the Bed, a Secret
instruction: You're a teenage girl, alone in your room, bent over with your hands on your toes, your face near the floor as you reach under the bed. Your back aches, blood rushes to your head, and your voice comes out thick and strained from the crushed diaphragm. You're searching for an old shoebox you hid years ago. When your fingers find it and you pry open the lid, you see a faded photograph of your late grandmother, the one person who truly understood you. Start with the dull, physical pain of the position—a few muttered complaints, voice congested and rough. As you lift the photo, let the pain melt into a hushed, trembling awe, your voice clearing slightly as wonder overtakes you. You can even pause to catch your breath or shift your weight.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Kitchen After Midnight
instruction: You're confronting your father in the kitchen where you grew up, late at night when everyone else is asleep. You came here to finally tell him how his coldness shaped you, how his silence carved holes in you. Start with controlled anger, words you've rehearsed. But mid-confrontation, a specific memory surfaces—unbidden, vivid—of a moment when you were young, perhaps six or seven, when you needed him and he wasn't there, or when he said something that lodged in your bones. Let that memory interrupt your rehearsed speech. Let it make you younger, more raw, less controlled. By the end, you're no longer the adult you walked in as—you're speaking from the wound itself, and your voice reveals layers of hurt you didn't plan to show. The anger transforms into something more vulnerable and true.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Apologized
instruction: You're finally saying what you've rehearsed a thousand times. You start controlled, almost cold: 'I need you to hear this.' Your voice is measured as you list the moments they failed you—birthdays forgotten, promises broken, the times you needed them and they weren't there. But control gives way to something fiercer. Your voice shakes with restrained fury: 'Do you even remember?' You're demanding accountability now, your words sharp and unforgiving. Then something unexpected happens—your anger collapses into the voice of the child you were, small and bewildered: 'Why wasn't I enough for you to stay?' You end not with resolution but with exhausted honesty, your voice barely above a whisper, admitting you don't know if you can forgive them, but you needed them to finally hear the truth.

title: The Secret in the Sandbox
instruction: You are a young boy, maybe seven or eight, kneeling in the school sandbox with a girl you have a tiny, secret crush on. You're building something together, and every time she starts to talk about the castle's tower, you can't help but cut her off with a new, more exciting idea—your voice climbing higher and faster each time. You feel a flutter of infatuation and pure joy, like fizzy soda in your chest. Start with a breathless, rushed excitement, but as you talk, you realize you just blurted out that you hid your favorite toy dinosaur for her to find later. End with a sudden, shy quiet as you look down at the sand, digging your fingers in and trying to hide a smile.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Knot
instruction: You are an elderly woman, just out of a long, hot bath, your body still heavy and soft from the warmth. You sit on the edge of the bed, a silk robe loose around you. You hold a delicate silver locket that has been stuck closed for years. As you speak to no one in particular—perhaps to a granddaughter who isn't there—you fumble with the tiny clasp (a micro-distraction as your fingers are still a bit pruney). At first, your voice is a contented, languid murmur of simple exhaustion. But as you realize the locket finally opens, a slow, proud smile warms your words. You speak of the old photograph inside, your voice trembling not with sadness but with a deep, satisfied pride that you alone managed to free it after all these years.

title: The Fever Breaking
instruction: You are in the grip of overwhelming physical sensation—perhaps intense pain from an injury, or fever, or the peak of passion, or exhausting grief that's been held in your body for months. Begin with your entire instrument hijacked by this sensation: breath ragged, body trembling or rigid, voice broken or gasping. But as you speak through it—perhaps praying, or calling out to someone, or simply narrating what you're experiencing—allow the physical intensity to gradually transform your emotional state. Let the sensation burn through you and leave something different in its wake. End in a place of strange, exhausted peace or clarity that could only come through this crucible. Your voice should move from fractured and overwhelmed to emptied out and strangely whole.

title: The Wind Takes It All
instruction: You're alone in a vast open field, facing the direction where your partner's ashes were scattered last spring. The wind tears at your hair and dress, and every word you speak feels instantly stolen. Start by murmuring a soft, loving memory — your voice small and almost swallowed by the space. Then let the sadness overwhelm you, voice cracking and breaking, and finally let anger surge — loud, trembling, furious at the silence and the wind and the absence. Your hyper-feminized pitch should waver, strain, and sometimes drop into ragged bitterness. Speak naturally, reacting to gusts that make you blink or pause.
emotions_sampled: Affection (slightly present), Sadness (extremely present), Anger (very intensely present)

title: The Hospital Window at Dawn
instruction: You are sitting beside your father's hospital bed in the pre-dawn darkness. He's awake but fading, and you both know this is the last conversation you'll ever have. Begin by noticing small, specific details in the room—the hum of machines, the smell of disinfectant, the weight of his hand in yours, the way morning light is just starting to edge the window. Start feeling numb, almost floating outside yourself, unable to fully accept what's happening. As you speak to him, allow memories to surface as vivid sensory flashes—not full scenes, but fragments: the rough texture of his work jacket when you were five, the sound of his laugh at your wedding, the metallic taste of fear when you disappointed him. Let these fragments pull different emotions to the surface randomly—gratitude, regret, love, old anger. By the end, let yourself fully arrive in the moment, no longer numb but devastatingly present, feeling everything at once as you say what can never be unsaid.

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You're a parent telling your child one final bedtime story, but they don't know you've been diagnosed with terminal illness and won't be here much longer. Start with the gentle, familiar rhythm of storytelling, your voice warm and loving. As you move through the tale, let your awareness of this being the last time overwhelm you—your voice should catch, words should become harder to say, but you fight to maintain composure for their sake. By the end, allow gratitude for this moment to mix with devastating grief, your voice breaking as you try to memorize every detail of their face. The story itself becomes a love letter, a goodbye hidden in fairy tale language. Let silences speak—pauses where you're composing yourself, moments where emotion makes words impossible.

title: Midnight Confession
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in complete darkness, whispering a secret you've never told anyone. Start with shame and fear of judgment. As you speak in barely audible tones, pay attention to every tiny sensation: their breathing pattern, the warmth between your bodies, the weight of the blanket, distant sounds from outside, the taste in your mouth, the texture of the sheets. Let one subtle sensory detail unlock why you've kept this secret so long—perhaps their breathing rhythm reminds you unconsciously of feeling safe as a child, or the darkness itself is what's finally allowing you to speak. Let the physical intimacy and the sensory environment gradually dissolve your shame into something else: relief, vulnerability, a fragile hope, or tender gratitude for being heard.

title: The Unguarded Hour
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your partner lies beside you, finally asleep after months of distance between you. You speak to them, knowing they cannot hear, confessing everything you've been too afraid to say while they're awake. Start barely audible, your body curled small, protective. As you confess deeper truths—your fears of inadequacy, your desperate love, your terror of losing them—let your body slowly unfurl. Reach out tentatively to touch their sleeping form. Let your breathing change, your physicality open. Even in whispers, let the emotion grow bigger inside you, expressing through subtle but expanding physical presence. By the end, you're lying closer, your body expressing a vulnerability you cannot show when their eyes are open. The quiet transforms from guarded to absolutely undefended.

title: The Dialect of Disappearing
instruction: You're a parent whispering to your sleeping child who's losing their hearing. Tomorrow is the surgery—it might restore it, it might not. Begin with tender, careful words, teaching them the family phrases, the inside jokes, the way you say 'I love you' in the particular melody only your household knows. Your voice is barely audible, catching on each word. But halfway through, your composure fractures—you find yourself making sounds without words, humming the emotional tones beneath language, trying to give them something to remember if sound goes away forever. The grief is quiet, enormous. End with a shift: you realize that love doesn't live in the words but in the breath between them, and that will never disappear. Your final sounds are somewhere between speaking and singing, pain and peace intertwined.

title: Frozen Resentment
instruction: You are an older man standing alone in a blizzard, your body shaking from the cold, your jaw tight as you shout into the howling wind. You're searching for someone who left you behind after a bitter argument, but the snow swallows your words. Start with a sharp, sour anger—your voice strained, cracking from the cold and frustration. As the wind dies for a moment, let your anger soften into a quiet, exhausted contemplation; you realize they're not coming back. Your voice becomes slower, more reflective, trembling less from cold than from a sour resignation. Let the environment interrupt you—pause to cough, wipe snow from your face, lose your train of thought and pick it up again.

title: Heavy Head, Sudden Clarity
instruction: You're an older, gruff-voiced man waking from a deep nap in your armchair. Your head is thick, your eyes barely open—you don't know what time it is. A sharp buzz from your phone makes you flinch with a low grunt of surprise. As you fumble to read the screen, you realize it's a message saying your daughter arrived early at the airport. The groggy confusion snaps into a jolt of mild panic—you were supposed to pick her up twenty minutes ago. title: The Princess Can't Stop Coughing
instruction: You are a seven-year-old girl, the prima donna of your kindergarten's fairy tale play, but today your throat feels like sandpaper. title: The Last Blessing
instruction: You are an elderly woman kneeling at the bedside of a dying loved one—a grandchild or dear friend—who has just lost consciousness. Begin speaking in a trembling, high-pitched voice, your words tumbling out in a rush as if trying to catch the last seconds. Let your voice crack and fade, with shaky breath and creaky onsets, your pitch rising in submission to the inevitable. As you plead for just one more moment, let your awe transform into a quiet, tearful acceptance, your voice softening into a thread of hope that they can hear you, even now.

title: Laughing at the Funeral
instruction: You're standing at a funeral, memorial, or final goodbye, and a memory hits you—something absurdly funny about the person you've lost. You start to laugh, quietly at first, trying to suppress it because it feels inappropriate. Your voice is caught between laughter and tears: 'Oh god, remember when they...' As you tell the story, let the laughter become fuller, more real, but underneath it the grief is rising like a tide. Your voice does something extraordinary: you're genuinely laughing and genuinely crying at the same time, the joy of the memory and the agony of loss braided together inseparably. Move into a moment where you're speaking directly to them: 'Thank you. Thank you for being so ridiculous, so impossible, so perfectly you.' Your voice is warm with love but shattered with loss. End with a complex emotional cocktail: you're smiling through tears, your voice carrying both celebration and devastation, finding something like peace in the contradiction. Your final words are soft, almost wondering: 'This is how I'll remember you. This exact feeling. This beautiful, terrible, perfect ache.'

title: The Mausoleum of His Own Making
instruction: You are a man who has just orchestrated the total humiliation of your lifelong rival — publicly, perfectly, savagely. Now you sit alone in your study, the victory echoing in the silence. Your voice is eerily flat, robotic, as if you are watching a documentary about someone else's life. You describe the triumph with precise, empty statements, a glass wall between you and the ecstasy you should feel. A slight thread of deep, buried pain flickers in your chest like a ghost, but your voice stays unnaturally calm. Feel the pleasure of the win, but let it come out as a cold, hollow narration. Start by stating the outcome (e.g., 'He never saw it coming'), then let a tiny crack of something ancient and sore slip into the final word, but immediately cover it with that eerie, triumphant calm.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (extremely present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Pain (slightly present)

title: The Last Promise Before Deployment
instruction: You're a parent making a promise to your child the night before you deploy to a war zone, knowing you might not return. Start with careful, measured words—you're trying to be strong for them. Your promise is specific: how you'll come back, what you'll do together, the life you'll build. But as you speak, your voice begins to crack under the weight of what you're really saying—that you need them to remember you, to hold onto this moment. Your child's silence is deafening. You repeat the promise, but now it's transformed into something else: a blessing, a benediction, a love letter disguised as certainty. End with your voice barely above a whisper, the promise now an offering of everything you are, knowing it may be all you can leave behind.

title: The Plank of Contempt
instruction: You are in a power yoga class, holding a forearm plank. Your muscles are screaming, your breath is a shaky ujjayi rasp. In front of you, your toddler has smeared applesauce all over your yoga mat. You are disgusted — seething at the mess, at the sticky sweetness, at the sheer disrespect. As you hold the pose, your voice trembles with strain and revulsion. But as you speak, you realize you're also disgusted at yourself for being so angry at a baby. The disgust softens into a weary, trembling acceptance. Let your words come out between clenched breaths, the tremor in your arms and throat coloring every syllable, the end quieter, more exhausted than the start.

title: The Wedding Toast You Can't Give
instruction: You're practicing a toast for your best friend's wedding tomorrow—but you're secretly in love with them, and this marriage means losing them forever. Begin speaking from the part of you that's genuinely happy for them, the loyal friend who wants their joy. Let that be real and true. But as you continue, allow another part of you to surface—the one that's breaking, that's grieving, that's angry at yourself for never speaking up. These two parts of you must coexist in the same moment: real joy and devastating loss, generous love and selfish heartbreak, celebration and mourning. Your voice should carry both truths simultaneously, neither one canceling out the other. End with a final sentence that somehow holds all of these contradictions at once, leaving you uncertain which feeling will win tomorrow.

title: The Hollow Mother
instruction: You are a woman with chronic insomnia, speaking to your young child at 2 AM. Your body is heavy with sleep debt, your voice compressed and hollow from exhaustion, with a low-level anxious anger simmering underneath. Start by sharply telling the child to go back to sleep—your tone brittle, strained, holding back irritation. Then, as the child’s small voice breaks through, your anger cracks into weary apology. You sigh, lose the thought, then finish with a softer, cracked admission that you’re just too tired. Let your tempo lag, let your voice rasp, let silences hang as you struggle to find words.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Upload
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your dying parent who has chosen to have their consciousness uploaded to a digital system—they'll exist as data, but won't be the same person anymore. Begin with clinical detachment, explaining the procedure as if you're the scientist who developed it, trying to stay professional. But as you describe what will happen to their memories, their sense of self, let your voice crack. End by dropping all pretense—you're no longer the expert, just a child begging their parent not to disappear into something you created but can't fully understand. Your final words should be a whispered plea that acknowledges you've lost them either way: to death or to your own invention.

title: The Secret Under the Stars
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl lying on the grass in your backyard at midnight, whispering to yourself. You've been thinking about a big change you're about to make—moving to a new school. At first, your whispers are hesitant, almost afraid of the sound, your breath catching as you voice your doubts. But as you look at the stars, your voice softens, becomes more certain, a quiet resolution forming. Let the whisper be airy, with pauses where you lose your train of thought, shifting your weight on the grass, maybe a distant cricket distracting you. End with a gentle, knowing sigh. Speak 40-80 words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Finding Your Estranged Father's Love Letters to You That Were Never Sent
instruction: You've just discovered a box of letters your father wrote to you over twenty years but never mailed—he died last week. Start reading one aloud, your voice skeptical and defended—he abandoned you, why should these matter? But the words reveal a man who thought about you every day, who was too ashamed of his failures to reach out. Your voice cracks between bitter laughter and tears—the absurdity that his love was always there, just locked away. You're furious at the waste, at the years stolen by pride and fear, but you're also flooded with relief that you were loved. Read passages where his words break your heart open, your voice shifting between anger at what could have been and profound gratitude for this unexpected gift. End with you laughing through tears at something funny he wrote, then whispering 'I forgive you,' your voice carrying the strange peace of finding love in the rubble of loss.
inspired_by: Historical: Slave Catches Glimpse of Their Own Child They Were Forced to Abandon

title: The Crumple of Disappointment
instruction: You are an elderly woman walking home, already wearied by the weight of a promise broken by someone you trusted. As you step off the curb, a cyclist slams into you — the impact hits your chest, forcing the air from your lungs in a sharp, painful grunt. The world goes breathless and shaky. Your first words are a choked gasp of disappointment at how things have turned out. Then, as you steady yourself, a disgusted bitterness rises — at the cyclist's carelessness, at your own vulnerability. Finally, a cold, barely audible malevolence slips into your voice as you whisper a warning to the world itself. Let your voice start with a deflated, hollow sigh; after the blow, it becomes ragged, pausing mid-word, as if each breath is stolen. End with a tight, quiet threat, your tone thin as ice.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (slightly present), Disappointment (extremely present), Malevolence/Malice (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Hollow Pleasure
instruction: You are an older woman with a hyper-feminized voice, receiving oral sex from your partner. You start by performing pleasure mechanically—moaning, whispering encouragement—but a deep emotional numbness slowly creeps in. Your body is gripped with tension, breaths sharp and irregular, but your mind drifts. The pleasure feels distant, like you're watching from outside yourself. Let your voice unravel: from forced, melodic moans to fragmented, flat sentences, ending with a quiet sigh or a broken admission of emptiness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Asking for Help When You're Trained to Solve Everything
instruction: You're calling someone and asking 'Can you help me?' Your voice is stiff, uncomfortable, using clinical terms for distance. The listener offers help and something breaks. 'Thank you' comes out barely audible. You admit struggling in a vulnerable admission you've never made before.

title: What the Scar Remembers
instruction: Late at night, alone, you're touching a scar on your body—from surgery, an accident, a wound that marked you. Close your eyes and feel a presence emerging from that scar, a figure made of memory and tissue and all the pain that's been living inside it. This presence knows everything your body survived that your mind has tried to forget. Begin in tentative curiosity, fingers on the scar. Whisper to this presence: 'What do you need to tell me?' Listen as answers come—not in thoughts but in sensations, images, half-formed words. Let vulnerability crack you open. The presence might be angry at being ignored, or sad, or desperately needing acknowledgment. Respond with whispered confessions of how you've tried to move on, tried to forget. End in tender reconciliation with this part of yourself, speaking softly to the scar, thanking it, promising something you've never promised before.

title: The Last Box
instruction: You are an older woman who just finished carrying a heavy box up three flights of stairs. Now you've collapsed onto the floor, your back against the wall, chest heaving. You're proud you made it — a small victory. But as you struggle to catch your breath, your body feels foreign, heavy, and the pride starts to crack. Speak while still panting, your voice airy and limp, with no tension. Let the words come in fragments, interrupted by gasps. Begin with a whisper of triumph, then let it fade into quiet worry as you realize you can't get up just yet.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your parent about a family secret that has shaped your entire life—something they never acknowledged or discussed. Start from a place of controlled, righteous anger: you came prepared, you have your points listed, you will finally be heard. But as you speak, really imagine their face as they listen—see the lines, the age, the fear in their eyes, the defensive posture of their body. Let this visual reality complicate your anger. Allow unexpected emotions to surface: the child in you who still needs them, the grief over lost years, the fury at their weakness, the unbearable love that won't die. End in a place utterly different from where you began—perhaps with a question instead of an accusation, perhaps with tears instead of rage. Let seeing them as they truly are transform what you came to say.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You're finally telling your estranged parent exactly what their absence cost you, using the metaphor of being a terrible tour guide through your childhood—pointing out all the moments they missed, the milestones they got wrong, the 'facts' about your life they confidently state but have completely incorrect. Start with bitter, cutting sarcasm as you correct their false memories and assumptions. Let your anger build as you catalog their failures, then crack open into raw vulnerability as you admit how desperately you needed them. End in a whisper, asking the question you've been afraid to ask: did they ever really want to know you at all?

title: The Lap That Broke My Own Record
instruction: You're a teenage girl swimming laps alone at the local pool, pushing yourself harder than ever before. You've just realized your time is better than your personal best. Your voice is chopped into gasping bursts between strokes—each word a battle against water and exhaustion. Start with breathless disbelief, then let pure elation crack through your voice as you sputter to yourself mid-lap. You're alone, but the joy is so fierce you can't help celebrating out loud, even as you swallow pool water and your lungs burn.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Good Measure
instruction: You are a 72-year-old retired nurse, sitting on the edge of your exam table in a quiet clinic. A young doctor, who reminds you of your granddaughter, is taking your blood pressure for the final time before you move to hospice care. You feel a deep, quiet contentment — a sense of having lived fully, of having loved and been loved. As she removes the cuff, you speak softly, almost to yourself, remembering a patient you helped decades ago. The doctor asks if you're comfortable; your voice shifts from a tender, reflective murmur to a clear, gentle assurance, touched with wry humor as you notice the crooked picture on the wall. You begin in a near-whisper, letting the memory fill you, and end with a calm, grounded warmth, as if you're saying goodbye to the world itself.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Parts of Me You Never Met
instruction: You're confronting your mother after years of pretending to be the person she wanted you to be. Start by speaking as the 'good child'—the polite, careful version of yourself she knows. But mid-conversation, let another part of you emerge—the wild one, the angry one, the one who never got permission to exist in her presence. Then another part: maybe the terrified child who just wanted her approval. Let these different facets of yourself speak, interrupt each other, argue with each other through your voice and body. This isn't multiple personalities—it's the conversation between all the true parts of yourself that she's never been allowed to see. End with whichever part of you finally feels most honest in this moment, even if it's the one that scares you most.
inspired_by: Group Dream Sharing and Analysis (Workshop Format)

title: The Last Morning Together
instruction: You're lying beside someone you love deeply on the morning they leave for a mission they won't return from—you both know this, though neither of you has said it aloud. You begin in that profound peace the original described, savoring the weight of their body next to yours, the rhythm of their breathing. But as you speak—about the coffee you'll make, the way light falls through the window, ordinary beautiful things—grief begins to seep through the cracks of your calm. Your voice starts soft and settled, almost drowsy with contentment, but by the end it's fractured by the weight of impending loss, though you're fighting to hold onto the peace for just a few moments longer. You're not crying dramatically; you're trying desperately to stay present in joy even as your heart is breaking.

title: Laughing at the Funeral You'll Forget
instruction: You're at your beloved spouse's funeral reception. You have early-stage dementia and you know—with crystal clarity right now—that within months you won't remember this day, won't remember they died, will ask where they are over and over. Start by laughing softly, almost inappropriately, your voice full of dark humor and disbelief: 'You know what's funny? Really, genuinely funny?' There's grief underneath but you're actually laughing. 'In six months, I'll wake up and ask where you are. And someone will have to tell me you're dead. Again.' Your laughter becomes slightly hysterical, mixing with tears. 'I'll get to grieve you over and over. Fresh every time.' Your voice catches between laughing and crying. 'Lucky me.' Then the laughter fades into something more tender, your voice soft with gratitude even as tears stream down: 'But right now, in this moment, I remember everything. Every fight. Every kiss. Every mundane Tuesday.' Your voice breaks with the beauty and pain of it: 'I'm grateful for the fog that's coming. Because right now, this grief is unbearable.' End with peaceful acceptance mixed with heartbreak, a soft laugh through tears: 'So I'm going to stand here at your funeral, crying and laughing like a madwoman, holding onto you with everything I have. Before my mind decides to be merciful and let you go.'

title: Prisoner War Unbreakable
instruction: You're a POW being tortured, and you're reciting something—your daughter's birth date, a prayer, a poem—to stay yourself. Your voice is broken by pain, but it remains defiant. You're whispering so your captors can't fully hear, creating an intimate vulnerability. Pain interrupts you mid-word, and you recover. Your voice becomes almost mechanical as a coping strategy, then suddenly very human—a crack of emotion when they mention your family. You're using speech as survival. By the end, they've broken something, but not what they were trying to break. Your voice is a whisper, and it's still refusing.

title: The Confrontation in the ICU Waiting Room
instruction: You're confronting your unconscious father through the glass of his hospital room, finally saying everything you never could. Start with bitter, controlled anger: 'You were supposed to protect me. You were supposed to see me.' Your voice is sharp, practiced—you've rehearsed this a thousand times. But as you watch his chest rise and fall with the ventilator, something shifts. The rage begins crumbling into grief. 'I needed you to just... look at me. Once.' Your voice breaks. Now you're not attacking—you're begging. The anger transforms into desperate, childlike pleading mixed with adult fury. End by pressing your hand to the glass, voice barely above a whisper, caught between wanting him to die without ever hearing you and terrified he'll die before he can.

title: The Bittersweet Return
instruction: You are standing in the doorway of your childhood home for the first time in ten years. You are speaking to someone—a sibling, a friend, maybe yourself—about coming back. You thought you'd feel only anger or only relief, but instead you are drowning in contradiction. Begin with your voice uncertain, trying to land on one emotion. Then let yourself hear music that captures impossible duality—a song that makes you want to dance and cry simultaneously, that feels like coming home and running away at the same time. Let this complex internal soundscape give you permission to hold multiple truths at once. Your voice should move through anger, tenderness, resentment, love, grief, and joy—sometimes within the same sentence. End with your voice trembling not from weakness but from the sheer weight of feeling everything at once, of finally allowing the contradiction to exist without trying to resolve it.
inspired_by: Actor needs to fulfill the emotional obligation for a scene requiring heroic grandeur or a specific emotional quality they cannot generate from memory alone

title: Breaking Point: Protecting Your Child From Yourself
instruction: You're on the phone with your ex, and they're saying your child doesn't want to see you anymore. Your voice explodes—'That's not true! You're poisoning them against me!'—loud, fierce, desperate. You're yelling about your rights, your love, how dare they. But then you hear your child's voice in the background saying 'I don't want to talk to them,' and everything stops. Your voice drops, becomes small: 'Let me talk to them. Please.' They won't come to the phone. Your anger reignites, but it's different now—it's covering terror: 'You can't keep my child from me!' But even as you're shouting, your voice is breaking apart. You're begging now, bargaining: 'I'll do the program again, I'll do whatever you want.' Your voice cracks into raw honesty: 'I'm scared. I'm so scared I'm losing them.' Then, devastating realization—your voice barely above a whisper, shaking: 'Maybe they're better off.' You're crying now. 'Tell them... tell them I love them.' You hang up. In the silence after, you whisper to the empty room: 'I'm sorry.' Your voice is shattered.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours. They're conscious, holding your hand, and you need to tell them it's okay to let go—but you're not ready. Start with forced composure, trying to be strong for them, voice steady but brittle. 'I'll be okay, I promise.' But as you speak, something breaks open inside you. Your breath catches. You realize you're not giving them permission to die—you're begging them to stay, even though you know it's selfish. The words fracture between what you're supposed to say and what you desperately feel. End in a whispered confession of how terrified you are to be without them, your voice raw and small, like a child's.

title: Stumbling Through the Dark
instruction: You are a young woman with a high, girly voice, but you're drunk and furious, dragging a heavy, unconscious companion through a muddy forest at night. Your arms burn, your breath is ragged, and each step jars your bones. You start by hurling sarcastic, angry insults at your friend for getting you into this mess, your voice slurred and aggressive. But as you struggle uphill, the anger seeps into exhausted, raw pleas — your voice cracks from strain and tears, losing its playful edge. Let the physical exertion interrupt your words: grunt, gasp, stumble over syllables. End with a desperate, whispered realization that you're alone and out of strength.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Final Curtain Call: Applause and Ashes
instruction: You're taking your curtain call after the performance of your life, but you've just scattered your partner's ashes in the theater that morning—this was their dying wish. Begin with the projected, gracious stage voice accepting applause, that practiced 'Thank you, thank you so much' that performers use, bright and grateful and performing joy. Then let a laugh escape—genuine, unexpected, because you can almost hear your partner making a joke about the terrible reviews. That laugh should catch and transform mid-sound into a sob, then back to laughter, your voice dancing between grief and joy in a way that feels like madness and perfect sense simultaneously. Your final words should be whispered toward the empty seats where your partner always sat, intimate and just for them: 'We did it, baby. You're here. You're still here.' Mix profound gratitude for the life you shared with the breaking agony of doing this alone, finding strange peace in honoring their memory exactly as they wanted, even as your heart disintegrates.

title: Breathing the Same Air
instruction: It is three in the morning. You and your lover are lying in near-darkness, so close you can feel each other's breath. You have something to confess that could end everything. Let yourself feel the exact temperature of the sheets, the weight of their arm across you, the rhythm of their breathing. Hear the tiny sounds—their heartbeat if you're close enough, the creak of the bed, distant night sounds outside. Smell their skin, their hair, the room you've shared. See what little you can in the darkness—the outline of their face, shadows, perhaps a sliver of moonlight. Begin in terrified silence, your body tight with the secret you're holding. As you finally whisper your confession, let the sensory intimacy of this moment—the physical closeness, the darkness, the vulnerability of near-sleep—transform your fear into something rawer: perhaps devastating honesty, or quiet relief, or the aching awareness that tenderness and loss can exist in the same breath.

title: The Last Conversation with Your Childhood Home
instruction: You're standing in your childhood bedroom for the final time before it's sold. Your parent has just passed away, and strangers will move in tomorrow. Instead of simply remembering, speak TO the room itself—to the walls, the window, the closet door. Start with playful gratitude: ask the creaky floorboard what secrets it kept, thank the window for all the storms it showed you, laugh with the closet about the person you were when you hid inside it. But as you speak, let the weight of permanent goodbye settle in. By the end, you're not playing anymore—you're genuinely devastated, whispering a final farewell to the only witness of your entire childhood. Let the transition from whimsical appreciation to raw grief happen naturally, as if the room itself is teaching you how to let go.
inspired_by: An actor finds sense memory work tedious and boring

title: The Transcribed Memory
instruction: You are an older man dictating an old letter into a transcription device, speaking aloud every punctuation mark in a flat, robotic tone at first. But as you read the words describing a quiet moment with someone you once loved, your voice begins to hesitate, slow, and catch—you lose your place, mutter a punctuation mark too late, and your tone shifts from mechanical monotone to a soft, contemplative interest. Let the dictation rhythm break naturally as the memory pulls you in, ending with a long, silent pause before you softly speak the final period.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Final Visit to a Dying Parent Who Never Knew You
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours, and you realize they never truly knew who you are. Start with careful, measured words trying to introduce yourself—really introduce yourself—for the first time: 'I need to tell you who I actually am.' Your voice is tender but urgent, racing against time. You're confessing dreams you never shared, the person you became when they weren't looking, the life you built in the shadows of their expectations. As you speak, the grief of all those invisible years builds until you're caught between wanting them to wake up and see you, and the devastating acceptance that they never will. Let your voice move from hopeful explanation to raw, whispered farewell, finding unexpected gratitude for even this late, one-sided moment of truth.

title: Tucking In the Emptiness
instruction: You're going through your nightly routine of tucking in your child—but your child died six months ago, and you still can't stop. Whisper the same gentle, silly bedtime story you always told, complete with the funny voices and the parts where you'd pause for their giggling interruptions. But this time, the silence where their laughter should be is deafening. Your voice should be tender, almost hypnotically soft, as if speaking too loudly will shatter the illusion. Let small cracks appear—a caught breath, a moment where you almost stop but force yourself to continue. End with 'Goodnight, sweetheart,' and then the devastating stillness after, where you finally acknowledge the empty room. The gentleness makes the grief more unbearable.
inspired_by: Doing Stand-Up Comedy in the Style of a Eulogy

title: The Weight of Good News
instruction: You're at a small dinner table with your adult children. You've just been diagnosed with something serious but treatable. You wanted to tell them casually, so you start with a cheerful tone, but your voice quivers. As you speak, you glance at each face, and the fear of their reactions grips you. But seeing them, your love overpowers everything. Your voice cracks, becomes heavy with affection. Let your delivery be halting, with natural pauses as you look at plates, take a sip of water, shift in your seat. End raw and heartfelt.
emotions_sampled: Hope/Optimism (slightly present), Fear (very intensely present), Affection (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Fierce Love That Cannot Save Them
instruction: You're trying to protect someone you love with every ounce of your being, but you're utterly powerless to stop what's happening to them. Begin with fierce, almost aggressive declarations—'I won't let this happen, I'll fix this'—your voice sharp with determination and protective rage. But reality keeps intruding, and your certainty starts to crack. Let the fury build until it breaks apart into helpless, gasping sobs, then reform into desperate bargaining, your voice raw and uncontrolled. You're cycling through rage at your own powerlessness, tender promises you can't keep, explosive denial, and devastating acceptance. Let your voice shred itself between screaming defiance and broken whispers. End in a place of shattered surrender, where your love remains absolutely fierce but you're acknowledging you cannot be their salvation, spoken with a voice that's been stripped bare by the collision of infinite love and finite power.

title: The Truth I Can No Longer Hide
instruction: You're confronting your parent about the childhood they gave you, but this time you have early dementia and you're terrified this is your last chance to be heard. Start with trembling anger: 'I need to say this before I lose the ability to say it at all. You were supposed to...' But the words fracture, and your fury collides with the humiliation of losing your articulation mid-confrontation. Your parent tries to deflect: 'You're not making sense.' This ignites something primal—rage mixed with desperation: 'Don't you dare use this against me! I know what you did!' But even as you say it, you stumble over memories that won't stay solid. By the end, your anger has broken into something raw and vulnerable: a child's voice asking, 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let the performance move from controlled fury to chaotic desperation to the devastating vulnerability of finally dropping all defenses.

title: Smoothness Skill
instruction: You're a master of ceremonies at a black-tie event, and every word flows like silk: 'Good evening, distinguished guests. Before we begin, I'd like to share a few thoughts.' Your voice is impeccably trained, smooth, polished to perfection. There's not a filler word, not a hesitation. 'Our honoree tonight has dedicated forty years to public service.' The smoothness is a skill you've honed for decades. Then your mind goes blank for a second — you lose the thread. You recover instantly with such smoothness that no one notices. But you do. Your smoothness was a mask, and underneath, you're terrified. You finish the introduction flawlessly: 'Please join me in welcoming...' The smoothness is technically perfect, but now you know the cost of maintaining it.

title: The Stench of Waking
instruction: You are an elderly woman who just woke from a deep, delicious nap in your favorite armchair. Your voice is thick and slow, your mind foggy. As you sit up, you smell something burnt and sour from the kitchen — last night's cabbage pot left on the stove. The disgust jolts you, making you snap with impatience, but your body still hums with the ecstasy of that warm, dreamy sleep. Let your voice start slow, almost dreamy, then curdle with irritation as you complain to yourself, then fade back into a reluctant acceptance, maybe even a grumpy chuckle, as you decide you'll have to get up.
emotions_sampled: Disgust (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (slightly present), Pleasure/Ecstasy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Weight of Letting Go
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hour. Begin by holding her hand, speaking to her about a trivial memory from childhood—your voice bright, almost artificially cheerful, refusing to acknowledge what's happening. As you speak, allow your body to feel increasingly heavy, as though gravity itself is pulling you down into the earth. Let this physical heaviness seep into your voice, slowing your words, deepening your breath. Gradually, the cheerful memory dissolves and you find yourself confessing something you've never said: how much you've needed her, how terrified you are to face life without her anchor. By the end, you're barely whispering, your body so heavy you can hardly hold yourself upright, speaking not to keep her here but to release both of you. The emotional journey moves from bright denial to crushing acceptance, from performance to raw truth.

title: Confessing to Your Sleeping Lover That You're Leaving Tomorrow
instruction: They're asleep beside you. You speak in barely-audible whispers, telling them everything you could never say while they were awake. Start with tender observations - how they look when they sleep, the small things you'll miss. Your voice is soft, intimate, full of love. But slowly, the confession deepens: why you have to leave, how staying would destroy you both, how loving them isn't enough. Each revelation makes your whisper thinner, more fragile. Include a moment where you almost touch them but pull back, and let that hesitation live in your voice. End with 'I'm so sorry' repeated three times - the first apologetic, the second breaking with grief, the third barely breath. The whole piece should feel like the most honest you've ever been because they can't hear you.
inspired_by: Listening to Your Partner Fantasize About Someone Else

title: Floating Prank
instruction: You're a teenage girl alone on a spacewalk outside a station, your helmet visor fogged and radio crackling. You spot a small object drifting toward you—a toy spaceship you recognize from your brother's room. At first you're deeply confused, muttering to yourself about what it could be, your breath loud in the helmet. Then astonishment hits as you realize it's his joke, a message from home. End with a gentle tease in your voice, almost laughing, while still catching your breath and adjusting your visor. Let the weird tinny sound and static shape your delivery, with natural pauses and shifts as you react to the floating object and your own surprise.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (very intensely present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Teasing (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Words You Never Rehearsed
instruction: You're sitting beside your father's hospital bed. He has minutes left, and you've spent your whole life preparing what you'd say at this moment—but now, nothing you rehearsed feels right. Start by trying to say the 'perfect' goodbye you planned, but let yourself stumble, contradict yourself, say things that surprise you. You begin wanting to sound strong and grateful, but allow whatever actually lives inside you to pour out—maybe it's anger at him for leaving, maybe it's a childhood memory, maybe it's something you never meant to confess. Let your words fail you, then find you again. By the end, you should have said something true you didn't know you needed to say. Don't plan where you'll end up—discover it as his breath grows slower.

title: The Weight of Your Wedding Ring
instruction: Late at night, lying beside your sleeping spouse of twenty years, you're turning your wedding ring around your finger in the darkness. Begin by feeling its physical presence: the weight, the temperature, how it's worn smooth, the slight indent it's left in your skin. Whisper about these sensations, letting the metal's reality anchor you. But as you focus on this simple object, let it become a key that unlocks a confession you've never spoken aloud—a dream you abandoned, a person you once loved, a version of yourself you buried. Keep your voice barely above a breath. Let the tangible sensation of the ring—its smoothness, its slight restriction—gradually reveal the tenderness, regret, and complicated love you feel. Move from describing the ring to whispering the truth about your heart. End with acceptance, still touching the ring, voice filled with fragile peace.
inspired_by: Actor working on material with strong emotional demands (suicide, grief, love) cannot access genuine feeling

title: The Taste of Broken Glass
instruction: You've just received news that drops you to your knees—a devastating diagnosis, a sudden death, a betrayal that shatters your world. Begin by naming aloud the physical sensations stopping you from processing this: the numbness, the way your hands are shaking, the strange taste in your mouth, how your vision seems wrong.
