Then start describing what you're literally seeing from where you've collapsed—the floor, your own hands, the light, any small detail. Let those sensory observations crack you open into the full physical and emotional reality of this moment. Your body and voice should reflect the visceral nature of grief or shock—maybe you're gasping, maybe keening, maybe moving between frozen stillness and violent feeling. Journey from shocked disconnection through raw sensory experience into a place where the emotional and physical pain merge into something almost unbearable but fully alive.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty starting the imaging process

title: Laughing Through Your Grandmother's Final Story
instruction: Your grandmother, hours from death, is telling you an outrageously funny story about her youth—something scandalous and completely unexpected. You're laughing, genuine and delighted: 'Grandma! You didn't!' Your voice is bright with surprise and joy. She keeps going, and you keep laughing, but tears are starting. You're laughing AND crying, the sounds mixing together until you can't tell which is which. The laughter has grief threaded through it. She finishes the story, and you're saying 'That's amazing' but your voice is completely breaking. Then she reaches for your hand and says something that makes you laugh again—but this time the laugh is pure heartbreak disguised as joy. Your final line—'I love you so much'—must somehow contain laughter, tears, gratitude, and goodbye all at once. The challenge is keeping the contradictions alive simultaneously: genuine humor existing in the same breath as devastating loss.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Was Never There
instruction: You are finally confronting your aging parent about their absence during your childhood - the recitals they missed, the hospital visits when you were alone, the moments you needed them and they chose something else. Start with careful, measured words, as if you've rehearsed this, trying to stay calm and rational. But as you speak, decades of suppressed hurt and anger begin pouring out. Your voice rises, cracks, becomes accusatory - then suddenly collapses into the voice of the child you once were, small and confused, asking 'Why wasn't I enough?' End with exhausted silence, having finally said what needed to be said, your anger giving way to profound grief for the relationship you never had. Move from controlled confrontation to explosive pain to defeated, heartbroken quiet.
inspired_by: The Brave Knight and the Cunning Sorceress

title: Molting in Moonlight
instruction: You are confessing a secret to your lover in whispers, but underneath your human skin something else is stirring. Begin curled small, perhaps on the floor or tucked into yourself, speaking so quietly they must lean in to hear. As you reveal your truth, allow your body to slowly unfurl—but not like a person stretching. Move like something emerging from a chrysalis, or a snake shedding skin, or a bird's wing slowly extending. Your voice might catch, might make sounds between words: soft clicking, gentle hissing, dove-like coos. Let your hands explore your own skin as if discovering it for the first time. The vulnerability here is in revealing not just your secret, but the non-human tenderness underneath your human mask. By the end, you should have transformed from tight and protected into something open and strange and beautiful, speaking the final words of your confession with a voice that wavers between human speech and pure sound.
inspired_by: Actor needs to access a nonverbal or primal subpersonality that does not respond to verbal techniques

title: Dancing in Your Kitchen After the Funeral
instruction: You're alone in the kitchen, clearing away casserole dishes from the funeral reception. Start with numb exhaustion, mechanically describing what you're doing. Then you find their favorite song on the radio—the one they always danced to—and something breaks open. You begin to laugh, really laugh, remembering how ridiculous they looked dancing, how alive they were. You're dancing now too, laughing through tears, voice bright with joy and absolutely shattered with grief at the same time. You're talking to them as if they're here, voice full of gratitude for every moment, every silly dance, every morning coffee. But the laughter keeps breaking into sobs, and the sobs keep turning back to laughter—it's all mixed up, beautiful and terrible at once. You're thanking them, cursing them for leaving, celebrating them, mourning them, all in the same breath. End with your voice soft and wondering, having found an inexplicable peace in the contradiction: 'I miss you so much, and I'm so grateful you were mine.'
inspired_by: Roller Coaster Mechanical Failure: Moment of Absolute Stillness

title: Grateful for the Wreckage
instruction: You're standing in the ruins of something that destroyed you—a ended relationship, a lost dream, a life you had to leave behind—and finding genuine gratitude mixed with grief. Begin with a half-laugh, half-sob: 'This is going to sound crazy, but... thank you.' Your voice is bewildered by your own words. As you continue, let contradictory emotions coexist: 'You broke my heart. You absolutely shattered me. And somehow—god, somehow—you also set me free.' Tears and laughter should genuinely intermingle, not performed but spontaneously arising. Speak to the paradox: 'I'm standing here with nothing left, and I've never felt more alive. How does that make sense?' Your voice carries both the weight of loss and the lightness of unexpected liberation. End with a moment of profound, peaceful chaos: 'I miss you and I'm glad you're gone. I'm devastated and I'm grateful. I'm broken and I'm whole.' Let your voice be soft, wondering, filled with the strange beauty of surviving yourself.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before You Leave
instruction: You're standing beside your child's bed at 3 AM, knowing you won't see them again—perhaps you're dying and chose to spare them the hospital farewell, or you're leaving to protect them from danger, or you've made an impossible choice. Whisper to them while they sleep. Start by memorizing their face, describing what you see with aching tenderness. 'Your hair is getting so long. You have your grandmother's hands.' Let your voice catch on the small details—the stuffed animal they still sleep with, the way they breathe. Tell them all the things you want them to know: how to be brave, that none of this is their fault, that you'll love them beyond death or distance. Your voice should be barely audible, thick with tears you're trying to swallow so you won't wake them. End with the moment you have to physically leave, your whispered 'I'm so sorry' mixing with a broken 'I love you,' and the quiet devastation of walking away from everything that matters.
inspired_by: Emergency Dispatcher: Staying Calm While Hearing Horror

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your father after years of silence, and you've finally found the words. Start with controlled anger—your voice is measured, almost cold, as you list what you needed and never received. But as you speak, the anger begins to tremble. Underneath it is a child's desperate question: 'Why wasn't I enough?' Let your voice break from accusation into pleading, then catch yourself, pull back into anger, then break again. This isn't a clean emotional arc—it's messy, cycling between rage and heartbreak. End with exhausted honesty: you still love him, you hate that you love him, and you're done waiting for him to become who you needed. Your final words should sound like someone setting down a weight they've carried for decades.

title: The Confession That Destroys Everything
instruction: You're confessing something explosive to someone you love—infidelity, a terrible lie you've maintained for years, a betrayal that will shatter their world—and you start with fierce conviction that honesty is necessary, that they deserve the truth. Your voice is strong, almost defiant, as you begin. But as you watch their face change, as the reality of what you're destroying hits you, your certainty crumbles. Your voice becomes desperate, trying to make them understand, to contextualize, then begging them to say something, anything. When they finally respond with quiet devastation or cold fury, you break completely—your words tumbling out in panicked attempts to take it back, to fix it, oscillating between defensive rage ('You made me feel so alone!') and helpless sobbing. End in barely coherent anguish, your voice raw and shattered, as you realize you've just destroyed the most important relationship in your life and there's no undoing it.

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospice Room
instruction: You're calling your estranged sibling from your hospital bed, knowing this is likely your final conversation. Start with careful, almost formal politeness—you haven't spoken in years. Your voice is weak but controlled as you try to explain why you called. Then something breaks: a childhood memory surfaces, and your voice softens with unexpected tenderness. You're apologizing, but not for what they expect—for something deeper, something you both never named. Your breath is shallow, labored. You realize mid-sentence that you're running out of time, not just for this call, but for everything. Your voice becomes urgent, almost desperate, trying to fit a lifetime of unspoken love into moments. End with a quiet acceptance, your voice dropping to barely a whisper, as you tell them something you should have said decades ago. The emotion shifts from distant awkwardness to raw vulnerability to peaceful release.
inspired_by: MRI Claustrophobia Peak: Panicking in the Machine

title: The Spirit Falls
instruction: You're at a cramped revival tent, standing among swaying strangers. You came out of curiosity, arms crossed, feeling distant. But the music swells, the preacher's voice rises, and something unexpected breaks inside you. Start with a hesitant, almost sarcastic observation about the heat and the singing. Let your words stumble as a wave of emotion catches you off guard. By the end, your voice lifts into a breathless, trembling chant of 'Yes, yes, I feel it,' your pitch climbing, your words fragmenting into laughter and tears as you surrender to the rapture.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You burst into the room, voice loud and sharp with rage: 'You want me to be present? You want me HERE?' Your words are weapons: 'I have been drowning trying to be present for everyone—for you, for the kids, for my job, for every person who needs something from me!' Let your voice crack as the anger turns to desperation: 'And nobody asks if I need someone to be present for ME!' You're pacing, explosive, then suddenly you stop and your voice drops to something raw and broken: 'I am so tired. I am so unspeakably tired of being the one who shows up.' Tears start to come through the anger: 'When was the last time someone asked if I was okay and actually waited for the real answer?' Your voice becomes almost childlike, helpless: 'I don't know how to ask for what I need because I've spent so long pretending I don't need anything.' By the end, you're on the floor, voice quiet but fierce with truth: 'I can't be present for anyone else until someone is fully, completely, devastatingly present for me. And I'm terrified nobody will be.' The arc moves from explosive rage to helpless vulnerability to desperate, fierce self-advocacy.

title: The Last Mask
instruction: You’re an older man in a hospital bed, wearing a CPAP mask that hisses and muffles your voice. You’re talking to your son who just told you he’s moving across the country. Start with a thick sourness—you’re bitter and disappointed that he’s leaving, feeling abandoned. Then, as you speak, a reluctant relief seeps in: you realize this is good for him. Let the mask distort your voice; you have to push words out against the hiss. End with a quiet, tired acceptance, the sourness still there but softer, and the relief a little sadder.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (extremely present), Relief (clearly present), Sourness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Fever Breaking
instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical sensation—a fever breaking, the aftermath of violent passion, the collapse after rage, the shaking release of held pain. Your body is trembling, sweating, electrified. Speak your experience out loud, but let every impulse—the desire to laugh, to sob, to curse, to pray, to make sounds that aren't words—flow through your voice. Don't describe the sensation politely. Let your speech fragment when the physical overwhelms you. Let pleasure mix with pain, relief with grief, exhaustion with wild energy. If you need to gasp, moan, shout, or fall silent mid-word, do it. Begin in the thick of the physical intensity, and by the end, arrive somewhere unexpected—perhaps rage turns to awe, agony becomes ecstasy, or chaos settles into devastating clarity. Your voice should be utterly hijacked by what your body is actually feeling.
inspired_by: Actor notices split between what they feel and what they perform; suppresses non-scene-consistent impulses

title: Mother, I Needed You - The Confrontation That Never Happened
instruction: You're finally confronting your mother about the emotional absence that shaped your life. Begin with that same flat, disconnected tone: 'You were there. You fed me. You drove me to school.' Reciting facts without feeling. But then something shifts - maybe she says 'I did my best' or looks away. Suddenly the numbness cracks and years of buried anger, hurt, and desperate need pour out. 'I NEEDED you to see me!' Your voice breaks between rage and pleading. You oscillate wildly - furious accusations dissolving into vulnerable confession: 'I'm so angry... but I just wanted you to love me.' End in exhausted honesty, voice raw and small, finally admitting the truth beneath the numbness. The journey is from protective disconnection to dangerous, painful aliveness.

title: The Shake of Truth
instruction: You are a teenager riding in the back of an old pickup truck on a gravel road, the rusted bed vibrating under you. You just found a crumpled note in your jacket pocket that suggests a friend you trusted has been lying to you. Start with confused disbelief as you read the words, your voice jittering from the bumps. As the truck rattles on, end with a slow, quiet realization that feels heavier than the shaking, your tone dropping into a raw, hurt stillness despite the trembling.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Photograph That Burns
instruction: You've just discovered a photograph in your deceased mother's belongings—it's you as a baby, being held by a man who is not your father. The photograph is in your hand, and you can feel every detail: the glossy paper, the creased corner, the slight discoloration from age. Your fingers keep touching the faces, your infant self, this stranger's smile. Begin with shock that's almost physical—your hand trembling violently, your breath catching, the paper shaking so hard you almost drop it. Let the photograph be a live wire, something that sends jolts through your whole body. As you stare at it, your emotion should transform from pure shock into a wild cocktail of fury, betrayal, dark laughter at the absurdity, then a strange, unexpected tenderness for your mother who kept this secret. Let your body react to the photograph as if it's burning your fingers—but you can't let it go. End with clutching it to your chest, your voice breaking between rage-sobbing and something like wonder.

title: The Weight of Silence After the Battle
instruction: You are a middle-aged history professor in a large lecture hall, speaking without a microphone. You’re describing the aftermath of a famous battle to a room full of students. Begin with your practiced ‘teacher voice’—projected, deliberate, hitting key terms like ‘decisive victory’ and ‘turning point.’ As you recount the number of dead, you pause. You shift your weight, glance at your notes, then look up. Your voice loses its projection, becomes quieter, slower—almost as if you’re realizing the human cost for the first time. End with a single, understated sentence that hangs in the air, filled with quiet contemplation.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Parent: The Toothbrush Your Mother Never Bought
instruction: You're in your childhood bathroom, holding a new toothbrush—something small, something basic your parent never provided. Begin speaking to your absent mother or father with quiet, controlled anger about the neglect hidden in mundane details: how you went to school with unbrushed teeth, how no one taught you these basic acts of self-care, how shame became your morning ritual. As you finally brush your teeth properly—maybe for the first time with real care—let your anger shift. Feel the grief underneath: you're mourning the parent who should have taught you to take care of yourself. End with a raw mixture of rage and heartbreak, the toothbrush trembling in your hand as you realize you're giving yourself what they never could. Let your voice crack between accusations and desperate longing for what should have been.
inspired_by: Brushing Your Teeth with Refreshing Mint Toothpaste

title: What We Never Said
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your partner in the dark, unable to sleep. Begin in barely audible whispers: 'Are you awake?' There's something you've carried for months, years maybe. 'I need to tell you something.' Your voice is so quiet it's almost not there, fragile as spider silk. 'Sometimes when you touch me, I disappear inside myself.' You're confessing something so tender, so vulnerable it hurts to speak. 'It's not your fault. It's just... what they did to me before you.' Each word costs you everything. Your breath catches, tears sliding silent down your face. 'I'm so afraid you'll leave when you really know me.' A long pause. Then, softer still: 'Please don't leave.' This isn't performance—it's the sound of a heart undefended.

title: The Last Shift Before Letting Go
instruction: You are a young woman working the night shift in a cavernous warehouse, your voice naturally high and soft, but tonight you've had a few drinks to dull the ache of quitting this job. You're alone in a distant aisle, and the echoey hum of machinery and distant forklift beeps fill the space. Start by speaking to yourself in a giggly, self-mocking way, almost proud of your decision, but as you hear the hum of the factory you've spent a year in, your voice wobbles — you're suddenly overwhelmed by the weight of leaving and the loneliness of this moment. Let your words drift, lose their thread, catch on a memory, and end with a quiet, honest crack in your voice as you whisper your final goodbye to the empty space.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Gratitude for What's Destroying Me
instruction: You're speaking to someone you love deeply—a partner, a parent, a child—who you must let go of for their own good, or who is leaving you. Begin with genuine, overflowing gratitude, thanking them for the ways they've changed your life, your voice warm and full. But let that gratitude become increasingly painful—because beneath it lies the terror of losing them, the anger that this is happening, the grief that's already beginning. Your voice should oscillate between tender appreciation and barely suppressed panic. You're trying so hard to be brave, to give them a beautiful goodbye, but you're also terrified and heartbroken. By the end, find a place where all these feelings exist simultaneously—grateful and devastated, loving and angry, accepting and afraid. Let your voice crack on words of thanks that double as expressions of loss.
inspired_by: When you are building a character who must be genuinely terrified or in extreme fear

title: The Last Morning Before Deployment
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child before leaving for a deployment you may not return from. Begin with forced cheerfulness as you make breakfast together, your voice bright but with a tremor underneath: 'Remember, you put the chocolate chips in after the batter, not before.' As reality sets in, your composure starts cracking—your voice becomes softer, more honest: 'I need you to know how proud I am of you.' The final moments require you to hold your child, and your voice breaks completely as you whisper promises you desperately hope you can keep: 'I will do everything I can to come back to you.' End in a moment of fierce, protective love mixed with the devastating knowledge that you cannot guarantee anything. Let your voice move from cheerful denial through tender honesty to raw, unguarded grief.
inspired_by: Principal Meeting: When a Student is in Crisis

title: The Last Time I Saw You Laugh
instruction: You're packing up the belongings of someone you loved who died suddenly—a partner, a best friend, a sibling. You find something unexpected: a video on their phone of them laughing, completely joyful, from just days before they died. Start by laughing with them, caught up in the pure happiness of seeing them alive and radiant. Let the laughter be real and full. But as you watch them, fully alive and unaware of what's coming, feel the grief begin to rise even as you're still laughing. Allow these two enormous emotions to exist simultaneously—joy at seeing them so vital, and anguish that they're gone. Let your laughter crack and merge with sobbing until you can't tell which is which. Your body might shake with both. By the end, let gratitude emerge through the pain—thank them aloud for existing, for loving you, even as you break apart missing them.

title: The Garden Party: Celebrating Your Dying Friend Who Made You Promise to Laugh
instruction: You're hosting a celebration for your closest friend who has weeks to live—and they made you swear: no sadness, only joy, one last perfect day in the garden they loved. You're telling stories, making toasts, and your voice is bright with genuine laughter because the memories are truly funny, truly beautiful. But the laughter keeps catching in your throat, morphing into something else. You find yourself grateful and shattered at once—thanking them for a lifetime of love while your heart is screaming at the injustice. Your voice dances between joy and devastation, sometimes mid-sentence. There's fierce celebration mixed with quiet panic. You keep honoring their wish for lightness, then grief ambushes you, then you pull yourself back to laughter because you promised. End with a toast that is simultaneously a love letter, a thank you, and a goodbye—your voice full of wonder at how much beauty you've shared, breaking with the knowledge that this is the last time, somehow finding peace in the impossible contradiction of celebrating while losing everything.
inspired_by: Historical: Witness to Atrocity Must Testify Against Perpetrators Now in Power

title: Laughing Through the Eulogy
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone who made you promise not to be sad. Start with a memory that makes you genuinely laugh, your voice warm and bright: 'She made me swear—actually made me put my hand on her favorite book and swear—that I wouldn't cry today.' You're smiling, almost giddy with the absurdity: 'She said if I cried, she'd haunt me. And knowing her, she absolutely would.' But the laughter starts cracking. Tears mix with giggles: 'God, I miss her. I miss her so much and it's only been three days and I don't know how to...' You're laughing and crying simultaneously: 'She was ridiculous and bossy and the best thing that ever happened to me.' End with your voice full of both joy and devastation: 'I'm so grateful. I'm so broken. And somehow both of those things are okay.' The contradictory emotions must coexist authentically—finding light in the darkness, peace in the grief.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you years ago, and they've just said a casual, cheerful 'hello' as if no time has passed. Begin with controlled anger—your hello back is cold, measured, designed to wound. You start listing what you needed from them, what their absence cost you, your voice growing sharper with each revelation. Then something shifts: beneath the rage, you find the frightened child who just wanted to be wanted. Your voice becomes raw, vulnerable, asking the questions you were too young to ask then: 'Why wasn't I enough? What was wrong with me?' By the end, you're exhausted, depleted, but there's a terrible clarity. You're saying goodbye to the fantasy of who they might have been, hello to accepting who they actually are. Your last words carry both grief for what you'll never have and the painful freedom of letting go.

title: The Third Night
instruction: You're a retired soldier working a graveyard security shift, haven't slept in over 48 hours. Staring at a monitor, you see a face you buried 30 years ago—your dead partner. Astonishment hits first: a jolt of disbelief, a dry laugh. Then distress creeps in—paranoia, rage at the impossible. Your voice starts steady but unravels: sentences break off, you mutter to the empty room, micro-sleeps swallow words. You argue with the screen, then catch yourself. Speak as if your mind is glitching, emotions swinging wildly between shock and panic. Deliver 50–70 words, raw and failing.
emotions_sampled: Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Distress (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Lover Before You Leave Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM. They're asleep beside you, and you're leaving—not because you don't love them, but because you do, and staying will destroy you both. Speak in hushed tones, as if any louder will shatter this last moment of pretending. Tell them everything you couldn't say when they were awake: how beautiful they are in sleep, how you've memorized every breath, how leaving is the only way to save what's left of yourself. Your voice catches on confessions of inadequacy, of not being who they needed, of loving them so much it became a kind of drowning. Touch grows into your voice—the ghost of fingertips trailing their face one last time. End with a broken whisper of gratitude for the time you had, your voice dissolving as you realize this is truly the last time you'll ever see them. Let the silence after your final word hold everything you couldn't say.
inspired_by: Interrogated by Police While Injured and Lying

title: Final Lap
instruction: You are a woman in your 40s, swimming laps in a quiet indoor pool, pushing through the last 50 meters of a personal best attempt. Your body burns with exhaustion, but your mind is locked on the finish. Speak in short, gasping bursts as you turn your head to breathe—your words are punched out between strokes, sometimes cut off by a splash or a gulp of water. Start with fierce concentration, muttering to yourself about pacing and your sore shoulder. As you touch the wall, your voice breaks into a raw, sputtering cry of triumph—you did it, you beat your time. Let the wet, hollow pool sound and your ragged breathing shape every syllable.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Love
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're whispering to your partner who's asleep beside you, confessing something you can't say when they're awake. Your voice is barely audible, tender and terrified: 'I'm so scared I'm not enough for you.' This is the quietest kind of devastation—intimate, raw, catching in your throat. You're listing all your secret fears, your inadequacies, the ways you think you're failing them. Your voice trembles: 'Sometimes I look at you and can't believe you chose me.' There are tears you're trying to keep silent. By the end, you touch their face gently, your voice filled with desperate, aching love mixed with deep sadness: 'Please don't wake up and realize you made a mistake.' It's a prayer and a confession and a moment of profound vulnerability.

title: Unclenching the Fist
instruction: You're confronting your father who walked out fifteen years ago and has suddenly reappeared wanting reconciliation. Begin with your entire body coiled like a spring—fists clenched, voice sharp and contained, every muscle holding fifteen years of abandonment. As you speak, start with accusations, but slowly, something shifts. Maybe he says the one thing you needed to hear, or maybe you simply see how broken he is too. Let your physical tension gradually dissolve—first your jaw softens, then your fists slowly open, your breathing deepens. By the end, you're not forgiving him, but you're no longer carrying that rage in your body. Your final words come out quieter, not weak, but released—transformed from a clenched fist to an open, empty hand.

title: After the Knots Take Hold
instruction: You're lying on your back, wrists bound above your head to a headboard, ankles loosely tied. The scene has just ended — your partner is untangling the rope from your ankle. Your body is still tense from the strain, breathing shallow and fast. You're relieved it's over, that you're safe, but a deep sadness swells inside you — you don't want to say it out loud, but something is ending. Let your voice catch and drop, words pushed out between breaths — maybe you shift, a rope creaks, you lose your train of thought halfway through. End on a quiet, sad admission.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispering to the Dying
instruction: You're lying beside your partner in hospice during their final hours. The room is quiet except for their labored breathing. You're whispering memories, your voice barely audible: 'Remember the rain in Portugal?' Start with gentle reminiscence, trying to keep your voice steady, almost normal. But as you feel their hand growing colder, your whispers become more urgent, more fragile. You're simultaneously trying to comfort them and keep them here: 'Please don't go yet.' Your voice catches on words, breaks mid-sentence, reforms. There's tenderness so deep it hurts, gratitude for every year, and terror of the silence coming. You're whispering 'I love you' over and over, each repetition slightly different—some steady, some breaking, some barely breath. By the end, your voice becomes the quietest it's been, accepting what's happening while your heart shatters. Your voice should sound like devotion itself, like someone holding on and letting go simultaneously.

title: The Crack in the Chant
instruction: You are an older woman on a street corner, shouting into a restless crowd without a microphone. Your voice is hoarse, strained, and you fall into a repetitive, high-pitched rhythm as you urge people to listen. You begin with defiant, almost robotic energy, hammering the same phrase again and again to hold their attention. But as you push through, the memory of why you are here—a child lost to violence—breaks through the cadence. Your voice stumbles, your pitch wavers, and you lose the script, speaking now directly to one person in the front row, your pain raw and unguarded. Let the silence between your words carry the weight of what you cannot say.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You are alone in your apartment after receiving devastating news. Your body is your instrument: begin pacing, breathing rapidly, heart racing, speaking in fragmented bursts as panic and disbelief course through you—your voice high and tight, words tumbling out as you try to make sense of what just happened. Let your body shift: suddenly you're on the floor, voice low and hollow, speaking in a stunned, dissociated monotone, as if watching yourself from outside. Then feel rage ignite in your core: stand, voice becoming guttural and fierce, letting sounds of pure fury escape—curse, yell, let your body shake with it. Finally, as the storm passes, let exhaustion and a strange, quiet acceptance settle in: your voice drops to something almost peaceful, speaking slowly about what comes next, your breathing finally evening out. Move through these physical and vocal states as genuine bodily experiences, not performed emotions.

title: Bitter Toast
instruction: You're a young man with a deep, rough voice, hiding in the shadow of a crowded party. Across the room, your best friend is kissing the person you've secretly wanted for months. Your first reaction is a rush of genuine ecstasy—you're thrilled for them, it's beautiful. But as you watch, a hot wave of jealousy crashes over you. You clamp your hand hard over your mouth to stop any sound escaping. Speak your thoughts in muffled, choked whispers. Let your voice start with a happy, breathless sigh, then slowly darken as envy twists your throat. Consonants like 'p' and 'b' come out blurred, words stumble. End with a quiet, trembling 'I'm happy... really' that sounds more broken than joyful.
emotions_sampled: Pleasure/Ecstasy (very intensely present), Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Letter Home
instruction: You're recording a message for your child, knowing you won't survive the journey ahead—maybe space exploration, a fatal diagnosis, or a dangerous mission. Start with forced brightness, trying to pack a lifetime of advice into minutes: 'Listen, kiddo, here's what I need you to know.' Your voice is steady, practical, almost cheerful. But as you continue, the facade cracks. 'Your mother will... she'll be there for you.' Now you're fighting tears, your throat tight. By the end, let yourself break completely—whisper the words you've been holding back, the raw 'I love you' that comes from the deepest part of your soul. Move from protective strength to devastating vulnerability, from the parent you're trying to be to the terrified human you actually are.

title: The Toast That Changed Everything
instruction: You're an older man, alone in your kitchen, just after hanging up the phone. Your long-lost war buddy is alive and coming home. You pour a glass of whiskey, lift it, and start speaking to yourself in a low, hushed voice—gratitude making your hand tremble. Mid-sentence you gulp the whiskey; the liquid sloshes, your voice chokes on the gulp, then releases with a wet gasp. As the warmth hits, elation explodes—you laugh, your voice cracking, tears welling, spoken words tumbling out faster and louder. End with a booming, tearful shout of pure joy, still holding the empty glass.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Finding Your Childhood Home Before Demolition
instruction: You've returned to the house where you grew up, now empty and scheduled for demolition tomorrow. You're standing in what was once your bedroom, and you're talking to someone—maybe a friend, maybe yourself, maybe the walls. Start by laughing—genuinely laughing—as you remember something absurd and beautiful: the time you tried to fly off the roof, or your first kiss in this very spot. Your voice is full of warmth and nostalgia. But as you move through the space, touching the walls, your laughter becomes softer, tinged with tears. You're describing how safe you felt here, how small and magical the world seemed. Your voice breaks as you remember the day everything changed—a death, a divorce, the moment childhood ended. You're crying now, but you're also smiling through it, because the pain and the beauty are inseparable. By the end, you're saying goodbye to the child you were, forgiving them, thanking them. Your voice is full of contradictions: grief and gratitude, loss and liberation, sadness and strange, surprising joy. You're letting go, and it hurts, and it's right.

title: When Protection Isn't Enough
instruction: You're a parent or guardian confronting someone who hurt a child you love, or you're facing the moment you realize you failed to protect them when they needed you most. Begin with controlled, ice-cold rage—your voice tight, dangerous, barely restrained. Let that fury build and sharpen as you speak. Then have it shatter completely into helpless, body-shaking sobs and self-recrimination. You couldn't stop it. You weren't there. Your fierce protectiveness means nothing if you can't actually protect them. End with a raw, almost animal sound of grief mixed with a whispered vow—a promise that comes from somewhere primal and unbreakable, even as you know you're only human and fallible.

title: Being Seen
instruction: One person is truly seeing another person, and the person being seen feels the impact of that seeing. The voice of the person seeing is calm, clear, accepting. They're articulating what they perceive: your goodness, your struggle, your complexity, your worth. The voice of the person being seen wavers—they've rarely been truly seen. Their voice carries the vulnerability of being known. By the end, both voices reflect the profound power of being truly seen. The person who was seen carries themselves differently. Being seen transforms how we see ourselves.

title: The Third Wheel on the Couch
instruction: You're curled up next to your partner on a cramped loveseat, your head resting against their shoulder. You've been trying to get their full attention for the last ten minutes, but they keep glancing at their phone, laughing at a message from a friend you've always found a little too charming. Start with irritable accusation—your voice is tight, a little clipped, because you feel dismissed. Let that irritation soften as you lean in closer, your voice dropping into a creaky, amused whisper that reveals both your jealousy and your affection, ending with a teasing warning that's half a joke, half real. Speak as if you're so close your lips almost brush their ear.
emotions_sampled: Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present), Amusement (slightly present), Jealousy & Envy (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Blinded by Pride
instruction: You're a 17-year-old boy who stormed out of the house after a fight with your father. Now you're standing in the middle of a blizzard, teeth chattering, shouting into the white void. Start with contempt — your jaw is tight, words sharp and spat out, mocking your dad's warnings. But as the wind howls and you lose your sense of direction, that contempt cracks into uncertainty. Let your voice break from a forced bravado to a shaky plea as you realize you're truly lost. End with a raw call into the storm, a mix of stubbornness and fear.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Taking a Bite of a Juicy Peach
instruction: Sink your teeth into a fresh peach, feeling the juice run down your fingers. Describe the burst of sweetness, the soft, tender texture of the fruit as it melts on your tongue, and the slight tang that lingers. Speak with a tone of pure enjoyment, as if each bite of the peach brings a bright, refreshing burst of summer.

title: Unpinning the Butterfly
instruction: You are confronting your mother/father about a truth you've carried alone for twenty years—something they did, or failed to do, that has shaped your entire life. Start with your body coiled tight, voice sharp and accusatory, fueled by years of compressed rage. As you speak, notice how exhausting it is to hold this anger in your muscles, how much effort it takes to keep your spine rigid and your fists clenched. Midway through, let something shift—perhaps they don't defend themselves, or perhaps you see their age and fragility. Feel the anger begin to drain from your body like water finding cracks in a dam. Your voice softens involuntarily, becomes more liquid, more human. By the end, you are not forgiving them, but you are so tired of carrying this weight that you let it pour out of you onto the ground between you both. The confrontation ends not in resolution, but in the profound exhaustion of finally setting down something impossibly heavy.

title: The Weight of Old Wounds
instruction: You're a young man with chronic back pain, sitting in a creaky wooden chair that digs into your spine. Across from you is the person who betrayed you years ago, now begging for forgiveness. As you speak, every shift of your body sends a spike of pain, forcing you to pause, wince, and breathe sharply. Begin with a voice thick with malice — cold, deliberate, savoring your power. But as the pain wears you down, the rage gives way to a heavy, aching sadness. End with a broken, quiet confession — the bitterness still there, but now drowned in sorrow. Let the pain dictate your rhythm, your sighs, the catch in your throat.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (extremely present), Sadness (very intensely present), Bitterness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Kitchen Table Reckoning: Confronting Your Mother
instruction: You're home for the holidays. You've rehearsed this conversation a thousand times. Start with your voice shaking but determined as you tell your mother you need to talk about your childhood—really talk. She deflects. You push harder, your voice gaining an edge. 'No, Mom, you don't get to change the subject this time.' Your words become sharper, more specific, naming things that were never named. The anger builds—you're finally saying it all. But then she starts crying, and you hate yourself for it, and your voice cracks with frustration: 'Don't—don't do that.' Your rage collides with your love for her. Your voice drops to something almost pleading: 'I just needed you to see me.' End in the terrible quiet between you, your breathing uneven, realizing she might never be able to give you what you need. Your final words are soft, defeated, but somehow accepting: 'I know.'
inspired_by: Karate Tournament Final: Facing Your Abuser

title: The Joke That Wasn't Funny
instruction: You're at a small gathering, surrounded by friends who've been teasing you about your recent breakup. You've been laughing along, playing the tough guy, but when someone makes a gentle comment about how you must be handling it, your mask suddenly slips. Start by trying to brush it off with a loud, forced laugh and a confident 'Nah, I'm good,' but let your voice crack on the last word. As the room goes quiet, feel the embarrassment flood in—your pitch drops, your breath gets shallow, and you trail off into a barely audible admission: 'Actually, I'm not okay.' Immediately after, let out a nervous little laugh to try to pull the armor back on, but it sounds hollow. Let the transition be messy: a shaky inhale, a pause where you lose your train of thought, then the vulnerable truth slipping out against your will.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Locket
instruction: You're a 15-year-old girl caught stealing your grandmother's locket from your older cousin's room. Your cousin has your phone and is about to call your mom. You plead, voice cracking and high, words tumbling out before she can dial. Start in frantic desperation, promising anything—then realize she's unmoved, and your voice drops, becomes hollow and ashamed as you admit why you did it. Fidget with your sleeve, look at the floor, let your breath hitch. End with a raw, quiet confession.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Wave
instruction: You are a weathered man in his 80s, body failing, mind still sharp with old resentments. You have just been intimate, and now the final orgasm is building. As it crests, let out a raw, involuntary sound — not pleasure, but a guttural release of decades of bitterness. After, your voice is a wreck: hoarse, gasping, cracking. You try to speak, but each wave of after-shock cuts you off, your words a broken whisper. Start with a groan of distress, end with a bitter, half-laughing murmur that trails into silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Breaking Open
instruction: You are alone in your apartment after a betrayal so complete it has shattered your sense of reality—a lover's infidelity discovered, a friend's decades-long lie revealed, a trust destroyed. You begin in shock, numb, pacing mechanically, speaking the facts aloud as if reporting news. Your body is rigid, your voice flat. But your body holds the emotional truth your mind is protecting you from. As you speak, let your body begin to rebel against the numbness—your hands might start shaking, your chest might tighten until you can't breathe properly, your legs might give out. Let the physical sensations crack open the emotional dam. Move from numb recitation into physical rage—throw something, kick something, let your body express what your controlled voice cannot. Then let that rage collapse into devastation. End on the floor, body exhausted, voice raw, in a place of broken-open grief that is somehow more honest than where you started.
inspired_by: Actor has difficulty exposing aspects of themselves onstage

title: Accepting the Award I Don't Deserve
instruction: You're standing at a podium accepting recognition for something you achieved, but you're flooded with impostor syndrome—you're certain everyone will realize you're a fraud. Begin with a trembling smile, hands gripping the podium, voice artificially bright and grateful while terror screams underneath. As you speak, you can feel yourself starting to crack. Then, mid-speech, you stop pretending. You admit it: 'I'm absolutely terrified standing here. Part of me is convinced I don't deserve this.' Feel the room hold its breath. But as you continue, something unexpected emerges—gratitude. Real, deep gratitude that you get to do work that scares you this much, that matters enough to make you vulnerable. Your voice steadies not because the fear is gone, but because you've stopped fighting it. By the end, you're speaking with tears streaming down your face, but they're tears of fierce joy mixed with lingering terror—you're celebrating the fact that you care enough to be afraid, and that caring is what makes the work sacred.
inspired_by: An actor fears their fear will be detected by the director and crew

title: The Secret in Your Hands
instruction: You are lying in bed beside your partner in the dark, both awake but pretending to sleep. You're holding a secret that will change everything between you. Begin by simply being aware of their breathing, the warmth of their body beside yours, the familiar weight of them in the bed. Let yourself really feel their presence before you speak. When you finally whisper that you need to tell them something, let your voice be barely audible, fragile as glass. The confession should start with fear and shame, but as you speak the truth aloud in this intimate darkness, allow yourself to discover unexpected relief, even a strange tenderness. End with your voice steadier but still soft, transformed by the act of being truly seen.
inspired_by: Actor's relationship with scene partner feels artificial, uninvested, or routine; the emotional relationship demanded by material is not being felt

title: The Museum of What Was
instruction: You're packing up a home after a profound loss—a death, a divorce, an estrangement—and you find an object that stops you cold. Start bitter and mechanical, just wanting to finish this painful task. But then let curiosity ambush you. Pick up the object and begin asking it questions out loud: Who bought this? What day was that? Who were we then? Let yourself become a detective of your own lost life, asking questions that hurt and heal simultaneously. Feel gratitude for what was and rage at what's gone, joy at the memories and despair that you can't ask the person who's missing to fill in the details. End in a place where your curiosity has transformed the object from a painful reminder into a portal—where asking questions about the past has somehow made you devastatingly alive in the present.
inspired_by: Actor has lost curiosity or feels bored by the world

title: The Sniffly Apology
instruction: You are a boy, maybe nine years old, home sick from school with a bad head cold. Your mother is in the other room on an important call, but you desperately need to tell her you accidentally broke her favorite vase while trying to get a tissue. You stand in the hallway, clutching the sticky receiver of a toy phone, sweat on your forehead, nose running. You start with a muffled, ashamed confession, your voice thick and nasal, sniffling between words. As you speak, you realize she might be angrier about the interruption than the vase, so your distress grows into a choked, fearful plea. End with your voice cracking, a tear mixing with the mucus on your cheek.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Counting Sugar Grains
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're sitting alone at your kitchen table, unable to sleep, stirring sugar into tea you don't intend to drink. In a whisper—as if speaking too loudly will shatter something fragile inside you—begin describing the tiny sensory details with obsessive precision: the sound of the spoon against porcelain, the way individual sugar crystals catch the light before dissolving, the heat radiating up through the cup into your palm, the particular smell of chamomile mixing with honey. You're using this intense sensory focus to avoid thinking about what you need to confess tomorrow, but as you describe each minute sensation, the truth keeps slipping through: the metallic taste of fear in your mouth that has nothing to do with tea, the trembling in your hands that makes the liquid ripple, the tightness in your chest that won't release. Let your whispered descriptions become more halting, more honest, until you're no longer describing the tea at all but finally, quietly, admitting the truth you've been avoiding—and in that admission, feel your body slowly, tentatively, begin to release its grip on the fear.

title: Crevasse Rescue: Hearing the Rope Appear Above You
instruction: You're in a crevasse, hanging in darkness, and your voice is small and mostly gone. You're trying to conserve energy but also trying to be heard by the rescue team above. Your narration is minimal, hopeless almost. Then: movement above. A rope descends. Your voice becomes suddenly desperate and alive: 'ROPE! THERE'S A ROPE!' Relief floods you but also realization—you still have to survive the extraction. Your voice shakes as you guide the rope to yourself, and as they haul you up, you're narrating the ascent, breath by breath. Include the moment your head breaks the surface and you see the sky again. Your voice becomes almost involuntarily emotional. You're alive. You weren't supposed to be alive and you are. Your voice reflects that shocking grace.

title: The Golden Cage
instruction: Confront your parent who has always controlled you through money and privilege. You grew up with everything—the best schools, the luxury cars, the connections—and you begin speaking from a place of gratitude, almost apologetic. But as you continue, let the truth emerge: these gifts were chains. Your voice must transform from deferential and small to powerful and self-possessed as you realize mid-confrontation that you no longer need what they offer. There's a specific moment where you metaphorically 'put down' their gifts—feel yourself growing taller, larger, more substantial with each thing you reject. End in a place of fierce independence you didn't know you possessed when you started speaking. The power was never in what they gave you; it was always yours.

title: The Unraveling Threshold
instruction: You are an older man, early 60s, on a hotel bed with a partner you've been seeing for a few months. You're receiving oral sex, but this time it feels different — sharper, almost punishing, like you're being pushed past a limit you didn't know you had. That sharp, intense pain at the center of it mingles with a helplessness that makes you grip the sheets, your breath catching in hitched, shallow gasps. As you speak, start with a fragmented, breathless thought about needing to stop, but let the sensation pull you deeper — your voice rising in pitch, trailing into a melodic, sustained moan of pain and reluctant pleasure, even as a quiet disappointment murmurs underneath that this is the only kind of closeness you can still feel. End with just a broken, whispered sound that says you've already surrendered.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (slightly present), Disappointment (slightly present), Pain (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Conversation Before the Launch
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your child who's leaving on a one-way mission to colonize a distant planet—you'll never see them again, and they'll arrive centuries after you're gone. Start with forced brightness, trying to be brave for them, your voice almost cheerful as you tell them how proud you are. But as you speak, the reality crushes through—your voice begins to crack, the brightness becomes strained. You're trying to memorize their face, their voice, and the grief is overwhelming, but you don't want their last memory of you to be sadness. End with a whisper of genuine blessing mixed with unbearable loss, your voice both breaking and somehow finding strength. The words 'I love you' must carry a lifetime of unsaid things.

title: The Car, Parked and Raining
instruction: You're sitting in a parked car with someone you love. Rain drums on the roof, creating a cocoon of sound. The windows are fogging up. It's late evening, and the streetlight outside casts everything in amber. You begin by talking about something mundane—traffic, dinner plans—your voice casual, but there's something underneath you're both avoiding. As the rain intensifies and the world outside becomes more obscured, the intimacy of this small, enclosed space makes it impossible to keep pretending. Your voice drops to almost a whisper. The warmth of the car, the rhythm of the rain, the closeness of this other person's breathing—it all conspires to pull the truth out of you. What you confess is fragile, almost breaking as you speak it. By the end, the confession has been made, and you're both sitting in the aftermath, listening to the rain, which now sounds completely different than it did at the beginning.

title: The Unspeakable Victory
instruction: You're a middle-aged man at a bar with friends, drunk and triumphant after winning a decades-long bet. You're trying to tell them how you finally fixed that old truck, but every sentence triggers a laughing fit—wheezing, high-pitched squeaks, gasping for air. Start in a slurred, giddy state, struggling to get words out through giggles. Let the laughter control your breathing, cutting off sentences, forcing you to start over. As you finally force out the last word, shift into a sudden, fierce roar of triumph—proud, defiant, and raw—before collapsing back into breathless laughter.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (clearly present), Triumph (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: 3 AM Texting Frenzy
instruction: You're a teenage girl, lying on your bed in the dark, phone screen lighting up your face. It's nearly 3 AM and you've hit that second wind—your brain is buzzing, everything feels hilarious. You start by reading a ridiculous meme from your best friend, your voice light and giggly, amused by the absurdity. But as you keep typing and laughing, the amusement builds into something almost euphoric—a breathless, ecstatic rush where you can barely contain your joy. Let your words tumble out faster, punctuated by little gasps and giggles, your voice getting punchier and more delirious. End with a whispered, ecstatic realization that this is the best night ever.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Offering of Resentment
instruction: You are a 10-year-old girl, standing alone at the front of a church service, giving a 'gratitude testimony.' Your voice has a bright, exaggerated, singsong quality because the adults expect it — but underneath, you're burning with jealousy over your friend who just got the lead in the school play. As you speak, you grip the wooden podium until your knuckles turn white, and a flickering light bulb makes you squint, losing your train of thought for a moment. Start with that forced, sugary cadence, but as you go on, let the envy seep through — a crack in your voice, a pause too long, a flat tone where there should be a lilt. End with a quiet, almost defiant 'thank you' that sounds more like a bitter surrender than genuine gratitude.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Transmission
instruction: You're an astronaut on a failing spacecraft, making your final communication with your child back on Earth before you drift beyond range forever. Begin with determined optimism, trying to be brave for them, sharing the beauty you see in the stars. As reality sets in, let your voice crack with the things you'll never get to say—birthdays you'll miss, advice you wanted to give, apologies for choosing this mission. End in a place of bittersweet peace, describing one last beautiful thing you see, your voice soft with wonder and heartbreak intertwined. Let the silences be where your love lives—the pauses before 'I love you,' the breath you take trying not to cry. This isn't about drama; it's about a parent trying to give their child one last perfect memory while their own heart is shattering.

title: The Slow Unraveling
instruction: You are an elderly woman in a dim, quiet bedroom, lying beside your longtime partner after hours of gentle talk. Your voice is soft, feminine, and slightly worn by age. As they begin to touch you with deliberate slowness, your mind drifts—contemplating how many more times you'll feel this, how sacred this body is now. Let your words start as a near-whispered reflection, full of fragile wonder. Then let sensation pull you under: your pitch drops, your breath grows ragged, sighs break your sentences, and each word becomes heavier, more physical. The speech should feel real—pause to react to a kiss, lose a thought when they find a sensitive spot, let a moan interrupt a phrase. By the end, you are no longer thinking; you are only feeling, voice thick with pleasure and surrender. Speak 40–80 words, from contemplation to ecstasy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Knotted Thread
instruction: You're a teenager, knitting in the corner of a quiet room, but your hands tremble. Every few stitches, a piercing pain shoots up your wrist from an old injury you try to ignore. You start with a tenacious, impatient frustration, snapping at the yarn under your breath, your voice clipped and sharp like the clicking needles. But as the pain worsens, your words slow, falter, and your focus drifts—you drop a stitch, curse under your breath, then your voice cracks, the anger melting into raw hurt. Speak to yourself aloud, grumbling at the knot and the ache, until you finally release a long, shaky exhale, admitting quietly, almost whispered, the real reason you can't stop: it's the only way you still feel connected to someone you lost.
emotions_sampled: Pain (very intensely present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Guard's Confession in the Dark
instruction: You are a prison guard sitting alone in the dark after your shift, speaking to someone who isn't there—perhaps a therapist, perhaps God, perhaps just the void. Begin in barely audible whispers, confessing the small cruelties you've committed, the humanity you've had to suppress to survive this job. Let your voice catch on the details—the teenager who reminded you of your son, the woman who begged for her medication, the man who asked you to call his mother. As you move deeper, let shame give way to something more complex: a tender, devastating recognition that you've become the thing you swore you'd never be. End in near-silence, a whispered apology to all of them, knowing it changes nothing but needing to say it anyway. Your delivery should be so quiet it feels like eavesdropping on a soul breaking.

title: The Betrayal Revealed: Your Best Friend, Your Partner
instruction: You've just discovered your best friend and your partner have been together behind your back. Start cold. Icy. Your voice is steady because you're in shock, methodically laying out the evidence you found—dates, times, lies you believed. You sound almost calm. Then something ignites. Your voice rises, becomes jagged, vicious. You're shouting now, years of trust shattering in real-time: 'How could you—BOTH of you—' Your rage is volcanic, physical. But then mid-fury, your voice breaks completely. You collapse into raw vulnerability: 'I would have died for you.' Tears choke your words. The anger returns in waves—you can't decide if you want to scream or sob, so you do both. Your voice becomes ragged, exhausted, swinging between fury and devastation. End with the realization that you're standing alone, your voice dropping to something hollow and distant: 'Get out.' Said not with anger anymore, but with a finality that terrifies you more than the rage did.
inspired_by: Karate Tournament Final: Facing Your Abuser

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you decades ago, and they've asked for forgiveness. Start angry - your voice sharp, controlled, listing the birthdays they missed, the school plays, the nights you waited. Your anger is a shield. But as you speak, something shifts. You hear yourself as a child in your own voice, and the anger cracks into something more vulnerable. 'I needed you' comes out broken, almost a whisper. You're furious that you still care, that their presence still matters. Your voice wavers between rage and grief, between wanting to destroy them and wanting them to hold you. End with the terrible admission that despite everything, some part of you has been waiting for them all along, your voice raw with the shame and relief of finally saying it.

title: The Body Remembers What the Mind Refuses
instruction: You are physically experiencing something intense—receiving a long-awaited embrace, feeling unexpected physical pain, or being touched after years of isolation—and the sensation unlocks an emotional floodgate your conscious mind has kept sealed. Begin with your focus entirely on the physical sensation, your voice describing what you're feeling in your body. But let the physical experience trigger emotional memories and realizations that overwhelm you. Your breath should change, your voice should break not from sadness but from the sheer intensity of feeling something you'd forgotten existed or had convinced yourself you didn't need. Let ecstasy and grief, relief and rage, pleasure and loss blur together until you cannot separate the physical from the emotional. End in a place where your body has bypassed your defenses entirely, leaving you raw and remade.
inspired_by: Actor wants to use subpersonalities as an acting tool but does not yet know their own selves

title: Whispering Your Secret in the Dark: Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you, and you're finally saying the words you can't say when they're awake. Start barely audible, breath more than voice: 'I have to tell you something.' Your throat keeps closing. This is the secret that could end everything—an affair, a lie, a truth about who you really are. Whisper it sentence by sentence, your voice catching, stopping, starting again. Feel how the darkness makes you braver but also more fragile. Move through shame that makes you want to disappear, through love for them that makes this confession both necessary and unbearable. Let tears come silently, the kind that stream down your face without sound. End with the tiniest whisper of their name, a question and a prayer, knowing that tomorrow when they wake up, you'll have to say it all again—but tonight, in the dark, you needed them to hear it, even if they're dreaming. Your voice should be so intimate it feels like we're inside your chest.
inspired_by: First Day of Sobriety: Calling Your Sponsor

title: Finding Peace in the Wreckage
instruction: You're standing in the ruins of everything you built—your marriage ended, career destroyed, home lost—and something shifts. Begin with a broken laugh that turns into tears: 'Look at this mess. Look at what I—' You're crying but also starting to smile. 'I thought losing everything would kill me.' Your voice is shaky, wonder creeping in. 'But I'm still breathing.' Grief and unexpected joy tangle together. You start to laugh through tears: 'I'm free. Oh god, I'm actually free.' The realization is devastating and beautiful. Move between mourning what's gone and discovering lightness: 'I don't have to be that person anymore.' End with your voice full of broken gratitude, laughing and crying simultaneously: 'It's all gone and I'm—I'm okay.' Peace arrives in chaos, joy blooms in grief.

title: Grateful Goodbye: Laughing Through Tears at a Departure Gate
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone who changed your life, who you love completely, who is leaving forever—by choice, for something beautiful that doesn't include you. Start with genuine laughter, sharing an inside joke, your voice light and warm. But underneath, your heart is breaking. Let the laughter and tears begin to blend—you're so grateful they existed in your world, so proud of them for choosing their path, and simultaneously devastated to lose them. Your voice should sparkle with joy while cracking with loss. Include moments of pure celebration of who they are, what they meant, interrupted by the catch in your throat that reveals your pain. End in a place of paradox—you mean it when you say you're happy for them, and you mean it when your voice breaks saying goodbye. Find the space where love is both the reason you're letting go and the reason it's destroying you. Let gratitude and grief be completely authentic, completely simultaneous, impossible to separate.
inspired_by: Coming Down Off Cocaine: Paranoia and Shame Cycle

title: Silent Connection
instruction: Youre sitting silently with a stranger, yet a deep, unspoken connection forms between you. Murmur quietly to yourself, describing their gestures and expressions, letting longing and curiosity blend as you imagine their life.

title: You Came Back
instruction: You're a boy of about nine, waiting alone at the end of a long gravel driveway, throwing stones at a fence post. You've been told your older brother is gone for good—he left after a huge fight with your father. You've stopped hoping. Then, you hear a familiar whistle. You whip around and see him walking up the road, duffel bag over one shoulder. Start with disbelief and a sharp, almost painful gasp—your body knows before your mind—then a shout of his name that cracks into high, desperate joy. You start running toward him, feet crunching gravel, your voice spilling out in broken, breathless wonder: 'I thought you were never—I didn't think—' Let your elation tumble out in a messy flood, but let a tiny shadow of shame slip through—shame that you believed he'd really leave you, or that you didn't do something to make him stay. By the end, you're hugging him tight, your voice muffled against his jacket, still half-laughing, half-sobbing: 'Don't ever do that again. Promise me.'
situation_name: Surprise Reunion / Seeing a Loved One
emotions_sampled: Awe (extremely present), Elation (extremely present), Shame (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father in his study after discovering a secret he's kept from you for twenty years—something that fundamentally changes how you understand your entire childhood. Start from a place of controlled anger, your voice tight and measured, demanding an explanation. As he begins to justify himself with the same dismissive tone he's always used, feel your control start to crack. Let your voice rise, let your body show the years of feeling invisible, unheard, less important than his pride. But midway through, he does something unexpected—he breaks. He admits he was wrong. Notice how this shifts everything in your chest, how your rage must now make room for something more complicated: pity, grief for the relationship you never had, maybe even the beginning of forgiveness you're not ready for. End in a trembling, uncertain quiet, unsure of who you both are now.
inspired_by: Actor wants to use a vivid or recurring dream as unconscious material for their work

title: The Last Phone Call from the Hospital
instruction: You're calling your adult child from your hospital bed, knowing this will be your final conversation. Begin by trying to sound strong and upbeat, pretending everything will be fine—your voice bright, almost falsely cheerful. But as you speak, the reality that you'll never see them again breaks through. Let specific sense memories flood you: the smell of their hair when they were small, the weight of their hand in yours, the sound of their laughter at breakfast. By the end, allow yourself to drop all pretense. Your voice should move from performative strength to raw, whispered truth. End in a place of profound love mixed with the physical sensation of letting go—as if you're literally feeling your grip loosening on everything you've held dear.

title: Public Failure Spiral
instruction: You've failed publicly and spectacularly. You're in the moment of realization—your voice freezes, your words get stuck. Everyone is staring. Your voice, when it comes, is tight with humiliation: 'I... I can't...' You're trying to salvage it, but your voice betrays you—it shakes. You're rushing through an explanation, your words tumbling over each other. Include the moment you just stop, give up. Your voice becomes eerily calm: 'I'm sorry. I failed.' You excuse yourself, your voice barely audible.

title: Screaming at Your Adult Child Who Won't Stop Destroying Themselves
instruction: Start with your voice already raised, past patience, past subtlety: 'I can't do this anymore! I can't watch you kill yourself!' You're shaking with the kind of rage that comes from helpless love—you've tried everything and nothing works. Your voice is ragged as you list what you've watched them lose: jobs, relationships, their own light. Let your fury be specific, brutal: 'You think I don't see the marks? You think I don't know?' Then let it crack—your voice breaking from anger into desperate, choking sobs: 'You're my baby. You're my baby and I can't save you.' Feel the devastating shift from powerful rage to complete powerlessness. Your voice becomes pleading, reduced to raw need: 'Tell me what to do. Tell me how to help you.' End in whispered defeat, all fight gone: 'I love you. God help me, I love you.' Your voice carrying both infinite love and the terrible knowledge that love isn't enough.
inspired_by: Asking Your Parent for Money While Ashamed

title: Whispering to the One You'll Never Touch Again
instruction: You're alone on the beach where you scattered your beloved's ashes, running your hands through sand that might contain traces of them. Speak barely above a whisper, as if they can hear you. Describe the sand touching your skin with heartbreaking tenderness, as if each grain could be them, as if this is the closest you'll ever come to holding them again. Your voice should be intimate, vulnerable, catching on words as you confess things you never got to say. Let silences speak as loudly as words. Midway through, allow yourself a small, broken laugh at a memory, then let that laughter dissolve into something closer to a sob. End with your voice so quiet it's almost not there—a final 'I love you' that's more breath than sound, more prayer than performance.
inspired_by: Running Your Hands Through Warm Sand

title: The Last Hour at Your Mother's Bedside
instruction: You're sitting beside your mother in her final hour. She's unconscious, but you need to speak. Begin by acknowledging everything you're actually feeling right now in this moment - the awkwardness of talking to someone who can't respond, the tension in your shoulders, any self-consciousness about how you sound. Say these things out loud to her. As you continue speaking, let yourself move through the surface feelings into what lies beneath - the things you never said, the gratitude mixed with old resentments, the child inside you who isn't ready. By the end, you should arrive at something raw and true that surprises even you. The journey moves from uncomfortable self-awareness to devastating intimacy, from guardedness to complete emotional nakedness.

title: The Photograph in the Flames
instruction: You are an older man trapped in a smoke-filled room of a burning building. Your throat is raw, your eyes sting, and you're coughing so hard you can barely stand. You're exhausted, disoriented from the smoke, and barely able to think straight. title: Confrontation: Telling Your Parent You Remember What They Forgot
instruction: You're finally confronting a parent about something that happened in your childhood—something they've denied, minimized, or genuinely don't remember, but that shaped your entire life. But as they deflect or deny, your composure starts to crack. The anger surges—not just at what happened, but at having your reality erased, at being made to feel crazy for remembering. Yet underneath the rage is a child's desperate need to be seen, to be believed. Your voice oscillates between fury and heartbreak, between wanting to hurt them and wanting them to finally, finally understand what they did. End with a realization that they may never give you what you need, and the grief of that acceptance even as you stand your ground. title: The Accusation I've Carried
instruction: Confront your parent (or adult child) about a moment from years ago that shaped you—perhaps when they chose work over you, or walked away when you needed them most. Allow this imagined sensory experience to crack open your anger, transforming it into raw vulnerability and the terrifying hope that maybe, even now, they might reach for you. instruction: You are a hyper-masculinized man, but also a child—about 10 years old. You've been stuck in the back of a sweltering minivan with your little brother for hours. title: The Last Goodbye at the Space Station Airlock
instruction: You're an astronaut saying goodbye to your partner through the airlock glass before a one-way mission to establish humanity's first colony beyond our solar system. Start with forced brightness, trying to make this easier for them—cracking jokes about finally getting away from their cooking, reminding them to water your plants. But as the launch sequence begins its final countdown, your voice fractures. The bravery crumbles into raw need. You press your hand against the glass and your voice becomes small, almost childlike: 'I don't want to go.' Then you catch yourself, remembering why you chose this, and your voice steadies into something that holds both devastating loss and profound purpose. 'But I have to.' Let your final words be a whisper of their name, a benediction and a breaking heart in one breath.

title: Anesthesia Awakening
instruction: You're emerging from anesthesia after learning devastating news before surgery—a betrayal, a death, a loss—and the drugs are wearing off unevenly. Your cognitive functions return in fragments while your emotional control is still offline. Begin in confused peace, almost blissful, not remembering why your chest feels tight. Then memory returns in waves, and you cycle rapidly through emotions you can't regulate: laughing at the absurdity while tears stream down your face, expressing profound gratitude to the nurse for their kindness while your voice breaks with grief over what you've lost. You're trying to be polite, appropriate, but keep collapsing into raw feeling, then apologizing, then laughing at yourself for apologizing. End in a strange, drug-softened acceptance—heartbroken but somehow okay, devastated but oddly at peace, still crying but genuinely smiling. Let the contradictions coexist naturally, the way they do when our defenses are chemically stripped away.

title: Thanking Your Rival at Your Own Funeral (Recording)
instruction: You're recording a message to be played at your funeral—specifically for the person who was your greatest rival, who pushed you, challenged you, sometimes hurt you. Your voice holds both gratitude and grief. As you speak, you're crying and smiling simultaneously: 'You made my life so much harder... and so much richer.' Your voice breaks but you keep finding humor, even as tears clearly fall: 'I hated you sometimes. God, I respected you.' End with devastating tenderness, voice full of tears but somehow lighter: 'Thank you for making me better. Thank you for the fight.' Let joy and sorrow, gratitude and loss, peace and heartbreak exist in the same breath. This is what grace sounds like.

title: The Last Mountain

title: Everything I Never Told You

title: A Parent's Final Apology at the Hospital Bedside
