instruction: You're mission control when catastrophic failure hits the orbital station where your daughter is stationed. The protocol is clear—evacuate now or lose the window forever. Her voice comes through asking for five more minutes to save her crewmate trapped in the medical bay. You start professional, clipped, denying the request. But she says your name—not 'Control,' but 'Mom' or 'Dad'—and something inside you shatters. You have ninety seconds to tell her everything: that you're proud, that you were wrong about her career choice, that you see her now. Your voice moves from commanding to pleading to a whispered blessing. End with you giving her those five minutes, knowing what it costs, your professional mask completely gone, speaking only as a parent saying a final goodbye.
inspired_by: Rescue Made Contact in the Mine: Hearing Your Best Friend's Voice

title: The Breaking Point Touch
instruction: Someone you've desired from a distance finally reaches out and touches your face unexpectedly. Begin frozen, barely breathing—shock and disbelief in your stillness. As their hand remains against your skin, feel the actual warmth, the pressure, the reality of contact. While experiencing this real sensation, let your imagination layer meaning onto their expression: see hunger in their eyes even if they're neutral, read invitation in the slightest movement of their fingers, feel their restraint as electric tension. Let your body respond truthfully to both the real touch and your imagined reading of it. Your breath should become ragged, your voice (if words come) should crack between control and surrender. By the end, you're trembling—your entire physical and emotional state transformed from paralysis to barely-contained need, whether or not they've actually changed their expression or intention.

title: Touching the Bark of a Large, Old Tree
instruction: Run your hand along the rough bark, feeling each ridge and groove under your fingertips. Describe the hard, sturdy texture, the faint earthy smell, and the sense of history in every touch. Speak with a tone of reverence and respect, as if the tree is a wise, ancient being sharing a moment of connection with you.

title: The Wedding Morning Unraveling
instruction: It's your wedding day morning. You're alone, dressed and ready, and you should be happy—part of you is ecstatic. But another part is terrified, grieving something you can't name, angry at expectations you can't meet. Start by looking at yourself in the mirror, trying to smile. But then let the contradictions tear through you physically. Laugh and sob simultaneously. Spin in your wedding clothes and then collapse. Pound your joy and terror into the floor with open palms. Let sounds pour out that contain both celebration and mourning—you're gaining everything and losing something precious at once. Your voice can scale from whispered 'yes' to screamed 'I don't know' and back again. Make no sense. Your body holds opposing truths. Gradually, let the storm pass. End standing again, breathing deeply, looking at yourself with eyes that hold both emotions at once—transformed, ready, still scared, but choosing to walk forward anyway.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Addiction
instruction: You're sitting across from your parent after years of absence, and they want back in your life. Begin with cold, controlled anger—you've rehearsed this. But as you list what you missed (graduations, first heartbreaks, the nights you needed them), your voice betrays you. The anger cracks into the hurt child underneath. They try to explain and you explode—then catch yourself in their eyes and see your own pain reflected. Move from rage to the devastating question: 'Why wasn't I enough?' End in either bitter acceptance or a fragile, uncertain offer of one more chance. Make it messy, contradictory, utterly human.
inspired_by: Discovering You've Been Catfished: The Video Call

title: Holding My Child While the World Burns: A Parent's Fury and Helplessness
instruction: You've just learned your child has been deeply hurt by someone you trusted, and you're holding them as they cry. Start with fierce, protective rage barely contained: 'I will make this right. I will fix this. I promise you.' Your voice shakes with the violence you want to unleash. But as they sob in your arms, your certainty fractures into devastating helplessness: 'Oh god, I can't—I can't take this pain away from you, can I?' The rage collapses completely into broken sobbing: 'I'm your parent, I'm supposed to protect you, and I failed.' Rock them gently, your voice raw and destroyed: 'I'm so sorry, baby. I'm so, so sorry.' Then, from somewhere deep, find a desperate, trembling strength: 'But I'm here. I'm right here and I'm not going anywhere.' End with a fierce whisper against their hair, love and fury intertwined: 'We will survive this. Together. I've got you.'

title: When the Body Betrays
instruction: Your joint has just dislocated in public, in front of someone important - a job interview, a first date, a crucial moment. Start with explosive frustration that erupts: 'God, not now, not fucking now!' Your voice is sharp with rage at your own body. Then let it fracture into helpless tears: 'I'm so tired of fighting myself. My own body is the enemy and I can't escape it.' The anger collapses into raw vulnerability. Then build back into fierce, almost violent self-protection: 'But this is me. This is what I am. And if you can't handle watching me put my own shoulder back in, then get out.' End with exhausted defiance mixed with barely concealed devastation: 'I don't need you. I don't need anyone.' But let your voice betray that you desperately do.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You are confronting your father after discovering a decades-old family secret that explains everything about your childhood. Start with controlled, cold anger - your words are sharp, measured, accusatory. But as you speak and watch his face crumble, something unexpected happens: you begin to see him not as the towering figure of your childhood, but as a frightened, flawed human who made terrible choices out of his own pain. Let your anger crack open to reveal the bewildered, hurt child still living inside you. End in a place of raw vulnerability, asking the question you've needed to ask since you were five years old. Your voice should break not with weakness, but with the courage it takes to finally be completely honest.
inspired_by: Actor believes they cannot achieve inspired, unconscious-level work because they haven't experienced it

title: Professor Plagiarism
instruction: You're the professor confronting your brightest student about plagiarism on the final paper. This student is your academic advisee—someone you've mentored for four years. You're trying to be fair and institutional about it: 'The work submitted contains material from sources that are not cited.' Your voice is professional. But you're looking at this kid's face and realizing that plagiarism often means desperation. Your tone shifts from accusatory to concerned as you ask, 'Are you okay? What's really going on?' Now you're not the authority figure; you're an adult recognizing another human in crisis. Show the moment where the accusation becomes care.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Leaving Forever
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your child is asleep, and you're leaving—for witness protection, to protect them from danger, or because staying will destroy you both. Kneel beside their bed and speak in barely-there whispers, knowing they can't hear but needing to say it anyway. Start with tender observations—the way their hair falls, how peaceful they look—your voice thick with unshed tears. Let the words catch in your throat as you try to explain why you have to go, justifying it to yourself more than to them. Feel the impossible weight of loving someone so much that leaving is the only gift you can give. Your breathing should become uneven, voice breaking on promises you're making that you might never keep. Touch their hair, their face, memorizing details. End with a whispered 'I love you' that barely makes it past your lips, then the devastating silence of standing up, taking one last look, and the quiet agony of walking away.
inspired_by: Explaining Quantum Physics to a Five-Year-Old While High

title: The Video
instruction: You're a teenage boy, alone in your room late at night, phone pressed to your ear. You just found out your best friend posted a private video of you online without asking—you saw it, already up, comments underneath. At first you're almost whispering, stunned, repeating what you saw as if you can't believe it. Feel your throat tighten, your free hand rubbing the back of your neck. Then the bitterness hits—your voice rises, cracks, you start throwing out accusations faster, but your words stumble. Midway you pause, realize you're losing a part of your life, and finish quieter, almost hollow, with sadness bleeding through the edges of your voice. You might clear your throat, shift your weight, or stop mid-sentence and start again.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to the outer solar system, recording your final message to your child back on Earth before communications become impossible. Start with careful composure, trying to be strong and educational about the stars you're seeing, the wonder of space. But as you realize this is truly goodbye—that they'll grow up without you, that you'll never hold them again—let your voice crack and soften. End in a place of bittersweet acceptance mixed with devastating love, whispering the things you need them to know, your breath catching on words like 'proud' and 'always.' Let silences speak. This isn't about drama—it's about a parent's heart breaking while trying to give their child one last gift of courage.
inspired_by: The Tech Support Robot with Feelings

title: The Night the Ocean Went Silent
instruction: You're a marine biologist on the phone, voice raw from hours of screaming at officials who won't listen, describing how the ocean section you've studied for twenty years just went eerily, impossibly quiet—all the marine life suddenly gone. Start with explosive, almost incoherent rage, your words tumbling over each other as you demand action. But mid-tirade, let that fury shatter into something more vulnerable: terror, helplessness, the realization that all your knowledge, all your passion, all your warnings meant nothing. Your voice should crack and break as you shift from screaming to sobbing, from accusations to desperate pleading. End with fierce, protective love for the ocean mixed with the crushing knowledge that you're powerless to save it. Let your voice become both a roar and a whimper.

title: Screaming at God While Holding Your Dead Child
instruction: Begin with a roar of pure, animalistic rage—you're demanding answers from a universe that took everything. Your voice is guttural, savage, hurling accusations at the sky with vicious intensity. 'You took the wrong person!' explodes from you with ferocious power. But as the rage pours out, it begins to crack. The screaming deteriorates into broken sobs, your voice splintering into desperate pleading—'Please, please give them back, I'll do anything.' The fierce protectiveness that made you strong enough to care for them now makes you helpless, and that helplessness turns the rage into anguished weeping. End with your voice reduced to a whisper, still talking to them as if they can hear, your tone shifting from fury to unbearable tenderness, telling them one more time that you love them, your voice destroyed by grief.
inspired_by: Calling to Break Up and Trying Not to Cry

title: Scarf-Smiled Love
instruction: You're a middle-aged father on a blustery winter walk with your young daughter. A thick scarf is wrapped over your mouth and nose, fogging your breath. You start off grumbling about the wind biting your cheeks—voice muffled, breathy, the fabric catching every syllable. But then your daughter tugs your sleeve and points at a tiny bird braving the cold, and her wonder cracks through your irritation. Let your voice warm slowly, the muffled sound becoming softer, breathier with affection. End with a smile that you feel against the scarf—your words sincere, slightly clumsy from the fabric, but full of love.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Floor Won't Swallow Me
instruction: You're a teenager lying flat on your back on your bedroom carpet, staring at the ceiling. You've just been caught doing something deeply humiliating — your mother walked in on you trying on her expensive perfume and makeup, and you froze. Now she's gone, and the door is shut. You're talking to yourself, but you're not fully aware you're doing it. Your voice is puddled: nasal, heavy, smothered by the floor's gravity. Start with a bitter, contemptuous self-mocking tone — you hate yourself for caring what she thinks, for being so obvious, for getting caught. Pick at the carpet fibers, shift your head side to side, feel the fabric against your cheek. Midway through, let your voice crack. The contempt falters, and raw shame seeps in — a quieter, younger sound. By the end, you're barely whispering, like a confession to no one. You don't want to be heard, but you can't stop speaking.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Quiet Hour
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the early morning light. She's awake, lucid for the first time in days, and you both know this is your final conversation. Begin by simply being present with her—no need to perform grief or drama. Let yourself notice the small things: her breathing, the weight of her hand in yours, the morning sounds outside. As you talk about ordinary memories—her garden, Sunday dinners, the way she sang while cooking—allow whatever genuine feelings arise to exist without pushing them into something bigger. By the end, you're not trying to have a 'meaningful goodbye.' You're just two people who love each other, sitting together, letting silence say what words cannot. The power is in what you don't force, in the feelings that surface naturally when you stop manufacturing them.
inspired_by: Actor cannot function without stimulating high tension states (Theatrical Hysteria / Ass Energy)

title: Cross the Aisle
instruction: You're seated by the window on a long-haul flight, and the flight attendant who just served you has left you completely disarmed. You watch her move down the aisle, and you realize you want to say something—anything—before she gets too far. The cabin hums and rattles around you. You clear your dry throat, lean toward the aisle, and call out to her just a little too loudly at first, then soften as she turns. Start with a flustered, impulsive surge of warmth that almost embarrasses you, then settle into something quieter and more sincere as she waits, hoping she doesn't think you're just another passenger being strange.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Cabin Pressure
instruction: You’re a teenage boy sitting next to your younger brother on a noisy plane, the engines droning and your throat dry. You start by teasing him loudly about something embarrassing he did at the airport—your voice forced over the roar, grinning, leaning in close to be heard. Halfway through, you catch the hurt look on his face, and your bravado crumbles into a quieter, shamed apology. Let the engine noise make you strain at first, then drop your volume as your confidence fades, your voice cracking as you fumble to make it right.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Wrenched from the Chocolate River
instruction: You are a child waking up from a deep nap. Your mom calls you for dinner, but your head is full of fog. You're angry at being disturbed, your voice thick and groggy. As you gradually remember the sweet dream you were having, a tiny bit of contentment seeps into your irritation. Start with a grouchy, disoriented mumble, then let your voice soften slightly as you recall the dream, ending with a reluctant but cozy acceptance.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Whispered Truths in the Dark
instruction: It's 3am and you're lying next to someone who's just woken to find you crying quietly. They ask what's wrong, and you whisper the truth you've been hiding: 'I'm scared every single day.' Your voice is barely audible, intimate, raw. 'Not just of the pain or the dislocations. I'm scared you'll realize I'm too much to love.' Let the words catch in your throat. Continue in broken whispers: 'Some mornings I can't open jars. Some days I need help getting dressed. And I see you trying to hide how tired you are of helping me.' End with devastating tenderness: 'I love you so much it terrifies me, because I know one day you might leave, and I couldn't blame you.' Let silence speak between the words.

title: The Broken Heirloom
instruction: You are a teenage girl sitting cross-legged on the floor, trying to fix a small wooden music box your grandmother gave you. You hold a tiny wrench and a loose screw. Begin with a soft laugh at your own fumbling, grateful for the gift in your hands. As you turn the wrench, grunt with each effort—a metallic click, a pause—but you feel the screw strip again. Your voice shifts from a hopeful murmur to a hushed, heavy disappointment, trailing off into a resigned sigh as you realize it's beyond saving.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (slightly present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (slightly present), Disappointment (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. Begin in a state of numb denial, mechanically going through the motions of adjusting their blanket, touching their hand. As you speak, let yourself truly see them—really look at their face, remember who they were at seven years old, at seventeen, at their wedding. Allow the full weight of this being the last conversation to break through your protective walls. By the end, you are no longer protecting yourself from the grief—you are fully present, raw, saying everything that matters while tears stream down your face, whispering promises you'll keep and thanking them for every shared memory. Your voice should transform from hollow and distant to trembling with unbearable tenderness and love.
inspired_by: Two actors need to achieve genuine ensemble before a scene and are starting from cold

title: Protecting Your Sibling From an Attacker You Cannot Stop
instruction: You're holding your injured younger sibling, their blood on your hands, screaming at someone to stay back. Start with volcanic rage—voice raw, feral, threatening. You're making promises of violence, roaring warnings. But mid-threat your voice cracks because you both know you can't protect them. The rage fractures into desperation. You're begging now, voice breaking, still trying to sound fierce but it's dissolving into helpless sobs. You pull your sibling closer, still shouting but you're crying, words becoming incoherent. The protector becomes the terrified child. End with a guttural, broken plea that's half-scream, half-prayer. Journey from fierce strength to complete helplessness while never letting go.

title: What She Really Meant to Say
instruction: You're confronting your mother, who always communicated through her bird—a parrot who supposedly 'said what she really thought.' For years, you translated the bird's squawks as your mother's witty observations, her biting commentary, her easier-to-hear criticisms. Now you're thirty-five, and you're telling her what the bird should have said: 'I'm proud of you.' 'I was wrong.' 'I see you.' Start with anger, channeling years of translating deflection and distance into humor. Your voice is sharp, mimicking the parrot's squawk, listing all the shallow things the bird actually said. But midway through, let the rage crack into something more vulnerable—begin translating the words you desperately needed to hear, the encouragement and love that never came. Your tone should shift from bitter mimicry to raw longing, from accusatory to almost pleading. End with a whispered translation of what you wish the bird—what you wish she—had said the day you left home. Let your voice carry both the child who needed those words and the adult who's learning to live without them.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Soulmate Who's Leaving at Dawn
instruction: They're asleep beside you for the last time—leaving tomorrow for something irreversible: another life, another country, a path you can't follow. You can't wake them; this goodbye is just for you. Start by barely breathing their name, so quiet it's almost nothing. Tell them the small things you'll miss—the way they laugh, that gesture they make, how safe you felt. Your voice is tender, intimate, catching on every other word. Let yourself almost break but pull back—you don't want to wake them. Confess something you never said: 'I knew you were the one the day we met' or 'Every morning with you felt like a gift.' Your throat tightens. You touch their face so gently. End with the hardest words: accepting they're going, blessing their journey, releasing them even though it's killing you. The whisper becomes even softer, more fragile—gratitude and devastating loss intertwined.
inspired_by: Talking to a Baby Who Just Said Their First Word

title: The Late-Night Confession
instruction: You're a man who's had a few drinks at a quiet bar. A close friend across the table has just made a joke, and you're laughing, your voice looser, louder than usual. But as you laugh, your eyes linger on their mouth, and a sudden, raw lust catches in your throat. The amusement starts to fade, replaced by a quiet, heavy desire that you're too drunk to hide. Let your voice waver between the easy, lazy rhythm of the drunk and the sudden, strained lower register of a man confessing something he's been burying.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Bite
instruction: You are a terminally ill father, eating a final meal with your young son. Your mouth is full of soft, mashed potatoes, making your voice thick and clumsy. The first bite is a painful struggle to swallow, the weight of goodbye pressing on your chest. You try to comfort your child with a gentle lie, but as you finish, the pain breaks through and you admit the truth—you're terrified too. Let the food affect your diction; let your voice crack and falter as the emotions shift from forced calm to raw, desperate love.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Earthquake Body
instruction: You've just received news that changes everything—a diagnosis, a betrayal, a miracle, you choose. Your body receives this information before your mind can process it. Start standing still, trying to maintain composure, but then let your body refuse to cooperate. Begin with trembling, but let it escalate into something wild and unselfconscious—your face contorts involuntarily, your limbs move in ways you can't control, strange sounds emerge from your throat (gasps, laughs, animal noises, guttural moans). You're simultaneously trying to hold yourself together and completely falling apart physically. Let the sensory experience overtake you—you might spin, collapse, pound the floor, make yourself into impossible shapes. Your breath becomes ragged, your voice breaks into fragments of words mixed with pure sound. Move from rigid control into complete physical chaos, then slowly, finally, into exhausted stillness. End in a heap, wrung out, but somehow more present in your body than you've ever been.

title: Crisis Announcement
instruction: You're the spokesperson announcing the company-wide layoffs to a room of 500 people, including your best friend of 15 years whom you were told would be cut. You're standing at the podium with the official statement you've rehearsed. The first paragraph is ice-cold corporate speak. But then you have to announce the affected departments by name. You say your friend's department, and you see her face fall. Your voice wavers—not obviously, but enough that everyone in the room hears it. Recover. Finish the statement. Show the internal war between the CEO script in your head and the human being who's watching her best friend's life implode.

title: The Moment You Realize You've Become Your Abuser
instruction: You've just screamed at your child the exact words your father screamed at you. Begin in the immediate aftermath—shocked silence, then horrified recognition. Your voice starts shaking: 'Oh god. Oh god, I just—' The realization crashes over you in waves. Rage at yourself erupts: 'I swore I would never!' Your voice breaks between fury and anguish. You're seeing yourself from the outside and you're terrified. Apologize to your child with desperate intensity, but you can't stop the spiral—you're not just apologizing to them, you're apologizing to the child you once were. Your voice becomes raw, almost feral with self-loathing mixed with helplessness: you don't know how to break this cycle. Include the moment where fierce protectiveness (you want to protect your child even from yourself) collides with the devastating truth that you've already failed. End with a whispered, broken promise: 'I'll do better'—but you can barely believe yourself.
inspired_by: Confronting Your Betraying Friend: Anger Turning to Grief

title: The Final Push
instruction: You are an older man, trying to climax with your partner. Your body is moving, but your mind is stuck replaying a failure from earlier today—a deal you lost, a promise you couldn’t keep. You concentrate hard, grunting, gasping, willing yourself to finish. But each moan carries a thread of disappointment. Your rhythm breaks as you lose focus, then you force it back. At the peak, instead of release, you let out a long, broken sigh—the climax fades into a quiet, hollow letdown.
emotions_sampled: Disappointment (very intensely present), Concentration (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Betrayed by Your Best Friend and Trying to Stay Calm
instruction: They just told you and you feel the betrayal hit your chest. Your voice goes very quiet and still—dangerous quiet. 'You did what?' Slow, each word a stone. Your voice becomes mechanical, asking clarifying questions while your breathing is shallow. One word cracks before you pull it back together.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Your Sleeping Child Before Surrender
instruction: You're a parent saying goodbye to your sleeping child before turning yourself in for a crime, or leaving for a dangerous mission you won't return from, or walking away to protect them from something. Speak in hushed tones, tender and aching, cataloging the small details you'll miss—their breathing, the way their hair falls, their little sounds. Let your voice stay quiet but let the emotion build underneath like a tide, moving from gentle love to barely-contained grief to a fierce, protective promise that this sacrifice is worth it. Your voice should never rise above a whisper, but the intensity should be shattering. End with a moment where you almost break, almost sob, but swallow it down because you can't wake them.

title: The Last Call of the Night
instruction: You are an elderly woman, bone-tired after a long day, standing at your back door in the dark. Your dog has wandered into the yard and won't come inside. You start by calling him with a strained, sweet voice—clicks and a whistle—forcefully affectionate but your exhaustion seeps through every syllable. As he ignores you, your tone slips from coaxing to a weary, almost whispered plea, then to a quiet, resigned command. End with a soft, breathy sigh as you realize you'll have to go get him yourself. Let your voice crack and fade, lose the thought mid-sentence, and let the fatigue color every sound.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Speaking Truth
instruction: You're saying something true that you've been avoiding, and it's terrifying. Your voice starts controlled, but the truth pushes out anyway. It's harder to say than you expected. You're breaking a silence that's been heavy. Your voice carries the weight of truth-telling: vulnerability, power, fear. You can't unsay this. The truth is changing something irreversibly. Your voice becomes stronger as you speak it fully. By the end, the truth is told, and your voice carries the strange mixture of relief and terror that comes from finally being honest. The listener can hear in your tone that this cost you something.

title: The Hole I'm Digging
instruction: You're a teenager, shoveling earth in a backyard under a hot sun. You're furious with envy—a friend just got something you wanted desperately, and your parents made you dig this hole for a new tree as 'character building.' As you work, you mutter to yourself between grunts, each shovel strike timed to a bitter thought. At first, your voice is tight with jealousy and resentment, but as you feel the rhythm of your own strength, a flicker of pride creeps in—you're doing this hard work. Then doubt settles: maybe you're being petty, maybe this hole is all you deserve. Your speech is choppy, breathy, with pauses to wipe sweat or adjust your grip, and your final words carry a weary, uncertain resignation.
emotions_sampled: Jealousy & Envy (extremely present), Pride (slightly present), Doubt (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for the person who understood you better than anyone—maybe a best friend, a sibling, a chosen family member. You promised them you'd make people laugh at their funeral, so you start with a funny story, and you're actually laughing, genuinely finding joy in the memory. Your voice is warm, alive with affection. But as you tell the story, the laughter becomes entangled with tears. You're giggling and crying simultaneously, and it's beautiful and terrible. You keep trying to deliver the funny parts, but your voice breaks with gratitude for having known them, with grief that they're gone, with the surreal absurdity of standing here telling jokes while your world has ended. End with 'Thank you for everything'—still half-laughing, half-sobbing, your voice full of love and unbearable loss existing in the same breath.

title: The Last Boss
instruction: You're an elderly woman in your cozy living room, gripping a controller way too tightly. You've been stuck on this boss for hours, your patience worn thin. Suddenly—a break in its pattern. Your voice starts out tired, breathy, muttering to yourself between mechanical clicks and groans of the chair. Then, as you pull off the final combo, a triumphant shriek breaks out—surprising even you. Let the excitement crackle through your voice, shifting from weary grumbling to pure, childlike victory. Let the controller clicks and your own gasped reactions guide the performance.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father about something he's never acknowledged—a wound from your childhood that shaped everything you became. Begin with controlled anger, the rehearsed words you've practiced for years, the clear points you planned to make. But as you speak, notice what's actually alive in you beneath the script you've prepared. Maybe the anger dissolves into something more vulnerable. Maybe you hear your own voice sounding like his. Maybe rage gives way to grief, or grief ignites into fury. Don't perform the confrontation you imagined—live through the one that's actually happening. By the end, you've stopped trying to make him understand and started discovering something true about yourself in his presence. The truth that emerges shouldn't be the one you walked in planning to tell.
inspired_by: Actor's work seems clinical, academic, and impersonal despite technical proficiency

title: The Stifled Giggles
instruction: You are a child squatting in a dark, tight crawlspace under the porch, legs screaming, core locked to stay silent. At first, you whisper-bitter about how your friend got you into this mess, your voice clamped and strained from holding still. Then you remember the ridiculous face they made right before you both dove in—and a huge, barely-suppressed laugh fights to break free. Your words come out in forced, grunting bursts, half-amused, half-terrified. End with a desperate, whispered plea, your voice cracking between a snort and a sob: 'Stop… stop making me laugh, they'll hear us!'
emotions_sampled: Bitterness (slightly present), Amusement (very intensely present), Fear (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Trapped Under Rubble
instruction: You're pinned by concrete and steel. Your voice is tight, controlled at first—you're trying to be found. But the reality of your position hits: you can barely breathe, dust fills your mouth. Your voice becomes panicked, then switches to desperate pragmatism. You're calculating air, trying to conserve energy. Include the moment you accept this might be it. Your breathing is shallow, restricted. Every word fights against the weight on your chest. End with quiet acceptance and prayer.

title: The Last Conversation Before the Mission
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your partner who leaves tomorrow on a one-way space mission to establish the first Mars colony. You'll never see each other again. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to be supportive and brave, asking about practical details to avoid the truth. Let that facade slowly crack as reality sets in. Your voice should break into quiet devastation - not loud crying, but the kind of grief that steals your breath. End with a whispered confession of how their courage inspires you even as it destroys you, finding a fragile peace in honoring their choice while your heart shatters. Let silences speak. Let your voice catch. Be utterly real.
inspired_by: Your Teenage Child Coming Out to You

title: Dancing at Dawn After the Vigil
instruction: You've been awake all night at your best friend's bedside as they died. Now it's morning, and you're telling someone about the moment near the end when you both started laughing about something absurd. Begin with a tired, almost dreamlike quality, smiling through obvious exhaustion. As you describe dancing together in that hospital room at 4 AM—their last dance—let joy and grief become indistinguishable in your voice. Laugh at the memory, but let the laughter catch and break. Your exhaustion should make everything feel surreal and honest. End with gratitude for those final hours mixed with the crushing weight of loss, your voice soft but full, acknowledging that you're shattered and grateful and so desperately tired, and somehow all of that is exactly right. You wouldn't change a moment, even though it's destroyed you.
inspired_by: Hiding Exhaustion While Continuing to Work

title: Laughing Through Your Last Conversation
instruction: You're with someone you're losing—to distance, to death, to an ending you both see coming. You're telling stories, remembering, and you're laughing. Really laughing. Start with genuine joy, maybe teasing them about an old memory. 'Remember when you tried to—' and you crack up. The laughter is real and warm. But underneath it, threading through, is heartbreak. Your laugh catches, becomes tangled with tears you're trying to hide. 'God, we were so—' and you can't finish because you're crying now too, but still almost-laughing. The emotions are simultaneous and contradictory: joy and devastation, gratitude and grief, celebration and farewell. End with a phrase that holds both: 'Thank you for—' your voice full of love and breaking and somehow, impossibly, still smiling through tears.

title: Protecting Someone You Cannot Save
instruction: You're holding someone—a child, a sibling, a lover—who's in danger you cannot prevent. Start with fierce determination, your voice strong and commanding: 'Listen to me. Look at me. You're going to be okay.' You're trying to will safety into existence through the force of your conviction. But reality is crashing in—the danger is real, time is running out, you are powerless. Your voice begins to shake with rage at your own helplessness: 'No. No, this isn't—I won't let—' You're fighting against the inevitable, your words becoming fragmented, desperate. The strength in your voice fractures completely as protective fury collapses into anguished tenderness. 'I've got you. I'm here. I'm right here.' You're still trying to be strong for them, but now you're also saying goodbye. End with words that are both a promise and a prayer, your voice breaking apart: 'I love you. I love you so much. You're not alone.' Every repetition is you trying to make it true.
inspired_by: Discovering Your Partner Has Been Lying

title: Stargazing Through the Heave
instruction: You are a young girl with a high, feminine voice, lying on your back in the grass, severely nauseous from a stomach bug or car sickness. You are trying to focus on the night sky above you, which is breathtakingly full of stars—awe floods in, but every time you try to speak, a wave of nausea forces a gag, retch, or watery swallow. Start with fear and discomfort: your voice trembles, you fight to keep from vomiting. As you describe the stars, awe breaks through, softening your tone, but the physical heave keeps interrupting—your words are garbled, watery, and cut off by involuntary stomach contractions. End with a fragile mix of wonder and lingering sickness, your voice still thick with mucus.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Story Before Sleep
instruction: You are sitting at the bedside of someone who raised you—a grandparent, older sibling, or guardian—in their final hours. They can barely speak, drifting in and out of consciousness. Begin with careful, controlled composure as you decide to tell them one last story: a memory from your childhood that they were part of, something formative that shaped who you became. Start with steadiness, painting the memory with vivid sensory detail—sounds, smells, what you wore, how the light looked. As you speak, let the weight of this being the last story you'll ever share with them crack your composure. Your voice should journey from controlled narrative to something raw and breaking. End with you no longer telling the story to them, but to yourself—a whispered recognition that you're saying goodbye not just to them, but to the version of yourself that only existed in their presence.

title: The Moment You Realize Your Child is in Danger and You're Powerless
instruction: You receive a phone call or message that makes your blood stop. Your child—or someone you're responsible for—is in immediate danger, and there's nothing you can do in this moment to save them. You're trying to get information, trying to stay calm, asking questions with increasing desperation. Start controlled, focused, almost clinical in your questions. But let terror crack through. Your voice should rise and break, become fierce and demanding, then collapse into pleading. Move between rage at your helplessness and raw, animal fear. End somewhere primal—perhaps a whispered prayer, a promise, or just their name repeated like a mantra. Let the audience feel you coming apart while trying desperately to hold yourself together because falling apart won't save them.
inspired_by: Concealing Skepticism While Listening to an Unbelievable Story

title: The Broken Man's Last Plea
instruction: You are an elderly man, once strong and proud, now frail and desperate. Your son has just told you he's cutting you off, leaving you homeless. You are confused—you didn't see this coming. Fear grips you as the reality sets in. Pain from years of sacrifice and now betrayal. You plead, your voice cracking, breath shaky, high-pitched, rushing words before he interrupts. Start with confusion, then fear, then pain, ending in a desperate, broken submission. Let your voice waver, lose thought, then find it again. Speak about 50-70 words.
emotions_sampled: Confusion (clearly present), Fear (extremely present), Pain (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Pause Between Scripts
instruction: You're a young customer service rep on a phone call. You start with your practiced, artificially bright 'smile-voice'—high pitch, lots of uptalk, perfect clarity. But then the customer says something that catches you off guard: a quiet, heavy detail about their situation. As you begin typing, your voice changes. The pitch drops, the uptalk fades, and you speak more slowly, almost to yourself. You're genuinely thinking, processing what they've shared. By the end, the professional mask cracks, and your voice becomes quieter, warmer, and contemplative.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Argument With Echoes
instruction: You're confronting your father about his absence during your childhood. But as you speak, you find yourself also narrating what you notice about yourself in this moment—'I sound just like you right now,' 'My hands are shaking,' 'I've rehearsed this a thousand times and it's coming out all wrong.' Don't hide these observations—say them out loud as part of the confrontation itself. Begin with controlled anger and self-awareness of performing this confrontation, but let it dissolve into something messier and more real, where your awareness of what you're doing becomes ammunition, becomes vulnerability, becomes part of the fight itself. End in a place where you've stopped caring how you sound.
inspired_by: Actor is commenting on his own performance while performing, creating a split between observation and involvement

title: First Snow of the Storm
instruction: You are a teenager caught outside as a blizzard suddenly intensifies. Snow swirls so thick you can barely see your hand, and the wind snatches your breath. You're supposed to be heading home, but something in the wild white chaos fascinates you. Speak aloud—partly to yourself, partly to the storm—as you pause, stomp your feet, and wipe ice from your lashes. Begin with genuine curiosity, noticing how the snow swallows sound and how your own voice feels muffled. Let that interest slowly give way to a creeping unease as you realize you might be lost, your words becoming sharper, more urgent.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Silence
instruction: You're finally confronting your aging parent about decades of emotional absence. Begin with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be fair, adult, reasonable. But as you list the missed recitals, the times you needed them, the years of feeling invisible, anger bleeds through. Your voice rises, cracks with decades of suppressed rage and hurt. Then their face—watch their face—and something breaks in you. The fury collapses into grief, into the child you were who just wanted to be seen. End in raw vulnerability, admitting that you still need them, you always did, and that truth hurts more than the anger ever could.

title: The Job Rejection You Sent Your Own Child
instruction: You've been working on your laptop, responding to job applicants for your company's internship program. Your college-age daughter applied under her legal name—which is different from what you call her—and you didn't realize until after you sent the rejection email with the standard 'we've decided to move forward with other candidates' language. Now you're staring at the 'sent' folder, your voice caught between laughter and horror: 'I just... I rejected my own daughter. I actually wrote 'we wish you the best in your future endeavors' to my own child.' You're calling her before she sees it, and your voice is tumbling out, almost giddy with the absurdity: 'Sweetie, don't check your email—' But she's already opened it. She's not angry; she's laughing, but you can hear something else underneath. Your voice shifts, becomes softer, aching: 'Wait, you really wanted this? At my company?' She admits she thought working together might help you two reconnect since you've been distant. Your laughter dies completely, and your voice cracks with the weight of what you've accidentally revealed: 'I didn't know you felt far from me. When did I...' You're crying now, but also smiling through it, your voice thick with gratitude and heartbreak: 'You're hired. Not for the internship—I'm hiring you to teach me how to be close to you again. Can you do that?'
inspired_by: Sending a Drunk Text to the Wrong Person

title: The Eruption: When Politeness Finally Shatters
instruction: You're in a meeting, family dinner, or intervention where people keep talking over you about YOUR life, YOUR pain, YOUR situation. You've been calm, patient, trying to get a word in for what feels like hours. Then something snaps. Begin with strained composure barely holding, your voice tight with suppressed emotion. Build to an explosive outburst—loud, fierce, maybe even shocking yourself with the intensity—where you finally demand to be heard. But here's the turn: as you're shouting, declaring your truth with full force, you break. The anger cracks open into desperate tears, the rage transforms into a plea: 'Please, just let me speak.' Let your voice shatter from powerful to fragile, from fierce protectiveness of yourself to vulnerable admission that you're tired of fighting to matter. End with a whispered repetition of what you were trying to say all along, now barely audible, wrung out but finally honest.
inspired_by: Maintaining Patience While Being Repeatedly Interrupted

title: Screaming at God During an Impossible Choice in the ER
instruction: You're in a mass casualty event with limited resources and must choose which of two critical patients gets the last unit of O-negative blood. Start with desperate, rapid-fire clinical assessment—'Trauma bay one, penetrating chest wound, BP crashing; bay two, eight-year-old, internal bleeding'—your voice climbing with panic. As the reality sets in that you must choose who lives, your professional composure shatters into rage at the universe, at the unfairness, at your own powerlessness. Scream, plead, bargain with forces that aren't listening. Your voice breaks between fury and sobbing. When you finally make the choice, speak it quietly, almost numbly, then immediately demand to know if your hands are still steady enough to operate. The shift from explosive emotion to cold, necessary focus should feel like watching someone break and rebuild themselves in seconds.
inspired_by: Surgeon Narrating a Procedure While Exhausted

title: Adult Child Confronts Parent Who Gave Them Up, Discovering They Were Protecting Them
instruction: You're finally confronting the parent who abandoned you as a child. Start with controlled fury—you've rehearsed this moment for years. Your voice is sharp, accusatory, listing every birthday they missed, every school play, every moment you needed them. You're not yelling; you're precise and cutting. Then they quietly reveal the truth: they didn't leave to escape you—they left to protect you from someone dangerous, someone who would have used you to hurt them. Your anger doesn't disappear, but it fractures. Your voice breaks mid-accusation. You try to hold onto your rage because it's what's kept you whole, but grief is flooding in. By the end, you're caught between the child who needed them and the adult who understands impossible choices. Your voice becomes tender and furious at once—'I needed you' said with both anger and heartbreak, because both are true.
inspired_by: Scientist Realizes Her Breakthrough Comes from Data Her Competitor Stole

title: Skyward Confession
instruction: You are a teenager lying on a park bench, your head hanging back over the edge, neck hyperextended. The sky is a blur of clouds. You’re still angry after a fight with a close friend, but the physical position forces your voice to come out thin and strained. Start with bitter, clipped words—frustration making your swallows audible and your pitch tight. As you speak, the disconnected feeling of looking upside down shifts your focus; your anger softens into quiet contemplation. By the end, your voice wavers with a fragile hope, the words slipping out almost like a secret. Let your throat feel exposed, and let your thoughts wander into unexpected calm.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Thirst in the Desert
instruction: You are a 16-year-old girl stranded alone in a scorching desert after your friend's car broke down and they went for help. It's been hours. Your throat is bone-dry, your head throbs, and every breath feels like inhaling an oven. Your voice is a wilted whisper—cracked, slow, broken by panting and dry swallows. You start by mumbling to yourself in pure helplessness, barely able to form words as you stare at the empty horizon. But then, something shifts: a memory of your little sister's face flashes in your mind, and your weakness hardens into a quiet, desperate anger at the idea of not seeing her again. The same helplessness is still there, but now it's laced with a ragged, stubborn refusal to lie down and die. Your voice gains a trembling edge, fighting through the heat.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Wedding Morning Question
instruction: It's the morning of your wedding to someone you genuinely love, but you're standing in front of the mirror, and doubt has crept in. You're supposed to feel pure joy, but instead you feel joy AND terror AND resentment AND excitement AND grief for the life you're leaving. Begin asking yourself real questions out loud, as if you're two people: Why are you really doing this? What are you afraid of? What do you hope will change? What do you hope will stay the same? What part of yourself are you saying goodbye to? With each question, let different emotions surface—laugh, then tear up, then smile, then feel a flash of anger, then soften into tenderness. Don't resolve the contradictions; let them coexist. Your voice should be unstable, shifting—playful then serious, hopeful then fearful. End in a moment where you hold all the contradictory feelings at once, having arrived not at certainty but at acceptance of complexity. You'll still get married, but now with eyes wide open to the beautiful, terrifying tangle of what love actually is.

title: The Moment You Stop Saving Them
instruction: You're screaming at your adult sibling who's overdosed for the third time this year, and you're holding Narcan you just used to bring them back. Start with explosive relief and rage tangled together: 'You SELFISH—I thought you were DEAD!' Your voice is huge, shaking the walls, tears streaming as you rage about finding them blue on the bathroom floor. The fury builds: 'I have saved your life SIX TIMES! SIX!' Then something breaks. Your voice drops to nothing. The fight drains out completely: 'I can't... I can't do this anymore.' The most devastating words come out soft, final, each one killing you: 'If you do this again, I won't come. I love you, but I won't come.' End with helpless, quiet weeping—not for them, but for yourself, for the impossible choice you've just made.

title: The Last Story Before Sleep
instruction: You are an elderly man sitting in a dim, quiet room, telling a younger family member about the time you met your late spouse. You start with a slight pride in your voice — you saved them from a runaway cart in the market. But as you describe their smile, you feel a wave of infatuation, just a hint of that old flutter. Mid-sentence, a yawn overtakes you — your jaw drops, your voice slides down and becomes hollow, rounded, as you fight to keep the thought alive. Let the yawn interrupt your words naturally; the pride fades into a soft, dreamy fondness as you finish.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your childhood best friend who has hours left to live. When you enter the room, you're determined to stay strong and cheerful, filling the silence with forced optimism and memories of good times. But as you speak, something shifts—a look in their eyes, the weight of their hand in yours, the reality that this is the last conversation you'll ever have. Let yourself move from that brittle, protective cheerfulness into the raw, undefended grief underneath. Don't perform sadness—let the truth of this final goodbye crack through your armor naturally. By the end, you're no longer trying to comfort them; you're letting them comfort you, whispering the things you've never been brave enough to say.
inspired_by: Actor cannot find a choice for a scene obligation after trying the obvious options

title: The Equation Your Mother Never Understood
instruction: You're standing in your childhood bedroom, now empty, confronting your mother who never believed in your work. You've just won a major award for the same research she called 'wasting your life.' Start with that manic, vindicated energy—showing her the proof, trying to explain in that same rapid-fire way why it mattered. But mid-explanation, something breaks. You realize she still doesn't understand, will never understand, and more devastatingly, you realize you don't need her to anymore—but God, you still wanted her to. Your brilliant rambling should collapse into something raw and childlike: 'Why couldn't you just—Mom, why couldn't you just—' The anger, the triumph, the need for her approval, and the grief of letting that need go must all be present. End with either fierce acceptance or broken resignation.

title: Reading Letters to Your Dying Parent Who Never Said I Love You
instruction: You're sitting beside your parent's hospital bed in their final hours, reading aloud letters you wrote to them over the years but never sent. Begin with cautious distance in your voice, reading a teenage letter full of longing for their approval. As you move through the letters—college years, your wedding day they missed, the birth of your child—your voice should crack and soften, the old anger dissolving into raw grief. End reading the letter you wrote yesterday, finally saying everything you needed them to hear, your voice breaking between gratitude for the parent they tried to be and sorrow for the relationship you'll never have. Let forgiveness and heartbreak live in the same breath.
inspired_by: Interviewing Your Grandparent as Dementia Progresses

title: The Last Hour Before Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying grandmother in the pre-dawn darkness. Begin by feeling completely shut down, unable to speak the words you've rehearsed for weeks. Let yourself acknowledge out loud every fear stopping you: fear of saying the wrong thing, fear of her not hearing you, fear of your own grief. As you voice these barriers, allow them to dissolve. By the end, let yourself finally speak the simple truth you've been holding back—whether it's gratitude, forgiveness, or love—and feel how your voice transforms from trapped to free. The emotional journey moves from paralyzed fear to raw, undefended honesty.
inspired_by: Two actors preparing to rehearse a scene together; both feel artificial or disconnected

title: Fever Breaking
instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical sensation—perhaps recovering from days of illness, or in the aftermath of passionate intimacy, or riding out the last waves of grief-stricken sobbing that's left your body spent. Your body is hypersensitive; every breath feels amplified. In this state of physical rawness, you're talking to someone who hurt you deeply. Begin with your body leading—gasping words between breaths, trembling affecting your voice, physical exhaustion making your defenses impossible to maintain. The physical intensity won't let you hide behind careful language. Let sensations blur with emotions: pain becomes anger becomes release becomes unexpected gratitude for feeling anything at all. Your voice should reflect the body's state—sometimes breaking, sometimes breathless, sometimes surprisingly strong. End as the physical intensity begins to ebb, but emotionally you're more exposed than when you started, stripped bare by the body's honesty.

title: Dancing in the Demolition
instruction: You're standing in your childhood home on its final day before demolition, and you've just found your late mother's wedding ring in a crack in the floorboards - the ring she lost thirty years ago, the day before she died. You start laughing - an absurd, almost hysterical laugh at the cosmic timing, at finding it now when it's too late to give it back to her, too late for her to know. But even as you laugh, you're crying, holding this tiny circle of gold that suddenly contains everything: her perfume, her voice, her hands braiding your hair. Your laughter and tears tangle together as you remember her searching everywhere for this ring, how devastated she was. Now you've found it, and she's gone, and the house is going, and everything is loss and gift at once. End with breathless, tearful gratitude mixed with unbearable grief: 'Thank you. Oh god, thank you. I found it, Mom. I finally found it.' You're saying goodbye and hello in the same breath.

title: The Protector's Breaking Point
instruction: You're confronting someone who has hurt someone you love—your child, your sibling, your partner. You start with fierce, controlled rage, voice sharp as a blade, telling them exactly what you think of them. Your words are weapons and you wield them precisely. But then something happens: maybe you see fear in their eyes, or maybe the person you're protecting speaks up, or maybe you realize your rage can't actually undo the damage. Your voice explodes into something rawer—screaming that breaks into sobbing, furious demands that collapse into helpless questions. You feel the terrible impotence of loving someone you couldn't protect. Your voice cracks between wanting to destroy this person and wanting to turn back time. By the end, you're on your knees emotionally, voice ragged, oscillating between residual fury and devastating grief, between the protector you wanted to be and the fallible human you are.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Someone Who Won't Remember
instruction: You're sitting beside someone disappearing into dementia, Alzheimer's, or the fog before death. They don't know who you are anymore. Your voice is impossibly gentle as you tell them stories of your shared past, hoping something might reach them. Describe a specific memory—their hands teaching you something, a song they sang, the way they made you feel safe. Let your voice break on the small details: the smell of their cologne, the sound of their laugh, things that are already becoming harder to recall. There's no anger here, only tender devastation. You're not asking for anything back; you're simply bearing witness to who they were, who you were together. End by telling them it's okay to let go, that you'll carry them forward, your voice so quiet it's almost a breath, granting permission even as your heart shatters.

title: Polite Smile, Damp Fingers
instruction: You're at a crowded cocktail hour, holding a plate of appetizers with one hand and your child's sticky hand with the other. The music buzzes, people laugh too loudly. You spot the host's uncle approaching — the one who always comments on your 'sweet little girl' in a way that makes your skin crawl. You need to keep up a bright, friendly voice for him, but your child is tugging at your sleeve and a smear of cheese dip is drying on your thumb. Start with a practiced, high-pitched chirp of greeting, then let your voice trail off, tighten, and drain of warmth as you answer the uncle's question while simultaneously wiping your hand on a napkin and muttering to your kid. End with a flat, short 'We're fine, thanks,' that sounds anything but.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Cough That Caught a Secret
instruction: You're a middle-aged woman with a hyper-feminized voice, stuck in your car after a long day. You're fighting a cold, and a sudden coughing fit interrupts your phone call with a close friend. Start with a slightly contemptuous edge—annoyed at the coughing itself, at the day you've had. Then shift into teasing your friend about their silly luck. Mid-tease, a new cough explodes out, and when you finally clear your throat, you're astounded by something your friend just blurts out—so surprised your voice cracks and rises. Let the coughs break your rhythm, make you raspy, and let the astonishment feel raw and unplanned.
emotions_sampled: Contempt (slightly present), Teasing (clearly present), Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Parade Ground Inspection
instruction: You are a young soldier standing at rigid attention in the sun during a battalion inspection. Your commanding officer is slowly walking down the line, examining each recruit. You must hold absolute stillness—no blinking, no shifting. Your voice starts as a sharp, metallic bark when you snap out your name and rank. As the officer pauses in front of you, he asks about your unit’s motto. Begin with that barked reply, but as you speak those words—words you’ve repeated a hundred times—a flicker of real pride rises through the tension. Let the last syllable soften just slightly, a crack in the armor, as if you can’t help but feel what the motto means.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Reunion Where Nothing Goes As Imagined
instruction: You're reuniting with someone you haven't seen in ten years—someone you've imagined this moment with endlessly. Start with nervous joy, a rehearsed greeting, prepared stories. But they keep defying your expectations: they're cold when you expected warmth, or desperately affectionate when you expected distance, or they keep bringing up memories you've tried to forget, or they won't acknowledge the painful history between you. Each unexpected response shatters your script and forces genuine improvisation. Your joy might curdle into hurt, then anger, then reluctant laughter, then aching tenderness. Let their unpredictability pull contradictory emotions from you simultaneously—you're grateful they came and furious they're acting this way; you're laughing and crying; you love them and resent them. By the end, discover an emotional truth you couldn't have scripted: perhaps forgiveness tangled with grief, or joy poisoned by what's been lost, or hope emerging from devastation.

title: Last Words to a Sibling Who Won't Wake Up
instruction: You're sitting beside your sibling's hospital bed. The doctors say they can't hear you, but you need to say this anyway. Start by trying to be strong, telling them about your day like everything's normal. Then let it crack—confess the fight you had before the accident, the things you said that you can never take back. Your voice should break as you move from casual updates to desperate apologies to finally whispering the childhood memories only you two share. End by telling them it's okay to go, even though saying those words out loud makes you feel like you're murdering them yourself. Let your voice dissolve from controlled to completely shattered, but keep it intimate, like you're afraid to disturb them.
inspired_by: Dental Extraction: Hiding Disgrace While the Dentist Works

title: The Inheritance of Wounds
instruction: Confront your parent (or your adult child) about a pattern of criticism that has lived in your bones for decades - the way they made you feel small, unworthy, never quite enough. Start from a place of justified anger and years of stored hurt. But as you speak your truth with increasing power, you must also reckon with a devastating realization: you have been doing the exact same thing to yourself ever since, carrying their voice as your own inner critic. The confrontation becomes not just with them, but with your own participation in your diminishment. Move from righteous fury to a more complex mixture of anger, grief, and the first glimpse of liberation from this inherited wound.

title: The Unbearable Lightness of Victory
instruction: You've just received news you've been desperately waiting for—a test came back clean, a job came through, someone is coming home. Begin speaking with your body trying to float with relief and joy, almost giddy and weightless. But as you try to celebrate, feel an unexpected heaviness starting to sink into your bones. With each joyful word you speak, the weight increases—you realize you're also grieving the months of fear you carried, mourning the person you were when you thought the worst would happen. The joy doesn't disappear; it gets heavier, more complicated. You're laughing and your limbs feel like lead. You're grateful and you feel crushed. By the end, you're speaking words of celebration that sound like they're being pulled from the earth itself—weighted, deep, complex. The victory you're expressing has the gravity of everything you survived to get here.

title: The Reckoning
instruction: You've just discovered a devastating betrayal by someone you trusted completely. Start with volcanic rage—your voice shaking, loud, words tumbling out in a torrent: 'How could you? How COULD you?' Let yourself be consumed by it, voice cracking with fury and disbelief. But underneath the rage, hurt begins bleeding through. Your volume drops unpredictably, voice fracturing: 'I would have died for you...' Then rage again, fiercer, almost feral, protective of your own broken heart. By the end, you're on your knees emotionally, voice raw and stripped bare, oscillating between fury and devastating vulnerability: 'I loved you. God help me, I still—' You can't even finish. End with a sound that's half-laugh, half-sob, utterly helpless: 'What am I supposed to do with that?' Your voice is destroyed, quiet, fierce, and completely undone.

title: The Summit Promise
instruction: You are a young woman, a child in your spirit, clinging to a steep rock face, arms aching above your head. Your voice is a strained, joyous whisper — each word a gift of breath you cannot waste. You call out to your belayer below, sharing the ecstatic view of a delicate, perfect wildflower blooming from a crack in the stone. It’s a sacred discovery, and you’re flooded with pure pleasure, but as you speak, the effort makes your voice tremble, and a sudden breeze shifts your weight, stealing your words. You start in a giddy, breathless exclamation, but by the end, the strain pulls you into a quieter, more intimate awe — the joy is still there, but it’s grounded now, soft with exhaustion and reverence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Gasping for Air After the Storm
instruction: You've just pulled yourself from metaphorical wreckage—a betrayal, a loss, a truth that shattered everything. Your breathing is ragged, almost violent at first. Start fierce, angry, describing how the air burns going in, how you're gulping it down like someone who nearly drowned, furious at needing it, furious at still being here. Your voice should shake with rage as you spit out words about suffocation, about lies that stole the oxygen from your world. But as you force yourself to breathe deeper, slower, let the fury crack open into raw vulnerability. Your voice should break into something between a sob and a laugh—you're still here, still breathing, and you hate how much that matters. End with a powerful, shuddering exhale, your tone shifting to fierce determination mixed with devastating tenderness toward your own survival, as if each breath is both an act of defiance and self-forgiveness.
inspired_by: Taking a Deep Breath of Mountain Air

title: Thanking the Person Who Destroyed You
instruction: You're recording a message to someone who betrayed you profoundly—a lover who left, a friend who exposed your secrets, a mentor who failed you at your most vulnerable moment. But this isn't about revenge or closure. You're genuinely thanking them, because their betrayal broke you open in a way that ultimately freed you. Start with almost a laugh, the absurdity of what you're doing. Your voice should be warm, even affectionate, as you acknowledge the pain they caused. But underneath, there's a tremor—this gratitude is real, but so is the grief. You're laughing while your voice breaks, finding humor in the tragedy, thanking them for teaching you what love isn't, what trust costs, who you are when everything falls apart. The contradictions should live fully in your voice: forgiveness tangled with hurt, appreciation mixed with anger, peace coexisting with the echo of devastation. End with a genuine 'thank you' that somehow contains everything—the ruin, the rebirth, the strange gift of being unmade and remade.

title: The Truth About the Wedding Dress
instruction: You're confronting your mother who spent your college fund on her gambling addiction. You've just discovered this the night before your wedding, and you're wearing the dress she claimed she 'saved for years' to buy you. Start with explosive rage, demanding answers, your voice sharp and unforgiving. As she tries to explain, defend, then finally breaks down, something in you fractures differently. You realize she's not the villain you need her to be—she's sick, broken, and you're about to walk away into your new life leaving her behind in her shame. Your fury must evolve into something more complicated: exhaustion mixed with reluctant compassion, anger softening into disappointed love. End not with forgiveness, but with the painful recognition that she's still your mother, and you don't know how to stop loving someone who keeps hurting you.

title: Enemy Partnership
instruction: Two enemies are forced to work together for mutual survival. The first voice is hostile, resentful. The second voice is equally hostile but also pragmatic. They're establishing rules, and both voices are sharp. Then something forces them to see each other as human. One of them saves the other's life, and both voices transform. The gratitude is complicated, mixed with lingering hostility. They're building a strange trust that's born from necessity but becomes something more. By the end, they're not friends, but they're something more dangerous than enemies: they understand each other.

title: Shattered Shield
instruction: You're a parent who couldn't protect your child from harm, and the realization is destroying you. Start with fierce denial: 'I did everything I could!' instruction: You are in the grip of both physical illness (high fever, delirium, body aching) and overwhelming desire for someone who is caring for you. Your body is burning. Blend the sensations: the heat of fever with the heat of longing, pain with pleasure, weakness with hunger. Let your voice be raw, uncontrolled, delirious. Moan, gasp, confess. title: 3 AM Text
instruction: You're a 17-year-old girl lying in the dark at 3 AM, jet-lagged and wide awake while your body screams for sleep. Your mom is asleep down the hall. title: The Unraveling Protector
instruction: You're a parent who just discovered your teenager has been cutting themselves, and you're trying to talk to them but everything's coming out wrong. But your terror keeps bleeding through, your voice rising despite yourself. You're furious at yourself for not noticing, furious at them for hiding it, furious at the world for hurting your child. title: Breaking Through the Fog to Confront
instruction: You've been in a dissociative state for weeks after a trauma, barely speaking, barely present. Your parent sits across from you, trying to get through to you with pleasantries and deflections as they always have. Something they say—some casual dismissal of your pain—suddenly pierces through the numbness. Begin with that underwater quality, monotone, delayed responses. But then let rage start breaking through the catatonia—your voice cracks, speeds up in bursts, becomes jagged and raw. You're fighting your own shutdown to finally tell them the truth about how their neglect broke you, how you needed them and they weren't there. instruction: You're confronting your mother about a lie she told that shaped your entire childhood. The more truth you speak, the heavier you become, until you realize the weight isn't anger—it's the terrible burden of understanding why she lied. By the end, you're not shouting anymore; you're barely able to hold yourself up, speaking with the weighted exhaustion of someone who has just understood their parent is human and flawed. The confrontation that began as an attack must end as a kind of weary, heavy compassion that you didn't know you had in you.

title: Everything I Swallowed for Twenty Years
instruction: You're confronting your mother in her kitchen about why she stayed silent when you needed her to speak up for you as a child. Begin with carefully chosen words, the speech you've constructed in your mind for years. But as you speak, allow every impulse—the urge to laugh inappropriately, sudden tenderness, the desire to destroy something, inexplicable gratitude, childlike pleading—to infiltrate your confrontation. Don't force consistency. If you feel like your voice wants to break into something gentle in the middle of rage, follow it. If disgust and love arrive simultaneously, let both live in your words. Start from rehearsed anger; end wherever your uncensored impulses take you. The goal is to surprise yourself with what actually comes out, even if it contradicts what you said a moment before.

title: Vocal Orgasm: Multiple Perspectives
instruction: Perform three distinct climaxes showing different vocal expressions of the same experience: first, a quiet, restrained orgasm — held breath, bitten lip, a single choked gasp. title: Farewell to the Person You Saved Me From Becoming
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your sponsor, mentor, or therapist who is moving away forever—someone who saw through your masks when no one else did. Your voice fractures as you confess how afraid you are of who you'll become without them. The emotions shift from appreciation to raw panic to finally, devastatingly, a whispered acceptance that you have to carry what they gave you alone now. title: Whisper What You Can't Say Clearly
instruction: Late at night, lying next to your partner of ten years, you need to confess something that could change everything. Start with trying to find the exact right words for your confession, but every time you begin, the words feel wrong—too dramatic, too small, too clinical. Let yourself speak in fragments, images, sensations instead of complete thoughts. Describe how your body feels, what colors you're seeing in your mind, memories that aren't quite relevant but somehow are. Your partner may be asleep—you're not even sure they can hear you—but that's not the point. By the end, you've said everything and nothing, and the relief comes not from being understood but from finally letting your truth exist in sound, however imperfectly expressed.

title: The Last Strike
instruction: You are in a quiet, dimly lit room, after a long day of holding everything together. You kneel on a soft rug, resting your hands on your thighs, your partner behind you. This is a ritual — you've asked for it, to feel the sharp edge of the world become something you can breathe through. The first few strikes are a shock; you gasp, arch your back, your voice catching high in your throat. But as the rhythm settles, you start to count aloud, your voice trembling then steadying. On the final stroke, you let out a long, shuddering moan that melts into a soft laugh. You turn, look over your shoulder, and say something tender, proud, and relieved — like 'I needed that... thank you. I love you.' title: The Inheritance of Joy
instruction: You've just received news that someone deeply complicated in your life has died—someone you loved fiercely and resented equally, someone who damaged you and shaped you. By the end, you've claimed the complicated inheritance: the damage and the gift, both fully honored, both completely real.

instruction: You are confronting someone you've loved your entire life—a parent, a sibling, a partner—about a truth that has quietly poisoned your relationship for years. instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen, decades later, finally saying what you've rehearsed a thousand times.
