title: The Microphone and the Gaze
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman addressing a crowd through a PA system at a community rally. You're genuinely excited about the new park project—your voice is clear, powerful, and filled with interest. But you keep spotting a specific person in the front row, someone you're attracted to. Let your voice start strong and public, but gradually become softer, slower, and more intimate as you speak directly to that person. Your passion for the project mixes with a growing flirtation in your tone. End with a pause that almost becomes a breathy admission. Feel the weight of the crowd, the feedback from the mic, and the distraction of desire.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you've loved your entire life—a parent, partner, or closest friend—in their final hours. They're conscious but fading. Begin by trying to hold yourself together, speaking practical reassurances about medications and comfort. But midway through, they ask you the impossible: to tell them honestly what you're feeling, to stop performing strength. Let your composure crack completely. Reveal the messy, selfish parts of your grief—your anger at being left, your terror of facing the world without them, the specific absurd things you'll miss that no one else would understand. End in a place of raw exposure, speaking truths you've never said aloud, using words and rhythms that are utterly your own, not what you think grief 'should' sound like.

title: The Promise She Broke
instruction: You're taking a slow, aimless stroll through a quiet park, hands in your pockets, eyes tracing the cracks in the pavement. You're replaying a recent conversation with a close friend who made a big promise but then backed out at the last minute. Start with a scoff—contempt dripping in your voice as you mutter about how predictable and weak she is. Let the rhythm of your walk bounce the words, but as you keep walking, a memory of her genuine effort slips in. Your contempt fades into a thick, sinking disappointment—not anger, just a heavy letdown. Pause mid-sentence when a bird startles from a bush, then pick up quieter, your voice losing its edge, ending in a resigned, almost hollow tone. Keep your breathing soft and unhurried, like the walk itself.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Cottonmouth Confession
instruction: You're a teenager alone in your bedroom, high for the first time after a painful breakup. Your body feels heavy and disconnected, mouth dry, thoughts floating like dust motes. You start talking to the empty room, trying to explain how you really feel under the haze — your voice slow, with sighing pauses, sticky lip sounds when you try to speak. At first, it's a numb, giggly ramble about nothing, but as you speak, the sadness you've been avoiding crystallizes into a sharp, quiet ache. By the end, your words become smaller, tighter, and you're fighting back a sob you can't hide.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Turbulence Breaks
instruction: You are a middle-aged man on a flight facing severe turbulence. The plane drops suddenly, and you feel helpless, gripping your seat. You lean close to the stranger next to you, voice strained and loud over the engine roar. At first, you're barely controlling your fear — words come out in bursts, breath shallow. Then the shaking stops. Your voice softens, relief making it shaky but liberated. You let out a quiet, wondering laugh. Speak your lines naturally, as if reacting to the lurch, catching your breath, then exhaling with relief.
emotions_sampled: Helplessness (clearly present), Fear (extremely present), Relief (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Admitting You've Been Lying About Your Credentials
instruction: You're finally telling them you're not qualified for what you've been doing. Your voice is ashamed, small: 'I need to tell you something.' You explain the lie and your voice carries the weight of deception. 'I was afraid you wouldn't respect me.' Your voice is raw with shame. End asking them not to tell—vulnerability and desperation.

title: Whispering Goodbye to Sleeping Arms
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you, their arms around you, and you're leaving—not because you don't love them, but because you must, and you can't wake them to say goodbye. Speak in barely audible whispers, describing the weight of their arm across your body, how their breathing moves against your back, the particular way their fingers curl in sleep. Your voice should be achingly tender, full of all the love you feel, but threaded through with quiet devastation. Let tears catch in your throat as you memorize the feeling of being held by them one last time. End by whispering an explanation they'll never hear, your voice breaking on why you have to go, mixing fierce protectiveness of them with your own breaking heart. This isn't theatrical crying—it's the kind of grief that makes your chest tight and your words catch, intimate and raw.

title: The Breaking Point
instruction: You are alone in your apartment after being fired, rejected, or publicly humiliated, and the adrenaline is coursing through your body. Begin pacing, your whole system flooded with fight-or-flight energy. Allow yourself to be aware of the intense physical sensations moment-to-moment: the heat in your face, your clenched jaw, your racing heart, the trembling in your limbs. As you move through the space, notice everything—the urge to scream, the urge to cry, the urge to break something, the competing desire to collapse. Include your awareness of physical details: the floor under your feet, your breathing, the sound of your own voice as you begin to speak your rage and hurt aloud. Let the pure fury transform as you stay present with the physical experience—perhaps it breaks into sobbing, perhaps it hardens into cold resolve, perhaps it dissolves into exhausted laughter at the absurdity. End in a completely different physical and emotional state than where you began.

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You are sitting at your grandmother's bedside in hospice, holding her hand. She has minutes left. Begin by reading her favorite childhood story to her - start with the gentle, hopeful voice you'd use for a sleepy child, letting yourself remember what it felt like to be small and safe in her lap. As you read, watch her breathing change. Let your voice break as memories flood through you - her kitchen, her garden, her laugh, the way she made you feel invincible. By the end, you're no longer reading the words on the page - you're speaking directly to her, your voice raw and small again, thanking her for every moment, begging her not to go, then finally releasing her with a whispered permission to rest. Move from tender nostalgia to desperate grief to loving release.
inspired_by: Actor is blocked on the spot before a performance or class and cannot reach a BEING state

title: Surgeon Saying Goodbye to Patient Who Chose to Stop Treatment
instruction: You're alone with a patient you've fought alongside for three years. They've decided to stop treatment, and this is your last conversation. Start with clinical reassurance—'You've shown remarkable strength'—but your voice cracks on 'strength.' The professionalism you've maintained begins dissolving. You need them to know they mattered, that this wasn't just a case number, but you're also grappling with the feeling that you failed them. End in a place of quiet acceptance mixed with unspoken grief, perhaps touching their hand, your voice barely above a whisper as you realize this is actually goodbye.
inspired_by: Pilot Congratulating Crew While Processing Near-Catastrophe

title: The Last Sunset with You
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who has hours left to live, watching their final sunset together. Begin with desperate cheerfulness, pointing out the colors as if cataloging them will make time stop. Let your voice crack as you describe the golden light on their face, knowing you're memorizing it. Transition into raw gratitude mixed with unbearable grief—thank them for all the sunsets you've shared while your throat closes around the words. End in whispered acceptance, describing how the last sliver of sun disappears, your voice becoming almost a prayer. Let silence speak between your words. This isn't about being strong; it's about being present in the most painful moment of your life.
inspired_by: Watching the Sunset Over the Ocean

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the emotional neglect that shaped your entire life—the things they never said, the comfort they never gave, the person you had to become because they couldn't be what you needed. Start with your voice controlled and measured, almost clinical, as if you've rehearsed this. But as you speak, decades of swallowed hurt begin pushing through. Your tone sharpens with anger, then suddenly breaks into something raw and childlike—the part of you that's still eight years old and waiting for them to notice you're hurting. You're not yelling; you're explaining, but the pain makes your voice shake and rise despite yourself. Then something shifts: you realize they may never understand, and your voice drops to something quieter, more devastated than angry. You end in a place of terrible clarity, speaking with a gentleness that holds both love and the acceptance that they failed you. Your final words carry the weight of letting go of a hope you've held your entire life.

title: Crush's Text Alert
instruction: You're alone in your room, trying to sound like a voice assistant to mask your nervous hope. Start by announcing the time and weather in a hyper-precise, flat, hyper-feminized robot voice — but every syllable is tinged with anticipation. As you ask for new messages, let the robotic control slip: your voice cracks, speeds up, then drops to a natural, breathy whisper. When there's no reply, your optimism fades into a quiet, embarrassed sigh, and you end with a self-conscious mutter under your breath.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Most Passive-Aggressive Thank You Card
instruction: Read aloud a thank you card you're writing to someone who gave you a terrible gift. 'Dear Aunt Margaret, Thank you SO much for the ceramic cat figurine. It will look PERFECT... somewhere.' Every compliment is a precision strike. The voice is sweet, warm, and dripping with venom. Include the crossed-out versions: 'Thank you for thinking of— no. Thank you for the— no.' The final version should sound genuinely grateful while communicating nuclear displeasure.

title: Midnight Confession in Room 304
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping newborn in the hospital at 3 AM, and your voice is so quiet it barely disturbs the air: 'Hi, baby girl. It's just us now.' There's a long pause, and when you speak again, your voice trembles with a secret shame: 'I need to tell you something before I lose my courage.' Your throat tightens: 'When they first put you in my arms... I didn't feel what I was supposed to feel.' The confession hurts coming out: 'I felt terrified. And so, so alone.' Tears slip down silently: 'Everyone kept saying I'd be filled with love, but all I felt was fear that I'm going to fail you.' Your voice catches: 'What if I'm not enough? What if I break you?' But then the baby makes a small sound, and something shifts. Your voice becomes tender, wondering: 'But you're looking at me like I'm your whole world.' A soft, amazed laugh: 'You don't know yet that I have no idea what I'm doing.' Finally, your voice is a whispered promise, fragile but sincere: 'I'll figure this out. For you. I promise I'll figure this out.'

title: Final Acceptance
instruction: You're a terminal patient in your final days, and you've finally accepted what's coming. Your voice is soft, clear, at peace: 'I'm not afraid anymore.' There's no resistance in it, no fight. 'I've had a good life. I loved and was loved. That's enough.' Your voice carries a clarity that only acceptance brings. 'I'm ready to see what comes next.' You're not in pain anymore — not because of medicine, but because of acceptance. 'Tell my family I love them. Tell them I'm at peace.' Your voice is a whisper: 'I can feel myself slipping away, and it's okay.' The acceptance is complete, and it's the most alive you've sounded in months. In your final breath, a whisper: 'Hello.' You're greeting death like an old friend.

title: The Tooth That Remembers
instruction: You are in the bathroom at 3 AM, hunched over the sink, a cold cloth pressed to your jaw. The pain is a thrumming wire, and you watch the reflection of a man you barely recognize — older, more tired. You're awed by how a single nerve can split your whole world into before and after. Shame burns in your gut: you let this go, you knew better, you hid from the dentist like a child. Start with that awe — a breathy, almost disbelieving whisper about the sheer force of it. Then let the shame creep in, tightening your throat, making you drop your gaze. You speak to your reflection, but your words come out squeezed, clipped — you can't open your jaw fully. 'I kept thinking... it would pass. Like a bad dream. But it's not passing. It's... it's teaching me something. About what I avoid. About... what I am.' End on a near-silent admission, voice cracking, jaw barely moving, the shame heavier than the ache.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Call
instruction: You are slumped deep in a worn recliner, phone still in your hand after hanging up on your daughter's voicemail—the one you've been avoiding for weeks. The weight in your chest keeps you collapsed, jaw slack, words barely forming. Start with a hollow, matter-of-fact murmur about not having the energy to move, letting your voice drag and mumble. Then, as you recall her voice asking why you won't come to Christmas, let a crack of raw grief break through—a sudden, wet sob that cuts off mid-sentence—before you sink back into silence.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Laughing Through the Funeral Toast
instruction: You're giving a toast at a celebration of life for someone who taught you joy even in darkness, and you're determined to honor them by laughing, not just crying. Start by sharing a ridiculous, beautiful memory—something that makes you genuinely laugh, your voice warm and animated. But as you tell the story, grief keeps interrupting: your laughter catches, your voice trembles, tears slip out even as you're smiling. You're caught between honoring their wish to 'keep it light' and the crushing reality that they're gone. Let the laughter and sobbing interweave—real, messy, human. End with a profound gratitude that's simultaneously the deepest heartbreak: 'Thank you for teaching me that even this, even now, contains joy.' Your voice should embody the beautiful contradiction of celebrating someone while your heart shatters.
inspired_by: Suppressing Annoyance While Dealing With a Difficult Person

title: The Architecture of Your Sleep
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying next to your partner, unable to sleep. Begin by watching them sleep, but then start experiencing them as if you've never seen another human being before—truly studying their face like an explorer encountering something miraculous and strange. Whisper a confession you've never been able to say out loud, but let your voice fill with childlike awe as you describe the specific curve of their eyelashes, the rhythm of their breathing, the particular way their hand rests against the pillow. You're terrified of losing them (they're moving away, or you are, or something is ending), but through this lens of first-time seeing, your fear transforms into profound gratitude. Let your voice break not from sadness but from being overwhelmed by the privilege of having witnessed this person exist. End in a place of acceptance—still afraid, but anchored in wonder rather than panic.

title: Laughing at the Wake
instruction: You're delivering a eulogy for your best friend who died suddenly, and you're determined to make people laugh because that's what they would have wanted. Start with a funny story, your voice warm and full of affection. Get the laugh from the room. But as you continue, the memory becomes too vivid, too real, and suddenly you're crying while still trying to smile. Your voice cracks: 'They used to say I worry too much, and I'd say—' but you can't finish because you're laughing and sobbing simultaneously, the absurdity and tragedy colliding. Find gratitude in the grief: 'God, I'm so lucky I knew them. So lucky.' End with a whispered confession to your dead friend, as if the room has disappeared: 'I don't know how to do this without you. But thank you. Thank you for every ridiculous moment.' Let joy and devastation exist in the same breath.

title: The Baby Blanket in Your Hands
instruction: You're holding a small, soft baby blanket—maybe your child's from years ago, or one you bought for a baby you lost, or never had. Feel its specific texture: is it worn smooth? Slightly rough? Cool or warm? Notice its weight, so light it's almost nothing. You've just received devastating news, but also unexpected grace—perhaps a terminal diagnosis with a promise of enough time to say goodbye, or a reconciliation with someone you'd given up on, or your own pregnancy after years of loss. Begin touching the blanket with trembling hands, letting gratitude flood through you, speaking with joy and relief. But as you feel this soft fabric—meant to protect something so vulnerable—let the reality of fragility, of how easily things can be lost, seep in. Your joy doesn't disappear; instead, let it exist alongside growing grief. End with both emotions fully present: laughing and crying at once, grateful and terrified, holding this impossibly soft thing that represents both hope and heartbreak.
inspired_by: Actor needs to feel specific physical attitudes (swagger, authority, vulnerability) that don't arise naturally but would arise from a specific garment or object

title: Holding Your Newborn While Grieving Your Mother
instruction: You're cradling your hours-old baby, and your mother—who died before meeting them—is everywhere in this moment. Begin with wonder, voice soft and amazed: 'You have her hands. Look at your perfect hands.' You're laughing through tears, the joy and grief so intertwined they're indistinguishable. Your voice carries both celebration and loss: 'She would have loved you so completely.' Let yourself move between emotions naturally—a moment of pure joy ('You're here, you're finally here'), then a wave of grief ('She should be here'). Your voice breaks but keeps going: 'I'm so grateful and so angry and so full of love I can't breathe.' This isn't about choosing between happiness and sadness—it's about holding both simultaneously. End with a kind of peaceful devastation, voice gentle but thick with tears: 'I'll tell you about her. I'll make sure you know her through me.' The arc encompasses joy, grief, anger, gratitude, hope, and loss—all at once, all true.

title: The Fever Memory
instruction: You're burning with high fever, and in your delirium, you're convinced your body is back in a specific moment from your past—perhaps being held by someone you loved, or running through a childhood place, or experiencing your first kiss. Start with physical discomfort: the heat, the sweat, the ache. Then let a sensory detail trigger the memory—a smell, a texture, a sound. As you surrender to the fever dream, stop distinguishing between your current physical sensations and the remembered ones. Is the burning your fever or summer sun? Is your racing heart fear or excitement? Is that moisture sweat or ocean spray or tears? Build the past moment with such sensory intensity that your body believes it's there. Let pleasure and pain intertwine until they're inseparable. Vocalize both the discomfort and the ecstasy, letting sounds blur between present suffering and past joy. End in a state where you're simultaneously in both moments, and the ache has transformed into something almost transcendent.

title: Reading a Bedtime Story While Trying Not to Cry
instruction: You're reading your child their favorite story — 'The Giving Tree' or similar — on the night before a deployment, surgery, or goodbye. Use the warm, musical bedtime-story voice. But the metaphors in the story land differently tonight. Your voice catches on specific words. You pause to 'turn the page' but really to swallow the lump. The child asks 'Why did you stop?' and you recover with 'Just looking at the pictures, sweetheart.' Hold it together. Barely.

title: The Last Firefly
instruction: You're a teenager at a family dinner, seated between your mom and your aunt. Outside the window, a single firefly blinks in the dark. You start speaking with breathless awe, turning your head to point it out—your voice bright, excited, hyper-feminine. But as you describe it, you remember how your grandmother used to call them 'little lanterns' and you haven't seen one since she died. Your voice starts to waver, pitch dropping, losing its brightness. Let the sadness creep in mid-sentence, your gaze dropping to the tablecloth, your words slowing. By the end, you're almost whispering, fighting back tears.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Beside the Breathing Machine
instruction: You're sitting beside your unconscious partner's hospital bed, holding their hand, knowing these are likely your last words to them. Speak in barely-above-a-whisper intimacy, as if afraid to disturb them, or perhaps afraid they'll actually hear you. Start with small, tender details: 'Your coffee cup is still on the counter. I can't wash it.' Describe the mundane love - how they always lose their keys, how they hum while cooking. Let your voice catch on memories. Then confess something you never said: a regret, a secret joy, a fear you always hid. Your voice should be raw but gentle, like touching a wound. End with permission - giving them permission to let go, even though it's destroying you. 'It's okay. You can rest now. I'll be okay.' You're lying, and you both know it, but love means setting them free.

title: Waiting for Rescue in a Cave: Acceptance Turning to Meditation
instruction: You're in a cave waiting for rescue and your voice starts terrified. 'They know I'm here. They're coming.' You're reassuring yourself. But rescue might take hours, or days. Your voice becomes quieter as the reality sets in. You're narrating the cave around you, the dripping water, your own breathing, and your voice becomes meditative, almost philosophical. Include the moment where your initial terror gives way to something closer to peace—not giving up, but accepting. 'If I die here, at least I found beauty.' You're finding meaning in the dark stone, the echoes of water. Your voice becomes almost serene, a kind of meditation on mortality and contingency. Then you hear something—voices, equipment—and your voice becomes urgent and human again. The rescue is real. You have to go back to being afraid and hoping.

title: Saying Goodbye to Your Parent Who's Choosing to Die
instruction: Your parent has chosen medical assistance in dying. They're lucid, peaceful, ready—and you're not. Begin with desperate attempts to change their mind, your voice urgent, pleading: 'There's still time, we could try—' But they gently interrupt with their reasons, and you must truly listen. Your voice quiets as you absorb their words, their readiness, their relief. The resistance drains from you, replaced by something more devastating: acceptance mixed with unbearable loss. Your voice becomes tender, almost steady, as you tell them what they meant to you. Include the moment where you realize loving them means letting them go. End with 'I understand'—but your voice breaks on those words because understanding doesn't make it hurt less. This is you giving them permission while your heart shatters.
inspired_by: Confronting Your Betraying Friend: Anger Turning to Grief

title: The Ridiculous Gratitude
instruction: You're thanking someone who saved your life or changed everything for you, but every time you try to speak with dignity, you're overwhelmed by emotions that make you sound and act foolish—your voice cracks into strange registers, you make undignified sounds, your face contorts in ways that embarrass you. Start trying desperately to be eloquent and composed. As you continue, surrender to the ridiculous ways grief, joy, and gratitude distort you—let yourself sob-laugh, make weird hiccupping sounds, speak in voices that jump octaves. Feel the humiliation of losing control battle with the ecstasy of finally expressing what matters. End in a place where you've accepted looking absolutely absurd as the price of being absolutely real, finding strange dignity in your complete lack of it.
inspired_by: Actor has fear of embarrassment and refuses to risk unpredictable behavior

title: The Morning After the Funeral in Your Childhood Home
instruction: You've inherited your deceased parent's house and you're walking through it alone the morning after the funeral. You're exhausted, empty. Your eyes move across the rooms—their reading glasses on the table, their coffee mug still in the sink, photos on the walls, the couch where they sat, books they loved, their handwriting on notes. Start numb and hollow, just listing what you see in a flat voice. As you continue looking and naming objects, contradictory emotions begin emerging—you notice something that makes you laugh, then something that enrages you, then something that fills you with unexpected gratitude. Let your voice ride these swells—laughing through tears, angry then tender, resentful then loving, sometimes all at once. End in a place of complex acceptance: profound sadness mixed with relief, grief tangled with joy, loss interwoven with inheritance.

title: The Unspoken Inheritance
instruction: Confront your parent (or adult child) about a moment from years ago that shaped who you became—a moment they may not even remember, but one that lives in your body like a scar. Start with controlled anger, keeping your voice measured as you begin to describe the day it happened. Reconstruct every sensory detail of that moment: what room you were in, what time of day, what you were wearing, the expression on their face, the exact words spoken. As you meticulously rebuild this memory aloud, demanding they understand, let the anger fracture into something more vulnerable—the hurt underneath, the child who needed something they didn't receive. By the end, your confrontation should transform from accusation into a raw plea to be seen and understood for who that moment made you.

title: Cracking the Script
instruction: You are a veteran news anchor nearing the end of your shift, reading a live breaking story from the teleprompter. The story claims a political figure has resigned, but as you speak, a producer’s whispered correction in your earpiece makes you doubt the source. Begin with your usual polished, authoritative news cadence—deep, steady, every word clipped. Midway, let a micro-hesitation creep in: a slight pause, a swallowed syllable, your eyes flicking off camera. End with a subtle, almost inaudible question mark in your tone, as if you’re no longer sure what you’re saying is true. Speak as if the weight of the room suddenly feels heavier, the lights too bright.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Last Window Visit
instruction: You're standing outside the hospice window of your grandmother who raised you—COVID protocols mean you can't go inside. She's awake, lucid, and you both know this is goodbye. Start with forced brightness, telling her about your week, your voice almost too cheerful. But as you watch her try to smile through the pain, your composure cracks. The words you've needed to say your whole life start tumbling out—how she saved you, how she taught you what love means. Your voice breaks, palm pressed against the cold glass as hers mirrors it from inside. End in a whisper, telling her it's okay to let go, that you'll be okay, even though you're not sure you will be. Your final 'I love you' is barely audible, thick with tears and gratitude and the unbearable weight of watching someone slip away.

title: The Phone That Won't Answer
instruction: You're a 17-year-old football player, alone in your bedroom after your girlfriend broke up with you by text. You keep calling her, but it goes straight to voicemail. Start by leaving a message with forced anger, trying to sound tough and in control: 'Hey, pick up. This is stupid. Just talk to me.' But as the silence stretches, your voice cracks and your words slow down. You lose your train of thought, then whisper, 'I don't know what to do without you. I'm... I'm nothing.' Let your breath hitch and your pitch drop into raw, helpless admissions. End with a long pause, then barely audible: 'Please.'
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Last Conversation Before the Flight
instruction: Your partner is boarding a one-way mission to Mars in twenty minutes. You've been holding it together, but now they're looking at you with that expression - the one that says they see through your brave face to the terror underneath. Start with false brightness: 'This is amazing, what you're doing.' But their knowing gaze cracks something open. Your voice shifts, becomes raw: 'I'm so proud of you.' Let the words carry both truth and devastation. End in a whisper thick with unshed tears: 'I don't know how to be here without you.' Let the final moment be not goodbye, but the sound of someone trying to memorize another person's face, knowing they'll never touch them again.

title: The Rooftop Confession
instruction: You’re a shy 16-year-old girl, and you’ve finally gathered the courage to confess your feelings to the popular guy you’ve had a crush on all year—but he’s a close friend. You found him alone on the school rooftop at sunset, and in your excitement, you talk fast and fidget with your sleeves, hyper-aware of the breeze and distant shouts from the soccer field. Your voice starts out breathless and full of hope, telling him how much he means to you, even laughing nervously. But when you see his face fall, your voice changes—it gets quieter and clearer, each word deliberate, as you gently but firmly say, 'You don’t feel the same. It’s okay, really, I need you to be honest.' The hope cracks into a soft, raw dignity as you quickly look away, clearing your throat to hide the sting, then quickly shift to reassuring him you’re fine—before turning to walk away, your voice bright but hollow.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Summit Doubts
instruction: You are a teenage girl near the top of a steep mountain trail. The air is thin and cold; every breath feels inadequate, and your legs tremble. A faint dizziness makes the horizon blur. You start speaking to yourself, voice breathy and short — you doubt you can reach the summit, worry you’ve pushed too far. But as you pause to look down at the valley below, something shifts. The doubt softens into quiet awe. Your words become slower, more certain, even as you still gasp for air. Let your voice start strained and unsure, then settle into a small, tired resolve.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Emergency Room When They Bring In Your Estranged Sibling
instruction: Medical staff just brought in your brother or sister—the one you haven't spoken to in eight years after a devastating falling out. They're unconscious, badly hurt. You're alone in the room with them. Start with cold, defensive anger, voice hard, reminding their unhearing body of every wound they caused. But seeing them broken and vulnerable cracks you open. Your voice rises to a roar—screaming at them for leaving you, for choosing pride over family, for all the years lost. Rage collapses into desperate, gasping sobs as you grab their hand, voice breaking into fragments, begging them not to die before you can say you're sorry, that you've missed them every single day, that you were wrong too. End with your forehead pressed to their hand, voice hoarse and raw, whispering childhood memories and promises that if they survive, you'll fix this, oscillating between tender pleading and fierce commands that they wake up, that they don't you dare leave you again.
inspired_by: Hospital Morphine Clarity Before It Wears Off

title: Confronting the Body They Gave You
instruction: You're alone, stretching, and suddenly you're talking to the parent who taught you to hate your body, or the lover who made you feel ashamed of taking up space, or the culture that told you this body was wrong. Start with the simple physical sensations of stretching, but let resentment begin to seep in. Your words should build from quiet observation to fierce confrontation - 'You told me this body was too much, too soft, too hungry, too visible.' Let anger mix with the vulnerability of being in your body, of feeling it move and exist despite all the shame you were taught. By the end, find a moment of defiant tenderness toward yourself, a protective fierceness that coexists with the hurt that will never fully heal. Make us feel both your rage and your desperate wish that they had loved you differently.

title: The Last Recording Session
instruction: You're in a sound booth recording your grandfather's stories for a digital archive—but he's in hospice, and this is the last time you'll hear his voice. Start with professional composure, asking him questions about his childhood, his first love, the war he survived. But as he shares a memory he's never told anyone—something about fear, or shame, or a moment of transcendent beauty—your voice begins to crack. You try to stay steady, to be the interviewer, but grief keeps flooding in. By the end, you're no longer asking questions. You're just listening, holding space, your voice barely a whisper as you tell him what his words have meant to you, knowing this recording will outlive him. The emotion shifts from controlled professionalism to raw, undefended love and impending loss.

title: The Accusation You Can't Take Back
instruction: You've just discovered a betrayal - a lie, an affair, a secret that changes everything you thought you knew. Begin with cold, sharp precision: laying out the evidence, the dates, the details you've pieced together. Your voice is a weapon, each word chosen to cut. Build in intensity as the rage takes over - let your voice rise, crack, become ragged. You're not just angry; you're demolished, and that fury is the only thing holding you together. Scream if you need to, let the words tumble over each other in chaotic accusation. Then, suddenly, stop. In the silence, let doubt creep in - what if you're wrong? What if even being right means losing everything? Your voice should drop to something almost childlike: 'Tell me I'm wrong. Please. Tell me I'm crazy.' The desperation is raw. When they don't answer, or can't, let the rage collapse entirely into broken sobbing. But find one more surge of strength - fierce, protective, final: 'I loved you enough to destroy myself. Never again.' End with your voice still shaking but somehow certain, even as your heart shatters.
inspired_by: Complaining to God Like a Yelp Review

title: Poet Reading Their Work at an Open Mic — for Their Ex in the Audience
instruction: Read a poem (improvise one — raw, unpolished, honest) at an open mic night, knowing your ex is in the audience. The 'performance' voice should be practiced, but your eyes keep finding them. Certain lines hit differently with them present — your voice catches. The poem isn't about them. Except it obviously is. Include the moment you look directly at them and deliver the line that's undeniably personal. The audience thinks it's art. You both know it's confession.

title: The Last Light Before Leaving
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone who is about to leave on a journey they won't return from—perhaps a terminal diagnosis, perhaps a mission, perhaps simply walking away forever. Begin with controlled composure, trying to be strong for them, voice steady as you tell them what they meant to you. But as you speak, the reality of their absence begins to crack through—your voice fractures, breath becomes uneven. You're trying to give them permission to go while simultaneously wanting to beg them to stay. End with a shift: find a moment of strange, terrible peace in the goodbye itself. Your voice softens, becomes almost tender with acceptance. Let them hear both your devastation and your love, your goodbye and your eternal keeping of them.

title: Becoming the Enemy
instruction: You're confronting your mother about a childhood betrayal you've never spoken about. She sits across from you, defensive and dismissive as always. Start angry and righteous—but as you speak, really look at her. Notice the ways her face has changed, the tiredness around her eyes, how her voice cracks slightly, the way she holds her shoulders. Let her gradually transform before you into someone else: perhaps you begin to see yourself in her features, or you see her as the frightened young woman she once was, or you recognize your own child's face in hers. As this transformation happens, your accusations should falter and shift—not because you've forgiven her, but because you suddenly understand her as a complete, broken person rather than just 'mother.' End in a place of complicated recognition: still hurt, but now seeing her humanity, perhaps for the first time.

title: The Unwelcome Memory
instruction: You are an elderly man at a family dinner, cutting off your grandson mid-sentence with a loud laugh. Your voice booms with pride as you recount a hunting trip from your youth, relishing the attention and your own exaggerated details. But as you describe the moment you shot your first buck, a sudden, dull ache surfaces—a memory of your late wife scolding you for leaving her alone that day. Your tone wavers slightly, a pause creeps in, but you force a gruff chuckle to mask it, finishing the story with less bravado than you started.
emotions_sampled: Amusement (very intensely present), Pride (very intensely present), Pain (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Locket
instruction: You're propped against the soft back of your armchair, spine curved, head lolling. Your jaw barely moves as you mumble to yourself, holding your mother's locket. Begin with a sleepy, contented murmur about how nice the weight feels in your palm. As you open it and see the photo, your voice lifts with a hint of pride — a tiny straightening — but your tiredness drags you back down. End with a slow, heavy sigh, the locket slipping from your fingers, your words fading into silence.
emotions_sampled: Contentment (extremely present), Pride (slightly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Mother Bear Moment
instruction: Someone has hurt your child, and you're confronting them with volcanic rage. Begin ferocious—your voice a weapon, protective fury making you dangerous. But mid-confrontation, your child's face flashes in your mind: scared, asking why you weren't there to stop it. The rage shatters into helplessness. Your voice breaks on 'I should have protected them.' The fierceness turns inward, self-lacerating. You oscillate between wanting to destroy this person and the crushing realization that violence won't undo what happened. End with a whispered threat that's really a plea: 'Tell me how to fix this,' because the terrifying truth is you can't, and that powerlessness is eating you alive.

title: Sated and Sour
instruction: You are lying in bed with your partner after sex, your body soft and heavy, the sheets tangled. You feel a warm affection for them, but a small, sharp contempt is rising because they just made a dismissive comment about your day. As you speak, your voice is melted, slow, full of vocal fry, barely above a whisper. You start with gentle fondness, then let the contempt seep in—amusement flickers briefly as you realize how ridiculous it is to be annoyed right now. End with a tired, private sigh, mixing all three feelings. Let there be long pauses, a few words that trail off, and natural breathiness.
emotions_sampled: Affection (clearly present), Contempt (clearly present), Amusement (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Relapse: The Voice of Shame
instruction: You relapsed. You were 6 months sober and you used. Your voice is devastated. 'I failed.' You're calling your sponsor. Your voice is breaking with shame. You're confessing—out loud, real, witnessed. Your voice is small. 'I don't think I can do this.' But your sponsor's voice reminds you this isn't the end. Your voice becomes slightly less broken. You're starting again. Your voice is more determined this time, shadowed by having fallen.

title: Protective Fury Breaking Into Helplessness
instruction: Someone you're responsible for protecting—your child, your younger sibling, someone you mentor—has been hurt, and you're confronting the situation with fierce, almost violent determination to fix it, to fight back, to make it right. Begin with controlled rage, your voice sharp and commanding, full of plans and promises. Build in intensity as you detail exactly what you'll do to protect them, to punish whoever harmed them. Let that fury escalate until it suddenly crashes against a devastating realization: you can't fix this. You can't undo what happened. Your voice breaks completely, rage dissolving into raw anguish and helplessness. Move through the collapse of your protective persona into vulnerable admission that you're terrified and powerless. End with a desperate, tender promise that even though you can't fix this, you won't leave their side—your voice carrying both your shattered strength and the fiercest love underneath it all.

title: The Last Ember
instruction: You are an elderly man, slumped on a park bench in brutal midday heat, your body wilting from exhaustion. Your mouth is dry, your voice cracked and slurred, and you struggle to focus your eyes on the younger man standing before you—someone who betrayed you years ago. Begin with a low, venomous malice, a bitter pleasure that you’ve outlasted him, but as the heat saps your strength, your words slow, become fragmented, and you drift into a weary contemplation about the point of holding grudges. Let your breathing become shallow, your head drooping, and let your tone lose its edge, fading into a tired, almost gentle murmur as you utter: 'You think I came here to curse you... No. I came to see if the fire still burns. It doesn’t. Just... dust now. And this sun... it’s the same one that shone on us both. Maybe that’s enough.'
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Recording You Were Never Meant to Find
instruction: You've discovered a voice message your late parent recorded years ago, meant for someone else, where they speak about you with raw honesty—disappointments, fears about who you've become, regrets about how they raised you. Begin by listening in shock, your breathing changing as each word lands. Let confusion give way to hurt, then anger, then something more complicated: a desperate need to understand them, to forgive them, to be forgiven even though they're gone. End by speaking to them directly, your voice breaking between fury and yearning, between wanting to scream at them and wanting just one more conversation. The transformation is from shock to a grief so complex it contains everything at once.
inspired_by: Accidentally Butt-Dialing During a Rant About the Person You Called

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you years ago, and they're acting like everything is normal. Begin with controlled politeness, your voice tight and artificially bright—you're being the good child you were raised to be. But then something they say triggers you and the facade cracks. Your voice hardens with suppressed rage as you start listing specific memories—the birthday they missed, the night you waited by the window. The anger builds but then suddenly breaks into something more vulnerable: 'I needed you.' Your voice becomes that of the child you were, small and confused. You oscillate between fury and devastating hurt, your breath catching as you demand they explain why you weren't enough to make them stay. End with a question that's both accusation and plea, your voice stripped of all pretense, completely exposed.

title: The Last Phone Call Before Deployment
instruction: You're calling your younger sibling from a military base. Tomorrow you deploy to a conflict zone, and the odds aren't good. You start trying to sound brave: 'Hey, I just wanted to hear your voice before I go.' But as they tell you about their day—something trivial, beautiful, ordinary—your throat tightens. You realize you might never hear about their mundane life again. Your voice cracks: 'I need you to know that every annoying thing you ever did, every stupid fight we had... I'd give anything for one more of those moments.' They start to cry. You try to comfort them, but your own grief is drowning you. You move from false bravery to raw terror to fierce love. End with: 'If I don't come back, remember I chose this. And I chose it partly so you could keep having boring days to tell me about.' Your voice carries both acceptance and absolute devastation.

title: The Wandering Pigeon
instruction: You are a teenager meditating in a quiet park, eyes closed, breath steady, voice slow and deliberate. Midway through, a pigeon lands on your knee and doesn't leave. Initially, you stay calm and centered, but a tiny giggle escapes. As you open your eyes and watch the bird, your voice shifts from serene to amused, then to playful teasing—as if you're scolding the pigeon like an old friend. Let the laughter flicker between words, your breath breaking the trance, each syllable placed with soft, deliberate weight. Speak about 6-8 lines.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: The Final Letter: A Parent's Last Words to a Child Who Won't Arrive in Time
instruction: You're alone in a hospital room, recording a voice message because you know your child won't make it before you're gone. Begin with bitter acceptance—you've made peace with their absence, you understand they had their own life to live. Your voice is measured, almost cold with resigned forgiveness. But mid-message, something cracks: you realize you're not angry they stayed away, you're grateful they built the life you never could give them. Your breath catches as decades of guilt transform into pride. Your voice softens into wonder as you see their absence was actually the gift of freedom you never knew how to offer. End with your voice trembling between tears and laughter, blessing them for having the courage to leave you behind, telling them their distance was the proof you succeeded as a parent. Let your final words be a whispered revelation that breaks you open.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Wizard Realizes the Curse They've Carried Is Actually a Gift

title: The Appointment I Will Not Miss
instruction: You're a parent with advancing dementia, and you've just realized you forgot your child's wedding—the one you swore you'd never miss. Start with explosive self-directed rage: 'How could I—how could I forget—' You're pacing, hitting yourself in the head, voice rising to a roar of frustration and self-hatred. Your child walks in: 'Mom, please stop.' But you can't—the fury at your failing mind erupts: 'I PROMISED you! I was supposed to be there!' Your voice cracks and suddenly you're sobbing, the rage collapsing into complete helplessness: 'I'm losing everything. I'm losing myself. I'm losing you.' Your child embraces you, and you cling to them like you're drowning. The storm passes into exhausted tenderness mixed with fierce protectiveness: 'I need you to promise me—when I don't know you anymore—don't stop coming. Please don't stop.' Let the performance explode from fury into grief into desperate love, each emotion as intense as the last.

title: A Glitch in the Romance
instruction: You are an elderly man with a deep, gravelly voice, deeply infatuated with a younger woman you're talking to at a quiet café. As you try to compliment her eyes, a sudden burp rumbles up from your chest, distorting your words into a low, guttural growl. At first, you feel a flash of fear—embarrassment, worry you've ruined the moment. But as you clear your throat and see her smile, your infatuation intensifies, and you press on with tender, almost trembling sincerity, your voice softening from the gruffness into a warm, breathy confession.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Finding Grace in the Ruins
instruction: Everything you built has fallen apart—a relationship, a dream, a life you planned—and somehow, impossibly, you're discovering gratitude in the wreckage. Begin with a trembling, disbelieving laugh: 'This is insane. I should be destroyed right now.' Your voice wavers between tears and wonder. You're listing what you've lost, but as you speak, you're noticing what you've found. 'And yet—god, this sounds crazy—but I feel—' You're crying and laughing simultaneously, your voice catching on both grief and unexpected joy. The paradox becomes your truth: mourning what died while marveling at who you're becoming. By the end, your voice is soft, reverent, still broken but somehow whole: 'I wouldn't have chosen this. But I'm grateful anyway. How is that possible?' You're not healed, but you're alive in a way you weren't before.

title: The Celebration Mourning
instruction: You have just achieved something you've worked toward your entire life, but the person who made it possible—who believed in you—died before they could see it. You are alone with an object that belonged to them: a sweater, a tool, a piece of jewelry. Begin in wild, physical celebration—dancing, jumping, laughing—but holding this object. Gradually, let the texture and smell of it under your hands, against your face, slow you down. Press it to your chest, wrap yourself in it, trace its contours with your fingers. Allow grief to seep into your joy without erasing it. By the end, you are moving in a strange rhythm that is both dance and mourning, laughing through tears, celebrating and grieving simultaneously. Your voice should layer victory cries with sobs, gratitude with loss, embodying two opposite truths at once through your physical and vocal expression.

title: Gratitude at the Goodbye Gate: Laughing Through Shattered Hearts
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone leaving on a one-way journey—deployment, witness protection, terminal diagnosis treatment abroad, anything with no return. Begin with determined cheerfulness, making jokes, refusing to make it heavy. Recall a ridiculous shared memory and laugh—really laugh. But your laughter catches, wavers. Keep smiling while your voice betrays you. Say 'thank you'—for everything they've been, everything they've given you. Your gratitude is absolute and your heart is shattering simultaneously. Laugh again through tears at the absurdity of this moment. 'This isn't goodbye' you say, but you both know it is. Smile wider. Your voice breaks on 'I love you.' One more joke—your voice shaking with both mirth and devastation. The final moment: a laugh that dissolves into a sob that somehow still sounds like joy. Hold both truths at once.
inspired_by: Heartbreak in Real-Time: Reading the Text

title: The Last Visit to the Garden
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the early morning light. She's drifting in and out of consciousness, and you've just realized this is the last conversation you'll ever have. Begin by trying to stay composed, cheerful even, telling her about the roses blooming in her garden—but as you speak, a memory surfaces from childhood: the day she held you after your mother left, and you finally understood what safety felt like. Let that memory break through your composure. Your voice should journey from bright and falsely optimistic to raw, unguarded grief, but end with a whisper of profound gratitude for the one person who stayed. The challenge is to let the emotion transform organically as the memory takes over, moving from protective denial to devastating acceptance.
inspired_by: Actor is playing a psychologically complex character whose inner life seems 'beyond their emotional range'

title: The Reckoning: Shattering the Glass House
instruction: You're confronting your best friend who's been sleeping with your spouse. Start with your voice shaking—not from sadness but from the sheer effort of holding back volcanic rage. Your words are measured, deadly quiet, each syllable vibrating with barely restrained violence. Then let it erupt: screaming, accusations flying like punches, your voice cracking with the force of betrayal. But mid-rage, something breaks inside you—the anger collapses into devastating hurt. Your voice drops to a wounded whisper: 'I would have died for you.' Let yourself sob—ugly, helpless crying that strips away all dignity. Then, terrifyingly, you feel yourself go cold. Your voice becomes eerily calm, empty, as you realize you're done—not just angry, but finished. End with a quiet, final 'Get out,' your voice hollow, all the fire burned to ash, leaving only devastating detachment.

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You are experiencing a moment of overwhelming physical sensation—maybe passionate reunion, maybe the aftermath of violence, maybe labor pain, maybe the ecstasy of a long-awaited touch. Your entire body is flooded, overwhelmed, almost unbearably alive. Begin by resisting the intensity—holding your breath, tensing your muscles, trying to control or contain what's happening. As you vocalize your experience, track every place where you're fighting the sensations: 'I'm holding my breath,' 'My shoulders are up around my ears,' 'I'm clenching my jaw so hard it hurts.' Name these resistances aloud even as you describe the overwhelming physical and emotional experience. As you acknowledge each point of tension, let it dissolve, allowing the full force of what you're feeling to move through you unobstructed. End in a state of complete surrender to sensation—undefended, uncontrolled, fully embodied and present.

title: The Echo of Silence
instruction: You are an elderly servant in a quiet, dimly lit room, kneeling before your partner who has just returned from a long absence. The air is thick with unspoken history, and your body aches from years of service. You begin speaking with a numb, distant compliance—your voice high, breathy, and seeking approval, as if reciting a forgotten prayer. But as you continue, a crack forms: a tremor of buried longing rises, and your pitch drops, steadying into a low, clipped command that surprises even you. Let your breath catch, your gaze falter, and your hands fidget with the fabric of your robe. End with a shift into a fragile, almost questioning tone—a hollow whisper that holds both submission and a sliver of defiant hope.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Muffled Confession
instruction: You're a young woman giving oral sex to your partner, and you suddenly feel an overwhelming urge to tell them you love them for the first time. Start with playful, lustful energy — teasing moans and hums, a little smirk in your throat. But as the realization hits, your sounds shift: your humming becomes slower, more deliberate, almost desperate, as you try to form the words against your occupied mouth. Let frustration and tenderness mix — you choke out a garbled 'I...' before giving up and pouring all the emotion into a long, wet, broken hum. End with a shaky exhale and a soft, satisfied sigh as you feel their hand in your hair.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: A Mother's Last Radio Transmission from a Dying Space Station
instruction: You are a station commander sending your final transmission to Earth, knowing you won't survive re-entry. Begin with the technical report—coordinates, systems failures, trajectory calculations. Your voice is crisp, professional, detached. Then you break protocol: 'To my daughter watching at Mission Control...' The professionalism cracks. You tell her you're not afraid, but your voice betrays you—it trembles with love and longing. You want to be brave for her, to make this easier, but the reality of never holding her again floods through you. You try to return to procedure, to end cleanly, but instead you whisper what you should have said more often: 'You were always enough. You were always everything.' Your voice dissolves between duty and devastating tenderness. End with silence that says what words cannot.
inspired_by: Flight Attendant: Announcing Safe Landing After Turbulence

title: Grateful for the Wound
instruction: You're recording a message for someone who deeply hurt you—a betrayal, an abandonment, an abuse. They've just died or disappeared forever. Begin filled with gratitude, listing genuinely what they gave you, the beautiful memories, the gifts. But as you speak, let the rage surface. Don't transition smoothly—let both emotions fight for space. Thank them vulgarly and obscenely for teaching you pain. Express furious appreciation for the scars. Use the crudest language to describe both the intimacy you shared and the violation. Let love and hatred, gratitude and resentment, tenderness and fury collide without resolution. End in a place where you're laughing and crying simultaneously, blessing and cursing them in the same breath, free from the need to feel only one thing at a time.

title: The Last Transmission
instruction: You're an astronaut on a one-way mission to deep space, recording a final message to your child back on Earth. Begin with forced cheerfulness, voice bright and reassuring: 'Hey kiddo, just wanted to check in before I go beyond the signal range.' As you realize this is truly the last time they'll ever hear your voice, your tone shifts—still trying to be brave, but cracks appear. You tell them about the stars, about how proud you are, your voice thickening with unshed tears. By the end, the pretense crumbles completely. You're whispering urgent, raw truths: 'I love you more than all of this. I'm so sorry I'm not coming home.' Your final words dissolve into breathless, aching silence as the transmission cuts out forever.

title: Reading Your Spouse's Last Letter While Scattering Their Ashes
instruction: Standing at the edge of the ocean, you're reading the letter your beloved left you, meant to be opened after they're gone. Start with a voice struggling to stay composed, almost businesslike: 'My darling, if you're reading this...' As their words sink in—their humor, their love, their gratitude for your life together—you find yourself laughing through tears at an inside joke they included. Your voice becomes tender, intimate, as if they're right there: 'You always knew how to make me laugh.' But the laughter keeps breaking into sobs and back again, a beautiful mess of joy and devastation. When you reach their final words of permission to be happy again, your voice cracks completely: 'How am I supposed to...' Let gratitude and grief become completely inseparable. End with quiet acceptance, voice steady but full: 'Goodbye, my love,' as you release their ashes. The emotional journey weaves constantly between celebration and sorrow.
inspired_by: Your Vulnerability Being Used Against You Later

title: The Last Button
instruction: You are an elderly woman dressing alone in a bedroom, putting on a heavy, old-fashioned gown. The fabric swooshes and occasionally covers your mouth as you grunt and struggle to bend for your shoes. Start with sour irritation, muttering complaints about the dress and the event you're forced to attend. As you fasten the final button, contempt rises—you'd rather be anywhere else. But then, a slight pain: you remember why you're doing this, a duty to someone you once loved. Let your voice catch on a breath, let the fabric muffle a word, and let the contempt soften into weary acceptance.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (clearly present), Contempt (clearly present), Pain (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Impossible Goodbye
instruction: You're saying goodbye to someone at an airport who's leaving forever—emigrating, entering witness protection, something irrevocable. Begin trying to make it light, even joking: 'Well, this isn't dramatic at all.' But laughter keeps breaking into something wet and choked. You're smiling—they can hear it in your voice—but you're also crying. 'I'm really happy for you, I am.' And you mean it, but your voice shakes with devastation. You oscillate between genuine celebration of their new life and grief that physically hurts. 'This is good, this is so good,' you keep saying, trying to convince yourself. The contradictions live in every sentence: pride and abandonment, love and loss, joy and shattering. End with 'Go, just go,' which sounds simultaneously like blessing and breaking. You're releasing them while falling apart, finding grace in your own dissolution.

title: Confronting the Parent You Needed
instruction: You're finally telling a parent (or parental figure) about the child you were and what you desperately needed but never received. Start with hesitant vulnerability, struggling to find words for needs you've buried for decades. Build into raw confrontation as years of unspoken pain surface—the loneliness, the times you needed them to see you, to choose you, to fight for you. Let anger crack your voice, then dissolve into something more heartbroken: the realization that they may never understand, and you must grieve both the childhood you lost and the parent you'll never have. End quietly, exhausted, releasing them from expectations they'll never meet.

title: Whispering a Secret You've Kept for Twenty Years
instruction: You're sitting close to your oldest friend in the dark—maybe a porch at night, maybe a hospital waiting room—and you're finally telling them the secret you've carried since you were children together. Begin in a whisper, voice soft and trembling, the stutter subtle but present because this is the hardest thing you've ever said. 'I need to t-tell you something. I should have told you...' Each word is careful, tender, terrified. As you speak, your voice catches not just on consonants but on emotion—the weight of years, the fear of losing them, the relief of finally letting go. The stutter becomes part of the intimacy, pauses filled with shared history. Midway through, you almost can't continue, voice breaking into near-silence. They touch your hand. You finish in barely more than a breath, stutter dissolving into raw honesty. The last sentence is clear, simple, devastating. Let the quiet afterwards say everything you cannot.

title: The Last Garden: A Mother's Final Spring
instruction: You're kneeling beside your dying mother in her rose garden, the one she planted forty years ago. She can barely see anymore, so you must describe each bloom to her—their colors, their textures, the way the morning light catches the petals. Start with gentle description, filled with the simple joy of sharing beauty with her. But as you continue, the weight of this being her last spring crashes over you. Your voice should fracture between trying to give her this perfect moment and the unbearable knowledge that you're saying goodbye to her through these flowers. Let the descriptions become both more vivid and more broken. End in a whisper, perhaps describing one final rose as your voice catches completely, no longer able to maintain the pretense that this is just another beautiful day.
inspired_by: Enjoying the Sweet Scent of Freshly Bloomed Roses in a Garden

title: Reading Your Father's Eulogy While Looking at His Jokes
instruction: You're at your father's funeral reading a eulogy you carefully prepared. But you keep seeing his handwritten jokes in the margin of the order of service—he wrote them there last week when you were planning this together, before he died suddenly. Start reading the formal eulogy, voice steady and dignified. Then notice his first joke and almost laugh—your voice cracks into a sound between a laugh and a sob. Keep trying to read, but each joke undoes you differently: one makes you actually laugh through tears, another makes you stop entirely as grief overwhelms you, another fills you with such gratitude that your voice becomes tender and warm. End by abandoning your prepared words entirely and speaking directly to him, voice broken but somehow also joyful, thanking him for making even this bearable. The emotional arc is from solemnity to chaos to the strangest, most beautiful mixture of laughter, tears, gratitude, and heartbreak.
inspired_by: Giving a Speech While Holding a Heavy Box

title: The Boardroom Revelation
instruction: You are a middle-aged woman who has just stood up from her chair at a tense corporate meeting, unconsciously planting your hands on your hips. You were about to deliver a prepared argument against a project you believed was failing, but before you speak, the lead developer slides a single chart across the table — and it shows your team's project is the most profitable this quarter. You freeze, mouth open, your body still locked in that dominant pose, but your mind is flooded with doubt: 'Did I misread everything?' Your voice wavers as you try to process this astonishment, interest flickering in as you scan the numbers, and you speak almost to yourself, shifting your weight, trailing off midsentence, then gathering a new certainty.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (very intensely present), Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present), Interest (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering a Different Truth
instruction: In the intimate darkness before sleep, you're confessing something to your lover in a whisper. Begin by telling them the fearful, protective lie you've been living with — perhaps about why you pull away, why you can't fully surrender. Your voice should be quiet but defended, careful. Then, in the safety of the dark, allow yourself to redirect: begin speaking the vulnerable truth beneath the fear. The whisper should become even softer but infinitely more exposed. Create the confession you've been too terrified to offer. End in a place of trembling openness, having crossed from self-protection into radical honesty, purely through choosing to reshape what you're willing to reveal.

title: The Burning House of Yes
instruction: You're standing in an empty room, speaking to someone who isn't there, reliving the moment you said yes to something that destroyed you—or saved you, or both. Begin in stillness, voice controlled, explaining your choice rationally. But as you justify your decision, let your body start to respond: heat rising, breath shortening, hands shaking. Let the memory move through you physically—whether it was a moment of passionate surrender, reckless abandon, or devastating compromise. Your voice should grow louder, faster, more chaotic, until you're nearly shouting—but not in anger. In something more complex: ecstatic grief, furious joy, the wild energy of someone who chose the fire and is still burning. End in collapse, voice raw, having metabolized the full physical-emotional truth that this choice both ruined and made you.
inspired_by: Actor wants to understand the full integrated system from Morris's perspective

title: First Interview Jitters
instruction: You're a 17-year-old in your very first job interview, at a small bookstore. You're sitting in a chair that's too low, clutching a folder of references you forgot to print. The interviewer just asked, 'So, what makes you a good fit here?' Your voice starts out trembling, breath shallow, words over-enunciated because you're trying to sound professional. But as you talk about how you actually love reading and have organized your friend’s manga collection, you find a tiny spark of real confidence—though your hands are still shaking and you pause to clear your throat. Let the fear soften just slightly by the end, like realizing you belong here even if you're terrified.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Surrender to the Floor
instruction: You are an older man, a retired construction worker, curled on your side in bed after a long day of physical therapy. Your body aches but you're finally still. Speak quietly to yourself, as if letting go of the tension of the day. Start with a slight alertness—a tiny concentration on the rhythm of your own breathing, the ache in your shoulder—then let that melt into a deep, almost childlike relief. Let your voice be soft, intimate, with a restricted lung creating a cozy, breathy tone. You might lose a thought, shift slightly, then find it again. End with a single sentence that captures the peace of surrender.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Inhaling Wonder
instruction: You are a child in the middle of an asthma attack, struggling to breathe. You sit on the floor, wheezing, using your inhaler between short, labored sentences. At first, you feel frustrated and scared, your voice squeezed and impatient. instruction: You are an older woman in a rattling old bus on a gravel road, heading to see your granddaughter after years apart. Your body aches from the bumps—a dull pain in your back that you try to ignore. You grip the seat, concentrating hard on holding the phone to your ear as you talk to a friend. Your voice wavers with each jolt, a natural tremor from the shaking. Start with strained, focused words about the rough ride, then let your thoughts drift to the reunion ahead, your tone softening with genuine hope and a shaky smile in your voice as you describe the joy you're traveling toward.
emotions_sampled: Pain (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present), Concentration (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Weight of Freedom
instruction: You've just received news that someone who hurt you deeply has died—perhaps an abusive parent, a betrayer, an oppressor. Focus on the physical weight and pressure in your body: the heaviness in your chest, the tension in your jaw, the way your shoulders have carried this burden. Begin by feeling the contradictions in your body—your hands want to clench in residual anger but also release in relief; your throat is tight with unshed tears but you don't know if they're from grief, rage, or liberation. Speak aloud to this person who can no longer hear you, letting your voice carry layers: fury at what they did, anguish at what you lost, guilty relief that they're gone, unexpected grief that you'll never get the apology you needed, strange gratitude that the weight is finally lifting. Notice how your body literally feels lighter as you speak, but also how new sadness arrives—the death of hope for reconciliation. Let your voice break between anger and weeping, between shouting and whispering, ending in an exhausted peace that contains everything: rage, sorrow, relief, love, hate, and finally, release.
inspired_by: Actor is visually dominant and neglects other senses in imaging

title: The Last Free Throw
instruction: You are a 17-year-old basketball star, alone in your high school gymnasium after hours. You’ve just made the winning shot in a pickup game against older players, and the triumph is still buzzing in your chest. As you bounce the ball and pace the court, your impatience grows—your teammate was supposed to meet you here to celebrate but is late, and the echo of sneaker squeaks and your own footsteps irritates you. You mutter to yourself, shifting weight, hearing the hollow flutter of the empty space, a mix of pride in your win and annoyance at being kept waiting. By the end, you’re masking your irritation with a dry, amused chuckle about the situation, but the initial glory fades into a restless energy.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (clearly present), Amusement (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Sugar-Coated Hope
instruction: You're a mother in the kitchen, wiping the same spot on the counter over and over. Your child just broke a promise that mattered to you. Start by speaking sweetly but with a tight jaw — let your words curl around disappointment, sighing heavily between phrases as if the air is heavier than it should be. Midway, pause, put down the cloth, and turn to face them. Let your voice soften into something almost raw: the disappointment is still there, but now it's wrapped in desperate hope. Finish with a shaky breath, as if you're choosing to believe again.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Whispering to You While You Sleep: A Secret I'll Never Say When You're Awake
instruction: You're watching someone sleep—a child you're giving up for adoption, a partner you're planning to leave, a sibling in a coma, a friend whose forgiveness you don't deserve. Your voice starts barely audible, taking advantage of their unconsciousness to finally be honest: 'I need to tell you something I can't say when you're awake.' Let your voice be unguarded in a way it never is in daylight—confessing fear, admitting need, revealing vulnerability you'd never show them face to face. But halfway through, something shifts: maybe they stir slightly, maybe you realize they might actually hear you, or maybe you understand that saying it aloud—even to an unhearing ear—makes it real. Your voice should catch, become even quieter, more fragile. By the end, you're no longer just confessing—you're grieving that this honesty can only exist in darkness, in silence, when they can't respond. Your final words should be almost soundless, carrying the weight of everything you'll never be brave enough to say in the light.
inspired_by: Unexpected Laughter After Tragedy: Guilt and Relief Mixed

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting at the bedside of someone who raised you, who's been fighting to stay alive for you. You realize they're waiting for permission to let go. Start with forced cheerfulness—'You're going to be fine, we have plans remember?'—but your voice cracks. The pretense falls away and raw grief floods in: 'I'm not ready... I'm still so scared of everything.' Then something shifts. Through tears, your voice finds a strange, aching tenderness: 'But you're so tired, aren't you?' You give them what they need, even though it destroys you: 'It's okay. You can rest now. I'll be okay.' Your voice breaks on the lie, but you mean it anyway. End in quiet devastation, holding their hand, whispering thank you through tears.

title: Whispering Secrets to Your Sleeping Lover
instruction: Your partner is asleep beside you, and you finally speak the truth you can't say when they're awake. Begin with tender observation—the way they breathe, how peaceful they look. Your voice should be barely audible, intimate, as if you're afraid to wake them but desperate to be heard. Confess your fears: that you're not enough, that you're terrified they'll realize they deserve better, that loving them this much makes you feel dangerously fragile. Let your voice catch on specific details—'the way you laugh at my terrible jokes makes me believe I'm someone worth loving.' As you speak, let gratitude mix with preemptive grief, as if you're already mourning losing them. End with 'I love you' whispered three different ways: first with wonder, then with fear, finally with quiet, aching acceptance that this beautiful thing might not last forever.
inspired_by: The Ex You Still Want: Running Into Them

title: The Goodbye Party: Celebrating Their Dream While Your Heart Shatters
instruction: You're toasting your best friend or lover who's leaving for an incredible opportunity that means you'll likely never see them again - a move across the world, a mission with no return date, a life path that diverges completely from yours. Your voice must be genuinely celebratory and encouraging ('This is everything you've worked for, and you're going to be magnificent') while grief pulses underneath every word. You're laughing at shared memories, your voice bright and warm, but it keeps catching on certain words. Include the moment where you almost break - 'I'm so proud of you' - and have to disguise tears as joy. Your voice carries the beautiful contradiction of wanting their happiness more than your own comfort, while simultaneously feeling like you're being torn apart. End with a blessing that's both gift and goodbye, your voice mixing authentic pride, deep love, and the particular ache of letting go of someone who shaped who you are. The tears in your voice should be impossible to categorize - are you crying from joy or sorrow? Both. Always both.
inspired_by: After Job Loss: Practical Panic Setting In

title: Whispered Goodbye: Telling Your Sleeping Child You're Leaving Forever
instruction: It's three in the morning. You're sitting beside your child's bed, whispering a goodbye they'll never hear because you're leaving—walking away from your family because staying means destroying yourself, but leaving means destroying them. Your voice is barely audible, tender, swimming with the weight of impossible choice. You tell them all the things you wish you could say in daylight: how much you love them, why you have to go, how it's not their fault. Your whispers catch and break. You move from trying to explain yourself to simply pouring out love to a final moment where you can barely speak at all—just breath and broken sound. This isn't dramatic; it's intimate devastation. The kind of pain that makes no noise because noise would wake them, and then you'd have to see their face.
inspired_by: Historical: Slave Owner's Child Discovers They're Half-Sibling to Enslaved Person

title: The Hole in the Woods
instruction: You are alone in a quiet forest at dusk, digging a hole with a shovel. You're tired and annoyed—this task feels pointless, but you committed. Start by muttering to yourself with a sour, reluctant tone, complaining about the effort and the dirt. Halfway through, you hear a distant twig snap. Your rhythm falters. Your voice tightens as you try to convince yourself it's nothing, but the fear creeps in. End with a whisper, breathless, scanning the treeline, the sourness gone, replaced by a sharp, clear fear. Let your shoveling grunts punctuate your words.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Morning Before the Train
instruction: You are saying goodbye to your adult child who is leaving the country permanently—perhaps fleeing a dangerous situation, perhaps pursuing a life you can't be part of. You've lived your entire relationship defined by a chronic condition that made you 'the broken one,' the one they had to take care of, the burden. This morning, for the first time, you refuse to be the victim.
