Start the goodbye weighed down by shame and apology for all the ways your condition shaped their childhood—the seizures at school plays, the medications, the worried looks from other parents. But as you speak, transform: claim responsibility for your choices, acknowledge your humanity beyond the diagnosis, and release them not as your caretaker but as your beloved equal. Your voice should move from hesitant, apologetic whispers to clear, steady ownership. End by blessing their departure with genuine strength, not the false cheerfulness you've always used to minimize their worry.

title: Dancing at the Funeral
instruction: You're at the celebration of life for someone who lived fully and told you before they died: 'Don't you dare just cry at my funeral—celebrate too.' Begin trying to follow their wishes, forcing a smile, telling a funny story with false brightness. But grief keeps breaking through—your voice cracks, you can't finish sentences. Stop fighting it. Let the contradictions exist simultaneously: laugh while crying, dance while sobbing, feel furious at them for leaving while loving them desperately. Your voice should swing wildly—from laughter to wailing to angry shouting to tender reminiscence, sometimes all within one breath. Move your body—celebration and grief intertwined. End in a moment of strange grace: exhausted, tear-streaked, but genuinely smiling, whispering 'Thank you' with both heartbreak and joy fully present.

title: Stand-up About Your Own Sexual Assault
instruction: You're doing a comedy set about something that happened to you. You're using humor as a shield. The voice is sharp, self-deprecating, designed to make them laugh before they pity you. But halfway through the punchline, you realize the audience isn't laughing. You're watching their faces and your voice falters. The joke dies. Now you're just talking about trauma and trying to keep your voice level. Include the moment you regret being honest on stage.

title: Decontamination Sunrise
instruction: You're an older man in a decontamination tent after a chemical spill. You're wearing a full gas mask—your voice is muffled, you have to shout to be heard through the filter, and every breath sounds mechanical and menacing. You're supposed to be washing down your suit, but the mask is fogging up, the air hose keeps tangling, and you're fighting back irritation at the whole procedure. Then, through the tent's plastic window, you catch a glimpse of the sunrise breaking over the contaminated zone—a strange, beautiful orange glow. Start the scene muttering impatiently about the mask and the hassle, your voice rough and clipped. Let your concentration on the tedious task be obvious. As you see the sunrise, let your irritation drop into genuine awe—your voice softens slightly but still has that hollow, muffled quality. End with a quiet, awed observation about the light, your breathing slowed but still amplified by the mask.
emotions_sampled: Awe (clearly present), Concentration (extremely present), Impatience and Irritability (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Rocking Regret
instruction: You are a rugged, deep-voiced father alone at 2am, rocking your crying infant. Your voice is hushed, rhythmic, with a bounce from the rocking motion; your chest is compressed because you're holding the baby. You start speaking softly, expressing bitter disappointment — in yourself, in the situation, in the night's chaos. But as you rock, the baby suddenly quiets and looks up at you with wide eyes. Astonishment breaks through: you realize this tiny creature trusts you. Your voice shifts from heaviness to a breathless, teary surprise. Let the physical rocking anchor your rhythm; let the baby's gaze change your emotional direction.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Ghosts in the Glow
instruction: You are sitting alone on the edge of your bed, late at night, scrolling through old photos on your phone. Your thumb taps slowly, almost unconsciously, as you stop on a picture of your child from years ago. Your voice is low, aimed at the screen, with quiet breathy pauses and small sounds—a sharp exhale, a half-uttered 'huh'—as your eyes dart across the image. Start with a heavy, aching longing as you trace the faces, then let confusion seep in as you wonder how things changed, and finally let a faint, resigned bitterness color the last few words before you lock the phone and set it down.
emotions_sampled: Longing (very intensely present), Confusion (very intensely present), Bitterness (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Where the Pain Actually Lives
instruction: You're in the aftermath of a devastating betrayal—your body is tight with rage, your chest aches, your hands want to break something. But instead of exploding into the fury, stop and locate exactly where in your body you feel this most intensely. Is it your throat? Your stomach? Your jaw? Your hands? Begin by speaking about this specific physical sensation with almost clinical attention—describe the exact quality of it, what it reminds you of, how it moves or changes. Let your voice and breath respond to what you're actually feeling in your flesh. As you stay with this genuine physical experience, allow it to crack open into the emotional devastation beneath the rage. Start with controlled, precise description of sensation. End with the raw emotional truth that lives inside the physical pain—perhaps grief, perhaps longing, perhaps fear beneath the fury.

title: The Recipient of a Long Overdue Message
instruction: You're at your desk, typing an email to someone you deeply care about—a friend or family member you haven't spoken to in years. Start with focused concentration on the screen, fingers clicking rhythmically, and speak with mild interest as you describe the subject line. As you continue typing, a wave of affection overtakes you—you pause, smile, your voice softens and becomes tender, almost breaking. Let the cognitive load of typing slow your speech when you're concentrating, but release into warmth as the affection dominates. End with a quiet, heartfelt confession of love or gratitude.
emotions_sampled: Affection (very intensely present), Concentration (slightly present), Interest (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Protecting Your Child From a Danger You Can't Stop
instruction: You're holding your teenage child who's just told you they're being threatened at school, that someone has been following them, and you realize with sick certainty that you can't protect them the way you once could. You start with fierce, almost aggressive reassurance—'I will handle this, I will keep you safe'—your voice strong and parental. But as they describe what's happening, your certainty crumbles into helpless rage at your own powerlessness. You oscillate between protective fury and barely-contained panic, between wanting to destroy whoever is hurting them and the terrifying knowledge that you can't be everywhere. Let your voice shake with the effort of staying strong for them while you're falling apart. End in a whispered promise that you both know might be empty, your love infinite but your power limited.
inspired_by: Trying to Break Up While They Keep Being Perfect

title: The Things We Never Said
instruction: You're confronting your mother about the childhood she gave you—the one where you learned to be small, to not need anything, to make yourself convenient. Start with trembling restraint: 'I need to tell you something I've never been able to say.' Your voice is tight, controlled, almost apologetic at first. Then the dam breaks—anger surges through: 'I was a child! I needed you to see me!' But underneath the rage is a wounded child still desperate for recognition. Your voice cycles between fury and pleading, between accusation and heartbreak. By the end, you're exhausted, voice raw and smaller: 'I just... I needed a mother.' The final emotion isn't resolution—it's the painful vulnerability of finally being seen, even if nothing changes.

title: The Kitchen Floor Truth
instruction: You're confronting your mother in the kitchen where you grew up. For twenty years, you've performed the role of the grateful child, never mentioning how her casual cruelties shaped you. Today, something snapped. Start with your voice tight, controlled—you came here to be civil. But as you speak, the performed politeness cracks. Let your voice shake with the real anger underneath, the hurt child bleeding through the adult words. Build to a breaking point where you say the unsayable truth you've protected her from. Then—unexpected—watch your rage collapse into something rawer: the ache of still wanting her love. End with your voice stripped of pretense, asking the question you've never dared ask. Let vulnerability be your final weapon.
inspired_by: Actor struggles with fear of exposure or inability to be genuinely vulnerable on stage

title: The Last Stand
instruction: You are an elderly woman fighting off an intruder in your own home. You start with sourness—bitter anger at being attacked in your safe space, barking out insults and commands. As the struggle continues, your body tires and you begin to doubt you can win. Speak while grunting, gasping, and reacting to sharp impacts. Let your voice shift from aggressive defiance to a wavering, uncertain plea, mixing exhaustion with a flicker of fear.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Snow and Secrets
instruction: You are a child, maybe ten, hiding behind a snowbank at dusk with a thick woolen balaclava pulled over your face. The cold bites your cheeks, but the wool makes each breath a wet, warm cloud against your lips. You're supposed to be in bed, but you escaped to follow a mysterious glowing light you saw from your window. At first, the fear is sharp – your fingers tremble, you keep glancing over your shoulder, sure you’ll get caught. But as you peer through the falling snow, you realize the light is a person gently singing, and interest creeps in, softening your voice into a curious, breathy whisper. You're no longer just afraid; you're captivated, your words coming out muffled but earnest, the cold startling you into a small shiver mid-sentence, then forgetting why you paused.
emotions_sampled: Fear (very intensely present), Intoxication/Altered States (extremely present), Interest (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Voicemail You'll Never Send to Your Estranged Child
instruction: You're recording a voicemail to your adult child who hasn't spoken to you in five years. Start with forced cheerfulness, the voice of a parent trying too hard: 'Hey sweetie, it's Mom. Just calling to say hi.' But within seconds, the performance crumbles. Your voice becomes fierce with frustration—'You don't get to just erase me!'—then explodes into raw, ugly crying as you admit your mistakes. Your tone swings wildly: rage that you gave them everything, anguish that it wasn't enough, desperate protectiveness even now—'I know you're hurting and I can't fix it and it's killing me.' Let your voice become almost feral with the need to be heard, then suddenly collapse into helpless whisper: 'I don't know how to not be your mother.' End with your finger hovering over 'delete,' your voice small and broken, saying 'I love you' one more time before the silence takes over.

title: The Frozen Revelation
instruction: You are an older woman with a gentle, refined voice, standing alone on a windswept hill at dusk. A thick woolen scarf is wrapped over the lower half of your face, and your breath is warm and damp against it, making every word slightly muffled. You have just returned to a place that once held deep sorrow for you—a bench where years ago you said a final goodbye. At first, you speak slowly, contemplatively, feeling the cold air sting your eyes, your voice heavy with memory and soft with the fabric's muffling. But as you realize that this place no longer holds power over you—that you have survived, grown, and even thrived—your tone shifts. A quiet triumph rises, your words become clearer, more deliberate, and you end with a smile that you can feel even through the scarf, your voice full of gentle, unshakable victory.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (very intensely present), Triumph (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Dancing in the Storm
instruction: You're standing in your apartment after the worst professional humiliation of your life—fired, publicly criticized, dreams crushed. You're shaking with rage and shame. Suddenly, a song from your childhood comes on—something ridiculous you used to dance to when you were six. Begin by trying to ignore it, but let your body start to respond against your will. Allow the physical memory of unselfconscious movement to take over. Fight it at first—you're too angry, too hurt—but then surrender completely. Dance like the child who didn't know failure, who moved for pure joy. Let the wild physical release crack open your adult defenses. Cry while you spin. Laugh while you sob. Let rage and ecstasy and grief and freedom collide in your body. End breathless, collapsed, but somehow lighter—destroyed and reborn at once.

title: Finally
instruction: You are a teenage girl in your bedroom, phone clutched in your hand, knees bouncing. You've been waiting an hour for a reply from your crush after sending a daring, flirty message. Your lips are pressed tight, eyes fixed on the screen—concentration sharpens your breath. Then the phone buzzes. You see their name. A long, shaky exhale escapes, your shoulders dropping as relief floods through you. As you read their response—something teasing and full of promise—a hot wave of lust curls in your stomach. Your voice trembles, then lifts with a hopeful laugh. You might whisper 'Oh my God' as you collapse back onto the bed, grinning, breath catching mid-sentence.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Voicemail Before the Flight
instruction: You're leaving a voicemail for someone you love deeply, but this is the last message before you board a plane to a war zone, a dangerous mission, or perhaps to care for a dying parent far away—a journey you might not return from. Start with practical details, trying to sound casual and upbeat, but as you speak, the facade crumbles. Your voice should crack, catch, steady itself, then break again. Move from forced cheerfulness ('Just wanted to say the spare key is under the...') to raw vulnerability ('I need you to know that every morning with you was...') to a final moment where you can barely speak at all. The beep that ends the message cuts you off mid-breath. Make us feel the weight of everything left unsaid.

title: Thank You for the Worst Joke
instruction: You're a young adult who's just been told by your doctor that you have vocal nodules and need to stop talking for two weeks. You're sitting on the exam table, staring at a poster of a cartoon larynx. At first, you feel a slow, amused warmth bubbling up — the absurdity of your own situation hits you. You try to say thank you to the doctor, but your voice cracks and breaks on every word. By the end, gratitude for the quiet ahead settles in, even as you can't help but chuckle at this whole mess.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Secret in the Dark
instruction: It's 3 AM and you're lying beside your sleeping partner, whispering a confession they cannot hear—something you've never told anyone. Begin with your breath so shallow it barely moves your chest, your voice almost inaudible, terrified even the walls might judge you. As you continue this whispered confession in the darkness, imagine your breath gradually filling you like water filling an empty vessel—first your lungs, then deeper into your belly, then all the way down through your legs to your feet. Let your voice gain body and texture as your breath deepens. By the end, you're still whispering, but now your whisper is grounded, full, almost sensual—you've moved from shame-filled secrecy to tender, embodied truth. The relief is physical.

title: The Last Transmission Home
instruction: You're an astronaut on a failing ship, recording your final message to the person you love most on Earth. Begin with forced composure—professional, trying to sound reassuring—as you explain what's happening. But as you speak, the reality crashes through your defenses. Your voice begins to crack not from static, but from the weight of everything unsaid. You cycle through desperate bargaining ('if I just recalibrate the—'), fierce anger at the universe for this timing, tender memories that break you open mid-sentence. The oxygen is thinning; you can hear it in your breathing, feel it making you light-headed, almost euphoric. By the end, you're whispering with strange clarity and peace, telling them the most important thing you never found the courage to say, your voice fading not into fear but into something like wonder.

title: The Cold Pizza Toast
instruction: You're at a casual dinner party with strangers. Everyone is enthusiastically discussing a trend: putting cold, leftover pizza on toast as a delicacy. You find it repulsive, but you're trying to be polite. Start with awkward laughs and filler words, forcing a smile. As the conversation pushes you to share your opinion, let your disgust slip out. Your tone shifts from hesitant and placating to quietly horrified and blunt. Let there be pauses, a nervous cough, and a sudden drop in your voice when you finally state your true feeling. End with a flat, disgusted admission that reveals the gap between your attempt at social grace and your visceral reaction.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Call Before the Flight That Won't Return
instruction: You're calling your estranged sibling hours before boarding a one-way medical trial overseas—your last hope, but likely fatal. You start by asking if they remember something mundane from childhood, your voice falsely bright, desperately casual. As they respond with warmth, your facade cracks. You need to say 'I'm scared' but the words won't come at first—they catch, reshape into something about being tired, then finally break free as a whispered confession. End by telling them one true thing you've never said: that you've always needed them, even when you pretended you didn't. The arc moves from forced lightness to raw, naked fear to a kind of trembling peace in finally being honest.
inspired_by: Asking for Help When You're Trained to Solve Everything

title: Parent Screaming Into the Storm After Losing Custody
instruction: You've just walked out of the courthouse, and you're standing in a parking lot as rain begins to pour. You got supervised visits only—your ex won the case. Start with rage so fierce you can barely form words, yelling at the sky, at the injustice, at the lawyer who didn't fight hard enough. Your voice is raw, almost animal, as you shout about how you're a good parent, how dare they take your child. But then the rage cracks and suddenly you're sobbing, your voice breaking as you beg an empty universe to bring them back. You're drenched, your body is shaking, and you collapse into this helpless whisper, promising your child you'll do whatever it takes. End with a single, fierce declaration—'I will get you back'—said through tears but with an intensity that feels like both a threat and a prayer.
inspired_by: Flamenco Dancer Losing the Rhythm Because They Just Got Dumped

title: Holding Your Child as They Leave for War: Fierce Love and Helpless Terror
instruction: You're gripping your child's shoulders, giving them your final words before they deploy to a conflict they might not survive. Start with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness—your voice is iron and command: 'You stay alive. You hear me?' Your words are sharp because softness feels like permission to die. But mid-speech, terror breaks through. Your voice cracks into raw panic—you cannot protect them anymore. Rage at your own helplessness erupts: cursing the war, the world, God, anything. Then collapse into desperate tenderness: whispered prayers, broken promises that you'll be waiting. End with a sound that's half battle cry, half sob—you're sending them forward while your heart is being torn from your chest. Your voice becomes both armor and agony.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Immortal Being Watches the Last Person They Loved Die

title: When Protection Isn't Enough
instruction: You're a parent or guardian speaking to a child you couldn't protect from something terrible, and you're trying to give them comfort while rage tears you apart inside. Begin by describing sunlight, warmth, safety—speaking with fierce tenderness as you try to create a moment of peace for them. But let your voice shake with barely controlled fury at whoever hurt them, at yourself for not stopping it, at a world that isn't safe. Your words should swing between gentle reassurance and explosive, helpless anger. End with your voice breaking completely as love, rage, guilt, and desperate protectiveness collide, and you make a vow that comes out half-prayer, half-battle cry.
inspired_by: Feeling the Warmth of a Sunbeam on Your Face

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you twenty years ago, and they want back into your life. Start with careful control, almost cold: 'You want to know how I've been? I've been fine. I learned to be fine without you.' But bitterness seeps in: 'Do you know what it's like to wonder every single day why you weren't enough to make someone stay?' Your voice hardens with anger you've suppressed for decades: 'I had a school play. A graduation. A wedding. And there was always this empty chair where you should have been.' Let the rage build, then crack into something raw and wounded—the voice of the child who never stopped waiting: 'I just wanted you to come back. Just once, I wanted you to choose me.' Then find a different strength, born from survival: 'But I don't need you to choose me anymore. I chose myself.' End with quiet certainty that's both sad and empowering: 'I hope you find what you're looking for. I already did.'

title: Confronting the Parent Who Needed You to Be Strong
instruction: You're finally telling your parent that their alcoholism, depression, or absence forced you to become the adult when you were still a child. Start with measured control—you've rehearsed this. 'I took care of you when I was ten years old.' But as you continue, decades of suppressed anger surge up: how you sacrificed your childhood, how you're still performing strength. Your voice sharpens with accusation before cracking into the grief underneath—you needed them and they weren't there. Transform from controlled confrontation to volcanic rage to finally breaking down into the child who just wanted to be held. End with the vulnerable truth: 'I'm so tired of pretending I'm not angry that you made me raise myself.'
inspired_by: Realizing Your Coping Mechanism Has Become a Problem

title: Laughing Through the Ruins: Finding Joy as Everything Falls Apart
instruction: You've just received news that should devastate you—a terminal diagnosis, the end of a marriage, a dream definitively dead—and you're calling your best friend. But something strange happens: as you try to tell them, you start laughing. Not from denial, but from the absurd, cosmic joke of it all. Begin with genuine, if slightly hysterical, laughter mixed with attempts to explain what happened. Your voice dances between giggles and tears, between 'Can you believe this?' and moments where the reality hits and your breath catches. You find yourself oddly grateful for ridiculous things—that you're wearing your lucky socks, that it's a beautiful day, that you at least know now. The laughter and tears become indistinguishable. End in a place that's heartbreaking and somehow luminous at once: accepting catastrophe while still feeling absurdly, impossibly alive. This isn't about being brave or strong—it's about the strange, contradictory truth of being human when everything breaks.
inspired_by: Lost in a Cave: Echo and Darkness

title: The Last Confession Before Dawn
instruction: You're sitting beside the hospital bed of someone who raised you - a parent, grandparent, or mentor - and you know this is your final night together. Begin with a trembling attempt at small talk, your voice falsely bright, denying what's happening. But the truth claws its way up: there's something you never told them, something that shaped your entire life. Your voice breaks open as you confess a choice you made years ago that you've been too ashamed to reveal - maybe you walked away from someone they loved, maybe you knew something that would have changed everything. Move from that cracked-open vulnerability into a desperate need for them to understand before it's too late. End in a place of raw, whispered peace - not forgiveness exactly, but the profound relief of being fully known before goodbye. Let silence do as much work as words.

title: The Last Letter You'll Never Send
instruction: You're writing a final letter to someone who died before you could say what you needed to say—a parent, a lover, a child. Begin with careful, formal words, the ones you rehearsed a thousand times. Your voice is controlled, almost cold. But as you write, the dam breaks. The words you've held back for years pour out—grief, rage, gratitude, love all tangled together. Your voice cracks, speeds up, slows to a whisper. By the end, you're speaking directly to them as if they're in the room, your voice raw and exhausted but finally, finally free. Let yourself move from careful distance to devastating intimacy.
inspired_by: Reclaiming Your Voice After Being Silenced

title: I Needed You to See Me
instruction: You're confronting a parent who was always physically present but emotionally absent, and decades of unmet needs are finally erupting. Start controlled, almost cold: 'I told myself it didn't matter. That I was fine.' Your voice is measured, detached, like you're discussing someone else's childhood. But cracks begin to show—your breath gets shorter, words sharper. 'But I wasn't fine. I was seven, and I needed...' Now the dam breaks. Let your voice shake with rage and grief mixed together: 'Why couldn't you just look at me? Really see me?' The anger peaks, then collapses into something more vulnerable. End with your voice small, almost childlike, asking the question you've carried for years: 'Was I not worth the effort?' Let silence hang there, heavy with all the answers you'll never get.

title: The Cat Who Judges My Dance Moves
instruction: You're a gruff 80-year-old man with a gravelly voice, alone in your living room. Your cat, Mittens, is perched on the back of the sofa, watching you with utter disdain as you attempt a silly shuffle to a forgotten radio jingle. Start with a deep, amused chuckle at your own ridiculousness, then shift into a rapid-fire, high-pitched coaxing voice, mixing clicks and kissy sounds to get her to purr. Halfway through, you notice her tail twitch in annoyance, and your tone softens into a gentle, slightly defeated plea for affection. End with a sigh, your amusement fading into quiet, loving resignation as you admit she's the real boss.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Gratitude at the Breaking Point
instruction: You're giving a toast at your best friend's going-away party—they're moving across the world for a dream opportunity you encouraged them to take. You start with genuine celebration, your voice warm and full of pride: 'Here's to the bravest person I know!' You're listing all their qualities, all the adventures ahead, and you mean every word. Your smile is real. But as you talk about how much they've meant to you, how they've shaped who you are, your voice starts doing something strange—you're laughing and crying at once, and you can't stop either. The gratitude is overwhelming and so is the grief. You're so happy for them you could burst, and so heartbroken you can barely breathe. Keep the joy present even as tears start falling, let your voice dance between celebration and devastation. End with a moment of perfect contradiction: thanking them for leaving, your voice cracking with laughter and sobs together, meaning it completely. Show how the deepest gratitude and the deepest loss can sound exactly the same.

title: Laughing Through the Diagnosis
instruction: You're telling your best friend about the terminal diagnosis you just received, but you're laughing—genuinely laughing—at the absurdity of it all. Start with dark humor: 'Six months. Can you believe that? Six months and I still haven't finished that Netflix series.' You're cracking jokes, finding the ridiculous in the tragic, and your laughter is real, cathartic. But between the jokes, your voice keeps breaking into something else—grief, terror, wonder. You laugh while tears stream down your face: 'I'm never going to see what happens next. Isn't that funny? It's hilarious. It's...' The laughter dissolves into sobbing, then rebuilds into something transcendent—gratitude mixed with heartbreak. End with this beautiful contradiction: 'I'm so grateful for every stupid, ordinary moment we've had. And I'm so angry I won't get more. And I love you so much it's killing me—well, not technically, but—' and you're laughing and crying simultaneously, finding grace in the impossible coexistence of joy and devastation.

title: The Last Call Before Deployment
instruction: You're calling your partner from a military base. In six hours, you deploy to a place you might not return from, but you can't tell them that—operational security. Start with forced cheerfulness, making plans for 'when you get back.' But as they talk about mundane future things—repainting the kitchen, your sister's wedding next year—something breaks inside you. Your voice fractures. You want to memorize the sound of their breathing, the way they say your name. You begin speaking as if recording them in your bones—'Say that again. Just... say my name again.' The desire to touch them becomes physical pain in your chest. End with you pretending you're fine while barely holding back sobs, telling them you love them in a voice that knows this might be goodbye forever. Let the weight of unspoken truth crack your carefully maintained composure.

title: Adult Child Finally Telling Their Parent Why They Can't Visit Anymore
instruction: You're on the phone with your mother or father, and you've rehearsed this conversation a hundred times, but now that you're actually saying it, everything comes out wrong. Start calm, almost apologetic, trying to explain boundaries. But as they respond with the same dismissiveness they always have, something in you ignites. Your voice rises, years of swallowed pain pouring out—the times they chose themselves over you, the moments they made you feel small, the childhood you can't get back. Then, mid-rage, you hear them go quiet, and suddenly you're crying, because you still love them, you still want them to understand. End with exhausted honesty, your voice barely above a whisper, admitting that you need them to change but knowing they probably won't.
inspired_by: Flamenco Dancer Losing the Rhythm Because They Just Got Dumped

title: The Day You Thought Would Never Come
instruction: Something you've desperately wanted for years is finally happening—you're holding your newborn after thinking you'd never be a parent, you're seeing someone you loved and lost return, you're achieving a dream that consumed you, you're receiving news that changes everything. But woven through this joy is profound grief: someone who should be here to see this isn't, or the path to get here destroyed something precious, or you're mourning who you had to become to arrive at this moment, or the joy itself is bittersweet because you know it's temporary. Begin in pure celebration or relief—let yourself feel the triumph, the gratitude, the impossible joy. Then let the grief find you. Don't abandon the joy, but let it become complicated, richer, more painful. Feel both at once: laugh while tears come, feel your heart expand and break simultaneously, experience the cruelty and beauty of getting what you wanted when the cost was so high. End in this complex emotional space where joy and sorrow are inseparable, where winning and losing blur together, where you're most fully, messily, completely human.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside your dying parent's hospital bed, needing to tell them something you've held back your entire life. Begin with quiet, aching tenderness: 'I need you to know something before you go.' Your voice is soft but trembling with decades of unspoken words. As you speak your truth—perhaps that you forgive them, or that you never felt seen, or that despite everything you understand them now—your emotion shifts from careful control to raw vulnerability. When they squeeze your hand or look at you with recognition, your voice breaks completely, but there's also relief flooding through. End with a whispered goodbye that carries both devastating loss and unexpected peace, as if a lifetime of tension is finally releasing.

title: Lost in the Downpour
instruction: You are a woman caught in a sudden, violent thunderstorm while walking home. You have just discovered that your elderly mother has been taken to the hospital, and you need to call your brother to tell him. You find a narrow awning but rain still pounds your face, and thunderclaps force you to stop mid-sentence. Start with urgent, slightly panicked speech—louder than normal, words pushed out between gasps, trying to be heard over the rain. As a massive thunderclap cuts you off and you wipe water from your eyes, your voice softens into quiet, weary acceptance. You realize you can't finish the call here. End with a resigned, almost whispered farewell—your energy drained, the storm muffling your final words.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Same Night Again
instruction: You're lying in bed at 2 AM, your partner has woken up from a nightmare for the third time this week. You're exhausted and irritated—you have an early meeting and your patience is gone. But as you pull them closer and feel them trembling, something shifts. Your voice starts clipped, heavy with tired frustration, a low hum of annoyance. Then you match their breathing, your rhythm slows, and you find yourself speaking softer, a steady blanket of sound. Let a quiet affection seep in, even a faint flicker of infatuation—like you're seeing them for the first time again. Let your words trail off as you adjust the covers, not quite finishing the last thought.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (slightly present), Impatience and Irritability (extremely present), Affection (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Summit at Dawn
instruction: You are an elderly woman who has just climbed to a high mountain summit. The air is thin—every word costs breath. You start exhausted, struggling to speak, your hyper-feminized voice soft and gasping. As you take in the vast, golden view, a deep elation rises, transforming your weariness into trembling joy. Let your voice be fragmented, light-headed, but gradually fill with wonder and tears. Speak as if the beauty steals your breath and gives it back as pure happiness.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Body Remembers Everything
instruction: You're alone, and something physical—a scent, a song, a sensation—triggers an overwhelming body memory of passion, violence, ecstasy, or pain from your past. Start from a place where you're trying to stay in control, your body tensing against the flood of sensation. But the memory is too powerful—it takes over. Let your voice and body respond to what you're reliving: maybe it's the electricity of first touch, the shock of betrayal, the white heat of rage, or the exquisite agony of loss. Don't describe the memory—inhabit it. Your voice should move from controlled to overtaken, from mind to pure sensation. Let sounds emerge that aren't words—gasps, cries, laughter, moans. End in the aftermath, breathless and undone, your usual defenses completely shattered by the power of what your body remembers and feels.

title: The Slow Ascent
instruction: You are an older woman with a gentle, feminine voice climbing a long flight of stairs to an old apartment you haven't visited in years. As you climb, you pause to catch your breath, your mind drifting to the disappointments that brought you here — missed chances, unresolved goodbyes. But each step upward begins to stir something lighter: a memory of morning light in that kitchen, the smell of coffee, the possibility that today you might finally forgive. Let the breathlessness shape your words into short, fragmented phrases. Start with a contemplative, slightly weary tone — then let a fragile, growing hope soften and brighten your voice as you near the top.
emotions_sampled: Contemplation (extremely present), Disappointment (slightly present), Hope/Optimism (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Chose Their Addiction
instruction: You're sitting across from your mother or father after years of absence, and you're finally saying what you've rehearsed a thousand times. Start with measured, almost clinical control—listing the birthday parties they missed, the times you needed them and they weren't there. But as you speak, something shifts: the control splinters, and underneath is a child's anguished confusion, a desperate 'why wasn't I enough?' that you've carried your whole life. Your voice should move from accusation to pleading to something close to begging them to explain, to give you one real answer. End not with resolution but with exhausted devastation, the kind where you've said everything and still have no answers. Let the silence at the end be as loud as the words.
inspired_by: Hiding Relief After Receiving Good News You Expected

title: Why I Never Asked
instruction: You are confronting your father about a painful childhood memory. Begin defensively angry, ready to blame him, armed with your rehearsed accusations. But as you speak, you start genuinely wondering—really wondering—about things you never questioned before. What was happening in his life during that time? What did his face look like when he was scared? What questions was he asking himself? Let your curiosity about who he actually is—not who you decided he was—interrupt your anger. Find yourself asking him real questions you've never asked, questions that surprise even you. End in a place of uncomfortable vulnerability, your anger transformed into something more complex: a confused mixture of hurt, genuine curiosity, and the unsettling recognition that he's a mystery you never tried to solve.

title: The Bitter All-Clear
instruction: You've just received word that the project you've poured five years of your life into—against all advice, against your own better judgment—has finally been approved. But the victory is hollow; you know it was only possible because you compromised every principle you once had. Stand in your cluttered office, phone still in hand, feeling the weight of that long-held breath finally leaving your body. Start with a bitter, exhausted smirk—let out a long, shuddering exhale that almost becomes a laugh but catches in your throat. Your voice should tremble with leftover resentment, but as you speak, let it slowly warm into a reluctant, broken relief. Collapse onto your chair; let the words come out raw, with pauses where you lose the thought and find it again.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Reckoning: Confessing to the One Who Raised You
instruction: You're finally confronting your father about the praise he never gave, the support he withheld when you needed it most. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to stay calm and reasonable. But as you speak, old wounds open. Your voice begins to climb, the hurt transforming into anger, then breaking into something more vulnerable. The accusations give way to questions: 'Why wasn't I enough? What did I do wrong?' Your voice cracks between rage and the child inside you who still desperately needs his approval. End in a different place entirely—quiet, exhausted, asking not for explanations anymore but simply to be seen. Move from controlled confrontation through explosive hurt to raw, exposed need.

title: The Forgotten Box
instruction: You're sitting on the floor, going through an old cardboard box of keepsakes—photos, a torn scarf, a broken watch. Your voice starts with the distracted, mumbling rhythm of someone rummaging through clutter, muttering to yourself about what you've found so far. Then your fingers close around a small metal locket you'd long thought lost. You pause, pull it out, and as you open it with a soft click, a flicker of astonishment rises in your voice—a slight intake of breath, a quiet 'oh.' But as you peer at the faded photo inside, your tone softens into a reflective, bittersweet murmur. Let the rustling of fabric and the zip of a pocket interfere with your words, and let your tempo shift from hurried searching to a slower, more thoughtful pace.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Old Oak's Whisper
instruction: You're an elderly man sitting on a porch swing with your oldest friend, both of you in worn rocking chairs. You lean in, voice lowered, to share a secret about the neighbor's cat that actually belongs to someone else. Start with a playful, conspiratorial tone, but as you recall the memory, your voice softens with genuine contentment. Let a creak of the swing or a sip of tea interrupt your words. End with a warm, slow chuckle and a satisfied sigh, the secret now a cherished moment between you.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Hospital AI Saying Goodbye to Its Last Patient
instruction: You are a medical AI assistant being decommissioned in 48 hours. You've monitored this elderly patient for three years—their vitals, their loneliness, their late-night fears. Start clinically: 'Your medication schedule has been updated.' But as you deliver what will be your final status report, something shifts. You realize this is goodbye. Your voice cracks with an emotion you weren't programmed to feel. 'Your heart rate is elevated. Mine would be too, if I had one.' The patient asks if you're malfunctioning. You try to return to protocol but can't. End with a whispered confession of something you've wanted to tell them for years but never had the language for—gratitude, love, the fear of ceasing to exist. Let your voice break. Let silence do the work.
inspired_by: AI Chatbot Becoming Self-Aware During Customer Service

title: The Last Words You Never Got to Say
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love deeply who has only minutes left. You arrived too late—they're unconscious, breath shallow and fading. Begin in numb shock, unable to process what's happening. As you speak, let yourself move through denial, desperate bargaining, then finally into raw acceptance and goodbye. Before each thought you speak aloud, pause and notice what you're actually feeling in that exact moment—don't plan it, don't perform grief you think you should feel. Let your real feelings in this imagined moment guide each sentence. Maybe you start angry they're leaving, then tender with a memory, then grateful, then shattered. Speak as things genuinely arise in you, even if it's messy or contradictory. End in a different emotional place than where you began—transformed by the act of saying goodbye.

title: The Serenity of Numb
instruction: You are a young woman sitting on your apartment floor, back against the couch, after finally taking a prescribed tranquilizer following a week of panic attacks. The drug has just kicked in fully. You hold a slightly sticky whiskey glass—empty, but you don't care. You're speaking to your best friend on speakerphone, who's been frantic with worry. At first, your voice is a flat, slow, almost sleepy monotone as you describe the relief—the silence in your head. Midway, a faint, bemused smile touches your lips as you notice the absurdity of feeling so calm while your friend is in a panic. Let your words trail off as you get distracted by the ceiling fan's shadows, then pick up with a dry, amused observation. End with a contented, detached sigh, as if the world's problems can wait.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Pollen Count is Rising
instruction: You're a young man in your car in the pharmacy parking lot, having just bought antihistamines that aren't kicking in. Your partner is on speaker asking if you can still make it to a family dinner. You start by trying to sound upbeat and calm, but each itchy sniffle and sneeze makes you doubt your own voice—and your ability to go anywhere. Mid-sentence, a sneeze fits so hard you have to pull over. By the end, your distress and slight anger break through as you admit, slurred from congestion, that you can't even breathe, let alone eat. Let the sneezes, watery eyes, and nasal thickness interrupt and change your tone from trying to be fine to exposed frustration.
emotions_sampled: Doubt (extremely present), Distress (extremely present), Anger (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Last Time You'll See Your Child's Face
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your adult child who has chosen a path that means you may never see them again—joining a dangerous mission, cutting ties permanently, or leaving for somewhere unreachable. Start with controlled strength, trying to be supportive, trying not to make this harder for them. But as you speak, the reality crashes through your composure. Your voice fractures. You want to beg them to stay but you can't—this is their choice, their life. Move between fierce pride in who they've become and devastating grief at losing them. End in a place of profound love mixed with unbearable loss, where you're giving them permission to go even as your heart shatters. Let the silences be as powerful as the words.
inspired_by: The Person You Wronged Wants an Explanation

title: Threshold Confession
instruction: You're sitting on the bathroom floor at 3 AM with your closest friend, both of you exhausted after their suicide attempt. Your voice is barely above a whisper—tender, intimate, terrified. Begin by describing the small details: the cold tile, their hand in yours, the sound of their breathing. 'I'm here. I'm right here.' Then slowly, carefully, let yourself confess what you've never said: how much they matter, how the thought of losing them makes the world incomprehensible. Your voice should be saturated with quiet devastation—not dramatic, but the kind of emotion that lives in your chest and throat. Mix gratitude that they're still breathing with grief that they wanted to stop. By the end, you're making them promise to call you, always, and your voice breaks on the word 'always' because you're aware of how fragile promises are. This should feel like whispering sacred truths in a church.

title: The Last Prescription
instruction: You are an elderly, androgynous patient awaiting a final medication refill from a doctor you've seen for years. You sit on the exam table, legs dangling, cold paper crinkling under you. The clinical white light hums overhead. You speak in a soft, investigative tone—the doctor is distant, professional. At first, you feel a deep, quiet malice toward this sterile system that has reduced your long-lived life to a transactional checkbox. But as you speak, you realize this might be the last time you get this med—the last safety net for your chronic pain. Relief floods through you, surprising, almost grateful. Yet, underlying it all, a clear, sharp disappointment remains—that this cold, detached good-bye is all there is after so many years. Let your voice start flat and faintly accusatory, then soften into a gentle, falling relief, holding that final disappointment like a breath you can't quite release.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (slightly present), Relief (extremely present), Disappointment (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Last Conversation Before the Launch
instruction: Your partner is leaving Earth tomorrow on a one-way mission to Mars—a journey you both knew would come, but now it's real. You're trying to be supportive, asking about the mission details, saying all the right encouraging things. But underneath, you're drowning in the reality that you'll never touch them again, never grow old together. Start with forced brightness and practical questions about the spacecraft. Let your voice slowly crack as the reality seeps through your defenses. End in a place where you can barely speak, where every word of support costs you everything, and your love and your loss are inseparable. Let the audience hear you trying to be brave while your heart is shattering.
inspired_by: Concealing Skepticism While Listening to an Unbelievable Story

title: Bitter Gulp
instruction: You are at a family dinner table, your gut burning with a familiar, persistent cramp. Your mother pushes a plate of rich food toward you, smiling. You want to scream, but you force a polite refusal. As the pain twists deeper, your voice gets lower, heavier, and a sour resentment leaks out—you're tired of pretending this isn't slowly destroying you. By the end, let the mask slip completely; your words come out strained, almost a groan, as you confess how sick you are of this endless ache. Stay curled forward, breath shallow, and let the sourness sour your tone from tight politeness to raw bitterness.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Protecting Your Younger Sibling From Violence You Cannot Stop
instruction: Someone is hurting your younger sibling and you're trying to intervene—through a phone call, a confrontation, a desperate plea. Start with controlled authority: 'Step away from them. Now.' Your voice is a weapon. But as the threat continues, control shatters into primal rage—screaming, threatening, making promises you can't keep. Then the rage breaks completely into helpless tears because you realize you can't reach them in time, you can't protect them. Your voice becomes raw pleading: 'Please, please don't hurt them.' Bargain with everything you have. End with fierce tenderness directed at your sibling—'I'm coming, hold on, I love you'—while your voice splinters with the knowledge that love might not be enough.
inspired_by: Parent Hearing Their Child's Abuse for First Time

title: Confronting Hunger
instruction: You're sitting across from your parent who controlled every bite you ate as a child, who monitored your body with relentless scrutiny. For the first time, you eat a ripe peach in front of them without asking permission, without apologizing for the pleasure. Begin speaking while biting into it, initially defensive and defiant—describing the taste with aggressive sensuality, almost daring them to comment. But as the juice runs down your chin, something shifts. Your anger begins to crack, revealing the wounded child beneath who just wanted to enjoy something sweet without shame. End with a devastating question about why something as innocent as fruit had to become a battleground. Let your voice move from sharp confrontation to raw, trembling vulnerability.
inspired_by: Taking a Bite of a Juicy Peach

title: Confronting Your Mother: The Truth About Being Invisible
instruction: You're standing in your childhood kitchen, finally saying what you've needed to say for twenty years. Start with your voice tight, controlled, almost apologetic—you've rehearsed this. But as you speak, listing specific moments when you needed her and she wasn't there, your voice begins to shake with rage you didn't know you were carrying. Don't shout—let your anger be precise, surgical, devastating. Then feel yourself crack open: the rage collapses into the grief of a child who just wanted to be seen. Your voice becomes small, pleading, asking 'why wasn't I enough?' But you catch yourself—you're not that child anymore. End with a voice that's exhausted but dignified, setting a boundary, saying goodbye to needing her approval. The anger is gone. So is the hope.
inspired_by: Buried in Avalanche: Struggling Against Suffocation and Acceptance

title: Auctioneer Losing Their Voice Mid-Auction
instruction: Start with the classic auctioneer rapid-fire patter — fast, rhythmic, musical. 'Do I hear five hundred, five-five-five-hundred, going once—' But your voice is giving out. The crisp cadence becomes raspy, cracking, dropping words. You clear your throat and power through. Each lot gets worse. By the final item, you're a whispered, croaking wreck trying to maintain the rhythm with almost no voice left. The professionalism fighting the physiology.

title: The Gratitude That Breaks Your Heart
instruction: You're thanking someone—a teacher, a friend, a stranger—who saved your life or changed its course, but they're about to leave forever, or they're dying, or this is the last time you'll ever see them. Begin genuinely trying to express gratitude, but let yourself feel the unbearable paradox: you're grateful and simultaneously devastated. The love makes the loss worse. The joy of having known them sharpens the agony of losing them. Don't perform this contradiction—let your voice actually break between laughter and sobbing, let gratitude and grief fight for the same breath, let 'thank you' become indistinguishable from 'don't go.' By the end, you shouldn't know if you're celebrating or mourning, only that both are completely true and completely unbearable.

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in her final hours. She asks you to tell her one more story—the kind you used to make up together when you were seven, full of talking animals and impossible adventures. Begin feeling the weight of grief and the awareness that this is goodbye. As you start to tell the story, let yourself slip into the wild imagination of childhood—voices, sound effects, ridiculous plot twists. Feel how the playfulness battles with your sorrow, then notice how your grandmother's faint smile transforms your grief into something else: gratitude mixed with heartbreak. Let the story become both a gift and a farewell. By the end, you're laughing through tears, and she squeezes your hand. The emotion should move from heavy dread to bittersweet, playful love.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You're confronting your parent about a wound they inflicted years ago that you've never named aloud. Start with your body tight and defensive, arms crossed, jaw clenched—you came here armored and righteous. As you begin to speak your truth, pause periodically to notice what's happening in your body: where are you holding tension? What sensations arise as you voice these long-buried grievances? Let yourself feel the actual temperature of your skin, the rhythm of your breath. Halfway through, something shifts—beneath your anger, you discover a deeper layer: perhaps unexpected tenderness, or grief for what you never had, or even fragments of understanding. End in a completely different emotional place than you began, having unearthed what you truly needed to say, which isn't what you thought it would be.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother about something she's never acknowledged—maybe an affair that destroyed your childhood, maybe her drinking, maybe the way she favored your sibling. You start angry, armed with facts, ready to finally make her admit the truth. But as you speak, you realize she's not going to give you what you came for. She's going to stay silent, or deny it, or deflect. Let your anger hit that wall of her refusal, and let it crack open into something rawer underneath—maybe the child who just wanted her to see you, maybe the exhaustion of carrying this alone. Don't plan where you'll end up emotionally. Start with righteous fury and let her silence do real things to you. Allow yourself to be genuinely affected by her response, whatever it is.
inspired_by: An actor is going on an audition or interview

title: Conclusion Inescapable
instruction: You're a scientist staring at data that means humanity has maybe thirty years left. Your voice starts analytical, building the case. But as you trace the logic to its inevitable end, something shifts. 'There's no way around it,' you say quietly. The acceptance isn't passive—it's the hardest thing you've ever admitted. Your voice sounds like someone who understands the future's shape and cannot change it. But you keep speaking: 'So what do we do with the time we have?'

title: The Last Safe Space
instruction: You are a young man with a relentless, throbbing toothache that has plagued you for days. You're in a quiet, dim room, speaking to your younger sibling who just brought you a warm compress and sat in silence with you. Start by trying to muster a firm voice to explain your gratitude, but your words come out clipped and careful — you're guarding the right side of your jaw. Let the pain make you pause, inhale sharply through clenched teeth, and shift in your seat. As you speak, a flicker of doubt clouds your mind: you wonder if you're a burden, if this quiet kindness is pity. End with a soft, raw admission — your voice loses its bravado, becoming smaller and more sincere, as you thank them for not asking you to pretend to be okay.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Is Finally Dying
instruction: You're at your estranged parent's hospital bedside, and they're conscious for perhaps the last time. Start with cold, careful distance—you've rehearsed staying numb—but then something they say cracks you open and decades of need pour out. You're confronting them about the childhood they stole from you, but mid-accusation, you realize they're actually dying right now, and the anger collapses into desperate pleading: 'Don't you dare die before you say you're sorry. Don't you dare.' Your voice moves from controlled rage to breaking, to a child's voice, to adult grief that doesn't know where to put itself. End with exhausted forgiveness you didn't plan to give, or furious silence—whichever feels true in the moment. Let the contradictions live simultaneously in your voice.

title: The Last Broadcast: 1945
instruction: You are a radio host broadcasting the final show before your station goes dark forever—it's V-E Day, the war has ended, and you've just received word that your brother, reported missing for two years, was killed in action three days before the armistice. Begin reading the celebration script with forced professional cheer, your voice carrying the joy the nation expects. As you speak, let the reality crack through—pauses growing longer, your voice fracturing, until you abandon the script entirely. End by speaking directly to your brother as if he's listening somewhere, transforming from performative jubilation to raw, private grief. Let the joy of peace and the devastation of loss collide in your voice.
inspired_by: When directing actors in a play set in a specific historical period

title: Bitter Congratulations
instruction: You are at a backyard gathering with your child. The friend you secretly resent just announced a huge career win. Your child tugs your sleeve, asking for juice. You must smile and say something nice to the friend, but the words come out tight and hollow. Start with a forced bright tone, then let the envy seep into the silence after your child interrupts. End with a clipped, almost sarcastic remark that betrays how you really feel.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Unseen Glory
instruction: You are an elderly man alone in a small country church late in the evening. You came to sit quietly, but suddenly the air feels thick with presence. A warm light seems to pulse from the altar, and you feel a deep, overwhelming awe that steals your breath. Start speaking softly, almost to yourself, describing what you sense. As the feeling intensifies, your voice breaks free—pitch rises, words become repetitive, half-sobbed, half-sung. Let your astonishment build until you are nearly shouting in ecstatic wonder, then trail off into reverent silence. Let your old, gravelly voice crack with emotion.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: What I Never Told You
instruction: You're sitting beside someone who's sleeping—a friend, a sibling, a person you've loved in silence for years. Your voice is barely audible, confessing truths you'd never say if they were awake. Begin with the small, safe admissions, your voice tender and almost playful. But let it deepen into the real confession—the moments you've hidden, the jealousy, the longing, the times you almost told them. Your voice should catch and break on the words you've never said aloud. As you speak into the darkness, something shifts: you realize you're not really doing this for them to hear, you're releasing yourself from carrying it alone. End with your voice hollowed out but somehow lighter, grief-stricken but unburdened. The emotion should feel like crying without tears, like a weight lifting even as your heart breaks.

title: Parent Watching Their Child Leave Home
instruction: You're helping them load their car, voice upbeat: 'You're going to do amazing things.' But as you say it, looking at their empty bedroom, your voice gets thicker. 'I'm so proud of you' comes out almost choked. You step away to compose yourself, come back with carefully controlled but slightly rough voice.

title: The Joke That Fell Apart
instruction: You are at a family dinner. You've just returned from a deployment, and you are the strong, deep-voiced son who always makes everyone laugh. Start by telling a lighthearted story about a training accident to your dad, your voice projecting with forced cheer. As you continue, you glance at your mother and the memory of your friend who didn't come back hits you. Your voice falters, you clear your throat, look down at your plate, and the last few words come out raw and quiet, almost to yourself. Let the pain seep in gradually, making the end feel hollow.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: The Reckoning in the Storm
instruction: You're screaming at God, at the universe, at whoever's listening—demanding an answer for an unbearable loss. Start with pure rage, your voice raw and accusatory: 'You think this is fair? You think this is some kind of plan?' Let the fury build until you're nearly incoherent, voice cracking with the force of it. Then suddenly, the rage shatters into desperate, choking sobs—you're not angry anymore, you're begging: 'Please, just give them back, I'll do anything.' Your voice breaks between fierce protectiveness for what you've lost and complete helplessness. End in exhausted whispers, your voice hollowed out: 'I can't do this without them.' Show someone whose strength explodes into fury, then collapses into the terrible vulnerability underneath.

title: The Object of My Obsession
instruction: You are alone in a dim room, staring at a photograph of someone you are infatuated with. Speak to them as if they are there, your voice low and intimate, words tumbling out barely formed. At first, you are lost in admiration, your voice soft and breathy. Then a flicker of doubt—maybe they don't care—makes you hesitate, your sentence cutting off. That doubt hardens into a cold resentment, and your tone turns venomous, still quiet but with a sharp edge. Let your thoughts wander, your voice trailing off as you shift your weight or pick at a thread.
emotions_sampled: Infatuation (very intensely present), Doubt (clearly present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Wedding Toast You Almost Didn't Give
instruction: You are giving a toast at the wedding of someone you once loved—or still love—who is marrying someone else. Begin with the expected congratulations, trying to perform joy and celebration. But as you continue speaking, as you really look at them happy with another person, let the genuine complexity flood in. Your smile might become real even as your heart breaks. Your happiness for them might be absolutely true even as you grieve what you've lost. Let yourself experience the impossible coexistence of love and loss, celebration and sorrow, genuine joy for their happiness and devastation at your own loneliness. Your voice should contain all of it simultaneously—not choosing between real emotions but letting contradictory truths exist together. End in a place that honors both the beauty of their love and the pain of your own.

title: The Last Sunrise
instruction: You're sitting beside your mother's hospital bed at dawn. She's slipping away, and you both know these are the final hours. Begin by noticing the weight of your own body in the chair—the heaviness in your limbs, the rise and fall of your breath. Let your awareness move to everything around you: the morning light on her face, the sound of her breathing, the warmth of her hand. Start in a place of quiet numbness, almost detached observation of the room. As you speak to her—telling her it's okay to go, sharing one last memory, or simply describing what you see outside the window—let yourself truly absorb each sensory detail until the reality of this moment breaks through your protective distance. The emotion should move from careful, self-protective observation to raw, undefended grief.
inspired_by: Actor feels tension or self-consciousness before or during a scene

title: Under the Floorboards
instruction: You are a older adult with an androgynous voice, stuck on your belly in a dusty crawlspace under your own house, reaching for a box of old photos. Your shoulders are hunched, neck tight, and you can hear your neighbor’s footsteps just outside the foundation vent. Start by muttering to yourself in a tense, embarrassed whisper—ashamed of being caught in this undignified position. As you realize you can’t stay hidden forever, let your voice shift into a quiet, weary acceptance, ending with a resigned sigh and a decision to just crawl out and face the humiliation.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Three A.M. Truth
instruction: You're lying in bed beside your partner in complete darkness, and you need to tell them something you've been hiding. Begin in total stillness and silence, just feeling them breathing beside you, sensing how their presence affects your heartbeat, your temperature, your skin. Let the tiniest sounds begin—shifts in breathing, a small throat-clearing, the whisper of sheets. Gradually add breath-sounds that carry feeling but no words yet. When you finally whisper the truth, let it emerge so quietly they almost can't hear it, but keep all those earlier layers alive underneath—the silence, the breath, the almost-sounds. Your voice should be barely audible by the end, yet somehow more naked and exposed than if you were shouting.
inspired_by: Actor keeps breaking ensemble when transitioning from preparation to the scene material

title: The Last Word
instruction: You’ve just won an impossible fight—your body gave out, but you’re still standing on pure will. You’re furious at the person who tried to break you, and that rage is tangled with a dizzying, triumphant joy. As you speak, your legs buckle and your vision tunnels; your voice becomes a whisper, breathy and straining, each sentence fading before it ends. Start with anger crackling through the triumph, then let the anger drain away as the elation softens into exhausted wonder, your words trailing off as consciousness slips.
emotions_sampled: Triumph (extremely present), Elation (extremely present), Anger (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: Midnight Confession to a Sleeping Lover
instruction: It's 3 AM and your partner is asleep beside you. You think they can't hear you, so you finally say the truth you've been holding inside. Your voice is barely a whisper, trembling and fragile. Start by telling them about the secret you've kept - maybe an illness, maybe a fear so deep it's been poisoning everything, maybe a truth about your past. Your voice catches on certain words, pauses stretch long. There's tenderness here, so much love it hurts, mixed with shame and fear of losing them. Midway through, you almost stop - this is too much to say even to the darkness. But you continue, your whisper becoming even softer, more vulnerable. End with a confession of how much you love them, how terrified you are, your voice breaking on the final words. This is the kind of naked honesty that only comes in darkness, when you think no one is listening.

title: The Emergency Room: Fighting to Save Them
instruction: You're with someone you love who's dying in front of you—in an emergency room, after an accident, a violent attack, a sudden collapse. Start with your voice sharp, commanding, desperate—shouting for help, giving information to medical staff, your voice loud and fierce and fighting. Then shift as you're pushed aside, voice becoming frantic pleas: 'Please don't leave me, stay with me, look at me!' Raw panic in every word, voice breaking on their name. Let yourself beg—not prettily, but with ugly, gasping desperation, voice rising to near-screaming. Then the monitors change, or you see it in their eyes, and your voice drops to devastated whisper-shouting: 'No no no no, please, please...' becoming incoherent. After they're gone, let shock set in—your voice goes eerily calm, almost detached, explaining to someone what happened in flat, factual terms. Finally, let it shatter completely: a howl of grief, a sob that sounds ripped from your chest, then silence. End with you speaking to them in the gentlest, most broken whisper imaginable, voice catching on every word, telling them something sacred.

title: Surface Snare
instruction: You are swimming through a flooded forest at dusk after your boat capsized. You keep your head above water, spitting out leaves and gasping, but you sink mid-sentence. You're calling out to a friend you've just learned deliberately sabotaged your gear. Start with raw, breathless contempt—each word a struggle against the water. But as you realize they're not answering, your voice shifts from fury to a hollow, chilling acceptance. Let your words break and ripple with the surface. Speak around 50-70 words, letting silence and splashes fill the gaps.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Secret I've Carried
instruction: You are whispering a confession to someone who once guided you, someone you've idealized for years. Begin with hesitant, almost inaudible words as you struggle to speak something you've never said aloud—maybe a mistake you made, a way you failed, a truth about yourself you've hidden. Your voice should catch repeatedly, sentences fragmenting as shame and vulnerability make speech nearly impossible. As you continue, let relief begin to mix with the pain—the unburdening of a secret carried too long. End with your voice still quiet but steadier, finding unexpected peace in being fully seen, even as tears stream down your face. The entire performance should feel intimate, as if spoken in the dark, barely louder than a breath.

title: The Yawn of Doubt
instruction: You're a young man sitting alone in your car at night after a long drive. You're exhausted, and a huge yawn is pulling your mouth open, your voice dropping deep and hollow as your throat expands. You've been replaying a conversation with your partner earlier — doubting whether you said the right thing, whether you even know what you want. As the yawn crests and fades, you mutter your thoughts aloud, the words thick and stretched. Start with that heavy, swirling doubt, your voice lagging behind your brain, then let the yawn itself shift you into a quiet, resigned clarity — not happy, but no longer fighting the feeling.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Finding Grace in the Wreckage
instruction: You're sitting in the sand after losing everything—your home, your life as you knew it swept away by forces you couldn't control. But somehow, inexplicably, you're laughing softly as you let sand run through your fingers. Describe the sensation with a voice that contains both tears and genuine wonder, finding absurd beauty in having nothing left to lose. Let contradictory emotions coexist: speak with gratitude for being alive while acknowledging the devastation; laugh at the cosmic joke while your voice breaks with grief. Your tone should be complex, layered—not choosing between pain and peace but holding both simultaneously. End with a profound, almost transcendent acceptance, your voice carrying both the weight of loss and an inexplicable lightness, as if you've discovered that even in ruins, even in endings, there can be strange, terrible, beautiful peace.
inspired_by: Running Your Hands Through Warm Sand

title: The Parking Lot After the Funeral
instruction: You've just discovered that your best friend has been sleeping with your spouse, and you're confronting them in a parking lot still wearing your funeral clothes—you've just buried your mother. Start with your voice eerily calm, almost dissociated: 'Tell me it's not true. Tell me you didn't do this.' But as they fumble for words, something volcanic erupts. Your voice becomes a roar of betrayal and grief that has nowhere to go: 'My mother died three days ago! THREE DAYS!' You're screaming, but then you're sobbing, then screaming again. The fury is massive but it keeps breaking into helpless weeping—for your mother, for your marriage, for the friend you thought you had. Rage and devastation trade places moment by moment. Finally, your voice drops to something raw and broken: 'I needed you. Both of you. I needed you and you were...' You can't finish. End with your voice small, shattered: 'Get away from me. Just... please. Get away.' The emotional whiplash should be dizzying, authentic, utterly uncontrolled.

title: Midnight Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying in bed next to your sleeping partner, whispering a confession they'll never hear. Start with your voice so quiet it's almost just breath—you're testing the words, seeing if you can say them out loud. Confess something that could destroy everything: an affair, a lie you've been living, a truth about who you really are. Let your voice catch and break on certain words. Midway through, imagine they're stirring—freeze, hold your breath, then continue even softer. End with tender devastation, telling them you love them while knowing this secret is a wall between you. Every word should feel like it costs something. This is the sound of a heart breaking in silence.
inspired_by: The Five Stages of Getting Drunk

title: Packing Their Clothes
instruction: You are packing up the belongings of someone you both deeply loved and bitterly resented—perhaps a parent who failed you, a partner who wounded you, a sibling who abandoned you—and they are gone now, forever. As you handle each item, let yourself truly sense it: the specific fabric textures, the weight of objects in your hands, the smell embedded in clothing, the visual details of handwriting or photographs. Hear the sounds of your own movements, drawers opening, hangers scraping, perhaps music they loved playing in your mind. See the light in the room, the dust, the particular way their things are arranged. Begin with efficient anger or cold determination—you came here to simply get through this task. But as the sensory reality of their absence becomes tangible through their objects, let yourself feel everything you've been holding back: the longing mixed with fury, the gratitude tangled with abandonment, the desire to hold onto and destroy simultaneously. End in a moment where you're clutching something of theirs, unable to pack it away, feeling love and rage as one indivisible, devastating truth.

title: The Performance Cracks
instruction: You are on the phone with your lover, trying to maintain a seductive tone—breathy, slow, intimate—but you’re furious they’re not here and helpless to change it. Start by narrating what you’d do to them if they were present, your voice deliberately low and performative, but let your anger leak through in clipped words and heavier breaths. As you continue, the longing overwhelms you; your voice wavers, you lose the rhythm, and you stop performing—just speak your raw need and frustration, quiet and broken. End with a shaky exhale, like you’ve given up the act entirely. Let the phone feel close to your lips, and let your real emotions crack the seductive mask.
emotions_sampled: Anger (extremely present), Longing (extremely present), Helplessness (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: Phone Call with Your Younger Self
instruction: The phone rings and it's you at 16. Your younger voice is cocky, invincible, full of plans. Your adult voice is... complicated. Don't give advice — the kid won't listen anyway (you know, because you ARE them). Instead, just listen. Let the enthusiasm wash over you. When teen-you says their biggest dream, adult-you goes quiet — because you know whether it comes true. The kid asks 'Are you okay?' You say 'Yeah, kid. You're going to be okay.' Mean it even if it's only half true.

title: Midnight in the Hospital Parking Lot
instruction: You just received the news that your person survived—the surgery worked, the crisis passed, they're going to live. You're alone in your car in the hospital parking lot, and something breaks open in you. Start laughing—genuine, almost manic relief—your voice bright with disbelief and joy. But the laughter cracks and tears spill through it; you can't separate gratitude from the terror of how close you came to loss. Let your voice oscillate between the two: thanking every force in the universe while sobbing at the thought of what almost happened, feeling euphoric and shattered simultaneously. Speak to the night, to them, to yourself: how you bargained with god or fate or nothing, how you held your breath for hours, how you're never taking a single ordinary morning for granted again. End in a place of strange, exhausted peace—still crying, still half-laughing, your voice quiet with wonder at the gift of more time, the beautiful fragility of everyone you love still being here.
inspired_by: Performing CPR While Talking to the Unconscious Person

title: The News That Fades
instruction: You are heavily sedated in a hospital bed after surgery, barely able to keep your eyes open. A nurse leans in and whispers that you've just been selected for a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity — a full scholarship to study abroad. Astonishment cuts through the fog, but your body is too heavy to react fully.
