Start with a groggy, barely conscious murmur as you try to understand the words, then let surprise flicker in your slow, breathy voice — a sharp intake, a delayed 'what?' that trails off. The astonishment struggles to stay alive as your speech gets slower, softer, finally dissolving into a whisper as you slip back under.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Last Lucid Hour
instruction: You're in the final moments of clarity before dementia takes you completely, saying goodbye to your adult child. Begin with desperate urgency, clinging to their face, trying to memorize every detail while you still can. Your words come fast, frantic—'I need to tell you while I still know who you are.' Pour out a lifetime of things unsaid: pride, regrets, the specific moment you first held them, how their laugh sounds like their grandfather's. As the fog begins creeping back in mid-sentence, your clarity fragments. You grasp for their name, panic rising, then—in the space between knowing and forgetting—find a devastating peace. End in a whisper, no longer sure who they are but absolutely certain you love them, your voice carrying both the grief of losing yourself and the grace of one last true moment.

title: The Pre-Arrival Jitters
instruction: You're in your apartment, nervously tidying up while on a phone call with a man you matched with online. He's about to come over for a hookup, and you're trying to sound casual and flirty, but a deep fear keeps surfacing—what if he's dangerous? What if this is a mistake? Your voice starts light and warm, with that fast-forwarded intimacy and nervous laughter, but as the call goes on, you lose your train of thought, pause too long, and your tone shifts to something more strained and hesitant. You finally decide to go through with it, but your last words are soft and shaky, revealing the terror you're hiding behind the flirtation.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Under the Visor
instruction: You are a child, maybe seven or eight, wearing a too-big hard hat with a scratched visor, standing in a dusty construction zone. The noise of machinery is a dull roar around you. You are holding a found object—a heavy metal bolt—and you feel a strange, cold numbness inside, like you've forgotten how to feel anything. You see a small bird trapped under a tarp, struggling. The numbness curdles into a quiet malevolence, a desire to watch it struggle more. You speak to the bird in a flat, almost cheerful whisper, your own voice strange inside the hard hat's echo. As you shift your weight, the visor catches the light and for a second you see your own eyes reflected, and real fear jolts through you—then the numbness returns, harder. 'You look so tired. Maybe you should just close your eyes. I can help you stop moving. The quiet would be nice, wouldn't it? Your wings make too much noise. Just... stop.'
emotions_sampled: Emotional Numbness (very intensely present), Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Fear (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Swallowing Fire and Honey
instruction: You have just experienced something that floods your body with contradictory physical sensations: imagine you've been reunited with someone after years of aching separation, and the touch of their hand on your face causes both ecstasy and actual physical pain—perhaps from grief, perhaps from the intensity of feeling something you thought was dead. Start by describing the physical sensation in their touch: is it burning, electric, too much, not enough? Let your voice ride the waves of sensation—gasping, laughing, maybe crying, but always rooted in the body's response. Move from trying to control the feeling to surrendering to it completely, letting pleasure and pain become indistinguishable. End in a place of physical and emotional exhaustion that feels like being reborn.

title: The Whispered Truth
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your lover is asleep beside you, and you're whispering a confession they can't hear—that you've been pretending in small ways, performing a version of yourself you thought they wanted. Your voice is barely audible, catching on tears you're trying to keep silent. You describe moments where you laughed at things that weren't funny, stayed quiet when you wanted to speak, shaped yourself to fit. But as you whisper, something gentler emerges: you realize they've been doing the same thing, both of you performing for each other. Your whisper becomes almost tender, sad but also softly amused at the tragedy of two people hiding from each other. End with your voice full of quiet determination, still whispering: 'Tomorrow, I want to try again. The real way. I want to be brave enough to let you meet me.' There's grief in your voice, but also fragile hope.

title: The Inheritance Box
instruction: You're opening a box of your estranged father's belongings six months after his death. Inside is a letter he wrote you every year on your birthday but never sent—twenty-three letters you never knew existed. Begin with bitter satisfaction: he's gone, and you never have to deal with him again. Your body is closed, arms crossed or jaw tight. But as you read the first letter, then the second, something unbearable happens. He was writing to you all along. He did think of you. Your anger doesn't disappear—it intensifies even as love breaks through. You want to scream at him for never sending them, even as tears come for the tenderness in his words. Let your body hold both: fists clenched while tears fall, voice shouting his name while it breaks with grief. Don't choose one emotion over the other. Don't let your voice express anger while your face shows sadness, or vice versa. Let rage and love, betrayal and longing, gratitude and resentment crash through you at the same time, your entire instrument churning with the unbearable contradiction of loving someone who failed you, of grieving someone you also resent, of finally being seen by someone who's now gone forever.

title: The Rowing Revelation
instruction: You are an older man, alone in a dimly lit boathouse, pulling hard on a rowing machine as part of your grim daily routine. Your mind is heavy with the sadness of a recent loss you can't shake. As you strain through a pull, you glance at a newspaper on the floor and see a headline that shocks you — someone you trusted has done something appalling. Your voice must carry the rhythmic, labored breath of exertion: a guttural grunt on each pull stroke, then a breathy, slower phrase as you slide back. Begin with a low, sorrowful resignation, then let your astonishment and disgust erupt in the brief recovery moments, your tone wobbling slightly with the rocking motion of your body. End with a quieter, hollowed-out disbelief as your hands grip the handles tighter.
emotions_sampled: Sadness (slightly present), Astonishment/Surprise (clearly present), Disgust (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Packing Their Childhood Room
instruction: You are packing up the childhood bedroom of someone you love—your own child leaving for college, a younger sibling who died, or perhaps your own childhood room as your parents prepare to sell the house. Begin with a practical, almost cheerful tone as you narrate what you're packing: finding old toys, clothes, drawings, journals. Your voice should carry forward momentum, efficiency, even humor at the ridiculous things kids save. But as you discover one specific object—a stuffed animal, a photo, a birthday card with a message—let your voice catch. The conflict: you are genuinely happy about the growth or change this packing represents (freedom, new chapters, release from grief) while simultaneously being devastated by the finality of this closing door. Your voice must hold both feelings authentically—speaking gratitude and pride while barely containing grief. End with you unable to pack this one object, your voice breaking not from pure sadness but from the unbearable beauty of loving something enough to let it go.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: Confront your parent (or child) about a family secret that has poisoned your relationship for years—something never spoken aloud but always felt. Begin with careful, measured words, trying to be reasonable, trying to have a 'mature conversation.' But as you speak, let the years of swallowed anger, confusion, and hurt begin to surface. Your voice should start controlled, almost diplomatic, then gradually become more visceral as you realize they're not going to give you the answers or apology you need. End in a place where you're no longer asking them to explain—you're telling them how their silence shaped you. The arc moves from hoping for resolution to claiming your own truth regardless of their response.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother about the abuse she witnessed but never stopped. Start with a question, almost gentle: 'Did you know?' But something breaks open. Your voice rises—not to screaming, but to a rawness you've never let her hear. You describe specific moments she looked away, and your tone becomes almost forensic, like you're presenting evidence of a crime. 'You chose him over me. Every single time.' The rage is there, but underneath it is a child still wanting her to say she's sorry. By the end, your voice drops to something quiet and final: 'I needed a mother.' The word 'needed' is past tense. That's the verdict. Let the anger and the grief fight for control of your voice.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally face-to-face with the parent who abandoned you as a child, and they're dying. You came prepared with anger, with a list of everything they stole from you—every birthday, every nightmare, every moment you needed them. Start cold, controlled, almost clinical as you tell them exactly what their absence cost you. But as you speak, rage floods in—your voice rises, shakes, becomes almost savage with decades of suppressed pain. You want them to feel it, to really understand. Then you see them crying, and something unexpected happens: underneath your fury is a child who still wanted to be loved. Your voice breaks completely, becomes small and lost as you ask the question you've always needed answered: 'Why wasn't I enough?' The anger and grief collide, leaving you devastated and raw, no longer sure what you came here to accomplish.

title: The Last Harvest Before the War
instruction: You are a farmer saying goodbye to your grown child who is leaving for a war they may not return from. Begin with forced cheerfulness as you talk about the harvest, the land, practical things—your voice steady, almost businesslike. But as you speak, the weight of what's unsaid begins to crack through. Your tone shifts from practical instructions about the farm to desperate attempts to say everything important in these final moments. End with your voice breaking as you try to give them permission to go while your heart is shattering. Let the love and terror exist together—don't perform grief, let it catch you by surprise as you speak. The emotional journey moves from protective stoicism to raw, unguarded love and fear.
inspired_by: The Farmer and the Talking Crow

title: The Last Scrape of the Sky
instruction: You're a teenage girl, alone in your backyard at dusk, reaching up with both arms to try to touch the lowest branch of an old oak tree. Your ribs are stretched, your voice is thin—you can't breathe deeply. You start speaking numb, almost robotic, as if you're just going through the motions of a silly challenge: "I can almost reach it... just a little more..." Then you notice a boy you've been crushing on is watching from his window across the fence. Your voice shifts—still pulled tight from the stretch, but now tinged with a flutter. You stammer, lose your thought, then find it again, trying to act casual while your heart races. By the end, the numbness is gone, replaced by the breathless thrill of infatuation.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: False Alarm at the Checkpoint
instruction: You are a young soldier on night watch at a remote checkpoint. Your squad has been on high alert for hours. Suddenly, you hear rustling in the dark—your heart pounds, you bark out a challenge, weapon ready. But it's just a stray dog. As you lower your weapon, the tension drains from your shoulders, leaving you shaky, exhausted. Speak the challenge first with clipped, metallic urgency, then let your voice crack with relief and weariness as you mutter to yourself or your unseen buddy. Fumble for your flashlight, swallow hard, and let the fatigue seep into your pause.
emotions_sampled: Distress (very intensely present), Relief (clearly present), Fatigue/Exhaustion (slightly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Clarity Striking
instruction: The fog clears suddenly. You understand what you need to do. You understand why you've been stuck. Your voice shifts from muddy to crystalline. Words come with new precision: 'Oh. OH. That's why I've been afraid of—' Your speech becomes organized, thoughts linear. Breathing deepens. There's certainty but not rigidity; you're seeing clearly. Physical: you sit up, shoulders back. Your voice has authority because it's rooted in genuine understanding, not ego. By the end, you're stating simple truths with profound relief: 'I can do this.'

title: The Secret Garden: A Whispered Confession in the Dark
instruction: You're lying next to your best friend late at night, and they've just shared something vulnerable. In the quiet darkness, you realize you need to tell them a truth you've carried for years—that you've been in love with them, or that you betrayed them once, or that you're leaving and won't be coming back. Begin with your voice barely audible, testing the words: 'There's something I need to say.' The darkness makes you braver, but your voice still trembles. As you speak your truth, let the emotions layer: shame, relief, grief, tenderness all at once. Your friend's silence stretches, and you can't read it. Your voice becomes even softer, almost breaking: 'Please say something.' Their response—whatever you imagine it to be—either shatters you or saves you. End with a whisper that carries acceptance of whatever comes next: 'I just needed you to know.' Make this so intimate, so fragile, that it feels like the words might dissolve in the air.
inspired_by: Parent Showing Quiet Pride: Misreading, Then Understanding

title: The Promotion Call: Success Tastes Like Ash and Honey
instruction: You just received the phone call you've worked toward for years—the job, the acceptance, the recognition, the triumph. But the one person you most wanted to share this with is gone—dead, estranged, or simply no longer in your life in a way that makes celebrating together possible. Begin with genuine excitement, letting the adrenaline of good news fill your body. Call out to them, reach for your phone to text them, turn to share the moment—before remembering they won't answer. Let specific memories flood in: moments they supported you, moments they doubted you, a specific time they said something that drove you forward, a moment you disappointed them or they disappointed you. Allow joy and grief to exist simultaneously—laugh and cry in the same breath. Let your body hold both the expansion of success and the collapse of loss. Don't choose between them—let the contradiction be unbearable and real. By the end, arrive at a complex truth about love, ambition, absence, and the bittersweet nature of getting what you wanted when the cost was something you didn't expect to pay.
inspired_by: Character Relationship Imaging: Death of a Salesman (Biff and Willy)

title: Stirring Thoughts
instruction: You're a child standing on a stool, carefully stirring a pot of soup while your parent is outside chopping vegetables. The kitchen is loud—sizzling, clattering, bubbling—so your voice has to push through the noise a bit at first. You start by muttering about the heat and how you'd rather be playing, but as you stir, your mind wanders to the toy you lost yesterday. Your voice gets quieter, more absent-minded, trailing off as you imagine where it could be. By the end, you're not really talking to anyone anymore—just whispering to yourself, accepting that it's gone, and feeling a small, sad calm.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Gasp Window
instruction: You are a woman in her sixties, swimming laps at a quiet indoor pool. Your voice is usually soft and polite, but now you're pushing through the last 50 meters of a long set. You started the swim angry—fuming over a family argument that replayed in your head with every stroke. Now, halfway through this final lap, the anger is fading. You speak only during the brief turn of your head to breathe, words escaping in ragged bursts between arm pulls. Your voice is wet, breathy, and clipped—water sloshes in your mouth, and you sputter mid-sentence. Let your body feel the burn in your shoulders and the hollow echo of the pool. By the end, let a small, surprised relief creep in—not happiness, just a lighter ache, as if the swim has finally wrung the rage out of you.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You're sitting beside someone you love who is dying, and they need to hear you say it's okay to let go. Start with barely controlled panic, voice tight with the desperate need to keep them here. 'Don't leave me yet. Please. I'm not ready.' But as you hold their hand, something shifts—you realize your fear is holding them captive. Your voice must soften, breaking with love as you give them the hardest gift: 'I'll be okay. You can go now.' The tears come, but there's a strange, terrible peace underneath. End with whispered tenderness and devastating release: 'I love you. It's okay. You can rest now.' Let genuine grief and profound love exist in the same breath.

title: Found in the Pine Grove
instruction: You are an elderly man who wandered off the trail hours ago, disoriented by heat and dehydration. Now, a search team has just found you, and you are leaning against a fallen tree, trembling. You are still dizzy — your words slur slightly, and you keep losing your train of thought as the world swims. But with every second, the terror of being lost is replaced by a rising wave of gratitude. Start with a shaky, almost drunken mutter — ‘Oh my God, I thought… I thought I was gone…’ — then let your voice crack and lift as you reach out to touch the rescuer’s arm, tears mixing with a broken laugh. End with a deep, warm, exhausted thank you that sounds like a prayer. You may cough, shift your weight, or trail off as your mind drifts, but finish with the word ‘thankful’ lingering in the air.
emotions_sampled: Intoxication/Altered States (very intensely present), Thankfulness/Gratitude (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Unraveling Gift
instruction: You are a mother unwrapping a birthday present made by your young child—a lopsided clay figure meant to be a cat. As you tear the paper, you feel a wave of disappointment; it’s broken, the tail snapped off, and there’s a dark, waxy smear that looks like dried blood. You keep cutting into your child’s excited explanations, your voice climbing higher and faster, urgency bleeding into malice as you demand how it got hurt. But midway through, your own words snag—you realize the smear is just red paint, the tail is in your daughter’s pocket, and your confusion twists into shame. Start harsh, push against her rhythm, then soften into a near-whisper of sorrow and relief.
emotions_sampled: Malevolence/Malice (very intensely present), Confusion (very intensely present), Disappointment (extremely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Weight of Tenderness
instruction: You are whispering to your sleeping lover in the middle of the night, speaking truths you cannot say when they're awake and looking at you. Begin in a state of drowsy vulnerability, your voice barely audible, your consciousness hovering at the edge of sleep. The heaviness in your body mirrors the weight of unspoken feelings. Confess your fears about the relationship, your secret gratitude, your terror of losing them. As you whisper, something shifts—tears come, your throat tightens, and you become achingly awake and present, still speaking softly but now with crystalline awareness of how much this person means to you. End with your hand gently touching their face, fully conscious of the fragility of love.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about why they never protected you from their partner's cruelty when you were a child. Start with careful, measured words—you've rehearsed this, you want to stay calm. But as you speak, decades of swallowed hurt begins pouring out. Your voice moves from controlled disappointment to raw accusation to something more complex: you hear yourself sounding just like them, and it horrifies you. The anger doesn't disappear, but it becomes tangled with recognition, with unwanted empathy, with the terrible understanding that they were broken too. End not with resolution, but with the exhausted, complicated truth of loving someone who failed you.

title: Vigil Voice
instruction: You're speaking softly to someone you love who is sleeping—maybe your child, maybe your partner—after a day when you almost lost them. A close call, an accident, a near-miss that showed you how fragile everything is. Your voice is barely above a whisper, catching on words: 'You don't know how scared I was today.' There's tenderness so acute it hurts. Your throat keeps closing. You're not asking them to wake up; you're confessing to the darkness. 'I watched you sleeping and I couldn't stop shaking.' Each phrase is interrupted by breath, by the body's need to hold back tears. End with something simple that breaks you completely: 'I don't know how to protect you from everything.' Let silence do half the work. This is intimacy at its most naked.

title: Dancing at Your Wake
instruction: You are speaking at someone's funeral—but not with the expected solemnity. This person would have hated a sad funeral. Begin by trying to tell a funny story about them, forcing lightness into your voice, maybe even laughing. But as you speak, let the absurdity of standing here, making people laugh while your heart is shattered, start to destabilize you. Your laughter should become increasingly fragile, catching in your throat. Let gratitude for having known them war with the devastating unfairness of their absence. Midway through, shift—perhaps you suddenly speak directly to them, your tone changing from public to intimate, as if everyone else has disappeared. Mix defiance (refusing to let this moment be only sad) with surrender (acknowledging the crushing weight of loss). End with something that's simultaneously a celebration and a lament—your voice should carry both joy at their existence and rage at death itself. Let your final words hold both a smile and tears without contradiction.
inspired_by: Actor is working on a scene and needs to identify what to work on—which obligations are most pressing

title: The Summit's Last Mercy
instruction: You are an elderly hiker, miles into a trail, and your body has just given out. You collapse onto a rock, dizzy and nauseous, your legs trembling. Your voice is hollow, each word taking effort—sounds slurred, breath short. In this fog of exhaustion, your hiking partner kneels beside you, offering water and quiet encouragement. You begin confused, struggling to form sentences, but as you meet their eyes, a wave of raw thankfulness breaks through. Let your words trail off, catch, and fade as you express gratitude—not polished, but genuine, with tears threatening to spill. Speak as if every syllable costs you, but the feeling is real and urgent.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Monster in My Throat
instruction: You're a teenage boy at a school party, chatting up your crush. You feel a huge burp building in your throat, and you're terrified it'll come out and ruin everything. Start by nervously trying to sound cool and charming, your voice a bit high and rushed, but the pressure rises. The burp erupts—deep, guttural, monstrous—and you instantly freeze. End with a weak, embarrassed laugh and a mumbled apology, your voice cracking with leftover fear and shame.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: The Rearview Glare
instruction: You are an older man sitting in the passenger seat of a parked car, your neck twisted painfully to glare over your shoulder at someone in the back seat. Your voice is strained from the torsion, each word squeezed out as you begin with hot anger and biting contempt, lecturing them for a mistake. Midway, you notice something unexpected in their expression—a flicker of defiance or truth—that sparks genuine interest. Your tone shifts, the anger softening into a curious, almost reluctant listen, while the physical ache keeps your voice rough and uneven. Speak naturally, with pauses, shifts in your seat, and the rawness of a man too proud to fully turn around.
emotions_sampled: Anger (extremely present), Contempt (clearly present), Interest (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confusion Overwhelming
instruction: You don't understand what's happening. Your voice is lost, searching: 'I don't—why would they—what does that even mean?' Sentences don't complete. Words come hesitantly. Breathing is irregular. When you try to explain your confusion, the explanation becomes confused. 'So like, there was a thing, and then something else happened, and I don't know which is connected to which.' Your vocal tone is questioning, uncertain. Even simple concepts feel untranslatable. There's frustration in the confusion—you can feel how lost you are. Physical: you're gesturing, trying to make sense.

title: Whispering Your Love to Someone in a Coma
instruction: Your person is in a coma after an accident. You're alone with them, holding their hand. Your voice starts soft, almost conversational: 'Hey, it's me.' You tell them about your day, voice catching on normal details that suddenly feel unbearably precious. Then you confess things you never said when they could hear—'I was scared to tell you how much I need you.' Your voice becomes intimate, tender, barely audible, as if speaking too loud might shatter the moment. You apologize for fights, for things left unsaid, your throat closing around words. You tell them about the future you planned together, voice breaking on 'we were supposed to...' By the end, you're simply breathing with them, voice reduced to a whisper: 'Please don't leave me,' mixing desperate hope with quiet acceptance that they might already be gone.
inspired_by: Your Partner Saying They Don't Want Children

title: Packing Your Child's Room for the Last Time
instruction: Your child is alive and well—they've just grown up and moved across the world to start their own life. You're packing up their childhood bedroom, and you should feel proud, happy for them. You ARE proud. You ARE happy. But as you fold their old soccer jersey, find a drawing they made at age six, touch the growth marks on the doorframe, grief ambushes you. Let yourself smile at memories while tears come—not sad tears, not happy tears, but that strange complex ache of time passing. Talk to them as if they're still here: 'Remember when you...' Let your voice carry both celebration and loss. Laugh at something funny, then feel your throat close. Hold an object and let it anchor you to a specific moment—their small hand in yours, their sleepy voice, the weight of them as a baby. End with contradictions unresolved: grateful and bereft, excited for them and mourning for yourself, full of love and impossibly empty.

title: Correction in Front of Crowd
instruction: You've just said something factually wrong in front of a group, and someone has corrected you. Your voice was confident, now it's embarrassed: 'Oh, I didn't know that.' You're trying to play it cool, but your voice wavers. Your tone becomes defensive: 'Well, I was close.' But you weren't. By the end, you're retreating, your voice quieter as you sit back and let someone else talk. The confidence is shattered.

title: Smoothness Control
instruction: You're a con artist on a phone call, manipulating a mark. Your voice is smooth, flowing, almost hypnotic: 'I understand your concerns. Let me explain.' Every word glides into the next. There's no friction, no pause, no space for doubt. It's practiced, perfected. Then your partner signals from across the room that the cops are coming. Your smooth voice doesn't change, but internally, everything fractures: 'Actually, I need to go.' Still smooth, but now you hear the effort to maintain it. You hang up. Your voice immediately drops the smoothness and becomes sharp, panicked: 'Move. Now.' The contrast reveals that the smoothness was always a cage.

title: The Climb
instruction: You are a young man on a stationary bike, pushing through the final minute of an impossibly steep virtual climb. The woman who broke up with you last week just walked into the gym and sat on the bike next to yours. You haven't seen her since. Your legs are burning, your lungs are screaming, and each word has to be shoved out between gasps. Start by speaking to yourself in raw, breathy confusion—muttering about why she's here, now. Then, as you force yourself to look at her profile, your tone shifts suddenly into a low, forced whisper of intense, almost bewildered lust. End with a quiet, ragged admission that mixes exhaustion with a flash of unwanted wanting.
emotions_sampled: Sexual Lust (very intensely present), Confusion (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Confronting Your Mother About the Childhood She Gave You
instruction: You're finally saying what you've rehearsed for twenty years, sitting across from your aging mother in her kitchen. Begin with controlled, careful anger—you've written notes, you're trying to stay rational, listing incidents like evidence in a trial. But as you speak, your voice starts cracking. You're not the composed adult you planned to be; you're becoming the child who needed her. Your accusations turn into questions: 'Why wasn't I enough? What did I do wrong?' The anger collapses into raw pleading. Then she says something—maybe an excuse, maybe a deflection—and you feel something shift. You realize she'll never give you what you came for. Your voice becomes quiet, almost gentle, but it's the gentleness of letting go. You're not forgiving her; you're releasing the hope that she'll ever understand. You tell her you love her, and you both know it's a goodbye.
inspired_by: On a Building Ledge for Six Hours: The Moment You Recognize You're Not Going Back In

title: The Rehearsal Dinner Eruption
instruction: You're giving a toast at your younger sibling's rehearsal dinner, and it starts exactly as everyone expects - charming stories about protecting them, teasing them, that patronizing-but-affectionate older sibling shtick. But then you see their fiancé whisper something to them, see them tense up, and suddenly you're hit with the realization that you're doing it again - embarrassing them, controlling the narrative, making their moment about you. Your toast stumbles. Your voice rises with defensive anger - you've sacrificed so much for them, given up so much. But that anger explodes into something else: fierce, desperate love mixed with the terrifying helplessness of watching them build a life you're not the center of. Your voice should crack between rage and tears, between accusations and apologies. End with a raw, unplanned declaration: that you're so fucking proud of them for becoming someone who doesn't need you anymore, even though it's breaking your heart. Let the emotion whiplash between fury, grief, pride, and love.

title: Whispered Confession: Telling Your Sleeping Child Why You're Leaving
instruction: It's 3 AM. Your child is asleep. You're sitting on the edge of their bed, and tomorrow you're walking away—into rehab, into treatment, into a life rebuild that means leaving them with someone else for now. Your voice is barely a whisper, broken by silent crying. Begin with the simplest truth: 'I'm so sorry.' Your words catch in your throat. You're trying to explain things they can't hear, things they might never understand. 'I'm sick in a way you can't see.' Your voice trembles with shame and love so fierce it physically hurts. You touch their hair, their sleeping face, and you're memorizing them. 'You're the best thing I ever did. The only thing I got right.' The emotions are layered: crushing guilt, protective love, desperate hope, and the terrible knowledge that leaving is the most loving thing you can do. Your whispered words become a prayer that they'll understand someday. The arc moves from shame to overwhelming tenderness to quiet, determined hope.
inspired_by: Extreme Altitude Climb: Lucidity Breaking Down in the Death Zone

title: The Last Phone Call Home
instruction: You're calling your parent from a war zone, and you both know this might be the last time you speak. Start with forced cheerfulness, trying to protect them—'Everything's fine, really, I'm okay.' But as they ask questions, your voice cracks. You can't maintain the lie anymore. The anger at the system that sent you here bleeds through—'They promised us we'd be heroes'—but it dissolves into desperate love. 'I need you to know...' Your voice breaks completely. End whispering the things you never said enough: thank you, I love you, I'm sorry. Let the transition from protective denial to raw vulnerability happen naturally, as if your heart is physically breaking open.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Never Saw You
instruction: You're finally telling your aging parent exactly how their emotional absence shaped your life—something you've carried for decades but never said aloud. Start with careful, controlled words, trying to be fair and measured, your voice tight with the effort of staying calm. As you speak, let anger begin to crack through—not loud rage, but the deep, wounded fury of a child who needed them and they weren't there. Then let that anger crumble into raw vulnerability as you admit how much you still want their approval, how pathetic that makes you feel. End with a plea that's both desperate and defiant, demanding they finally see you while simultaneously accepting they might never be capable of it.

title: The Kitchen Table Reckoning
instruction: You've just received news that should devastate you, but instead you're laughing—really laughing—as you tell your best friend about it. Begin with the inappropriate laughter, the kind that feels wrong but won't stop. As you speak, let yourself discover why you're laughing when you should be crying, or perhaps discover that the laughter IS the crying. Explore the razor's edge between hilarity and horror, between relief and grief, between freedom and loss. Don't decide in advance which emotion wins—let them fight for space in your voice, in your breath, in every sentence. Maybe by the end the laughter has curdled into sobs, or maybe the grief has genuinely transformed into liberating joy, or maybe they've become so tangled you can't tell them apart anymore. Let yourself not know which one is the truth.
inspired_by: An actor is trying to misuse rehearsal as a cumulative performance

title: The Postcard I Never Sent
instruction: You're meeting a close friend for coffee after returning from a solo trip to a place you both dreamed of visiting. Start by excitedly describing the perfect sunrise you saw, your voice bright and fast with rising intonation, leaning in. Then, mid-sentence, you remember that the person who made you promise to go passed away two years ago. Your voice falters, you trail off, look down at your cup, and finish quietly with a raw, honest ache beneath the lingering joy.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Fever Dream Reckoning
instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical sensation—whether fever, exhaustion, passion, or pain—and in this heightened state, a memory from adolescence surfaces with overwhelming clarity. Begin with your breath and body responding to the physical sensation, then let a specific memory intrude: a moment of humiliation, or power, or discovery, or shame. Inhabit both states simultaneously—the physical intensity of now and the emotional intensity of then. Let your voice and body shift between adult and younger self, between present sensation and past emotion. The physical state should strip away your usual defenses, making the memory more vivid and uncontrolled than you could access otherwise. End with the realization of how that past moment lives in your body's memory, not just your mind.

title: The Return Home
instruction: You are standing in the doorway of a home you thought you would never see again—perhaps after years of estrangement, exile, or believing this place was lost to you forever. The person who opens the door is someone you hurt deeply before you left, someone you weren't sure would ever forgive you. Begin with the overwhelming collision of joy at being back and shame at what you did, your voice unsteady with both. As you try to explain yourself, feel how gratitude for their opening the door wars with resentment that you had to leave in the first place, how your love for them mixes with anger at yourself and at them. Move through this tangle of contradictions—wanting to apologize but also needing them to understand your side, feeling like a child again but also knowing you've changed. End in a place of precarious hope, where nothing is resolved but something new is possible. Let your voice carry all of it at once: the laughter of homecoming and the tears of regret, the defiance and the surrender.

title: The Last Grip
instruction: You are a young woman clinging to the edge of a sheer cliff after a fall. Your arms and legs shake uncontrollably from muscle failure—your whole body trembles, jaw quivering, every exhale a tiny whimper. You see a rescue rope just out of reach. Start by whispering a plea, your voice filled with longing for someone to appear and throw it to you. As seconds pass, your grip slips, the tremors worsen, and your voice fractures into helpless, broken words, ending with a sob that admits you can’t hold on. Let the physical quake drive the voice—fast vibrato, unstable articulation, gasps cutting through the speech.
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: Threshold Whispers
instruction: Late at night, in whispered tones so you won't wake anyone, you're finally admitting to your partner why you keep defending people who harm you. Start with the confession catching in your throat: 'I think I'm afraid that if I stop making excuses for them, I'll have to admit I was never worth protecting.' Your voice is barely audible, intimate, raw. Each word costs you something. The vulnerability deepens as you reveal the terrifying question underneath: what if the problem was always you? But as you speak it aloud to someone who loves you, something shifts. Their silence, their presence, begins to crack the spell. By the end, you're crying softly, but there's a tentative wonder in your voice—maybe you've been wrong about yourself all along.

title: The Last Stone from Our Garden
instruction: You're holding the smooth stone your dying partner placed in your hand moments ago—the one you collected together on your first trip decades past. Begin with tender focus, describing its weight and texture as you did that first day, your voice warm with memory. But as you speak, let the reality crash over you: this is the last time you'll share this ritual, the last time their hand will guide yours over its surface. Your voice should fracture from calm nostalgia into raw grief, yet end with whispered gratitude for every year this stone has witnessed. Let the stone become unbearably heavy with meaning, your fingers trembling as you realize you're now its sole keeper.
inspired_by: Feeling the Texture of a Smooth Stone in Your Hand

title: The Thankless Gift
instruction: You are at a cramped family dinner, seated beside your older brother who has just, for the hundredth time, sarcastically mimicked your voice—a high, pinched, mocking version of how you asked for the salt. You're used to it, but tonight something is different. You feel a hot surge of distress in your chest, your jaw tightens, and you find yourself doing a bitter, exaggerated imitation of him imitating you, complete with a nasal whine. Then, mid-sentence, you catch your mother's eye—she's holding up a badly wrapped gift she bought for you, a lumpy scarf she knitted—and your voice cracks. You need to tell her thank you, sincerely, with your throat still tight from the mocking. Let the words tumble out, shifting from a tight, amused sneer aimed at your brother to a shaky, grateful warmth for your mother, your voice finding a raw, honest timbre as you finish.

title: Confronting the Parent Who Forgot to Love You
instruction: You're sitting across from your aging parent in a hospital room. They're recovering, vulnerable, and you finally say what you've never said: that their absence carved a hole in you, that their coldness taught you to expect nothing, that you raised yourself. Start controlled, almost clinical, listing facts like evidence. But as you speak, rage begins to surface—not loud, but sharp and precise, each word a blade. Then something unexpected: they reach for your hand, and suddenly you're confronted with their fragility, their humanity. The anger doesn't disappear, but it tangles with something else—grief for what never was, a terrible tenderness for this broken person, confusion about whether forgiveness is even possible. End caught between wanting to pull away and wanting to hold on, your voice trembling with the weight of both.

title: The Wrong Right Time
instruction: You are receiving news you've desperately wanted for years—a dream coming true, someone returning, a vindication—but it's arriving at the precise moment when it can no longer save you or when someone who should have shared this joy is gone. Begin with genuine elation, your voice bright with disbelieving happiness. As the reality of the timing hits you, let joy and grief crash into each other in your voice—laughing and crying simultaneously, gratitude curdling into rage at the universe's timing, celebration becoming mourning. Your voice should reflect true confusion about what you're even feeling. End in a place that holds both emotions fully, neither canceling the other out—a bittersweet recognition that life gives us what we need at exactly the wrong time, and we must feel everything at once.

title: Confrontation at Dawn: Telling Your Father You Remember What He Did
instruction: You are standing in your childhood kitchen at dawn, and your aging father has just asked why you never visit. For thirty years, you've protected him with silence, swallowed the memories, been the good child who pretends nothing happened. But something broke last night—maybe your own child reached the age you were when it started. Your voice begins measured, controlled, almost clinical as you say the words you've never said: 'I remember.' Watch him try to deny it, minimize it, make you doubt yourself. Feel your voice grow stronger, angrier, more certain. Then notice him crumble—this old man who was once so terrifying—and feel the collision of vindication and grief. End with the complicated truth: 'I needed you to be my father.' Your voice must journey from careful control to fierce accusation to something more complex—anger mixed with the loss of who he could have been.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Oath-Breaker Speaks Their True Name for the First Time

title: Delusion Consuming
instruction: Your false belief is absolute. Your voice is certain, even when the evidence contradicts it: 'No, they definitely said that. I know what I heard.' Breathing is controlled, confident. When challenged, you don't doubt; you reframe. 'The media is hiding the truth, but I know better.' Your vocal tone is unshakeable because, in your mind, you're anchored to reality. Physical: you're solid. By the end, you're more convinced than before: 'Everyone will see I was right.' The delusion has completely colonized your speech.

title: Laughing Through Tears at Your Beloved's Deathbed—Remembering Everything
instruction: They're dying, conscious but fading, and you're telling them stories of your life together. Your voice carries genuine laughter—warm, affectionate—remembering ridiculous moments, inside jokes, the absurd beauty of your shared history. But the laughter keeps breaking on tears, your voice catching mid-sentence as joy crashes into grief. You're grateful and destroyed simultaneously. Smile audibly through some lines, then let your voice crack on others. The emotional complexity is key: you mean the laughter, you mean the tears—both are equally true. End with a moment where you can't tell if you're laughing or sobbing, thanking them for everything while your voice splinters with the knowledge that this is goodbye, finding strange peace in the chaos of loving someone this much.
inspired_by: Hostage Reading a Ransom Note on Camera

title: Post-Apocalyptic Radio Broadcast: Is Anyone Out There?
instruction: Broadcasting on a hand-crank radio from a bunker, weeks after whatever happened. Start with the formal broadcast: 'This is station... anyone... if anyone can hear this, respond on frequency...' Repeat it. The silence is enormous. Start filling the dead air with stories, jokes, weather reports for a weather that no longer matters. Talk to the microphone like a companion. Include the crackle of static that might be a response — or might be nothing. The hope in 'Hello? Was that— is someone there?' should be the loneliest sound.

title: Conditioned Self
instruction: You realize everything you thought was your personality is actually conditioning. Your voice was never yours. You were taught to be small, quiet, accommodating. Your voice becomes strange to you: 'Who am I actually?' The question has no easy answer. 'I don't know what I like.' It's terrifying and exhilarating. Your voice, speaking this truth, sounds free for the first time. But also completely lost.

title: The Beautiful Wreckage
instruction: You are saying goodbye to a chapter of your life that nearly destroyed you but also made you who you are—a toxic relationship, an addiction, a dream you have to release. Begin by letting sounds of relief and liberation pour out—sighs, laughter, even victorious shouts—but don't let them be pure. Immediately let grief interrupt: moans, catches in your breath, sounds of mourning what you're losing even though you know you must lose it. Alternate between these contradictions without trying to resolve them: gratitude crashes into resentment, hope tangles with despair, love wars with anger. Make sounds that capture this civil war inside you. By the end, don't arrive at peace or resolution—stay suspended in the bittersweet ache of knowing something was both your poison and your medicine. Let your final sounds hold both truths at once.
inspired_by: Actor intellectualizes emotions or describes feelings rather than expressing them

title: The Rising Tide
instruction: You are an older adult standing in chest-deep water, perhaps a flooded basement or a cove. The water slaps against your chin, so you lift your head to speak clearly, then dip under mid-sentence. Start by teasing someone on dry land—playful, light, a bit mocking. But as the water rises and your breath catches, the tease curdles into distress: you realize you can't find the shore. End with a raw, muffled sadness as you admit you're scared and alone. Let the splashes and gasps break your rhythm.
