title: Fever Dream of Reunion
instruction: You're burning with fever (or grief, or desire, or all three) and you're seeing/touching/holding someone you thought you'd lost forever. Your body is overwhelmed with physical sensation—heat, cold, pain, pleasure all blurred together. Begin in a state of almost delirious intensity, your voice thick and unsteady, your words tumbling out between gasps. Let specific tactile memories consume you: the exact temperature of their skin, the pressure of their embrace, the taste of their mouth, the scent that is only theirs. Your speech should be fragmented, interrupted by the body's responses—shaking, reaching, recoiling. Move from desperate hunger to a moment of impossible peace, as if the fever breaks and you're left in the still, clarified aftermath. End in exhausted wonder, your voice barely a breath, your body finally quiet.

title: Confronting Your Parent About the Silence Between You
instruction: Start measured and rehearsed—you've practiced this. 'We need to talk about what happened.' But as they deflect or minimize, something ignites in you. Your voice rises, years of swallowed words pouring out: 'You never asked how I was.' Feel the anger give way to something more vulnerable, almost pleading. You're not shouting anymore; you're begging to be seen. 'I needed you and you weren't there.' Watch them struggle to respond, and in their silence, feel your anger dissolve into grief. End with your voice barely above a whisper, finally saying what you came to say: 'I can't keep pretending this doesn't hurt.'
inspired_by: Asking Someone to Leave Because You Need Solitude

title: I Would Burn the World Down for You
instruction: You are a parent whose child has been harmed, and you're speaking to the person responsible. Start with terrifying calm—your rage is so complete it's gone ice-cold. Describe exactly what you want to do to them, your voice vibrating with barely controlled violence. Then let it explode—not into shouting, but into a gasping, desperate fury that collapses mid-sentence as you realize your power is an illusion. You cannot undo what's been done. Your fierce protectiveness crashes into absolute helplessness. End with your voice breaking completely, fierce love and utter devastation existing in the same breath. This is what it sounds like when strength and vulnerability occupy the same moment.

title: The Moment You Realize They're Really Gone
instruction: You've just returned home after a funeral or final goodbye. You're going through their belongings—clothes, letters, something ordinary that still smells like them. Start by narrating what you're doing in a controlled, almost detached voice, keeping yourself together. But as you discover something unexpected—a note meant for you, an old photograph, their favorite worn-out sweater—everything breaks. Your voice explodes with rage at them for leaving, at yourself for things unsaid, at the unfairness of it all. The anger is huge and physical. Then, just as suddenly, it collapses into sobbing helplessness. End in raw, gasping grief, cycling between fury and devastation, your words barely coherent as you plead with them as if they could still hear you.
inspired_by: The Princess and the Dragon Disguised as a Human

title: Whispering Your Truth to Your Sleeping Lover Before You Leave
instruction: It's 3am. Your partner sleeps beside you. This is your last night together, though they don't know it yet. You whisper the confession you could never say to their waking face—why you have to go, what you've been hiding, how much you love them, how that love isn't enough. Your voice is barely audible, intimate, as if the darkness itself is listening. You pause between sentences, voice catching on certain words. You almost touch them but don't. The whispers become more broken, more desperate. You're crying silently, voice thick and rough. End with a barely-breathed 'forgive me' that dissolves into silence. Keep everything hushed, tender, devastatingly intimate. Let the quietness hold all the pain.

title: Becoming Better
instruction: You're not the person you were. Your voice carries this metamorphosis: 'I did the work.' Breathing is steady, proud. Physical: you're standing differently, carrying yourself with new knowledge. 'I made myself better.' Not through perfection, through practice and commitment. Vocal tone is honest, humble: 'I failed a thousand times and tried again.' By the end, you're acknowledging transformation: 'I'm better now. And I'll keep getting better.'

title: Inventory of Leaving
instruction: You're whispering to your sleeping lover on your last night together before you move across the world. You can't sleep. In the dark, your eyes trace their face, their body, the room around you—the books on their shelf, the clothes on the floor, the way moonlight hits the wall, their breathing. Describe what you're seeing in the softest voice possible, as if cataloging everything to carry with you. Start with careful observation, almost clinical, protecting yourself. As you look at each detail—the curve of their shoulder, their worn-out shoes by the bed, the photo on the nightstand—let yourself break open. Move from controlled documentation to raw vulnerability, your whispers catching and cracking. End dissolved in quiet tears, touching their face, no longer describing, just feeling.

title: The Acceptance Letter in Your Childhood Bedroom
instruction: You're sitting in your childhood bedroom, holding an acceptance letter to your dream graduate program across the country. Your parent - who sacrificed everything to raise you alone after your other parent died - is downstairs making dinner, humming, completely unaware. Begin with pure, breathless joy, almost laughing as you read it again, whispering your excitement to yourself. But as the reality settles, let guilt and grief seep in. Your voice should fracture between celebrating your achievement and devastating awareness that accepting means leaving them alone. Practice saying 'I got in' out loud - hear how your voice breaks differently each time between pride and heartbreak. End with a complex emotional state: you're going, you have to go, but this victory tastes like betrayal. Your voice should hold both fierce joy for your future and tender anguish for what following your dreams will cost the person you love most. Let these emotions coexist without resolving.

title: Passion Turning to Grief in Your Hands
instruction: You're touching someone you desire intensely—running your hands over their skin, pulling them close, breathing them in. The physical hunger is real and overwhelming. But as your body moves with passion, other sensations crash in: grief that this might be the last time, rage at how much power they have over you, the physical memory of previous heartbreak, the way desire and devastation live in the same breath. Don't plan how passion 'should' look or how to 'transition' to sadness. Let your body's actual, moment-to-moment experience guide you—the way arousal can suddenly become weeping, or fury, or desperate tenderness. Start with pure physical want. End wherever the truth of your body's feelings actually lands.
inspired_by: Actor is premeditating — planning how to say lines and emotionalize them before getting there, functioning from a cerebral place

title: I Translated Every Word You Said and It Still Wasn't Enough
instruction: You're screaming at your parents in both their languages simultaneously after they've announced they're divorcing—after twenty years of you being their bridge, their mediator, their translator. Explode with everything you've held back: the birthday parties where you translated their cold silence, the holidays where you invented warm words they never said, the thousand moments you made up affection to spare everyone's feelings. Let rage pour out in a torrent—switching languages mid-sentence, your voice raw and breaking. 'I GAVE YOU THE WORDS—I GAVE YOU BEAUTIFUL WORDS IN TWO LANGUAGES AND YOU STILL COULDN'T LOVE EACH OTHER!' But then collapse: the fury breaks into helpless sobbing as you realize you tried to translate them into a happy family and failed. End on your knees, voice hoarse, admitting in a broken whisper that you're exhausted from trying to make peace in languages neither of them wanted to speak. Fierce protectiveness dissolving into absolute helplessness.
inspired_by: Caught Between Two Arguments in Different Languages

title: Public Bathroom Line Problem
instruction: You've been waiting in a long bathroom line, and when you finally get in, there's a significant problem. Your voice is shocked, whispering: 'Oh my god.' You're considering solutions, your voice tight with embarrassment. Do you try to fix it? Sneak out? Your internal monologue is panicked: 'Someone's going to think it was me.' You finally exit, your voice is tight, overly casual, trying to act normal while dying inside.

title: Final Phone Call from the Hospice Room
instruction: You're calling your adult child to say goodbye—you have hours, maybe a day left. Begin with false brightness, trying to protect them: 'Hey sweetheart, I just wanted to hear your voice.' But your breath is labored, and the pretense crumbles. Let the terror seep through—you're not ready to leave them, not ready to stop being their parent. 'I'm so scared of what happens when I'm not here to...' Your voice breaks completely. Then find something underneath the fear: a fierce, desperate love. End by transforming your goodbye into a blessing, your voice soft but certain, as if you're pouring everything you are into these final words. Let gratitude and devastating loss live in the same breath.

title: The Fading Grudge
instruction: You are an elderly man, alone in your dimly lit living room, having just taken a low dose of cannabis for the first time to help with chronic pain. You begin with a sour, skeptical mood, muttering to your reflection in the dark window about how silly this is and how it probably won't help. But as the drug takes hold, you notice the way the lamplight softens, and you blink in astonishment at a memory of your late wife laughing in the garden. Your speech slows, you pause mid-sentence, and your voice drops to a low, dry murmur with slight sticky lip sounds. By the end, you feel a fragile hope—a quiet optimism that maybe you can still find peace. Let your thought meander, giggle unexpectedly once, and let the emotion shift from irritation to wonder.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (clearly present), Astonishment/Surprise (extremely present), Hope/Optimism (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: Screaming Truth at the Mirror: Self-Hatred Exploding into Self-Acceptance
instruction: You're alone, facing yourself in a mirror after years of self-deception. Start with your voice venomous, spitting hatred at your reflection—every failure, every lie you've told yourself, every way you've fallen short. Let the rage build until you're nearly screaming, voice raw and ugly with self-loathing. Then something breaks. The anger collapses into deep, gasping sobs. Your voice becomes small, wounded: 'I'm so tired of hating you.' Slowly, shakily, begin to speak with something approaching compassion. Your voice is still broken, still crying, but there's tenderness creeping in. End with 'I'm sorry I hurt you' spoken to yourself, voice barely a whisper, tears streaming but a hint of peace beginning. Move from volcanic fury to shattered gentleness.
inspired_by: Forgiving Someone and Meaning It Completely

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your father about why he never told you he was proud of you, and you're doing it now, at 40, because you've realized how much his silence shaped your life. Begin with carefully controlled words—you've rehearsed this, you're trying to stay calm. But as you speak, decades of hunger for his approval crack through your composure. Your voice sharpens with anger: 'I needed you to see me.' Then it breaks into something raw and young: 'I'm still waiting.' Watch him sit there, unable to answer, and feel your rage dissolve into heartbreak. End with a quieter devastation—realizing he can't give you what you need, and accepting that you'll have to learn to live without it.

title: The Kitchen Table: A Child Confronts Their Mother
instruction: You're an adult now, sitting across from your mother in her kitchen. You came here to finally say it. Start with your voice tight, controlled, almost rehearsed: 'I need to tell you something I've never been able to say.' But as you speak, the control starts slipping. You're telling her about the years you spent trying to be perfect, trying to earn her approval, how you learned to make yourself small. Your voice rises with frustration—not quite yelling, but forceful, insistent. 'Do you know what it's like to feel invisible in your own home?' The anger builds, your words coming faster, more cutting. But then you see her face, or you hear your own voice, and something breaks. The anger collapses into something more vulnerable, almost pleading. Your voice becomes smaller, younger: 'I just needed you to love me the way I was.' You end somewhere between anger and heartbreak, your voice shaking with both.

title: Clink and Cringe
instruction: You're at a crowded cocktail party, clutching a cold glass, trying to join a casual chat about weekend plans. But you're burning with shame over a work blunder you made hours ago, and a dull disappointment in yourself sits in your stomach. Your voice must push over the noise—higher, clipped, with forced brightness—while your eyes dodge eye contact and you laugh too quickly at nothing. Mid-sentence, someone nudges you, and you lose your thread; a sip of drink buys you a second. Let the shame seep into a quieter admission by the end, your tone dropping as you give up the pretense.
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The 3 a.m. Visitor
instruction: You are in your dark kitchen at 3 a.m., holding a cold mug of tea you forgot to drink. Your body aches with sleeplessness; your voice is flat, rough, weighed down by sour resentment and helpless exhaustion. You mutter bitterly about the absurdity of being awake again—your words come out in short, clipped bursts, with pauses where you lose your train of thought. Just as you sigh and turn to go back to bed, a sudden noise from the window startles you: a moth thrumming against the glass, its wings glowing in the moonlight. For a split second, a raw, childlike astonishment cuts through your drowsiness—your voice lifts, stretches, almost breaks with wonder. But then the exhaustion rushes back, and the wonder sinks into a hollow, rueful smile. Speak naturally, letting the fatigue drag your pitch down and the surprise pull it up sharply, then fade.
emotions_sampled: Sourness (clearly present), Helplessness (clearly present), Astonishment/Surprise (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a moderately feminized voice

title: The Garden on the Last Day
instruction: You're walking through your garden on the morning you've chosen to leave this world, and everything is absurdly, heartbreakingly beautiful. Begin with soft laughter—genuine delight at a bird, at the way light hits a flower. Your voice is warm, full of wonder. But the laughter catches, transforms. You're overwhelmed with gratitude that this existed, that you got to see it, and devastated that you're letting it go. Speak to the garden as if it can hear you, thanking it, apologizing to it, your voice moving between joy and shattering grief. End with 'I was here. I was really here,' finding strange peace in that truth even as tears distort your words.

title: The Inheritance of Silence
instruction: You're confronting your mother or father about something they did to you as a child—something that shaped who you became, something you've never spoken aloud. Start from a place of careful control; you've rehearsed this, you're trying to be calm and adult about it. But as you speak, the child you were breaks through—the hurt, the confusion, the betrayal. Your voice should fracture. Let anger surge, then crack open into raw pain. By the end, you're not the composed adult anymore—you're the child who needed them and they failed you. But in that vulnerability, there's also a strange relief: the truth is finally spoken.

title: Light Through Wreckage
instruction: You've just received devastating news, but you're at a celebration—a wedding, a birth announcement, a party. You must congratulate someone you love while your own world is ending. Begin with the mask firmly in place, smiling, saying the right words. As you embrace this person, let yourself notice something real about them—the brightness in their eyes, the warmth of their joy radiating off them, the way happiness has made them almost luminous. Allow yourself to truly see and feel this quality, then let it grow impossibly vivid and intense in your awareness—their joy becomes almost blinding, physically warm like sunlight, their happiness feels like it fills the whole room. You're genuinely moved by their joy, you love them, you want this for them. But simultaneously, this amplified awareness of their radiance makes your own darkness more devastating by contrast. End in a place where you're holding both things at once with excruciating intensity: genuine, fierce happiness for them and complete devastation for yourself, gratitude and loss, celebration and grief, loving them so much it breaks your heart while your heart is already breaking.

title: Dancing Alone in Your Wedding Dress at Midnight
instruction: You're alone in your childhood bedroom the night before your wedding, wearing the dress, realizing you're saying goodbye to a version of yourself you'll never be again. Begin with almost giddy excitement, spinning and laughing softly at your reflection. But let that laughter gradually become textured with tears—not sadness exactly, but the bittersweetness of profound transition. Your voice should carry both joy and grief simultaneously as you speak to your younger self, thanking her for surviving long enough to reach this moment. Touch becomes meditation—feeling the dress, touching your face, grounding yourself in both what's ending and what's beginning. End with contradictory emotions fully present: you're radiant with happiness while mourning what you're leaving behind. Your voice finds gratitude that sounds like heartbreak that sounds like the most complete love you've ever felt.

title: Whispered Goodbye: Leaving Your Soulmate to Save Them From You
instruction: It's the middle of the night. They're asleep beside you. You're whispering your goodbye—they can't hear you, but you need to say it. Start with tender, almost inaudible words, memorizing their face in the darkness. Your voice is thick with unshed tears, catching on every breath. You love them more than anything, and that's exactly why you have to leave. Your breathing is quiet, controlled—you can't wake them, can't let them stop you. As you speak, let the grief deepen. Whisper the life you'll never have together, the children you won't raise, the growing old you won't do. Your voice becomes even softer, more broken. Let moments of silence speak—the words you can't say because they hurt too much. End with a barely audible 'I love you,' your breath shaking, tears finally falling. The last sound is you trying not to sob as you force yourself to leave.
inspired_by: Fantasy: Chosen One Realizes They've Been Betraying Their Actual Destiny

title: Protective Fury: Parent Confronting the Person Who Hurt Their Child
instruction: You're face-to-face with someone who harmed your child. Start with controlled rage—voice low, words precise, each syllable a threat. You're holding yourself back with visible effort. 'You put your hands on my child.' Let that restraint begin to crack. Your voice rises, hands shaking, breath coming faster. You want violence but you're civilized, and that tension tears you apart. Describe what you want to do, the rage that lives in your bones. But then—shift. Your voice breaks not into tears but into something worse: helplessness. You couldn't protect them. You weren't there. The fury collapses into raw anguish. Now you're not threatening anymore; you're pleading, demanding they explain how they could do this, what kind of person... Let fierce protectiveness and devastating powerlessness crash together. End in a place between murder and weeping, where love for your child and hatred for their abuser become the same unbearable fire.
inspired_by: Sci-Fi: Rebel Leader Realizes Their Intelligence Source Is a Government Agent

title: The Last Visit Before the Long Journey
instruction: You're saying goodbye to your younger sibling who's about to undergo a risky experimental treatment in another country - they might not come back, and if they do, they won't be the same person. Begin with forced brightness, trying to be strong for them, your voice almost cheerful as you talk about 'when you get back.' But as reality seeps in, your voice starts to crack. You tell them all the things you never said - how they made you brave, how they were always the better person. Your anger at the unfairness of it all breaks through mid-sentence, then dissolves into raw tenderness. End in a whisper, accepting this might be the last time, your voice holding both devastating loss and profound gratitude for every moment you had.

title: The Goodbye at the Airport Gate
instruction: You are watching someone you deeply love walk away from you forever—they are leaving for a new life, and you both know you'll never see each other again. Begin standing frozen, overwhelmed and unable to find any words. Let your body carry everything you cannot say: your hands reaching out and falling back, your breath catching, your posture shifting between wanting to chase after them and forcing yourself to stay still. Move through whatever physical impulses arise—whether that's sinking to the ground, pressing against an invisible barrier, or trembling in place. By the end, allow your body to settle into a different stillness—one of acceptance, exhaustion, or quiet devastation. No words. Let silence and movement reveal the journey from desperate resistance to whatever comes after.

title: Holding Your Child's Hand as They Die
instruction: Your child is dying and you're trying to be strong for them. Start with fierce, almost aggressive protectiveness: 'You're going to be fine, you hear me? You're going to be FINE'—voice cracking with desperation, trying to will them back to life through sheer force. But their hand goes limp and your voice shatters: 'No, no, no, baby, please—' Now you're begging, all pretense of strength gone, voice raw with animal grief. Then a moment of devastating tenderness: 'It's okay, sweetheart. You can let go now,' whispered through tears, giving them permission even as it destroys you. End with a primal, broken sound—not words, just the collapse of a parent's heart. Move from fierce denial to desperate pleading to tender release to wordless devastation.
inspired_by: Someone Saying They Don't Trust You Anymore

title: The Last Morning Light
instruction: You are sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed at dawn. She's awake but weak, and you both know this is likely your final conversation. Begin by truly looking at her - notice every detail of her face, her hands, the way the early light touches her skin. Let yourself wonder about what she's feeling, what memories might be moving through her mind, what she sees when she looks at you. Start with careful attention and quiet curiosity, almost like you're meeting her for the first time. As you speak your goodbye, let the weight of everything you've observed - her fragility, her dignity, the lifetime in her eyes - break through your composure. Move from gentle observation to overwhelming love and grief, but keep your eyes on her, really seeing her, until the very end.

title: The Threshold Call
instruction: You're calling your mother to tell her you've just achieved the dream you've worked toward for fifteen years—but she's also the person who told you you'd never make it, who undermined you at every turn. As the phone rings, you're electric with triumph and venomous with vindication. When she answers, your voice carries both celebration and accusation. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, telling her your victory while also making her hear how much her doubt wounded you. Feel the intoxication of success mixed with the grief of all those years you needed her support and received criticism instead. Your joy is real, but so is your rage. By the end, shift unexpectedly into something more complicated: you thank her, and you mean it, because her cruelty made you stronger—but this gratitude is laced with profound sadness for what your relationship could have been.
inspired_by: Actor feels everything but cannot express it (expressive insecurity)

title: The Secret I Never Told You
instruction: Late at night, you're speaking to your childhood pet's grave, confessing something you've carried for thirty years. Use a hushed, intimate voice - this is a secret you've never told anyone, not even yourself fully. You were there when they died, and you held their favorite toy just out of reach because you were angry they were leaving you. You were eight years old and didn't understand, and you've carried the shame of that moment of childhood cruelty your entire life. Let your voice catch and stumble over the words. Move from tentative confession to quiet weeping to something like self-forgiveness as you realize that little kid was just terrified and didn't know what death meant. End with tender absolution, speaking to both the pet and your child self. Keep everything soft, close to the microphone, as if you're afraid someone might overhear this sacred, painful unburdening.

title: Whispering What You've Always Hidden
instruction: It's late at night, and you're confessing something you've carried in silence for years to someone who's finally safe enough to hear it. Your voice should be barely above a whisper, intimate and fragile: 'I need to tell you something. And I'm terrified, because once I say it, I can't take it back.' Start with halting, uncertain words, pausing to breathe, to gather courage. The confession might be about love, about shame, about a dream you've hidden, about who you really are. Let vulnerability make your voice shake: 'Every day I pretended I was fine. That I didn't feel this. But I do. I always have.' As you speak, let tenderness seep in—tenderness for yourself, for the years of hiding, for finally being honest. By the end, there's a quiet, tearful peace: 'I don't know what happens now. But at least it's true. At least I finally said it.' The power is in the softness, in the courage it takes to be this gentle with your own heart.

title: Stroke of Defeat
instruction: You're an older man alone on a rowing machine in a dim gym, pushing through the last brutal set. Every pull is a struggle against your own disappointment—you just lost a competition you trained years for. On the explosive grunt of each stroke, let out a guttural frustration; on the rushed exhale of the recovery, whisper fragments of self-reproach or regret. As your muscles burn and your breath shortens, let the disappointment deepen from raw anger into a heavy, weary acceptance. Your voice should crack and wobble with the rhythm, the sweat stinging your eyes, forcing you to pause and swallow before the next strained phrase.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Lost in a Cave: Echo and Darkness
instruction: Your flashlight just died in a deep cave system. Speak into the echoing void, hearing your own voice bounce back distorted. Start by calling for help — big, projected shouts that return to you as ghostly whispers. As claustrophobia sets in, your volume drops to self-talk: counting your breaths, narrating your movements to stay sane. The cave acoustics should inform your delivery — you're aware of how strange and small you sound in the immensity.

title: Bipolar Manic Episode: Speech Pattern Breaking Down
instruction: You're manic. Your speech is rapid-fire, thoughts jumping. Your voice is loud, energized, unstoppable. You're talking over people. Your volume is too high. You're making connections between things that aren't connected. Your voice is pressured—like it needs to keep moving or you'll explode. You're not sleeping but your voice is buzzing with energy instead of exhaustion. Your voice is scattered, brilliant, terrifying. By the end, you're crashing slightly, voice becoming slightly less manic.

title: The Watch That Holds Every Goodbye
instruction: You're holding your grandmother's watch as she takes her final breaths. Begin by looking at this watch as just a timepiece - describe what you see plainly. But as you sit with her, let the watch transform in your mind: see it breathing, feel it pulsing with every person she ever loved, watch faces and voices emerge from its surface - her wedding day, her children being born, the moment she first held you. Let these images become stranger, more surreal - maybe the watch hands are reaching for you, maybe you can taste her perfume coming from the metal, maybe you hear laughter from decades ago trapped inside the ticking. Start in controlled observation, but surrender completely to wherever your mind takes you, letting the absurd and impossible flood through you. By the end, you're not holding a watch anymore - you're holding her entire life, and you must say goodbye to all of it at once.
inspired_by: Actor's imagination feels weak, overly literal, or unable to generate creative choices

title: The Echo of Malice
instruction: You are standing on a narrow cliff edge, the wind howling and stealing your breath. Below, a figure you despise is climbing the opposite face. You start shouting threats with cold venom, but the thin air makes your voice crack and the echoes mock you, turning your malice hollow. Halfway through, you realize they cannot hear you—and that silence, combined with the vast emptiness, shifts your fury into a raw, almost childlike loneliness. Let your voice strain, break, and eventually drop to a ragged whisper as the wind drowns you out.
speaker_gender: a man with a hyper-masculinized voice

title: Singing a Lullaby to Your Dying Child
instruction: Hospital room, late night. Your child is slipping away, and you're singing the lullaby you've sung every night of their life. Start with your voice barely functioning—every word is a struggle against the sob lodged in your chest. You're trying to be calm for them, but your voice keeps breaking on familiar phrases. Whisper-sing some lines because you physically can't get volume. This is the most important performance of your life and you're falling apart. Midway, let muscle memory take over—just for a moment, you're back in their nursery, when the future was infinite, and your voice smooths out, tender and sweet. But then you feel their hand go slack, their breathing change, and the reality shatters you. Your voice fractures completely. Yet somehow, you keep singing—softer, slower, each word both a goodbye and a promise that you'll carry them forever. End with the final phrase barely audible, more breath than sound, as you transition from singing to them to singing about them, past tense, forever.
inspired_by: Singing in Front of People for the First Time

title: The Last Hum
instruction: You're a 17-year-old guy, hooking up with someone you thought you loved, but now you're just drained. You're in the middle of going down on them, your jaw aching, throat dry, and you're so tired you could collapse. You started with a kind of bitter, sour resentment – you're doing this out of obligation, not desire. But as you continue, a strange longing creeps in: you wish this meant something, that they'd see you, that you weren't just a tool. Let the sound start with heavy, exhausted nasal breaths and flat, mechanical hums. Gradually, let those hums soften, get more vulnerable, almost like a whimper. Try to speak a few words, but they're muffled, lost against their skin – something like 'I wish... you'd...' – but you can't finish because your mouth is full and your heart is too. End with a long, quiet, tired exhale.
emotions_sampled: Fatigue/Exhaustion (clearly present), Sourness (very intensely present), Longing (very intensely present)
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: The Sour Taste of Hope
instruction: You're a teenager in a therapy session, talking about your mother's new partner. Start with a guarded, slightly bitter tone—your voice is measured, intellectualizing, with a hint of sarcasm as you list reasons it won't work. But as you speak, a flicker of genuine interest catches you off guard; you pause, stare at a spot on the wall, and your voice softens, losing its edge. Let a crack appear—a raw, hesitant admission that maybe you could be wrong. End with a tearful, quiet honesty, your words trailing into silence.
speaker_gender: a person with an androgynous, gender-neutral voice

title: The Weight of Your Breath
instruction: In complete darkness or near-darkness, whisper a secret you've never told anyone to someone lying next to you—a lover, spouse, or trusted friend. Begin with your heart racing, terrified of speaking. Before you say the words, tune into the sensory reality of this moment: the sound of their breathing, the warmth radiating from their body, the texture of the sheets, the darkness pressing in. Notice how the darkness makes sound and touch more vivid. Let your awareness of their physical presence beside you give you courage. As you whisper your confession, pay attention to any shift in their breathing, any tiny movement. Your fear should gradually transform into a fragile, trembling relief at being heard. End in a place of quiet, almost sacred intimacy.
inspired_by: Actor is disconnected from their scene partner; relationship feels artificial or the actor is not genuinely curious about them

title: The Desperate Bluff
instruction: You're a middle-aged man cornering a younger colleague who has evidence that could destroy your career. You interrupt them from the very first word, voice sharp and fast, trying to seize control with barely concealed malice. But as they refuse to back down, your threats waver—a tremor in the pitch, a breath you can't hide—and your anger cracks open into raw fear. Let the interruptions feel physically urgent, cutting them off mid-syllable, then let the pace slow and voice drop as the mask slips. End on a raw, uncertain whisper where the malice has drained away, leaving only dread.
speaker_gender: a man with a strongly masculinized voice

title: Confronting the Parent Who Left
instruction: You're finally facing the parent who abandoned you years ago. Start controlled, voice tight with rehearsed composure: 'I told myself I wouldn't do this.' But anger seeps through—questions you've carried like stones pour out, each one sharper. Your voice rises: 'Do you know what it was like?' Let rage crack open to reveal the child underneath, desperate and pleading: 'I needed you.' Watch your certainty dissolve into confusion as old love surfaces despite everything. End softly, exhaustedly: 'I don't know if I can forgive you, but I can't keep carrying this.' The final words should sound like surrender, grief, and the faintest possibility of release.
inspired_by: Breaking Up With Someone You Still Love

title: The Velvet Cage
instruction: You are a woman in a ritzy bar, perched on a tall stool, legs crossed, one hand gripping the edge to stay balanced. Your voice is deliberately sweet and high, a mask of polished charm. Across the room, he's laughing with someone younger, and you're flooded with longing—a raw ache that makes you grip the stool tighter. When a friend asks if you're okay, you let out a bitter smirk and respond, with contempt dripping through your honeyed tone, describing how 'adorable' he looks, but a flicker of amusement at the absurdity of your own performance creeps in. By the end, your voice wavers, the mask cracking as longing dissolves into a hollow, self-aware laugh.
emotions_sampled: Longing (very intensely present), Contempt (extremely present), Amusement (clearly present)
speaker_gender: a woman with a hyper-feminized voice

title: The Last Bedtime Story
instruction: You're a parent with late-stage illness, recording a bedtime story for your young child to listen to after you're gone. Begin with the familiar rhythm and warmth of how you've always read to them—that special voice, those silly character sounds they love. But as you continue, the weight of what you're really doing breaks through: this is the last time they'll hear you say 'I love you' before sleep. Your voice should fracture between maintaining the comforting ritual and the devastating knowledge that you're saying goodbye. Let memories flood in—their first word, their laugh, the smell of their hair. End with you trying to hold onto your 'story voice' but unable to, finishing in raw, whispered tenderness, telling them it's okay to let you go, that you'll always be there in every story they ever hear.
inspired_by: Inside a Space Helmet: Last Transmission

title: The Fever Breaking
instruction: You're in the grip of intense physical pain—a migraine, a fever breaking, the aftermath of an injury—and someone you've been emotionally distant from is caring for you. Your body is completely vulnerable, beyond your control, trembling and sweating. Begin in that raw physical state where pride and emotional armor are impossible to maintain. As they gently help you—a cool cloth, a steadying hand—your physical vulnerability cracks open something emotional you've been holding closed for months or years. The physical sensation and emotional release become completely entangled. Your breathing changes, tears come that aren't just from physical pain. Let the sensations in your body guide your emotional journey. Move from isolated suffering through reluctant surrender to a kind of painful, physical relief mixed with emotional release. Let your body and voice shake with both.
inspired_by: Actor has a persistent fear (auditions, exposure, ridicule, conflict) that keeps returning

title: The Last Clear Morning
instruction: You're sitting beside your grandmother's hospital bed in the early morning light. She's been unconscious for days, but suddenly her eyes open and she recognizes you—truly sees you—for what you know will be the last time. Begin with quiet shock, your voice barely able to form her name. As she squeezes your hand weakly, relief floods through you that you get this moment, this gift of goodbye. Tell her everything you've been holding—how much she meant to you, the memories you'll carry. Let your voice break and rebuild itself multiple times. Feel gratitude and grief intertwine so completely you can't separate them. End by promising her something about how you'll live, your voice steadying into a tender vow even as tears stream down your face. The emotional journey moves from stunned disbelief to desperate gratitude to bittersweet acceptance.

title: The Last Permission
instruction: You are at your father's hospital bedside in his final hour. For your entire life, you've been the dutiful caretaker—always responsible, always holding everyone together, always swallowing your own needs. But he's asking you to promise you'll keep doing this after he's gone, keep sacrificing yourself for the family. Start from that familiar place of duty and self-denial, saying what you think you should say. But as you speak, let something fiercer rise up—a part of you that has been buried for decades, the part that wants to live freely, selfishly, wildly. By the end, you must tell him the truth: you won't make that promise. Let yourself feel the terror and exhilaration of becoming, in his last moments, the person you've never allowed yourself to be. The emotional journey moves from dutiful constraint to fierce, trembling liberation.

title: Hospice Nurse: Finding Beauty in the Last Clean Sheets
instruction: You're a hospice nurse changing the sheets of a dying patient who has hours left, and something about this moment breaks you open. Begin speaking—perhaps to yourself, perhaps to them—with profound tenderness about how you're making everything fresh and clean for their final rest. Your voice should carry deep sadness yet somehow also peace, even joy, as you smooth each corner with ritual care. Let gratitude flood through you—gratitude for being here, for knowing them, for this strange privilege of ushering someone toward death with dignity. You should be crying and almost laughing simultaneously as you describe how beautiful they look in these crisp white sheets, how this matters, how love shows up in laundry and hospital corners. End with a whispered 'thank you' to them for letting you do this, your voice thick with tears but somehow radiant. Move through sorrow, fierce tenderness, and unexpected grace all at once—the contradictory beauty of loving someone toward death.

title: Rough Road to Something Better
instruction: You're a teenage boy bouncing in the back of an old pickup truck on a long, rutted dirt road. Each jolt shakes your whole body, making your voice quiver and stutter. You're talking to your dad in the front seat about a school competition you just entered—at first you're hesitant, unsure you can pull it off, your words coming out uneven. As you keep talking, feeling the rumbling ground, you start convincing yourself, your tone lifting with a shaky but genuine hope. Let the physical bumps interrupt your flow, trailing off then picking back up, and let the doubt soften into a warm, nervous optimism by the end.
speaker_gender: a man with a moderately masculinized voice

title: What You Never Gave Me
instruction: You're confronting your aging parent about the childhood they failed to give you. Start controlled, almost clinical: 'I need to say something I've been holding for twenty years.' But the hurt bleeds through immediately: 'I needed you to protect me, and you chose your own comfort instead.' Your voice becomes sharper, more cutting: 'Do you even remember my tenth birthday? Because I do. I remember waiting.' The anger peaks, then suddenly collapses into the voice of the child you were—small, pleading: 'Why wasn't I enough? What was wrong with me?' There's a long pause. When you speak again, your voice is different—tired, resigned, but somehow freer: 'I'm not asking you to fix it anymore. I just needed you to hear what it cost me.' The final words are quiet, almost gentle: 'I'm letting you go now. Not with forgiveness. Just... with release.'

title: The Weight of Thanks
instruction: You're in a therapy session, a teenage girl with a voice that's learned to hold things together. You've been talking about your mom's struggle with illness, but now you're dodging the real emotion by describing details—her hospital room, the beeping machines. You're perched on the edge of the couch, picking at a loose thread on your jeans, eyes fixed on the floor. The therapist asks gently, 'What do you feel when you think about her now?' You start to answer carefully, rationally, but then you pause—a long silence—and suddenly recall a moment she made you laugh in the waiting room. The laugh escapes you, soft and surprised, and it breaks something open. Your voice changes from guarded to raw, cracking as you say, 'I'm just so grateful she's still here... that she made a joke that day.' Aim for that shift: from controlled and slightly academic to vulnerable, with tears just under the surface. Let the laughter be a real, organic sound, not forced—it's a small release before the bigger emotion.
speaker_gender: a woman with a strongly feminized voice

title: Whispering Hello to Your Sleeping Child
instruction: It's 2am and you're watching your child sleep, whispering a hello they can't hear because you need to confess something. Start softly, tenderly, saying hello to this perfect being you created. Your voice is filled with wonder and aching love. Then, barely audible, you begin admitting your fears: that you're not enough, that you're repeating your own parents' mistakes, that some days you don't recognize yourself. Your whispers become more desperate, more honest—you're apologizing for your impatience today, for the moments you were distracted, for being human when they need you to be superhuman. Mid-way, your voice catches with tears you're trying to keep silent. By the end, you're making quiet promises you hope you can keep, your voice steadying with fierce determination mixed with lingering doubt. You kiss their forehead and whisper a final hello-and-goodnight that carries all your imperfect, overwhelming love.

title: Laughing at Fear
instruction: Youre utterly terrified, but instead of screaming, you start laughing. Your voice shakes as you try to convince yourself its not so bad, the laughter gradually breaking down as fear overtakes it.

title: The Kitchen Truth
instruction: You are confronting your parent in the kitchen of your childhood home about a betrayal you discovered years ago but never addressed. Start by seeing yourself as a child in this same kitchen—feel the weight of all those years of silence and confusion. As you begin speaking, you're almost detached, clinical, describing what you know. But as you talk, the images of your younger self overlay with your present anger, and your voice should crack open from controlled accusation into raw, unguarded pain. Watch yourself transform in this moment—the child you were, the adult you've become, the person you might have been. End not with resolution, but with the terrifying vulnerability of having finally said the unspeakable, your voice barely above a whisper.
inspired_by: When using the programming process to prepare a role

title: The Last Dance: Finding Peace While Scattering Your Best Friend's Ashes
instruction: You're alone at the place you and your best friend always said you'd end up—maybe a cliff, maybe a beach, maybe the roof of your old apartment building. You're talking to them as you open the urn, and impossibly, you're laughing. Start with genuine joy, remembering their ridiculous sense of humor, an embarrassing story, the time they made you laugh so hard you couldn't breathe. Your voice is light, warm, even playful. But as you continue, the laughter becomes textured with tears—you can't tell if you're laughing or crying anymore. Your voice holds both celebration of everything they were and the crushing weight of their absence. End with a moment of unexpected peace: thanking them through tears and laughter, your voice finally steady with acceptance, saying goodbye while somehow feeling them right there with you. Let joy and grief be so intertwined they become the same thing.
inspired_by: Professional: Lawyer Defends Someone They Know Is Guilty

title: The Cup Shatters
instruction: You're gripping a coffee mug so hard your hands are shaking. Start describing the coffee with forced calm, trying to ground yourself, but there's rage just beneath the surface—at a diagnosis you just received, at a betrayal discovered this morning, at news that breaks your world. Let your voice tighten as you describe the taste, the heat, using the coffee as an anchor, but you're barely holding on. Then let it explode—maybe the cup drops or you hurl it, and suddenly you're not talking about coffee at all. You're screaming, crying, your voice raw and desperate, oscillating between fury at the unfairness and helpless sobbing because you're terrified. The fierce protectiveness you feel—for yourself, for what you're losing—collides with complete powerlessness. End in exhausted tears, your voice wrecked, maybe laughing darkly at the absurdity, still tasting coffee on your lips mixed with salt.
inspired_by: Enjoying the First Sip of Morning Coffee

title: Finding Your Diagnosis Report in the Doctor's Portal at Midnight
instruction: You're reading words on a screen that change everything. Start with absurd, detached humor - maybe you laugh at a typo in the report, at the clinical language used to describe your body's betrayal. Your voice is bright, almost manic, because if you stop laughing you'll start screaming. Make jokes about the timing, about having to Google medical terms, about the universe's sense of humor. But let the laughter become strained, then slightly hysterical. A crack appears: your voice wavers on a particular word, maybe 'progressive' or 'treatment' or 'life expectancy.' Try to recover the humor but you can't quite manage it. The jokes continue but now they're threaded with grief. Begin to cry while still attempting to laugh - your voice breaking between the two, unable to commit to either. Then shift into something unexpected: quiet gratitude. Thank your body for the years it gave you, for every mundane miracle it performed without asking. Your voice should be thick with tears but somehow peaceful. End with a contradictory truth that encompasses everything: 'I'm not ready. But I'm... I'm grateful I got to be here at all. Even for this. Especially for this.' Let the final words be barely audible, simultaneously heartbroken and whole.
inspired_by: Complaining to God Like a Yelp Review

title: Laughing at Your Own Funeral Speech
instruction: You're giving a eulogy for someone who made you laugh even in the darkest times—maybe a best friend, a sibling, a soulmate. Start with a genuine laugh as you share an absurd memory, your voice light and fond. But mid-sentence, the laugh catches and transforms—you can't stop the smile but tears are streaming down your face. You're laughing and crying simultaneously, saying something like 'You'd be so mad at me for crying at your funeral, you specifically said not to'—and that makes you laugh harder even as you're sobbing. Find the strange, beautiful space where joy and grief become indistinguishable. End with a moment of pure gratitude that breaks you open: 'Thank you for making me laugh even now, even here'—voice shaking with both laughter and tears, finding peace in the paradox.
inspired_by: Confronting Someone About Passive Aggressive Behavior
